delfeayo.blurb: New Orleans trombone, and a producer's ear.
delfeayo.bio: Delfeayo Marsalis, born in 1965, is an American trombonist who also produces and teaches, a musician who has spent as much time shaping other people's records as making his own. That producer's ear informs everything he does: he hears how a session should sit as a whole, not simply how the horn in his hands should sound. He stepped out under his own name with the 1992 debut 'Pontius Pilate's Decision', and returned in 2010 with 'Sweet Thunder', an Ellington-meets-Shakespeare suite that showed how far his writing had travelled. His trombone tone is warm and conversational, phrased closer to a singer than to the instrument's usual bluster. Mentored by Ellis Marsalis, he has recorded alongside Wynton, Branford and Jason Marsalis, and teaching remains as much a part of his working life as playing.

jason.blurb: The youngest Marsalis, on drums and vibraphone.
jason.bio: Jason Marsalis, born in 1977, is the youngest of the Marsalis brothers and the one who came to the family trade from behind the drum kit. The son of Ellis and Dolores Ferdinand Marsalis, he grew up inside the New Orleans jazz education his father built, and he was leading his own sessions while still in his early twenties, announcing himself with 'The Year of the Drummer' in 1998. He has recorded alongside all three of his brothers, Wynton, Branford and Delfeayo, and works as a composer, producer and bandleader in his own right. In later years the vibraphone became his second voice, a lighter and more melodic instrument that let him write and improvise away from the drum chair. Taught by his father like the rest of the family, he carries the Marsalis grounding in tradition into music that is playful, precise and unmistakably his own.

johnnygriffin.blurb: The Little Giant of the tenor saxophone.
johnnygriffin.bio: Johnny Griffin, born in 1928, was an American tenor saxophonist known as the Little Giant for his small frame and enormous, headlong sound. He began working in the mid-1940s and kept playing until the month he died in 2008. A pioneering hard bop voice, he recorded prolifically as a leader while also serving under the drummer Art Blakey and in Thelonious Monk's group, and he built a celebrated two-tenor partnership with Eddie Lockjaw Davis. His 1957 was extraordinary: 'The Way You Look Tonight' and 'Smoke Stack' both came from A Blowing Session, and 'The Congregation' gave him a title track that still gets called at jam sessions. He carried the big-toned tenor lineage of Coleman Hawkins forward at bebop speed. After moving to Europe in the 1960s he joined the Kenny Clarke and Francy Boland Big Band, and in 1995 Berklee awarded him an honorary doctorate.

frankrosolino.blurb: Fast, funny, fearless West Coast trombone.
frankrosolino.bio: Frank Rosolino, born in 1926, was an American jazz trombonist with one of the most agile and high-spirited sounds the instrument has produced. He came up through the big bands and found his footing in Stan Kenton's orchestra, whose demanding brass writing suited a player of his speed and range. Working out of the West Coast scene, he made 'Free for All' in 1958, still his best-known date as a leader, and followed it in 1961 with 'Turn Me Loose', an album that set his singing alongside his playing. The bebop trombone vocabulary that J.J. Johnson opened up runs through everything he recorded, though Rosolino added a comic exuberance entirely his own, a sense that the horn was there to be enjoyed. He died in 1978. Trombonists still study his solos for the combination of technical daring and irrepressible good humour.

tonybennett.blurb: American song sung straight from the heart.
tonybennett.bio: Tony Bennett, born Anthony Dominick Benedetto in 1926, was an American singer who moved between jazz and traditional pop for seven decades without ever losing his footing in either. 'Rags to Riches' made him a star in 1953 and 'I Left My Heart in San Francisco' became his signature in 1962, but the recordings musicians treasure most are the intimate duets with the pianist Bill Evans, including 'But Beautiful' from 1975. He also sang with Count Basie, a pairing of warm voice and hard swing. Away from the microphone he painted, and in Astoria, Queens he set up the Frank Sinatra School of the Arts together with Exploring the Arts, a charity for arts education. Named a Kennedy Center Honoree and an NEA Jazz Master, and the winner of twenty Grammy Awards, he sold more than fifty million records worldwide and died in 2023.

stankenton.blurb: Big band ambition, brass and bold harmony.
stankenton.bio: Stan Kenton, born in 1911, was an American pianist, composer, arranger and bandleader who ran one of the most ambitious jazz orchestras of the twentieth century for nearly four decades. 'Artistry in Rhythm' became his theme in 1943, 'Tampico' gave him a hit with the singer June Christy in 1945, and 'The Peanut Vendor' in 1947 showed how far he would push a big band towards Afro-Cuban rhythm. Pop hits came steadily from the early 1940s all the way through to the 1960s, yet the music always leaned forward, thick with brass and unresolved harmony. His band doubled as a school: Frank Rosolino, Art Pepper and Lee Konitz all passed through its ranks. In 1959 he founded the Stan Kenton Jazz Camp at Indiana University, an early landmark in jazz education. He died in 1979, his influence still audible in college big bands everywhere.

bolden.blurb: The first jazzman, heard only through legend.
bolden.bio: Buddy Bolden, born in New Orleans around 1877, is the first name in jazz and the hardest to hear. A cornetist and bandleader, he was remembered by contemporaries and by later scholars alike as the man who bent New Orleans ragtime into something looser and hotter, the music that would be called jass and then jazz. Not a note of it survives on record. What remains is testimony: the volume of his horn, the pull of his blues, the dancers who followed his band across the city. His influence passed directly to King Oliver, and through Oliver into every New Orleans band that came after, which makes him the source of a line running through the whole century. He died in 1931. Bolden exists now as legend and as lineage, remembered through those he taught and through everyone who learned from them in turn.

oliver.blurb: New Orleans cornet king, Armstrong's teacher.
oliver.bio: King Oliver, born in 1881, was an American cornetist and bandleader who carried the New Orleans sound of Buddy Bolden into the recording era and made it permanent. His Creole Jazz Band sessions of 1923 are the foundation stone: 'Dipper Mouth Blues' with its landmark cornet solo, 'Snake Rag' with its famous two-cornet breaks, and 'Canal Street Blues'. He was celebrated for his pioneering use of mutes, coaxing cries and growls out of the horn, and he wrote tunes still played today, among them 'Sweet Like This' and 'Doctor Jazz'. Lil Hardin Armstrong sat at his piano and Jelly Roll Morton was his great contemporary. Above all he taught Louis Armstrong, who insisted that jazz would have become a different music entirely had Joe Oliver never existed. He died in 1938.

morton.blurb: Jazz's first arranger and loudest self-promoter.
morton.bio: Jelly Roll Morton, born in 1890, was a Louisiana Creole pianist, bandleader and composer, and the first great arranger jazz produced. His achievement was to prove that a music built on improvisation could be written down and still keep everything that made it itself. 'Jelly Roll Blues' reached print in 1915, among the first jazz compositions ever published, and 'King Porter Stomp', which he recorded as a piano solo in 1923, became his most influential piece and a staple of the swing bands that followed. With his Red Hot Peppers he made 'Black Bottom Stomp' and 'The Chant' in 1926, records of astonishing balance between arrangement and freedom. A contemporary of King Oliver, he claimed outright to have invented jazz, a boast nobody could verify and few could entirely dismiss. He died in 1941.

bechet.blurb: The soprano saxophone's first great voice.
bechet.bio: Sidney Bechet, born in 1897, was one of the first true soloists in jazz, a clarinetist who made the soprano saxophone his own and played it with a vibrato wide enough to fill a room. He began recording in July 1923, only months after Louis Armstrong first recorded with the Creole Jazz Band of King Oliver, and the two men played together more than once. His 1939 'Summertime' remains the soprano saxophone landmark, while 'Blue Horizon' from 1944 is a clarinet blues of extraordinary depth. A famously erratic temper held his career back for years, and wide acclaim did not arrive until the late 1940s, by which time he had found a second home in France. There 'Petite Fleur' made him a popular star in 1952. France held him for most of his final years, and he died there in 1959.

armstrong.blurb: The trumpet and voice that invented jazz soloing.
armstrong.bio: Louis Armstrong, born in New Orleans in 1901, is the most influential figure jazz has produced, a trumpeter and singer whose career ran across five decades and several eras of the music. King Oliver taught him, Fletcher Henderson's orchestra took him to New York, and by 1928 his Hot Five solo on 'West End Blues' had rewritten what a jazz soloist could be. He recorded with Bessie Smith, Sidney Bechet, Earl Hines and Lil Hardin Armstrong, and his phrasing reshaped singing as thoroughly as his horn reshaped brass playing, a debt both Billie Holiday and Ella Fitzgerald acknowledged. Late fame brought 'Hello, Dolly!' to number one in 1964 and 'What a Wonderful World' in 1967. Known as Satchmo and Pops, he took a Grammy in 1965, a posthumous lifetime award in 1972, and sits in halls of fame across several genres.

henderson.blurb: Drew the blueprint for the big band.
henderson.bio: Fletcher Henderson, born in 1897, played piano, led bands, wrote arrangements and composed, and it was he who drew the blueprint for the big band. Working in New York through the 1920s, he set brass against reeds in call and response and left room for soloists to speak, a design that 'The Stampede' laid out in 1926 complete with a Coleman Hawkins solo. Hawkins was his star tenor for years, and a young Louis Armstrong passed through the band and changed how everyone in it phrased. Henderson's writing later became the engine of Benny Goodman's orchestra, his 1932 arrangement of 'King Porter Stomp' chief among the scores, which is how a Black arranger's pen came to define the sound of the swing era. Nicknamed Smack, he stands with Duke Ellington among the most influential arrangers jazz has had. He died in 1952.

ellington.blurb: Jazz's greatest composer, leading from the piano.
ellington.bio: Duke Ellington, born in 1899, led his own orchestra from 1924 until his death and wrote for it the way other composers write for a symphony, tailoring every part to the individual player. Johnny Hodges, Ben Webster and the young bassist Jimmy Blanton were instruments as much as bandmates. 'Mood Indigo' in 1930 and 'It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)' in 1932 named the era before it fully arrived, and 'Take the A Train', written by his indispensable collaborator Billy Strayhorn, became the band's theme in 1941. He worked alongside Count Basie and Mary Lou Williams, shared the stage of his generation with his peer Benny Carter, and mentored Abdullah Ibrahim. Musicians from Nina Simone to Wynton Marsalis have drawn on him. To the music critic Ralph J. Gleason, no American composer mattered more. He died in 1974.

strayhorn.blurb: Ellington's alter ego and quietly peerless composer.
strayhorn.bio: Billy Strayhorn, born in 1915, was a composer, pianist, lyricist and arranger whose partnership with Duke Ellington lasted nearly three decades and produced some of the most refined writing in American music. He gave the Ellington orchestra its theme with 'Take the A Train' in 1941, and in the same year wrote 'Chelsea Bridge', an impressionistic piece that stands closer to the French composers than to swing. 'Lush Life', a ballad of such harmonic and lyrical sophistication that singers still approach it warily, was first recorded in 1949 with Nat King Cole. 'A Flower Is a Lovesome Thing' belongs to the same body of work. Because so much of it appeared under the Ellington banner, his authorship was long obscured, and part of the pleasure of listening now is hearing where one writer ends and the other begins. He died in 1967.

basie.blurb: The leanest, hardest-swinging machine in big band jazz.
basie.bio: Count Basie, born in 1904, formed his orchestra in 1935, took it to Chicago the following year for the long engagement that produced its first recordings, and then led it for almost fifty years. Everything rested on the rhythm section, with Papa Jo Jones at the drums and Basie himself playing the fewest notes any major pianist has dared, a minimalist style owing something to Fats Waller. He split his tenor saxophones into two duelling voices, one of them Lester Young, and turned the riff into a structural principle. 'One O'Clock Jump' became his signature in 1937 and 'Jumpin' at the Woodside' followed in 1938. Billie Holiday and later Joe Williams sang with the band, Quincy Jones and Clark Terry passed through, and the New Testament orchestra gave him 'April in Paris' in 1955. He died in 1984.

hawkins.blurb: Made the tenor saxophone a jazz instrument.
hawkins.bio: Coleman Hawkins, born in 1904, made the tenor saxophone a jazz instrument. Before him the horn was barely acknowledged as one; he was the first to build a method of improvising suited to the saxophone itself rather than borrowed from the clarinet, and his rich, arpeggiated, vibrato-laden playing set the terms for everyone who followed. Nicknamed Hawk and Bean, he was the star soloist of Fletcher Henderson's orchestra, then recorded 'Body and Soul' in 1939, a wholly improvised chorus that remains a foundation text of the music. 'The Man I Love' followed in 1943. Lester Young offered the cool alternative to his heat, and the rivalry between them shaped a generation. Hawkins recorded with Thelonious Monk and Roy Eldridge and worked with Benny Carter and Ben Webster, while Sonny Rollins, Dexter Gordon and Johnny Griffin all descend from him. He died in 1969.

tatum.blurb: The pianist other pianists could not believe.
tatum.bio: Art Tatum, born in 1909, is widely held to be the greatest pianist jazz has known, a player whose technical command astonished his fellow musicians from the very start of his career. His 1933 'Tiger Rag' announced a soloist who could think and execute faster than seemed possible, but the deeper achievement was harmonic: he pushed jazz piano far past its stride roots through reharmonization, unusual voicings and touches of bitonality. 'Tea for Two' in 1939 is a showcase of that rebuilding, and 'Yesterdays' from 1954 comes out of the great late solo sessions. Earl Hines was his peer and Fats Waller a presence in his playing. Bud Powell, Charlie Parker and Nat King Cole took lessons simply from listening, and Oscar Peterson, Erroll Garner, Ahmad Jamal, Hank Jones and Marian McPartland all worked in his long shadow. He died in 1956.

goodman.blurb: The King of Swing on clarinet.
goodman.bio: Benny Goodman, born in 1909, was the clarinetist and bandleader crowned the King of Swing, the musician who carried the style out of the ballrooms and into mainstream American life. Fletcher Henderson and Mary Lou Williams wrote the arrangements that gave his orchestra its authority, and 'Stompin' at the Savoy' in 1936, 'Sing, Sing, Sing' with Gene Krupa's drums in 1937 and 'Don't Be That Way' in 1938 became defining records of the era. His small groups mattered just as much, and they mattered socially too: Teddy Wilson, Lionel Hampton, Charlie Christian and Cootie Williams played in his bands at a time when Black and white musicians rarely shared a stage. He recorded with Billie Holiday and Jack Teagarden and shared the swing years with his peer Glenn Miller. A formidable technician to the end, he died in 1986.

hampton.blurb: Vibraphone played with a drummer's joyful attack.
hampton.bio: Lionel Hampton, born in 1908, brought the vibraphone into jazz as a front-line instrument and played it with the attack of a drummer, which is what he had been. He joined Benny Goodman's small groups alongside Teddy Wilson, then built a big band of his own that ran hot enough to point straight towards rhythm and blues: 'Flying Home' in 1942, with Illinois Jacquet's roaring tenor solo, and the jump-blues hit 'Hey! Ba-Ba-Re-Bop' in 1945. He could write a ballad too, and 'Midnight Sun' from 1947 became a standard. His bands were a proving ground for singers including Dinah Washington and Betty Carter, and across a long career he worked with Charlie Parker, Charles Mingus, Quincy Jones and Buddy Rich alike. The National Medal of Arts came to him in 1996, and he died in 2002.

christian.blurb: Made the electric guitar a solo voice.
christian.bio: Charlie Christian, born in 1916, lifted the guitar clear of the rhythm section and made it a solo voice, and he did it in barely two years of national exposure. Among the first musicians to build a style around the electric guitar, he played single-string lines with the phrasing of a horn, an approach every lead guitarist since has inherited. From August 1939 to June 1941 he was the star of Benny Goodman's sextet and orchestra, recording 'Seven Come Eleven' in 1939 and 'Solo Flight' in 1941. After hours he went uptown to Minton's, where 'Swing to Bop' caught him working out harmonic ideas with Kenny Clarke and Thelonious Monk while bebop was still forming. Wes Montgomery and Tal Farlow followed the path he cut. He died in 1942, having permanently changed his instrument.

young.blurb: Pres: cool, floating, behind-the-beat tenor saxophone.
young.bio: Lester Young, born in 1909, played the tenor saxophone with a light, floating tone and a rhythmic freedom that seemed to hover just behind the beat, opening a second path for the instrument alongside the heat of Coleman Hawkins. The rivalry between the two defined tenor playing for a generation. Young made his recording debut with Jones-Smith Incorporated on 'Oh, Lady Be Good' in 1936 and became the great soloist of the Count Basie orchestra, where 'Lester Leaps In' arrived in 1939. Known as Pres, he found his ideal partner in Billie Holiday, and their reunion on 'Fine and Mellow' for the 1957 television broadcast The Sound of Jazz is among the most moving performances jazz has on film. Charlie Parker, Stan Getz and Lee Konitz all built on him. He died in 1959, his sound by then woven permanently into the language of the saxophone.

holiday.blurb: Lady Day, who phrased like a horn.
holiday.bio: Billie Holiday, born in 1915, sang jazz and popular song as though she were playing a horn, bending phrase and tempo with a freedom she took from instrumentalists, Louis Armstrong and Bessie Smith above all. She recorded with Benny Goodman, sang with the Count Basie orchestra, and found her closest musical partner in the tenor saxophonist Lester Young, who gave her the name Lady Day. In 1939 she recorded 'Strange Fruit', an unflinching song about lynching that no other singer of her stature would touch. 'God Bless the Child', which she co-wrote, followed in 1941 and 'Lover Man (Oh, Where Can You Be?)' in 1944. Anita O'Day, Carmen McRae, Dinah Washington, Abbey Lincoln and Cassandra Wilson all sing in her wake. She died in 1959, having changed how phrasing and tempo could be handled by a singer.

webb.blurb: The Savoy's drummer king who found Ella.
webb.bio: Chick Webb, born in 1905, was the drummer and bandleader whose orchestra held court at the Savoy Ballroom in Harlem through the 1930s. He played with a power and precision his peer Gene Krupa openly admired, and he drove the band from the drum chair rather than from the front of the stage. Two pieces the Webb orchestra introduced in 1934, 'Stompin' at the Savoy' and Edgar Sampson's 'Don't Be That Way', went on to become swing era standards in other people's hands. His most lasting act was to take on a teenage singer named Ella Fitzgerald and build the band around her: their 'A-Tisket, A-Tasket' in 1938 made her a star and gave him his biggest hit. He died in 1939, still a young man, having shaped both the sound of the Savoy and the career of the finest singer in jazz.

ella.bio: Ella Fitzgerald, born in 1917, was the First Lady of Song, celebrated for purity of tone, immaculate diction and a horn-like improvising gift that made her scat singing the equal of any instrumental solo. Chick Webb took her into his orchestra as a teenager and 'A-Tisket, A-Tasket' made her famous in 1938. Louis Armstrong shaped her sense of swing and phrasing. The Songbook albums of the 1950s, including the Porgy and Bess 'Summertime' of 1957, established the American standard as a serious repertoire. Live in Berlin in 1960 she forgot the words to 'Mack the Knife' and improvised her way through the wreckage into one of the best-loved records in jazz. She worked with Ray Brown, Oscar Peterson, Joe Pass, Hank Jones and Tommy Flanagan, was a peer of Nat King Cole and Mel Tormé, and died in 1996.

natcole.blurb: Velvet voice, and a pianist's pianist.
natcole.bio: Nat King Cole, born Nathaniel Adams Coles in 1919, was a jazz pianist of the first rank who became one of the most beloved singers of the century. His playing carried Art Tatum's harmonic sophistication into a lighter, more conversational setting, and the piano-led trio he fronted became a widely copied model. 'Straighten Up and Fly Right' gave that trio a hit in 1943, then 'Nature Boy' in 1948 and 'Unforgettable' in 1951 turned him into a singer first in the public mind, his voice warm and unhurried and impossible to mistake for anyone else. Across a career that began in the late 1930s and ran nearly three decades he placed more than a hundred songs on the pop charts, and he acted as well. A peer of Ella Fitzgerald and a model for singers since, Gregory Porter among them, he died in 1965.

anita.blurb: A voice used as a rhythm instrument.
anita.bio: Anita O'Day, born in 1919, was an American jazz singer who treated her voice as a rhythm instrument, cutting through the fastest arrangements with a dry, swinging delivery that never asked for sympathy. She learned from Billie Holiday but arrived somewhere else entirely, and she made her name singing with Gene Krupa's band, holding her own against the drums at any tempo. 'You're the Top', from the 1956 album Pick Yourself Up, shows the wit in her phrasing. Her defining moment came at Newport in 1958, where 'Sweet Georgia Brown' and 'Tea for Two' were filmed for Jazz on a Summer's Day and remain the most watched few minutes any jazz singer has left behind. A peer of Mel Tormé and admired by critics and musicians alike, she died in 2006.

django.blurb: Europe's first great jazz voice, on guitar.
django.bio: Django Reinhardt, born in Belgium in 1910 into a Romani family, was the first major jazz talent to emerge in Europe and remains its most distinctive. With the violinist Stephane Grappelli he founded the Quintette du Hot Club de France, an all-string band with no drums and no horns, unlike anything in American jazz, and gave it 'Minor Swing' in 1937. His playing drew on the example of Louis Armstrong and on Romani musical tradition in equal measure, and he composed as fluently as he improvised. 'Nuages', recorded in 1940, became a classic of the wartime years in France, and 'Djangology' followed in 1948. The style he made, now called Gypsy jazz, carries his nickname and is still played much as he left it, a whole European tradition descending from a single guitarist. He died in 1953.

grappelli.bio: Stephane Grappelli, born in France in 1908, was the violinist who proved his instrument could swing, and he went on proving it for more than sixty years. In 1934, with the guitarist Django Reinhardt, he started the Quintette du Hot Club de France, a group built from strings alone with no drums and no horns, and their recordings together, 'Minor Swing' and 'Sweet Georgia Brown' from 1937 and 'Nuages' from 1940, are the foundation of the style. Where Django was fire, Grappelli was elegance: a light, singing tone and a melodic imagination that never ran dry. The nickname that stuck to him, grandfather of jazz violinists, is fair enough, since Regina Carter and every swing fiddler since work ground he cleared. He collaborated with Toots Thielemans, was still touring internationally in his eighties, and died in 1997.

parker.blurb: Bird: the alto saxophone that rewrote jazz.
parker.bio: Charlie Parker, born in 1920 and known as Bird, was the alto saxophonist at the centre of bebop and one of the most influential improvisers in any music. He absorbed Lester Young's phrasing and Art Tatum's harmony and pushed both much further, introducing fast passing chords, altered chords in new forms and substitutions that jazz musicians have been working through ever since, all of it delivered at tempos nobody had attempted. 'Ko-Ko' in 1945 announced the new language, 'Now's the Time' came from the same year, and 'Ornithology' followed in 1946. Dizzy Gillespie was his partner in the revolution, with Bud Powell and Max Roach beside him and Thelonious Monk, Sarah Vaughan and Dexter Gordon in the same circle. He mentored the young Miles Davis. He died in 1955, and the music has never stopped catching up.

dizzy.blurb: Bebop's trumpet virtuoso and joyful ambassador.
dizzy.bio: Dizzy Gillespie, born in 1917, was a trumpet virtuoso, bandleader, composer and educator who built on the style of Roy Eldridge and added layers of harmonic and rhythmic complexity jazz had not heard before. With Charlie Parker he made bebop, and 'Salt Peanuts' in 1945 and his own 'A Night in Tunisia' in 1946 remain its calling cards. He also opened a second front: 'Manteca', recorded in 1947 with the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo, brought Afro-Cuban rhythm into jazz for good. Kenny Clarke and Thelonious Monk were in his circle, Sarah Vaughan and Milt Jackson worked alongside him, Tadd Dameron and George Russell wrote with him, Quincy Jones played in his band, and he mentored Lee Morgan while Hugh Masekela was among the many he inspired. The beret, the bent horn and the wit made him the music's great popularizer. He died in 1993.

monk.blurb: Bebop's great eccentric at the piano.
monk.bio: Thelonious Sphere Monk, born in 1917, was an American composer and jazz pianist whose improvising sounded like nobody else: angular, spacious, full of deliberate stumbles that turn out to be architecture. He gave the standard repertoire some of its most enduring themes, among them 'Round Midnight', first recorded for Blue Note in 1947, the blues line 'Straight, No Chaser' in 1951 and 'Blue Monk' in 1954. By 2009 he stood as the second most recorded composer in jazz history, after Duke Ellington. He came up in the bebop circle around Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Kenny Clarke and Charlie Christian, shared a band with Johnny Griffin, and recorded with Coleman Hawkins, Milt Jackson and Carmen McRae. His mentorship of John Coltrane remade that saxophonist, and pianists such as Vijay Iyer still work in his shadow. Monk died in 1982.

powell.blurb: Bebop's fire translated to the keyboard.
powell.bio: Bud Powell, born in 1924, was the pianist who carried bebop onto the keyboard, applying complex phrasing to an instrument that suddenly had to answer horns like Charlie Parker's. A pioneer of the style and of the jazz theory that grew out of it, he cut 'Bouncing with Bud' and 'Tempus Fugit' at Blue Note sessions in 1949, then made the astonishing 'Un Poco Loco' with Max Roach in 1951 for The Amazing Bud Powell. He worked alongside Parker, recorded with Fats Navarro and Sonny Stitt, drew on Art Tatum's example, and found an early champion in Mary Lou Williams, while Lennie Tristano explored the keyboard from another direction entirely. His playing shaped Walter Davis Jr., Barry Harris, Toshiko Akiyoshi, Kenny Barron, Tommy Flanagan and Bill Evans. Powell died in 1966, leaving bebop piano permanently in his image.

clarke.blurb: The drummer who moved time to the ride cymbal.
clarke.bio: Kenny Clarke, born in 1914 and known to musicians as Klook, was the American drummer and bandleader who rebuilt jazz time. Where earlier drummers kept the beat on the hi-hat, he moved it up to the ride cymbal and freed the bass drum to punch irregular accents, the dropped bombs that gave bebop its lift and its unpredictability. That approach is audible on the Charlie Parker session that produced 'Now's the Time' in 1945, and on his own Savoy dates of 1955, the title track of 'Bohemia After Dark' and 'Telefunken Blues', made with Jay Jay Johnson. He was central to the bebop circle around Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk and Charlie Christian. A direct line runs from Papa Jo Jones through Clarke to Max Roach and to virtually every drummer who followed. Clarke died in 1985.

roach.blurb: Bebop drumming raised to political statement.
roach.bio: Max Roach, born in 1924, was an American drummer and composer generally counted among the most important percussionists in the history of the music. A pioneer of bebop, he worked with Charlie Parker, Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins, Charles Mingus and many more, and co-led one of the great quintets of the 1950s with Clifford Brown, whose 'Joy Spring' they recorded in 1954. He then turned the drum kit toward politics: 'Driva Man', from the 1960 We Insist! Freedom Now Suite made with Abbey Lincoln, is among the starkest civil rights statements in jazz, while 'The Drum Also Waltzes' of 1966 showed what a solo drummer could compose. He played with Booker Little, taught at university level, and the DownBeat Hall of Fame inducted him in 1980, the Modern Drummer one in 1992. Roach died in 2007.

dexter.blurb: Long Tall Dexter, the bebop tenor giant.
dexter.bio: Dexter Gordon, born in 1923, was an American tenor saxophonist, composer and bandleader, and among the most influential of the early bebop musicians. He stood six feet six, which earned him the nicknames Long Tall Dexter and Sophisticated Giant, and his huge, unhurried, behind-the-beat sound carried the line of Coleman Hawkins forward into the language John Coltrane would inherit. His studio and performing career ran for more than forty years. The album Go! gave him 'Cheese Cake' and 'Three O'Clock in the Morning' in 1962, and 'Body and Soul', from Our Man in Paris the following year, is a definitive reading of that ballad. He moved in Charlie Parker's bebop circle, stood as a peer to Sonny Rollins, and recorded with the bassist Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen. Gordon died in 1990.

milt.blurb: Bags, the blues voice of the vibraphone.
milt.bio: Milt Jackson, born in 1923 and known everywhere as Bags, was the American vibraphonist who made his instrument sing the blues. His cool, unhurried swing was central to the Modern Jazz Quartet, where John Lewis's 'Django' became a signature piece in 1954, and he kept a lifelong appetite for playing alongside hard bop and post-bop musicians. That same year he recorded 'Bags' Groove' with Miles Davis, the blues theme that carries his nickname and remains one of the most called tunes in jazz; 'Bluesology' followed in 1956. He was a bandmate of Dizzy Gillespie and recorded with Thelonious Monk, and his example shaped the vibraphonists who came after him, Bobby Hutcherson and Gary Burton among them. He composed and sang as well. Jackson died in 1999.

vaughan.blurb: The Divine One, queen of bebop singing.
vaughan.bio: Sarah Vaughan, born in 1924, was an American singer and pianist whose voice was one of the twentieth century's extraordinary instruments: wide in range, elastic in rhythm, trained enough for the concert hall and free enough for bebop. Billed as The Divine One, known too as the Queen of Bebop, and Sassy to intimates, she came up in the big bands of Earl Hines and Billy Eckstine, moved in Charlie Parker's circle and sang with Dizzy Gillespie. 'Lullaby of Birdland', made with Clifford Brown in 1954, the pop hit 'Whatever Lola Wants' in 1955 and a definitive 'Misty' in 1958 show the span of her work. She won two Grammys from nine nominations, including the Lifetime Achievement, and an NEA Jazz Masters Award in 1989. Carmen McRae and Betty Carter were her peers; Dianne Reeves, Cécile McLorin Salvant and Samara Joy are among her heirs. She died in 1990.

carmen.blurb: Behind the beat, and sharp with a lyric.
carmen.bio: Carmen McRae, born in 1920, was an American jazz singer, pianist and actress, counted among the most influential vocalists of the twentieth century. Her art was one of timing and attitude: she sang behind the beat, letting the band move ahead of her, and read a lyric with a dry irony that could turn a love song inside out. She recorded with Thelonious Monk, and in 1955 gave the Monk-associated ballad 'Round Midnight' one of its definitive vocal readings, the same year as a superb 'Body and Soul'; in 1961 she sang a lyric version of 'Take Five'. Billie Holiday was the presence behind her phrasing, though the wit was her own. Alongside Sarah Vaughan and Nancy Wilson she defined what a jazz singer could be in her generation. McRae died in 1994.

betty.blurb: The most fearless improviser among jazz singers.
betty.bio: Betty Carter, born in 1929, was an American jazz singer and songwriter who treated a song the way a horn player treats a set of changes, bending tempo, scatting freely and rebuilding melodies in front of an audience. She learned the trade in Lionel Hampton's band and took her sense of line from Charlie Parker. Live performance was her real medium: 'Sounds (Movin' On)', from 1979, is an extended signature piece that shows how far she would travel from a written melody, while 'The Good Life', on 1988's Look What I Got!, applies the same imagination to a standard. Carmen McRae once remarked that there was really only one jazz singer, and she meant Carter. Sarah Vaughan and Sheila Jordan were peers; Cassandra Wilson and Cécile McLorin Salvant followed her lead. Carter died in 1998.

akiyoshi.blurb: Japanese tradition inside an American big band.
akiyoshi.bio: Toshiko Akiyoshi, born in 1929, is a Japanese pianist, bandleader, arranger and jazz composer who took the American big band and made it speak in a new voice. Her playing grew from close study of Bud Powell and Charlie Parker, but her lasting achievement is compositional. 'Kogun', recorded in 1974, took its theme from a soldier who had survived the war, and brought the timbres and gestures of Japanese music into a jazz orchestra without turning them into decoration. 'Long Yellow Road' followed in 1975 as the title piece for the Akiyoshi-Tabackin Big Band, and 'Children in the Temple Ground' appeared on Insights in 1976. As pianist, writer and conductor she has built a body of work in which bebop language and Japanese tradition sit together without strain.

miles.blurb: The restless architect of jazz's great changes.
miles.bio: Miles Davis, born in 1926, was an American trumpeter, bandleader and composer, and one of the most influential figures in twentieth-century music. Across nearly five decades he stood at the front of one stylistic change after another: bebop and cool jazz, hard bop and third stream, modal jazz, the avant-garde and finally fusion. Charlie Parker mentored him early, Gil Evans became his great orchestral collaborator, and the bands he assembled read like a roll call of the music, with John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Tony Williams and Chick Corea all passing through. 'Milestones' in 1958 opened the door to modal playing, and 'So What' and 'Freddie Freeloader' walked through it on Kind of Blue the following year. He painted too, and his legacy runs on into rock, funk, classical music and hip hop. Davis died in 1991.

gil.blurb: One of jazz's greatest orchestral colourists.
gil.bio: Gil Evans, born in 1912, was a Canadian-American arranger, composer, pianist and bandleader, widely recognised as one of the greatest orchestrators jazz has produced. He heard the large ensemble as a single instrument with an enormous palette, and his writing helped shape cool and modal jazz, free jazz and fusion in turn. The collaborations with Miles Davis are the heart of the legacy: 'Springsville' on Miles Ahead in 1957, 'Summertime' from the 1958 Porgy and Bess, and 'Concierto de Aranjuez' on Sketches of Spain in 1960, where trumpet and orchestra seem to breathe together. He also worked with Gerry Mulligan and recorded with David Sanborn, and his approach to orchestral colour runs directly into the writing of Maria Schneider. Evans died in 1988.

coltrane.blurb: The searching tenor who redrew jazz harmony.
coltrane.bio: John Coltrane, born in 1926, was an American saxophonist, bandleader and composer, and one of the most influential, most acclaimed figures jazz has known. He came up through Miles Davis's band and through an apprenticeship with Thelonious Monk that transformed his harmonic thinking, having already absorbed the tenor language of Dexter Gordon. 'Giant Steps', from 1960, set out a chord cycle so demanding it became a rite of passage for every player since, and the same year brought 'Naima', the tender ballad written for his wife. In 1961 he made 'My Favorite Things' his own on soprano saxophone. His quartet with McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones pushed toward modal and free playing; he worked with Eric Dolphy, recorded with Lee Morgan and moved in Ornette Coleman's orbit. He died in 1967, and Kamasi Washington and Jan Garbarek are among the many still answering him.

cannonball.blurb: Alto joy, from hard bop to soul-jazz.
cannonball.bio: Cannonball Adderley, born in 1928, was an American alto saxophonist and bandleader of the hard bop era whose sound carried the plain joy of the blues. He spent formative years in Miles Davis's band, and his own 'Autumn Leaves', from 1958's Somethin' Else, is among the best-loved performances in the music. Leading his own group he folded gospel and soul feeling into jazz: 'Work Song', written by his brother Nat, appeared on Them Dirty Blues in 1960, and 'Mercy, Mercy, Mercy', penned by his bandmate Joe Zawinul, became a genuine crossover hit in 1966. Jimmy Cobb played beside him, Nancy Wilson collaborated with him, and Charlie Parker was the alto voice standing behind his own. Adderley died in 1975, having done as much as anyone to keep jazz within earshot of a popular audience.

billevans.blurb: Impressionist harmony and a singing right hand.
billevans.bio: Bill Evans, born in 1929, was an American pianist and composer who worked mainly at the head of his own trio and changed what that format could be. His impressionist harmony, block chords, inventive voicings and rhythmically independent singing lines are still the grammar most jazz pianists learn. 'Peace Piece', a solo meditation from 1959's Everybody Digs Bill Evans, showed how much he could make of almost nothing, and the 1962 Village Vanguard recordings gave 'Waltz for Debby' and a heartbreaking 'My Foolish Heart'. He played with Miles Davis and George Russell, counted Scott LaFaro, Paul Motian and Eddie Gómez among his bandmates, and recorded with Jim Hall and Tony Bennett. Brad Mehldau, Shirley Horn and Michel Petrucciani are among those who took up his line. Evans died in 1980.

blakey.blurb: Hard bop's engine and greatest talent scout.
blakey.bio: Art Blakey, born in 1919, was an American drummer and bandleader, and for four decades the finest finishing school jazz had. Known for a time as Abdullah Ibn Buhaina after converting to Islam in the late 1940s, he drove his groups from the drums with enormous force and had an unmatched ear for young players. The Messengers, the band he co-founded with Horace Silver, gave the world Bobby Timmons's gospel-drenched Moanin' in 1959, Benny Golson's 'Blues March' the same year, and an explosive 'A Night in Tunisia' in 1961. The list of musicians he mentored is more or less the story of hard bop: Clifford Brown, Johnny Griffin, Jackie McLean, Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard, JoAnne Brackeen and, later, Wynton Marsalis. Roy Hargrove was among those who followed. Blakey died in 1990.

silver.blurb: The funkiest composer in hard bop.
silver.bio: Horace Silver, born in 1928, was an American pianist, composer and arranger who helped pioneer hard bop in the 1950s and gave the style much of its repertoire. His writing put gospel cadences and blues feeling into a bebop frame: 'The Preacher', from 1955, sounds like a church band that has learned to swing, 'Blowin' the Blues Away' drove hard in 1959, and 'Song for My Father', recorded in 1965 with a bossa lilt, became one of the most recognisable themes in jazz. He co-founded a band with Art Blakey before leading his own quintets, where Lee Morgan, Hank Mobley and Donald Byrd all played. Few composers of his generation left more tunes that musicians still call on the bandstand. Silver died in 2014.

brown.blurb: Trumpet brilliance cut short at twenty-five.
brown.bio: Clifford Brown, born in 1930, was an American trumpeter, pianist and composer whose sound was warm, fleet and startlingly clear, with a lyric sense that made even his fastest lines feel composed. He won the DownBeat critics' poll as New Star of the Year in 1954, the same year he wrote 'Joy Spring' and 'Daahoud', and co-led a quintet with Max Roach that also featured Sonny Rollins. 'Sandu', from 1955's Study in Brown, completes the trio of his compositions that became standards. He came through Art Blakey's tutelage, recorded with Sarah Vaughan and Tadd Dameron, and carried forward the line of Fats Navarro. A car crash killed him in 1956 at twenty-five, leaving four years of recordings; Lee Morgan, Booker Little and Freddie Hubbard all built on what he had done. DownBeat's Jazz Hall of Fame took him in 1972.

rollins.blurb: The colossus of the tenor saxophone.
rollins.bio: Sonny Rollins, born in 1930, ranks among the most important and influential musicians in jazz, an American tenor saxophonist and composer whose thematic improvising turns a tune inside out until a long solo feels argued rather than merely played. 'Oleo', from 1954, is his best known rhythm-changes original; 'St. Thomas', in 1956, brought a calypso lilt into the modern jazz repertoire, and 'Tenor Madness', from the same year, set him against Coltrane on record. He recorded with Miles Davis, played in the quintet Clifford Brown co-led, and made some of his most searching music in a group with Jim Hall. He carried the Coleman Hawkins tradition forward alongside his peer Dexter Gordon, and tenor players from Joe Henderson to Melissa Aldana have worked in his debt ever since.

mingus.blurb: Bass, temper and a composer's grand vision.
mingus.bio: Charles Mingus, born in 1922, was an American bassist, composer, bandleader, pianist and author, and a fierce proponent of collective improvisation. Over three decades he worked with Charlie Parker, Duke Ellington, Eric Dolphy and Max Roach, and wrote music that ran from advanced bebop and the avant-garde to the post-bop landmarks Pithecanthropus Erectus in 1956 and Mingus Ah Um in 1959, and on to big band experiments as ambitious as the 1963 album The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady. 'Goodbye Pork Pie Hat', his elegy for Lester Young, and the gospel-charged 'Better Git It in Your Soul' both come from Ah Um, and the baritone-led Moanin' opened Blues and Roots in 1960. Jackie McLean and Rahsaan Roland Kirk passed through his bands, Oscar Pettiford was a peer, Jimmy Blanton an ancestor, and Esperanza Spalding is one of many heirs. He died in 1979.

leemorgan.blurb: Blue Note's brashest trumpet, boogaloo and all.
leemorgan.bio: Lee Morgan, born in 1938, was an American trumpeter and composer, a cornerstone of the Blue Note label and one of the defining hard bop voices of the 1960s. He arrived more or less fully formed in his late teens, recording with Hank Mobley, Wayne Shorter, Curtis Fuller, Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane before taking his place in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, where his brash, vocal phrasing found its perfect setting. 'The Sidewinder', from 1964, rode a boogaloo groove to a crossover success few jazz records of the era matched, and 1967 brought the soulful 'Cornbread' and the graceful bossa ballad 'Ceora'. He played in Horace Silver's band and recorded with Joe Henderson and Billy Higgins, carrying the trumpet line of Clifford Brown into a new decade. Morgan died in 1972.

freddie.blurb: A trumpet tone that defined modern bop.
freddie.bio: Freddie Hubbard, born in 1938, was an American trumpeter whose bright, cutting and unmistakable tone opened new perspectives for modern jazz. From the early 1960s onward he moved between bebop, hard bop and post-bop, and his time in Art Blakey's band amounted to a bandstand education. 'Birdlike', a burning blues from 1962's Ready for Freddie, shows the hard bop player; 'Little Sunflower', on Backlash in 1967, is pure modal calm; and 'Red Clay', in 1970, married modal writing to a funk pulse and became his signature. He was also the trumpeter other leaders wanted, recording with Eric Dolphy, John Coltrane, Herbie Hancock, Oliver Nelson and Joe Henderson. Clifford Brown's example lay behind his playing, and Woody Shaw was his great contemporary on the instrument. Hubbard died in 2008.

wes.blurb: Thumb-plucked octaves that changed jazz guitar.
wes.bio: Wes Montgomery, born in 1923, was an American guitarist who changed the instrument by refusing a plectrum: he played the strings with the fleshy outer edge of his thumb and built solos in octaves, giving him a warm sound nobody could mistake for anyone else. Carrying forward the line of Charlie Christian, he recorded often alongside his brothers Buddy and Monk, and with the organist Melvin Rhyne. Up to 1965 his records sat in hard bop, soul jazz and post bop, among them 'Four on Six' and the waltz-time 'West Coast Blues', both from 1960. He then turned to instrumental pop albums that reached a far wider audience, including the Grammy-winning 'Goin' Out of My Head' in 1966, a later style that fed directly into fusion and smooth jazz. Pat Metheny, George Benson and Emily Remler all learned from him. Montgomery died in 1968.

jimmysmith.blurb: The man who made the Hammond swing.
jimmysmith.bio: Jimmy Smith, born in 1928, was the American musician who showed what the Hammond B-3 organ could do in jazz and, in doing so, built a link between the music and 1960s soul. He made a whole band out of one instrument, walking a bass line beneath his own bebop-schooled right hand. 'The Sermon', an extended blues jam from 1959, is the classic statement of the after-hours organ groove; 'Back at the Chicken Shack' followed in 1963, and 'The Cat' set the organ against a big band for a hit in 1964. He recorded with Wes Montgomery, Kenny Burrell, Grant Green and George Benson, shared the field with Shirley Scott, and left Larry Young and every soul-jazz organist since in his debt. Smith died in 2005.

getz.blurb: The Sound, and bossa nova's American gateway.
getz.bio: Stan Getz, born in 1927, was an American tenor saxophonist known simply as The Sound, after a tone so warm and lyrical it seemed to cost him no effort. His model was the wispy, mellow timbre of Lester Young, and he first drew notice in Woody Herman's big band in the late 1940s, before leading his own bebop and cool jazz groups. Hearing Antônio Carlos Jobim and João Gilberto redirected him: 'Desafinado', made with Charlie Byrd for Jazz Samba in 1962, and then Getz/Gilberto in 1964, with 'The Girl from Ipanema' and 'Corcovado', carried bossa nova to a huge American audience. Later bands drew on JoAnne Brackeen, Kenny Barron and Gary Burton, and he recorded with Chet Baker. The big-toned tenor tradition of Ben Webster runs through his playing. Getz died in 1991.

jobim.blurb: The composer who gave bossa nova songs.
jobim.bio: Antônio Carlos Jobim, born in Brazil in 1927 and known at home as Tom, was a composer, pianist, guitarist, arranger, songwriter and singer, and among the founding fathers of bossa nova. By folding the harmonic language of cool jazz into samba in the 1960s he made a music of extraordinary poise, and from the early years of that decade his songs travelled the world in the hands of singers and instrumentalists everywhere. 'The Girl from Ipanema', which he wrote, reached its most famous form on the 1964 Getz/Gilberto recording; 'Wave', from 1967, found him composing and playing piano on his own title track; and 'Aguas de Marco', written in 1972, shows the wit of a songwriter counted among the most celebrated of the twentieth century. He worked closely with Stan Getz and with João Gilberto. Jobim died in 1994.

gilberto.blurb: The whispering guitar that invented bossa nova.
gilberto.bio: João Gilberto, born in Brazil in 1931, was a guitarist, singer, songwriter and composer who gave bossa nova its sound in the late 1950s: a hushed voice, a guitar rhythm that reset the samba pulse, and an intimacy that made the microphone part of the instrument. 'Chega de Saudade', from 1959, is the founding single of the genre. Abroad he was called the father of bossa nova; in Brazil he was simply O Mito, the myth. Getz/Gilberto, made with Stan Getz, became in 1965 the first jazz album ever to take the Grammy for Album of the Year, and carried 'The Girl from Ipanema' around the world. Amoroso brought a further nomination in 1978, and João voz e violão won a Grammy in 2001. He worked constantly with Antônio Carlos Jobim, and in 1974 sang 'Aguas de Marco' with Elis Regina. He died in 2019.

abbey.blurb: A jazz voice raised for civil rights.
abbey.bio: Abbey Lincoln, born Anna Marie Wooldridge in 1930, was an American singer, songwriter and actress in jazz who built a career out of deeply felt readings of standards and, increasingly, out of her own material. From the 1960s she was also a civil rights activist, and the two strands met on We Insist! Freedom Now Suite, the 1960 record made with Max Roach, where her voice on 'Driva Man' carries the weight of the whole project. The later albums show the songwriter plainly: 'Brother, Where Are You?' appeared on People in Me in 1973, and 'Throw It Away', from 1990's The World Is Falling Down, is among her best known originals. Billie Holiday was the model behind her phrasing, though what she did with it was entirely her own. Lincoln died in 2010.

nina.blurb: The High Priestess of Soul, entirely uncompromising.
nina.bio: Nina Simone, born in 1933, was an American singer, songwriter, composer, concert pianist and civil rights activist, and the artist they called the High Priestess of Soul. Trained at the keyboard on baroque and classical music, and on Bach above all, she brought that discipline to a contralto of unusual weight and used both across classical, folk, gospel, blues, jazz, rhythm and blues and pop without ever settling in one of them. 'Mississippi Goddam', sung in 1964 on Nina Simone in Concert, is among the most direct protest songs of the civil rights era; 'I Put a Spell on You' and 'Feeling Good' followed in 1965 and are among her most widely heard performances. Duke Ellington was one of her touchstones, and musicians such as Esperanza Spalding carry her example forward. Simone died in 2003.

ornette.blurb: The alto that set jazz harmonically free.
ornette.bio: Ornette Coleman, born in 1930, was an American alto saxophonist, trumpeter, violinist and composer, and the principal founder of free jazz, a term taken from his own album of collective improvisation. His music let go of what jazz had been built on: tonality, chord changes, harmony-based composition and a fixed rhythmic frame. In their place came an experimental approach to improvising rooted in ensemble playing and in blues phrasing, which is why 'Lonely Woman', from 1959's The Shape of Jazz to Come, sounds plaintive rather than abstract. Ramblin' followed in 1960 and the double-quartet 'Free Jazz' in 1961. He played with Don Cherry, Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins, recorded with Scott LaFaro and Jimmy Garrison, stood beside Cecil Taylor and later worked with Pat Metheny. Once dismissed as a fraud, he is now celebrated as a fearless innovator. Coleman died in 2015.

cherry.blurb: Pocket trumpet at the heart of free jazz.
cherry.bio: Don Cherry, born in 1936, was an American trumpeter whose pocket trumpet became one of the defining sounds of free jazz. He came to prominence as a member of the Ornette Coleman Quartet, the group that pulled jazz loose from its chord changes at the end of the 1950s, and his playing on 'Lonely Woman' in 1959 remains a touchstone of the music. Alongside Coleman he worked closely with the bassist Charlie Haden and the drummer Billy Higgins, a partnership that reshaped what a rhythm section could do. As a leader he recorded the suite 'Complete Communion' for Blue Note in 1966, and 'Awake Nu' followed in 1971 on the album Orient. He also collaborated with the composer Carla Bley. Cherry died in 1995, one of the most restlessly curious improvisers of his generation.

dolphy.blurb: Alto, flute and bass clarinet visionary.
dolphy.bio: Eric Dolphy, born in 1928, was an American multi-instrumentalist and composer who moved between alto saxophone, flute and bass clarinet with equal authority. More than anyone he established the bass clarinet as a jazz instrument, and he was among the first significant soloists on jazz flute, while his alto playing stretched the vocabulary of the horn towards the edge of tonality. He worked inside Charles Mingus's bands and alongside John Coltrane, recorded with Freddie Hubbard, Andrew Hill, Bobby Hutcherson and Woody Shaw, and shared a front line with the trumpeter Booker Little. Ornette Coleman's example fed his own leap outward. The 1964 session 'Out to Lunch!' produced 'Hat and Beard', a jagged classic of the new music, and his unaccompanied bass clarinet reading of 'God Bless the Child' from 1961 stands alone. He died in 1964, far too early.

cecil.blurb: Piano as percussion, jazz at its outer edge.
cecil.bio: Cecil Taylor, born in 1929, was an American pianist and poet who treated the keyboard as a percussion instrument and built one of the most uncompromising bodies of work in jazz. A trained classical pianist, he arrived at a dense, physical manner of improvising that set aside conventional harmony and steady metre, and he never stepped back from it. 'Unit Structures' in 1966 gave the world 'Enter Evening', and the title piece of 'Conquistador!' came from the same year, while 'Bulbs' in 1962 caught him at full stretch. He stands with Ornette Coleman, Sun Ra and Albert Ayler as an architect of free jazz, and the saxophonist Archie Shepp was among his bandmates. Poetry ran through the work alongside the music. Taylor died in 2018, leaving a language on the piano that nobody else has quite spoken since.

sunra.blurb: Cosmic bandleader who sent jazz into space.
sunra.bio: Sun Ra, born in 1914, was an American composer, pianist and bandleader who wrapped his music in a cosmic philosophy and a theatre of costume and ritual. For most of his career he led the Arkestra, an ensemble whose name and line-up shifted constantly, working through bebop, free improvisation and fusion, with the synthesizer as much his instrument as the piano. 'Rocket Number Nine' in 1966 and the side-long title piece of 'The Magic City' from the same year show the range, while 'Space Is the Place' in 1973 became his declaration of intent. He and Cecil Taylor pushed at the same frontier from different directions, and the line running out of his music reaches forward to Kamasi Washington and Shabaka Hutchings. He died in 1993, leaving one of the strangest and most generous bodies of work in American music.

ibrahim.blurb: Cape jazz piano and an anti-apartheid anthem.
ibrahim.bio: Abdullah Ibrahim, born in 1934 and for years billed as Dollar Brand, was the South African pianist and composer who stands as the leading figure in Cape jazz. He grew up amid the mixed music of Cape Town's port districts, where traditional African song, AME Church gospel and Western styles all met, and he carried that mixture into a body of work that also drew deeply on Thelonious Monk and Duke Ellington. Ellington championed him early, a piece of mentorship that opened the wider world to his playing, and he stood alongside Hugh Masekela among the great South African musicians of his generation. 'Mannenberg', recorded in 1974, became an anthem of the struggle against apartheid, while 'The Wedding' in 1973 and 'Water from an Ancient Well' with his group Ekaya in 1985 held the same singing, hymn-like calm.

tyner.blurb: Thundering left hand of the Coltrane quartet.
tyner.bio: McCoy Tyner, born in 1938, was an American pianist and composer whose sound is inseparable from the classic John Coltrane Quartet, where he played from 1960 to 1965 beside the drummer Elvin Jones and the bassist Jimmy Garrison. His thundering left hand and open, fourth-heavy voicings gave that band both its ground and its lift, and the approach was imitated so widely that it became part of the standard language of modern jazz piano. After leaving Coltrane he built a long career of his own: 'The Real McCoy' in 1967 produced the surging 'Passion Dance' and the ballad 'Search for Peace', while the title track of 'Sahara' in 1972 reached towards African and Eastern colours. Honours followed: NEA Jazz Master, and five Grammy Awards. Tyner died in 2020, among the most influential pianists jazz has produced.

elvin.blurb: Drummer who turned time into rolling waves.
elvin.bio: Elvin Jones, born in 1927, was an American drummer of the post-bop era whose playing with John Coltrane's quartet from late 1960 to 1965 changed what a jazz rhythm section could be. Alongside McCoy Tyner and Jimmy Garrison he set up a churning, many-layered pulse that surrounded the beat rather than simply marking it, and it can be heard on 'My Favorite Things' in 1961, on 'Chasin' the Trane' from the Village Vanguard in 1962 and across 'A Love Supreme' in 1965. Hank and Thad, his brothers, were celebrated musicians in their own right, and the three occasionally recorded together. From 1966 he fronted groups of his own, a trio at first and later the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine, with Dave Liebman among the players who passed through them. The Modern Drummer Hall of Fame took him in 1995; Jones died in 2004.

shorter.blurb: Composer of riddles, saxophonist of few words.
shorter.bio: Wayne Shorter, born in 1933, was an American saxophonist, composer and bandleader, and one of the towering figures of modern jazz. Art Blakey mentored him early, after which he joined the Miles Davis Quintet, writing much of the book that band is remembered by, including 'Nefertiti' in 1968, and playing beside Herbie Hancock and Ron Carter. 'Speak No Evil' in 1966 and 'Footprints', first recorded on 'Adam's Apple' in 1967, became standards that players still turn to. With Joe Zawinul he co-founded a band of their own, where Jaco Pastorius later joined him. He passed it on in turn: Branford Marsalis drew from him, Esperanza Spalding became a collaborator, and Renee Rosnes was a bandmate. Six decades of work brought him the Polar Music Prize and twelve Grammy Awards. Shorter died in 2023.

herbie.blurb: Jazz pianist who keeps reinventing the future.
herbie.bio: Herbie Hancock, born in 1940, is an American pianist, keyboardist, bandleader and composer who has changed direction more often than almost anyone in jazz and been right nearly every time. He started out in Donald Byrd's group and had a hit of his own with 'Watermelon Man' from the 1962 album Takin' Off, followed by 'Cantaloupe Island' in 1964. Joining the Miles Davis Quintet beside Wayne Shorter, Ron Carter and Tony Williams, he helped redraw the role of the rhythm section and ranked among the primary architects of post-bop. In the 1970s he turned to fusion, funk and electronics, and 'Head Hunters' became his most influential record, while 'Rockit' in 1983 carried the same curiosity somewhere new again. Freddie Hubbard and Terri Lyne Carrington are among his many collaborators, and Robert Glasper one of his clearest descendants.

tony.blurb: Teenage prodigy who helped invent jazz fusion.
tony.bio: Tony Williams, born in 1945, was an American drummer who joined Miles Davis while still a teenager and became the engine of the Second Great Quintet alongside Herbie Hancock and Ron Carter. His loose, elastic sense of time freed the other players to move where they liked, and it can be heard on 'Nefertiti' in 1968 and on his own early record 'Life Time', which produced 'Tomorrow Afternoon' in 1964. With Davis and then with his own group The Tony Williams Lifetime he helped invent jazz fusion, and 'Emergency' in 1969 announced it at full volume with the organist Larry Young and the guitarist John McLaughlin. He also recorded with Andrew Hill. In 1970 the critic Robert Christgau ranked him very likely the finest drummer alive. The Modern Drummer Hall of Fame took him in 1986; Williams died in 1997.

corea.blurb: Fusion pianist with a Spanish tinge.
corea.bio: Chick Corea, born in 1941, was an American pianist, keyboardist and composer whose tunes became part of the standard repertoire. He played in Miles Davis's bands beside the bassist Dave Holland, then formed Return to Forever, the group that carried Latin colour and electric energy into jazz: 'La Fiesta' arrived on its 1972 debut, and 'Light as a Feather' in 1973 produced both 'Spain' and '500 Miles High'. Flora Purim and Avishai Cohen were among his bandmates over the years, and the drummer Roy Haynes and the reedman Anthony Braxton among his partners in very different settings. He recorded with Michael Brecker and made duo music with John McLaughlin, Bobby McFerrin and the pianist Hiromi. Corea died in 2021, having spent a lifetime moving between acoustic trios, electric bands and every space in between.

jarrett.blurb: Solo piano improviser of the Koln Concert.
jarrett.bio: Keith Jarrett, born in 1945, is an American pianist and composer who began his career with Art Blakey, moved on to Charles Lloyd and Miles Davis, and then turned to work of his own. His solo concerts, improvised whole in front of an audience with nothing written in advance, produced 'The Koln Concert' in 1975, the record most people mean when they speak of solo jazz piano. He draws on gospel, blues, folk and Western classical music as freely as on jazz. Jan Garbarek, Charlie Haden and Paul Motian were among the bandmates behind 'My Song' in 1978, and with Jack DeJohnette he ran a long-lived standards trio whose reading of 'God Bless the Child' dates from 1983. Brad Mehldau and Hiromi are among the pianists who grew up in his shadow.

zawinul.blurb: Austrian keyboardist who co-founded Weather Report.
zawinul.bio: Joe Zawinul, born in 1932, was an Austrian keyboardist and composer who stood among the inventors of jazz fusion. He first drew attention with the saxophonist Cannonball Adderley, for whom he wrote the gospel-soaked hit 'Mercy, Mercy, Mercy' in 1966, then wrote and played 'In a Silent Way' for Miles Davis in 1969, the piece that gave that turning-point album its title. With Wayne Shorter he co-founded Weather Report, the defining fusion band, composing 'Birdland' for it in 1977 and later sharing its bandstand with the bassist Jaco Pastorius. He was a pioneer of the electric piano and the synthesizer, and DownBeat readers named him their top electric keyboardist twenty-eight times. He went on to lead The Zawinul Syndicate. Zawinul died in 2007, having proved that electricity and jazz could share a stage.

mclaughlin.blurb: Guitarist who fused jazz, rock and raga.
mclaughlin.bio: John McLaughlin, born in 1942, is an English guitarist, composer and bandleader, one of the pioneers of jazz fusion. He served his apprenticeship in the important British bands of the early 1960s, then stepped out under his own name with 'Extrapolation' in 1969 before moving to the United States, where he joined Tony Williams's Lifetime and played across the run of electric Miles Davis albums from 'In a Silent Way' to 'On the Corner'. His own Mahavishnu Orchestra, with the drummer Billy Cobham, welded jazz and rock to classical and Indian influences at a punishing level of virtuosity: 'Meeting of the Spirits' opened 'The Inner Mounting Flame' in 1971, and 'Birds of Fire' followed in 1973. Shakti, the Indian-jazz group he helped found in 1974, gave 'Joy' in 1976. He has also worked with Larry Young, Chick Corea and Al Di Meola.

holland.blurb: Bassist who anchors freedom with firm ground.
holland.bio: Dave Holland, born in England in 1946, is a bassist whose sound has anchored some of the most adventurous groups in modern jazz. He played in Miles Davis's band alongside the pianist Chick Corea, and from that circle came the freer company he kept next: the multi-instrumentalist Anthony Braxton and the drummer Jack DeJohnette, players for whom musical form was something to be built rather than inherited. His own 'Conference of the Birds' in 1973 is the record his name is attached to, giving both the title piece and 'Four Winds', and it set the pattern for everything after, writing open enough to breathe played with a bass tone as firm as a floor. The Dave Holland Quintet carried that balance through to 'Prime Directive' in 1999, and Esperanza Spalding is among the bassists who have followed his lead.

pastorius.blurb: Electric bass reinvented as a lead voice.
pastorius.bio: Jaco Pastorius, born in 1951, was an American bassist, composer and producer, and by common consent the most influential electric bass player there has been. His 1976 solo debut announced everything at once, with a headlong reading of the bebop line 'Donna Lee' and the floating harmonics of 'Portrait of Tracy'. That same year he joined Weather Report alongside Wayne Shorter and Joe Zawinul, staying until 1981 and writing 'Teen Town' for the band in 1977. He also collaborated with Pat Metheny, Joni Mitchell and Herbie Hancock, and stood with Stanley Clarke among the players who dragged the electric bass out of the background and made it a lead instrument. Pastorius died in 1987, leaving a way of playing that every bassist since has had to reckon with, whether they follow it or resist it.

larryyoung.blurb: Hammond organ taken into modal frontiers.
larryyoung.bio: Larry Young, born in 1940, was an American organist and occasional pianist who did for the Hammond B-3 something like what John Coltrane did for the tenor saxophone. He started out deep in Jimmy Smith's soul jazz, then pushed the instrument towards a modal, exploratory language nobody had tried on it, heard most fully on 'Unity' in 1966, the record that gave 'Zoltan' and 'The Moontrane'. He recorded with the guitarist Grant Green and shared a scene with the organist Shirley Scott. When Tony Williams put together his new trio with John McLaughlin, Young was the third voice, and he was in the studio for Miles Davis's 'Bitches Brew', playing on 'Miles Runs the Voodoo Down' in 1970. He died in 1978, and the jazz organ has not sounded the same since.

brecker.blurb: Tenor saxophone titan of studio and stage.
brecker.bio: Michael Brecker, born in 1949, was an American tenor saxophonist and composer who appeared on more than nine hundred albums across four decades, in jazz and in popular music alike. The Brecker Brothers gave the funk-driven 'Some Skunk Funk' and 'Sponge' in 1975, while his own 'Don't Try This at Home' in 1988 produced 'Itsbynne Reel'. His playing took Coltrane's harmonic reach and matched it to an immaculate, hard-edged sound that a whole generation of saxophonists set out to copy. He recorded with Chick Corea and with Pat Metheny, and stood alongside Tom Scott among the players who moved freely between the jazz world and the studio. He received fifteen Grammy Awards, an honorary doctorate from Berklee in 2004, and, in 2007, a place in the DownBeat Hall of Fame; he died that year of leukaemia in New York.

garbarek.blurb: Nordic saxophone tone, cold and singing.
garbarek.bio: Jan Garbarek, born in 1947, is a Norwegian saxophonist and composer whose sound, clear and keening and edged with cold air, is among the most recognisable in European jazz. He came up under the spell of John Coltrane and found his own way out of it, working with equal seriousness in jazz, in classical music and in the folk traditions gathered under the name world music. He was a member of Keith Jarrett's European quartet and stood alongside the trumpeter Tomasz Stanko among the voices that made a distinctly northern kind of jazz. 'Molde Canticle' in 1990, from 'I Took Up the Runes', shows the folk root plainly, and 'Rites' followed in 1998. His 1994 meeting with the Hilliard Ensemble on 'Officium', improvising over early sacred polyphony on pieces such as 'Parce mihi Domine', reached far beyond the jazz audience.

wynton.blurb: Trumpet standard-bearer of the jazz tradition.
wynton.bio: Wynton Marsalis, born in 1961, is an American trumpeter, composer and educator, and directs Jazz at Lincoln Center. Taught first by his father Ellis and then mentored by Art Blakey, he arrived with a command of both jazz and classical trumpet, and remains the sole musician to have taken Grammy Awards in both fields in a single year. 'Black Codes (From the Underground)' and 'Knozz-Moe-King' in 1985, followed by 'Hesitation' in 1986, caught his quintet at its most restless. Nine Grammy Awards have come his way, and the Pulitzer Prize for Music went in 1997 to his oratorio 'Blood on the Fields', the first jazz work ever to win it. He has recorded with his brothers Branford, Delfeayo and Jason, and has argued tirelessly for Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington as the foundation of the music.

metheny.blurb: Guitarist of wide skies and long melodies.
metheny.bio: Pat Metheny, born in 1954, is an American guitarist and composer whose warm, wide-open sound has carried jazz to audiences well outside it. He learned from Wes Montgomery and Jim Hall, and was still very young when the vibraphonist Gary Burton took him into his band and effectively launched him. The Pat Metheny Group gave 'Phase Dance' in 1978, 'Are You Going with Me?' on 'Offramp' in 1982 and 'Last Train Home' on 'Still Life (Talking)' in 1987, music built on long singing melodies and a horizon-wide sense of space. He has also gone the other way, into free playing with Ornette Coleman and Charlie Haden, and has recorded with Michael Brecker and Joshua Redman. Bill Frisell and John Scofield are his peers on the instrument, and the bassist Linda May Han Oh a more recent bandmate.

redman.blurb: Tenor saxophonist of the 1990s jazz wave.
redman.bio: Joshua Redman, born in 1969, is an American tenor saxophonist and composer, and the son of the saxophonist Dewey Redman. He emerged in the early 1990s as one of the most fluent players of his generation, at ease with the bebop repertoire, as his 1993 reading of Charlie Parker's 'Moose the Mooche' shows, and equally at home with his own material, from the ballad 'Sweet Sorrow' in 1994 to the hard-grooving 'Jazz Crimes' in 2002. His bands have been proving grounds for others: the pianist Brad Mehldau and the bassist Christian McBride both played alongside him early on, and both went on to lead their own. Redman has since moved between quartets, trios and larger projects, keeping the same warm, conversational tone at the centre of everything he does.

mehldau.blurb: Jazz piano that thinks in counterpoint.
mehldau.bio: Brad Mehldau, born in 1970, is an American pianist, composer and arranger whose playing joins the harmonic lineage of Bill Evans and Keith Jarrett to a way of thinking closer to classical counterpoint, the left hand arguing rather than accompanying. He came to notice in Joshua Redman's band before leading his own trio, and he was among the first jazz musicians to treat contemporary songwriting as serious repertoire: his readings of Radiohead's 'Exit Music (For a Film)' in 1998 and 'Paranoid Android' in 2002, and of the Beatles' 'Blackbird' in 1998, opened a door that many have since walked through. Esbjorn Svensson and Joe Lovano are among his peers. Mehldau has gone on to write for voice, orchestra and solo piano, restless in a notably quiet way.

mcbride.blurb: Bassist with a foot in every era.
mcbride.bio: Christian McBride, born in 1972, is an American bassist, bandleader and composer, an eleven-time Grammy winner who has appeared on more than four hundred records as a sideman. He came up through the lineage of the great swinging bassists, learning from Ray Brown and Ron Carter and from the electric example of Stanley Clarke, and by 1995 he was leading his own dates, among them 'Gettin' to It' and a bravura 'Cherokee' from the same year. He played alongside Joshua Redman and the trumpeter Roy Hargrove in the wave of young musicians who reshaped jazz in the 1990s, and counts the pianist Renee Rosnes among his peers. He works across small groups and big bands, and has become one of the music's most visible advocates, a teacher as much as a player.

hargrove.blurb: Trumpet bridging hard bop and neo soul.
hargrove.bio: Roy Hargrove, born in 1969, was an American trumpeter and flugelhorn player who could swing as hard as anyone of his generation and had no interest in staying in one room. He arrived young: 'Mr. Bruce' came from 'Diamond in the Rough' in 1990, and he won Grammy Awards in 1998 and 2002 for two very different kinds of jazz. Hard bop was his home ground, learned in part from Art Blakey's example, but he moved easily into R&B, neo soul, alternative rock and hip hop, and said plainly that all that mattered was whether a musician could play. 'Strasbourg / St. Denis', from 'Earfood' in 2008, became the tune a generation of players learned. Christian McBride and Robert Glasper were bandmates, and Ambrose Akinmusire is among those who followed. Hargrove died in 2018.

glasper.blurb: Where jazz piano meets hip hop and soul.
glasper.bio: Robert Glasper, born in 1978, is an American pianist, producer, songwriter and arranger who has done more than anyone of his generation to dissolve the wall between jazz and black popular music. Trained in jazz and shaped by Herbie Hancock's example, he built a band sound around a rhythm feel borrowed from hip hop and neo soul, and his 2012 work with singers made the case in public: 'Afro Blue' with Erykah Badu, 'Cherish the Day' with Lalah Hathaway, 'Ah Yeah' with Musiq Soulchild and Chrisette Michele. He played in Roy Hargrove's band, and stands alongside Kamasi Washington among the musicians who brought a young audience back to jazz. Five Grammy Awards have followed. Glasper writes for film too, and produces for others as readily as he records under his own name.

kamasi.blurb: Saxophone epics that revived spiritual jazz.
kamasi.bio: Kamasi Washington, born in 1981, is an American saxophonist, composer, arranger and record producer, and a founding member of the collective West Coast Get Down. He works on a deliberately grand scale, with choirs and strings massed behind the horns, and his music runs directly out of the spiritual jazz of John Coltrane, Alice Coltrane, Pharoah Sanders and Sun Ra. 'The Epic' in 2015 opened with 'Change of the Guard' and found a young audience the music had stopped expecting; 'Truth', from 'Harmony of Difference' in 2017, and 'Fists of Fury', from 'Heaven and Earth' in 2018, followed. He belongs to a generation, with Robert Glasper, Esperanza Spalding, Nubya Garcia and Shabaka Hutchings alongside him, that has made jazz a living popular music again rather than a museum piece.

esperanza.blurb: Bassist and singer who rewrites the form.
esperanza.bio: Esperanza Spalding, born in 1984, is an American bassist, composer, singer and songwriter who sings intricate lines while playing them, a rare enough thing to have made her instantly recognisable. Her early records built outward from 'I Know You Know' in 2008, while 'Black Gold' in 2012 and 'Good Lava' in 2016 pushed further into soul, funk and free-formed song, each project setting itself a different problem to solve. Charles Mingus and Nina Simone stand in her lineage, along with the bassists Ron Carter and Dave Holland; Wayne Shorter and Terri Lyne Carrington have been collaborators, and Kamasi Washington and Regina Carter are peers. She has five Grammy Awards, two honorary doctorates and a teaching life running alongside the music. Spalding treats each record as an experiment rather than a product.

hiromi.blurb: Piano virtuosity with no genre boundaries.
hiromi.bio: Hiromi Uehara, known simply as Hiromi, was born in Japan in 1979 and is a pianist and composer famous for a technique that seems to have no ceiling and for live performances of enormous physical energy. Her writing pulls stride, bebop, post-bop, progressive rock, classical music and fusion into the same piece, often within the same minute, and her 2003 album 'Another Mind' introduced it with 'XYZ'. 'Spiral' followed in 2006 and 'Voice' in 2011. Chick Corea, who became a duo partner and champion, and the example of Keith Jarrett both stand behind her playing, though neither quite accounts for it. In 2021 she took the piano to the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, playing at their opening ceremony. Hiromi remains one of the few jazz musicians whose concerts are as much spectacle as recital.

mulligan.blurb: Baritone lightness and the pianoless quartet.
mulligan.bio: Gerry Mulligan, born in 1927, was an American baritone saxophonist, arranger and composer who made the heaviest horn in jazz sound weightless. He wrote for Claude Thornhill and Stan Kenton, and was among the arrangers around Miles Davis in the sessions that defined cool jazz, working beside Gil Evans. In 1952 he formed a quartet with the trumpeter Chet Baker and no piano at all, letting the two horns weave their own harmony, and the results, among them 'Bernie's Tune', 'Walkin' Shoes' and a famous reading of 'My Funny Valentine', remain a high-water mark for the whole cool school. He later worked with Dave Brubeck and counted Art Pepper among his peers. A number of his tunes entered the standard repertoire. Mulligan died in 1996, the reference point for anyone who picks up a baritone.

tadd.bio: Tadd Dameron, born in 1917, was an American composer, arranger and pianist who gave bebop its most lyrical writing. Where his contemporaries chased speed, Dameron wrote melody: 'Hot House' (1945), written for Parker and Gillespie, 'Our Delight' (1946), first recorded by Dizzy Gillespie's orchestra, and 'Lady Bird' (1948), cut by his own sextet and still one of the most played themes in the music. He collaborated with Gillespie, shared a band with the trumpeter Fats Navarro and later recorded with Clifford Brown, work that placed his charts at the centre of the fastest-moving decade jazz ever had. His harmony, warm and unhurried, taught a generation of arrangers that bebop could sing as well as sprint. He died in 1965, leaving a songbook players still return to.

russell.blurb: Theorist who opened jazz to modal harmony.
russell.bio: George Russell, born in 1923, was an American composer, pianist and theorist whose ideas reshaped how jazz musicians think about harmony. His 1953 book, the Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization, was among the first works of general music theory built from jazz rather than European practice, and it pointed toward the modal playing that Miles Davis carried to the wider world.
