Russell wrote 'Cubana Be, Cubana Bop' (1947) for the Dizzy Gillespie band, an early meeting of bebop and Afro-Cuban rhythm, then led his own groups on albums such as 'Stratusphunk' (1960) and 'Ezz-thetics' (1961) for Riverside. Bill Evans passed through his bands. Composer, educator and musicologist by turns, Russell spent a long career, ending in 2009, arguing that theory could itself be a creative act.

nelson.blurb: Arranger behind one of jazz's finest albums.
nelson.bio: Oliver Nelson, born in 1932, was an American saxophonist, clarinetist, arranger, composer and bandleader whose writing gave hard bop a clean, architectural shape. The Impulse! album he made in 1961, 'The Blues and the Abstract Truth', has long been counted a landmark of its era, and its centrepiece, 'Stolen Moments', became a standard; 'Hoe-Down' and 'Yearnin' followed in the same year. Nelson worked alongside Eric Dolphy, whose wilder lines set off his own orderly ones, and recorded with the trumpeter Freddie Hubbard. He came back to the idea with 'More Blues and the Abstract Truth' in 1964, then made 'Sound Pieces' in 1966, and worked increasingly as an arranger and conductor thereafter. He died in 1975, remembered as a saxophonist whose greatest instrument may have been the ensemble itself.

bennycarter.blurb: Alto pioneer and architect of swing arranging.
bennycarter.bio: Benny Carter, born in 1907, was an American alto saxophonist, clarinetist, trumpeter, composer, arranger and bandleader, and with Johnny Hodges one of the two men who defined the alto saxophone's place in jazz. He began arranging in the 1920s, and the charts he supplied to Fletcher Henderson's big band helped set the shape of swing itself; his own tunes entered the repertoire: 'Blues in My Heart' (1931) and 'When Lights Are Low' (1936), his signature, first recorded with Elisabeth Welch. Carter worked with Coleman Hawkins and with Hodges, and stood as a peer of Duke Ellington across a career of extraordinary length that lasted into the 1990s; 'Honeysuckle Rose' (1961), from 'Further Definitions', catches him in full maturity. Eight Grammy nominations and a Lifetime Achievement Award came late. He died in 2003.

carlabley.blurb: Composer who gave free jazz its wit.
carlabley.bio: Carla Bley, born in 1936, was an American composer, pianist, organist and bandleader, and one of the defining figures of the 1960s free jazz movement. Her songbook travelled further than she did: 'Ida Lupino' (1965) and 'Sing Me Softly of the Blues' (1965), first recorded by the Art Farmer Quartet, were taken up by players from Gary Burton and Jimmy Giuffre to George Russell, Robert Wyatt and John Scofield. Her jazz opera 'Escalator over the Hill' brought her wide acclaim, while 'Lawns' (1987) shows the plainer, hymn-like side of her writing. She worked with Don Cherry and Charlie Haden, stood alongside Archie Shepp among the era's radicals, and pioneered artist-owned record labels, with more than two dozen albums to her name, the first in 1966 and the last in 2019. She died in 2023.

schneider.blurb: Grammy-winning leader of the modern jazz orchestra.
schneider.bio: Maria Schneider, born in 1960, is an American composer and the leader of her own jazz orchestra, whose writing turned the big band into an instrument for long-form, richly coloured music. Gil Evans is the acknowledged influence, and something of his orchestral shading, all half-light and slow bloom, runs through her scores, though the sense of landscape in them is entirely her own. 'Hang Gliding' (2000), from 'Allegresse', shows her gift for building momentum without hurry; 'Concert in the Garden' (2004) widened the palette further; and the Grammy-winning 'Cerulean Skies' (2007), from 'Sky Blue', carries jazz composition toward tone poetry. She has won multiple Grammy Awards and stands with Wynton Marsalis among the leading American jazz figures of her generation. Her orchestra remains the measure against which modern large-ensemble writing is judged.

quincy.blurb: Arranger and producer across seven decades.
quincy.bio: Quincy Jones, born in 1933, was an American arranger, composer and record producer whose seven-decade career began in jazz and grew into one of the largest in popular music. He played and travelled in Dizzy Gillespie's band, was mentored by the trumpeter Clark Terry, wrote arrangements for Count Basie, and worked with Miles Davis and with his fellow arranger Melba Liston. Leading his own orchestras he made 'The Birth of a Band!' (1959) and 'The Quintessence' (1961), and in 1962 recorded 'Soul Bossa Nova', from 'Big Band Bossa Nova', still his most instantly recognisable tune. The harmonica player Toots Thielemans recorded with him. His accolades ran to twenty-eight Grammy Awards, a Primetime Emmy and a Tony, with Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations besides. He died in 2024.

dinah.blurb: The self-crowned Queen of the Blues.
dinah.bio: Dinah Washington, born in 1924, was an American singer, songwriter and pianist who ranked among the most popular Black women making records in the 1950s. A jazz vocalist first, she moved freely through blues, rhythm and blues and traditional pop, gave herself the title Queen of the Blues, and was known too as Queen of the Jukeboxes. She came up singing with Lionel Hampton's band, learned from Billie Holiday, stood among peers such as Eartha Kitt, and passed her cutting diction on to younger singers, Nancy Wilson chief among them. The Grammy-winning 'What a Diff'rence a Day Makes' (1959) carried her to the pop audience, while 'This Bitter Earth' (1960) and 'Mad About the Boy' (1961), made with Quincy Jones, show the bite behind the sweetness. She died in 1963.

torme.blurb: The Velvet Fog, singer and songwriter.
torme.bio: Mel Tormé, born in 1925, was an American singer, composer, arranger, drummer, actor and author, nicknamed the Velvet Fog for the soft, burnished tone that made his name. He wrote the music for 'The Christmas Song' (1945) and co-wrote its lyrics with Robert Wells, giving himself one of the most performed songs in the American calendar. As a singer he was a musician's musician, at ease with the fast, harmonically alert style heard on 'Mountain Greenery' (1954), from his famous Crescendo Club night, and on 'Lulu's Back in Town' (1956) with the Marty Paich Dek-Tette. He stood among peers such as Ella Fitzgerald and Anita O'Day at the top of jazz singing. Tormé won two Grammy Awards from fourteen nominations, and kept working until his death in 1999.

joewilliams.blurb: The blues singer in Basie's band.
joewilliams.bio: Joe Williams, born in 1918, was an American jazz singer whose big, unhurried voice gave the Count Basie Orchestra one of its finest chapters. Big bands were his natural home, Basie's above all and Lionel Hampton's besides, though he was just as convincing in a small combo; he also acted a little, appearing twice on film with the Basie orchestra. His 1955 recordings with Basie made his name: 'Every Day I Have the Blues' became his signature, and 'Alright, Okay, You Win' and 'The Comeback' followed from the same fertile year. Williams sang the blues without ever shouting, letting the band carry the heat while his phrasing stayed easy and conversational, and that model of the blues-rooted male jazz singer runs forward to Gregory Porter. He kept singing for decades before his death in 1999.

hendricks.blurb: The poet laureate of jazz singing.
hendricks.bio: Jon Hendricks, born in 1921, was an American jazz lyricist and singer, and one of the originators of vocalese, the art of setting words to recorded instrumental solos and handing whole big-band arrangements to voices. With Lambert, Hendricks and Ross he sang the Count Basie book back to itself on 'Sing a Song of Basie', which produced 'Cloudburst' (1957); the trio's 'Twisted' (1959) became a standard, and 'Gimme That Wine' (1959) was words and music of his own. He recorded with Basie and drew his rhythmic language from Charlie Parker's generation. Leonard Feather named him the poet laureate of jazz, Time called him the James Joyce of jive, and Al Jarreau rated him the finest jazz singer there had ever been. Kurt Elling is his clearest heir. He died in 2017.

shirleyhorn.blurb: Singer and pianist of luxurious slowness.
shirleyhorn.bio: Shirley Horn, born in 1934, was an American singer and pianist who accompanied herself with such independence that the arranger Johnny Mandel likened it to having two heads. Her voice was a smoky contralto, and her great subject was time: she took ballads slower than anyone else dared, trusting the silence between the phrases. Miles Davis was her champion and returned to play on 'You Won't Forget Me' (1990); Bill Evans's harmonic touch is audible in her piano. Her collaborators ran from Toots Thielemans and Dizzy Gillespie to Ron Carter, Wynton Marsalis and Carmen McRae, and Quincy Jones likened her voice to clothing. 'Here's to Life' (1992) became her signature album, with 'Estate' from the same record a masterclass in restraint. She died in 2005.

cassandra.blurb: Jazz singer who absorbed blues and folk.
cassandra.bio: Cassandra Wilson, born in 1955 in Jackson, Mississippi, is an American jazz singer, songwriter and producer whose dark, grainy contralto reshaped what a jazz vocal album could contain. Betty Carter and Billie Holiday stand behind her phrasing, but her records pulled blues, country and folk into the frame: 'Blue Light til Dawn' (1993) held a spare, haunted 'You Don't Know What Love Is', and 'New Moon Daughter' (1995) set the Son House blues 'Death Letter' beside the Monkees' 'Last Train to Clarksville' as though they had always belonged together. The critic Gary Giddins credited her with expanding the playing field. She has won two Grammy Awards, was named America's best singer by Time in 2001, and stands with Dianne Reeves among the leading jazz voices of her generation.

elling.blurb: Baritone heir to the vocalese tradition.
elling.bio: Kurt Elling, born in 1967, is an American jazz singer and songwriter whose wide baritone and appetite for words made him the leading male jazz voice of his generation. He took up the vocalese line from Jon Hendricks, writing lyrics to recorded instrumental solos and treating a song as a vehicle for poetry as much as for melody. John Coltrane is his other pole: 'Resolution' (2009), from 'Dedicated to You', sets Coltrane's music for the voice, while earlier records had already established the range, from 'My Foolish Heart' (1995) on 'Close Your Eyes' to a searching 'Nature Boy' (1997) on 'The Messenger'. Elling improvises text as freely as he improvises line, and keeps a difficult tradition alive without ever turning it into a museum piece.

cecile.blurb: Among the most acclaimed singers of her generation.
cecile.bio: Cécile McLorin Salvant, born in 1989, is a French-American singer, songwriter and composer of French and Haitian roots, and one of the most admired jazz singers now working, a regular winner of DownBeat critics polls. She sings mostly in English and in French, her first language, and has recorded in Occitan and Haitian Kreyòl too, drawing on old and forgotten songs as readily as on standards. Betty Carter and Sarah Vaughan are the ancestors she has claimed, and Samara Joy follows in the same line. 'For One to Love' (2015) won the first of her three Best Jazz Vocal Album Grammy Awards and holds both her sly reading of 'Wives and Lovers' and her own 'Fog'; six of her eight albums have been Grammy-nominated. She is also an illustrator.

mcferrin.blurb: Improvising voice that needs no band.
mcferrin.bio: Bobby McFerrin, born in 1950, is an American improvising vocalist, songwriter and conductor who turned the unaccompanied voice into a complete instrument. His technique leaps octaves mid-phrase, sustains a melody while sketching harmony around it, and takes in scat, polyphonic overtone singing and vocal percussion, so that one man alone can sound like a small band. 'Don't Worry, Be Happy' (1988), from 'Simple Pleasures', was built entirely a cappella and became a worldwide hit; 'Drive', from the same album, works the same method. He has moved as easily through classical music as through jazz, conducting orchestras and collaborating widely, and his reading of Chick Corea's 'Spain' (1992), from 'Play', catches two improvisers at close quarters. Few musicians have made so much from so little.

toots.blurb: He made the harmonica a jazz voice.
toots.bio: Toots Thielemans, born in Belgium in 1922, was a jazz musician best known for the chromatic harmonica, and also a guitarist, whistler and composer. The historian Ted Gioia rated his elevation of the humble harmonica into a legitimate jazz voice as his most important contribution, and by common consent he became the instrument's preeminent player. His composition 'Bluesette' (1962), whistled in unison with his guitar, entered the standard repertoire, while 'The Days of Wine and Roses' (1974), from 'Captured Alive', shows the singing legato that made him irresistible to arrangers. He collaborated with Stéphane Grappelli and recorded with Quincy Jones, and worked as a film composer alongside his jazz career. Belgian by birth and American by adoption, he played on into a long life, dying in 2016.

petrucciani.blurb: French pianist of dazzling, defiant virtuosity.
petrucciani.bio: Michel Petrucciani, born in France in 1962, was a jazz pianist who became one of the most accomplished players of his generation despite osteogenesis imperfecta, the genetic condition that gave him brittle bones, short stature and a short life. He played with a full, orchestral touch and an unmistakable joy, drawing on Bill Evans for harmony while keeping a rhythmic drive entirely his own. 'Looking Up' (1989), from 'Music', is the tune most associated with him; 'She Did It Again' (1989), from 'Michel Plays Petrucciani', shows how completely he could carry a trio; and 'Home' (1998), from 'Solo Live', finds him alone and unhurried at the keyboard. He stood beside Martial Solal as a pillar of French jazz piano. He died in 1999.

stanko.blurb: Poland's great trumpet voice of the avant-garde.
stanko.bio: Tomasz Stańko, born in Poland in 1942, was a trumpeter and composer who worked in free jazz and the avant-garde, and the most internationally known figure Polish jazz produced. His tone was cracked, dark and vocal, and Miles Davis stands behind it, though Stańko carried the sound somewhere colder and more elegiac. He was a peer of Jan Garbarek in shaping a distinctly Northern European jazz, patient and open-spaced. A late run of albums took that music worldwide: 'Soul of Things' (2002), whose seventh variation is among his best-known pieces, 'Suspended Night' (2004), and 'Dark Eyes' (2009), from which 'Terminal 7' comes. He also composed for film. Stańko died in 2018, having spent half a century proving that the avant-garde could also be beautiful.

avishai.blurb: Israeli bassist who leads from the bottom.
avishai.bio: Avishai Cohen, born in Israel in 1970, is a jazz double bassist, composer, singer and arranger who made the bass a lead voice and brought Middle Eastern melody into the heart of contemporary jazz. He came to wide notice as a member of Chick Corea's groups before building his own trios, where the writing favours strong tunes, odd metres and a singing, almost folk-like directness. 'Remembering' (2005), from 'At Home', and 'Smash' (2006), from 'Continuo', show the range between lyricism and attack, while the title track of 'Seven Seas' (2011) sets his own voice alongside the instrument. He stands with Tigran Hamasyan among a generation who treat inherited folk traditions as jazz material rather than local colour. His trio remains one of the most followed in the music.

tigran.blurb: Armenian folk melody meets jazz piano.
tigran.bio: Tigran Hamasyan, born in 1987, is an Armenian pianist, composer, singer and whistler whose music grows out of the scales and modes of Armenian folk tradition. He plays mostly his own material, and even his straight-ahead jazz playing is threaded with figures from Middle Eastern and Southwest Asian traditions; his solo record 'A Fable' leans furthest into the folk material, while 'Red Hail' shows a debt to progressive rock. 'Vardavar' (2011), from 'EP No.1', and 'The Court Jester' (2013), from 'Shadow Theater', catch the mix of intricate metre, hammering attack and sudden tenderness that defines him. He belongs with Avishai Cohen and Vijay Iyer among players who widened jazz by carrying their own traditions into it. Few pianists of his generation are so immediately identifiable.

masekela.blurb: The father of South African jazz.
masekela.bio: Hugh Masekela, born in South Africa in 1939, was a trumpeter, flugelhornist, cornetist, singer and composer, the man widely called the father of South African jazz. Dizzy Gillespie was an early model, and Masekela stood alongside Abdullah Ibrahim as the most visible voice of South African music abroad. He reached a mass audience with 'Grazing in the Grass' (1968), from 'The Promise of a Future', a number one pop hit in the United States that other artists have covered since. His lasting work, though, is political: 'Bring Him Back Home' (1987), from 'Tomorrow', became an anthem of the campaign to free Mandela, and 'Soweto Blues' belongs to the same fight. 'Stimela (Coal Train)' (1974) remains his great smouldering set piece. He died in 2018.

solal.bio: Martial Solal, born in 1927, was a French jazz pianist and composer whose playing was famous for its wit, its harmonic sleight of hand and its refusal to repeat itself. Charlie Parker's language shaped his ear, and Solal turned it into something wholly personal, forever recomposing a standard mid-flight rather than decorating it. His appearance at Newport in 1963 produced enduring versions of 'Jordu' and 'Round About Midnight', both issued on 'At Newport 63'. He also worked as a conductor and as a film composer, and he stood beside Michel Petrucciani as one of the two pillars of French jazz piano across successive generations. He remained an improviser to the last, playing solo concerts in which nothing seemed decided in advance. He died in 2024.

esbjorn.blurb: Swedish pianist who took jazz to rock audiences.
esbjorn.bio: Esbjörn Svensson, born in Sweden in 1964, was a jazz pianist and the founder of the Esbjörn Svensson Trio, known as e.s.t., the group that carried European piano jazz to audiences raised on rock. Keith Jarrett's touch lies behind his lyricism, and he shared with Brad Mehldau a generation's instinct for melody, but e.s.t. added electronics and rock dynamics, playing clubs and festivals more usually booked for bands. 'From Gagarin's Point of View' (1999) gave the trio its breakthrough album and title track, with 'Dodge the Dodo' from the same record becoming a signature, while 'Tuesday Wonderland' (2006) found the writing at its most expansive. Svensson died in 2008 and the trio ended with him, leaving a body of work that reshaped what a jazz piano trio could be.

ayler.blurb: Free jazz at its most primal.
ayler.bio: Albert Ayler, born in 1936, was an American avant-garde saxophonist and composer whose huge, shuddering tone pushed free jazz past harmony and into pure sound. He built his themes from marches, hymns and folk melody and then tore them open: 'Ghosts (First Variation)' (1964), from 'Spiritual Unity', is his signature theme, while 'Spirits Rejoice' (1965) and the side-long live 'Bells' (1965) show the same method at full stretch. John Coltrane collaborated with him and was among his advocates, and Ayler stood with peers such as Cecil Taylor and Archie Shepp at the centre of the New York avant-garde. His playing runs on into the European free scene, where Peter Brötzmann took up the same ferocity. Ayler died in 1970, his influence far outrunning his brief career.

pharoah.bio: Pharoah Sanders, born in 1940, was an American tenor saxophonist known for overblowing, multiphonics and the sheets of sound he could summon from the horn. He came to prominence in John Coltrane's mid-1960s groups, and that apprenticeship carried him toward the free and spiritual jazz he made his own, much of it alongside Alice Coltrane. 'The Creator Has a Master Plan' (1969), from 'Karma', with its vocal by Leon Thomas, is the defining statement of ecstatic jazz, while 'Astral Traveling' (1971) opened 'Thembi' in near-weightless calm. More than thirty albums followed under his own name. Late in life came 'Promises' (2021), made with Floating Points and the London Symphony Orchestra. Ornette Coleman rated him the best tenor player in the world; Kamasi Washington and Shabaka Hutchings both descend from him. He died in 2022.

alice.blurb: Harpist and priestess of spiritual jazz.
alice.bio: Alice Coltrane, born in 1937, was an American jazz pianist, harpist, organist, composer, bandleader and Hindu spiritual leader, known later as Swamini Turiyasangitananda, or simply Turiya. She performed with her husband John Coltrane in 1966 and 1967, and after his death made a run of albums for Impulse! that became the foundation of spiritual jazz. 'Journey in Satchidananda' (1971) is her signature: its title track and 'Shiva-Loka' float harp, modal drone and the saxophone of Pharoah Sanders into music that belonged to no existing genre, while 'Turiya and Ramakrishna' (1970), from 'Ptah, the El Daoud', shows her blues-rooted piano. One of the very few harpists in jazz history, a lineage she shares with Dorothy Ashby, she proved influential far beyond jazz, reaching players such as Kamasi Washington. She died in 2007.

shepp.blurb: Avant-garde tenor with a political edge.
shepp.bio: Archie Shepp, born in 1937, is an American saxophonist, educator and playwright who has been central to avant-garde jazz since the 1960s. John Coltrane's advocacy opened the door, and Shepp used it to make music that was formally radical and openly political: 'Hambone' (1965), from 'Fire Music', and above all 'Attica Blues' (1972), the Impulse! album that remains his fiercest political statement. He played in Cecil Taylor's band, stood alongside Albert Ayler and Carla Bley among the New York radicals, and found kindred spirits in Roscoe Mitchell and the German saxophonist Peter Brötzmann. 'Steam' (1976), recorded live in Nuremberg, catches the ballad player inside the firebrand. A long parallel career in the university classroom has made him one of the music's most articulate teachers.

braxton.bio: Anthony Braxton, born in 1945, is an American experimental composer, multi-instrumentalist, theorist and educator, best known on alto saxophone but at home across the reeds. Raised on Chicago's South Side, he became one of the earliest and most important members of the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, the collective that reimagined what a jazz composition could be. His 1969 double album 'For Alto' was the first full-length record given entirely to solo saxophone, and its 'Composition 8C' still sounds like a manifesto; 'Opus 23B' (1974), from 'New York, Fall 1974', and 'Composition 51' (1976), from 'Creative Orchestra Music 1976', show the reach of his numbered, diagrammed systems. He worked with Roscoe Mitchell, Dave Holland, Chick Corea and Sam Rivers, and mentored Mary Halvorson. Few musicians have built so complete a world.

rivers.blurb: Multi-instrumentalist between hard bop and freedom.
rivers.bio: Sam Rivers, born in 1923, was an American composer and multi-instrumentalist, famous above all on tenor saxophone but heard too on soprano saxophone, flute, bass clarinet, harmonica, piano and viola. His Blue Note debut 'Fuchsia Swing Song' (1964) remains his calling card, its title track and 'Cyclic Episode' balanced between hard bop form and free playing, while 'Beatrice', from the same album, became his best-known ballad and a favourite of later saxophonists. He recorded with Miles Davis, and stood as a peer of Anthony Braxton among musicians who treated composition and free improvisation as a single activity. Rivers died in 2011, after a long career spent moving between structure and abandon, and between more instruments than most players ever attempt.

roscoe.blurb: Cofounder of the Art Ensemble of Chicago.
roscoe.bio: Roscoe Mitchell, born in 1940, is an American saxophonist, composer and educator, and one of the architects of the jazz avant-garde. He helped found both the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians in Chicago and the Art Ensemble of Chicago, the collective that carried the AACM's ideas about small-group form, silence and instrumental colour around the world. His 1966 debut as a leader, 'Sound', broke with hard bop convention almost entirely, treating texture and space as material in their own right, and the 1977 solo alto piece 'Nonaah' remains a landmark of unaccompanied saxophone playing. A technically formidable if deliberately idiosyncratic player, he has worked alongside Anthony Braxton and shared the free-jazz frontier with peers such as Archie Shepp. Decades of teaching have passed his methods on to younger improvisers, and he is still counted among modern music's genuine iconoclasts.

frisell.blurb: Jazz guitar with an Americana accent.
frisell.bio: Bill Frisell, born in 1951, is an American guitarist whose sound, hazy and elastic and full of space, changed what the instrument could do in jazz. He emerged at ECM Records in the early 1980s, first as a session player and then as a leader with 'Throughout', from his 1983 debut In Line. In New York he became central to the Downtown scene, forming a long working partnership with the composer and saxophonist John Zorn, and he played for three decades in drummer Paul Motian's groups until Motian's death in 2011. From the late 1990s his own records folded in folk, country, rock and roll and Americana, as on his 1992 reading of 'Have a Little Faith in Me' and the solo 'Ghost Town' of 2000. Threads run back to Jim Hall and Derek Bailey and forward to Mary Halvorson.

zorn.blurb: Composer who refuses every category offered.
zorn.bio: John Zorn, born in 1953, is an American alto saxophonist, composer, conductor and producer who has built a career out of refusing to sit in any one category. Jazz, rock, hardcore, classical, surf, metal, soundtrack, ambient and Jewish music all pass through his writing, played by deliberately unlikely combinations of musicians and rarely twice the same way. 'Batik' comes from 1986's The Big Gundown; 'WS1935' from the 1989 album Spy vs Spy, where the tunes of Ornette Coleman, a formative influence, are fired through a hardcore lens; and 'Jair' from 1994's Masada Alef, the first volume of the songbook in which Jewish melody meets that same freedom. Bill Frisell has been a long-standing bandmate and Derek Bailey a fellow traveller in free improvisation. Operating almost wholly outside the mainstream, Zorn is among the most influential musicians of his time.

iyer.blurb: Pianist who thinks in rhythm and systems.
iyer.bio: Vijay Iyer, born in 1971, is an American pianist, composer, bandleader, producer and writer based in New York, and one of the most restlessly intellectual figures in contemporary jazz. Steve Coleman was an early mentor, and Coleman's rhythmic thinking runs through Iyer's own, as does the angular logic he draws from Thelonious Monk and from Geri Allen. His 2009 trio album gave him the title track 'Historicity' and a rebuilt 'Human Nature', taken from Michael Jackson; 'Hood', from 2015's Break Stuff, drives the same rhythmic rigour through a trio. He received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2013, was voted Jazz Artist of the Year four times in the Downbeat critics' polls, and in 2014 was appointed with tenure at Harvard in both music and African American studies. He works among peers including Jason Moran, Ambrose Akinmusire, Tigran Hamasyan and Linda May Han Oh.

moran.blurb: Stride piano rewired for the hip hop age.
moran.bio: Jason Moran, born in 1975, is an American pianist, composer and educator whose work reaches well past the bandstand into multimedia art and theatrical installation. Andrew Hill was his mentor, and the older pianist's oblique harmony sits alongside the two other presences in Moran's playing: Thelonious Monk and the stride tradition of Fats Waller and James P. Johnson. His 2002 album Modernistic made the argument plainly, setting Johnson's 'You've Got to Be Modernistic' beside a piano reading of Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock' and treating a century of Black music as one continuous conversation. Geri Allen was another shaping influence, and he moves in the same contemporary circle as Vijay Iyer. Equally at home with composition, curation and teaching, Moran has made the piano a place where jazz history and the present tense argue productively with one another.

halvorson.blurb: The most singular guitar sound in new jazz.
halvorson.bio: Mary Halvorson, born in 1980 and raised in Brookline, Massachusetts, is an American guitarist and composer whose sound is unmistakable within a bar: clean lines that suddenly bend and smear, as though the tape were warping underneath her. She studied with Anthony Braxton, who remains her most important mentor, and took a different kind of licence from Bill Frisell, whose openness to space and texture she pushed somewhere stranger. Her writing has grown steadily more ambitious, from the octet music of 2013's Illusionary Sea, with its title track and the winding 'Sinks When She Rounds the Bend', to 'Night Shift' on 2022's Amaryllis, where horns thicken the frame around her. Equally in demand as an improviser and as a bandleader, she has become the guitarist against whom a younger avant-garde measures itself.

scoleman.blurb: Architect of M-Base and its rhythms.
scoleman.bio: Steve Coleman, born in 1956, is an American alto saxophonist, composer, bandleader and music theorist, and the central figure in M-Base, an approach to improvisation built on layered, cyclical rhythm rather than conventional song form. Charlie Parker is the root of his alto language, but Coleman stretched it over meters that fold and interlock, as on 1995's 'Def Trance Beat (Modalities of Rhythm)', which remains the clearest statement of his method. His 1991 album Black Science yielded 'Cross-Fade' and 'Country Bama', both built from the same rhythmic logic. Geri Allen was a key bandmate in those years, and Coleman went on to mentor Vijay Iyer, passing his rhythmic thinking to a younger generation of pianists and composers. He was named a MacArthur Fellow in 2014, formal recognition of an influence long felt among musicians before critics caught up.

ambrose.blurb: Trumpet of rare tenderness and unease.
ambrose.bio: Ambrose Akinmusire, born in 1982, is an American trumpeter and composer who brought a fragile, searching tone into a tradition that often prizes brilliance. Roy Hargrove was a formative influence, though Akinmusire's own writing sits closer to the avant-garde, leaving jagged edges and long silences where a more conventional player would fill. 'Confessions to My Unborn Daughter' opens his 2011 album When the Heart Emerges Glistening with an almost confidential quiet, and the celeste-and-trumpet ballad 'Henya' from the same record shows how far he will strip a piece back. Three years later 'Our Basement (Ed)', sung by Becca Stevens, extended that hush into song. He belongs to a generation of peers that includes Vijay Iyer and Melissa Aldana, and he remains one of the most distinctive trumpet voices to emerge this century.

bessie.bio: Bessie Smith, born in 1894, was the greatest of the classic blues singers and the most popular of her age, known then and since as the Empress of the Blues. Her 1923 debut 'Downhearted Blues' made her a star almost overnight, and 'St. Louis Blues', cut in 1925 with Louis Armstrong answering her on cornet, is one of the defining records of early jazz: two enormous voices, one of them a horn. She sang with a weight and an unhurried authority that turned the blues into theatre, and 'Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out', from 1929, has long outlived its moment. Her phrasing shaped the singers who followed, Billie Holiday above all, and through them the whole language of jazz vocals. She died in 1937 and entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989.

lilarmstrong.blurb: Pianist and composer behind the Hot Five.
lilarmstrong.bio: Lil Hardin Armstrong, born in 1898, was an American pianist, composer, arranger, singer and bandleader who sat at the centre of jazz in the 1920s. She held the piano chair in King Oliver's band, where she played alongside the young cornetist Louis Armstrong, whom she married, and the two went on to collaborate on many of the decade's defining recordings. On the Hot Five sides she played, arranged and wrote: 'Struttin' with Some Barbecue', from 1927, is her own composition and became a standard, while 'Hotter Than That', from the same year, is among the most exhilarating records of the era. She led her own bands into the swing years, cutting 'Doin' the Suzie-Q' as a leader in 1936. Long filed away as somebody's wife, she was in truth one of the music's architects. She died in 1971.

marylou.blurb: The pianist who taught bebop its harmony.
marylou.bio: Mary Lou Williams, born in 1910, was an American pianist, arranger and composer whose career ran through nearly every era of the music, and who kept moving forward while others settled. She was the musical brain of Andy Kirk's Clouds of Joy, writing and arranging 'Froggy Bottom' and 'Walkin' and Swingin'' in 1936 and the boogie showpiece 'Roll 'Em' the following year. She wrote and arranged for Benny Goodman as well, and collaborated with Duke Ellington. To the young modernists she was friend, mentor and teacher, guiding Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell and Dizzy Gillespie among others as bebop found its harmonic footing. She left hundreds of compositions and arrangements and more than a hundred records, and stood as a peer to Marian McPartland and Vivian Garry. She died in 1981, still the most complete musician of her generation.

melba.blurb: Trombonist and arranger who wrote for everyone.
melba.bio: Melba Liston, born in 1926, was an American trombonist, arranger and composer, and the first woman to hold a trombone chair alongside men in the big bands of the 1940s. She played in Dizzy Gillespie's orchestra and worked with Billie Holiday, John Coltrane and Count Basie, but it was her writing that left the deepest mark: a long arranging partnership with the pianist Randy Weston produced some of the most distinctive orchestral jazz of the postwar decades, and she collaborated with Quincy Jones as well. Her own 1959 date Melba Liston and Her 'Bones gave her 'My Reverie' and the original 'Insomnia', a rare chance to hear her as leader and soloist at once. A peer of J.J. Johnson on the instrument, she opened a door that had been closed, and wrote charts nobody else could have written. She died in 1999.

mcpartland.blurb: Pianist, composer and radio's great jazz host.
mcpartland.bio: Marian McPartland, born in England in 1918, was a jazz pianist, composer and writer who made her career in the United States and became one of the music's most generous public voices. Her playing carried the harmonic richness she took from Art Tatum, applied with a light, conversational touch, and she wrote as well as interpreted: 'Twilight World', from 1958 and later given lyrics by Mercer, is her best-known composition, alongside 'In the Days of Our Love' from the same year and the Grammy-nominated 'Ambiance' of 1970. From 1978 until 2011 she hosted Marian McPartland's Piano Jazz on National Public Radio, playing duets with and drawing out three generations of musicians in the least formal setting any of them ever faced. A peer of Mary Lou Williams and an OBE, she died in 2013.

ashby.blurb: She made the harp play bebop.
ashby.bio: Dorothy Ashby, born in 1932, was an American harpist, composer and singer who did something nobody had managed before: she made the harp a real jazz instrument. Where it had been used as orchestral colour or as novelty, Ashby proved the harp could handle bebop lines as fluently as a saxophone or a piano, and she did it with a swing and a bluesy phrasing that left no room for argument. Her 1968 album Afro-Harping is her monument, opening with 'Soul Vibrations', a groove that producers would mine for samples for decades afterwards, and running on through 'Action Line' and a supple reading of 'Little Sunflower'. Undervalued in her lifetime, she is now recognised as one of the most unjustly overlooked players of her era, and her example opened the way for Alice Coltrane. She died in 1986.

brackeen.bio: JoAnne Brackeen, born in 1938, is an American pianist, composer and educator who came up through two of the toughest schools in jazz: she found a mentor in Art Blakey, and she later held the piano chair in Stan Getz's group. Both sharpened a style already notable for its harmonic daring and its rhythmic independence, the left hand often working against the right rather than supporting it. Her 1977 album Tring-a-Ling, with Michael Brecker on tenor, produced the title track and the knotty 'Haiti-B'; more than a decade later the solo 'Dr. Chu Chow', recorded live at Maybeck Recital Hall in 1989, showed how much she could sustain alone at the keyboard. She has spent decades teaching, passing on a compositional approach that few of her contemporaries could match, let alone imitate.

sheila.blurb: Bebop singer who sang with bass alone.
sheila.bio: Sheila Jordan, born in 1928, was an American jazz singer and songwriter who built a style out of almost nothing: a voice and an upright bass, with no chords to lean on. Charlie Parker was the presence that shaped her, and he is said to have introduced her from the stage as the lady with the million dollar ears; his phrasing stayed in hers for the rest of her life. Her 1962 album Portrait of Sheila is a landmark of jazz singing, from 'Falling in Love with Love' and 'Baltimore Oriole' to the voice-and-bass duo 'Dat Dere' with Steve Swallow that pointed towards the format she made her own. A gifted improviser of lyrics as well as melody, and a peer of Betty Carter, she taught for decades and stayed among the most consistently creative singers in jazz. She died in 2025.

flora.blurb: The voice that carried Brazil into fusion.
flora.bio: Flora Purim, born in Brazil in 1942, is a singer whose wordless, wide-ranging voice became one of the defining sounds of jazz fusion. She took the cool, conversational intimacy she heard in João Gilberto and stretched it across octaves, using the voice as an instrument among instruments rather than as a vehicle for lyrics. Her prominence came with Return to Forever alongside Chick Corea and Stanley Clarke, where she sang the title track of 1973's Light as a Feather and the soaring '500 Miles High'; the same year her own Butterfly Dreams established her as a leader in her own right. She has recorded with Dizzy Gillespie, Gil Evans, Stan Getz, George Duke, Santana and Jaco Pastorius, and above all with the percussionist Airto Moreira, her husband and lifelong partner. Few singers did more to make Brazilian colour native to modern jazz.

geriallen.blurb: The pivot between M-Base and modern piano.
geriallen.bio: Geri Allen, born in 1957, was an American pianist, composer and educator who joined the avant-garde, the bebop tradition and the rhythm-driven thinking of M-Base without ever sounding as though she were reconciling anything. Her 1984 trio debut announced her with the title track 'The Printmakers'; a decade later 'Feed the Fire', from Twenty One, showed the same combination of muscle and lyricism, and 'Unconditional Love', from 2004's The Life of a Song, found her at her most songful. She was a key member of Steve Coleman's circle, recorded with Charlie Haden and worked closely with Terri Lyne Carrington. As a teacher at the University of Michigan and the University of Pittsburgh, and simply as an example, she shaped the pianists who came after her, Jason Moran and Vijay Iyer among them. Her death in 2017 cut short a career still opening outward.

carrington.blurb: Drummer, producer and builder of bands.
carrington.bio: Terri Lyne Carrington, born in 1965, is an American drummer, composer, producer and educator who has spent her career both anchoring other people's music and reshaping the room it is played in. She has worked with Dizzy Gillespie, Stan Getz, Clark Terry, Wayne Shorter and the Yellowjackets, and spent the decade from 1997 to 2007 on the road with every band Herbie Hancock put together. As a leader she made The Mosaic Project in 2011, which yielded 'Transformation', featuring Nona Hendryx, and the churning 'Echo'; two years later came the delicate 'Fleurette Africaine (African Flower)' from Money Jungle: Provocative in Blue. Close collaborations with Geri Allen and Esperanza Spalding run through the same years. Her work as a producer and as a teacher has done as much as her playing to widen who gets to make this music, and on whose terms.

regina.blurb: Jazz violin with a Motor City heart.
regina.bio: Regina Carter, born in 1966, is an American violinist who took an instrument with only a thin foothold in modern jazz and gave it a broad, singing voice. The swing and elegance of Stéphane Grappelli are audible in her playing, but so is the soul music that runs through her 2000 album Motor City Moments, which turns Stevie Wonder's 'Higher Ground' into a violin feature without losing an ounce of its grit. She has ranged widely since, recording 'Cinema Paradiso' for 2003's Paganini: After a Dream, a project that set her between the classical and jazz traditions, and revisiting an older American songbook on 2006's I'll Be Seeing You: A Sentimental Journey. A peer of Esperanza Spalding among contemporary bandleaders, and cousin of the saxophonist James Carter, she has made the violin sound entirely at home in jazz.

reeves.blurb: Contralto of enormous range and warmth.
reeves.bio: Dianne Reeves, born in 1956, is an American jazz singer whose instrument, deep and elastic and capable of sudden power, descends most clearly from Sarah Vaughan, though she has always drawn as freely on gospel, soul and rhythm and blues. Her 1987 self-titled album gave her 'Better Days', an early signature that showed how naturally she could carry a story through a song. 'Endangered Species', from 1991's I Remember, is her most defiant performance, while 'Lullaby of Birdland', on 2001's The Calling, returns her to the standards tradition she came up in. She has won five Grammy awards from nine nominations. Alongside peers such as Cassandra Wilson and Dee Dee Bridgewater, she helped define what a jazz singer could be at the turn of the century, equally convincing whispering a ballad or riding a big band.

deedee.blurb: Singer and actress with a theatrical fire.
deedee.bio: Dee Dee Bridgewater, born in 1950, is an American singer and actress whose career has moved between the jazz stage and the theatre without ever settling on one. Ella Fitzgerald is the presence behind her scat singing and her sense of swing, a debt she repaid directly on 1997's Dear Ella, whose romp through 'Cottontail' is pure delight. Her 1974 debut Afro Blue announced a voice already fully formed in its title track; three decades later 'La Vie en Rose', from 2005's J'ai Deux Amours, found her entirely at home in the French songbook. She has won three Grammy awards and a Tony, hosted National Public Radio's JazzSet for twenty-three years, and serves as a United Nations Goodwill Ambassador for the Food and Agriculture Organization. A peer of Dianne Reeves, she remains a fearless and theatrical performer.

aldana.blurb: Chilean tenor with a Rollins lineage.
aldana.bio: Melissa Aldana, born in Chile in 1988, is a tenor saxophonist and composer whose big, unhurried tone descends directly from Sonny Rollins, along with the same willingness to build a solo slowly and let it find its own shape. She made her early mark leading Melissa Aldana and Crash Trio, the saxophone, bass and drums format that leaves a player nowhere to hide, as on 'Free Fall' from 2014. Her 2022 Blue Note debut 12 Stars gathered up the writing she had been working towards, from the searching title track to 'Los Ojos de Chile', which looks homeward. She belongs to the same generation of bandleaders as Ambrose Akinmusire, and stands among the most compelling tenor voices to arrive in the last decade, as much for what she composes as for what she plays.

lindaoh.blurb: Bassist and composer of great melodic precision.
lindaoh.bio: Linda May Han Oh, born in 1984, is a Malaysian-Australian bassist and composer whose playing combines a big, woody sound with a composer's ear for line. Ron Carter's example runs through her approach to the double bass, though her writing pulls in directions of its own, folding odd meters and long melodies into small-group formats. 'Yoda', from 2013's Sun Pictures, shows the agility of that writing; the title track of 2017's Walk Against Wind and the propulsive 'Firedancer' from the same album show its ambition. She has held the bass chair in Pat Metheny's groups and collaborated with Vijay Iyer, two very different sets of demands that she meets equally. Now an associate professor at Berklee and part of its Institute for Jazz and Gender Justice, she is shaping the players coming up behind her as well.

roncarter.blurb: The most recorded bassist in jazz.
roncarter.bio: Ron Carter, born in 1937, is an American double bassist and cellist, and by some distance the most recorded bassist in jazz, with more than two thousand two hundred sessions to his name. He anchored Miles Davis's second great quintet from 1963 to 1968 alongside Herbie Hancock, Tony Williams and Wayne Shorter, a band that rewrote how a rhythm section could function: 'E.S.P.' and 'Eighty-One', both from 1965, show him steering the harmony rather than merely marking it. That trio partnership resurfaced on 1977's 'Third Plane' with Hancock and Williams. Paul Chambers came before him and shaped the vocabulary he inherited; Christian McBride, Esperanza Spalding and Linda May Han Oh are among those who have taken it forward. Three Grammy awards and a solo career of more than sixty years have made him the instrument's elder statesman.

haden.blurb: The bass that freed itself from time.
haden.bio: Charlie Haden, born in 1937, was an American bassist, composer and educator whose career ran more than fifty years and began at the centre of the free jazz revolution. In Ornette Coleman's quartet with Don Cherry and Billy Higgins he abandoned the walking line for something looser and more melodic, sometimes shadowing the soloist and sometimes moving independently; 'Lonely Woman', from 1959's The Shape of Jazz to Come, is the result, and remains one of the most beautiful things in the music. The Liberation Music Orchestra, formed with Carla Bley, carried his politics openly on 1970's 'Song for Che'. He found another lifelong voice in duet, as on 'Cinema Paradiso' with Pat Metheny in 1997. Keith Jarrett, Geri Allen and Gonzalo Rubalcaba were among his many partners. He died in 2014.

blanton.blurb: He gave the bass its voice.
blanton.bio: Jimmy Blanton, born in 1918, was the American bassist who turned the double bass from a timekeeper into a solo instrument. He joined Duke Ellington's orchestra as a very young man and transformed it: 'Jack the Bear' and 'Ko-Ko', both from 1940, hand him lines that answer the band rather than merely underpin it, and the duets he cut with Ellington the same year, among them 'Pitter Panther Patter', were unlike anything recorded before, two instruments in genuine conversation with nothing else in the room. His pizzicato and his bowed playing were more complex than any bassist's before him. He died in 1942, after only a few years in the spotlight, but Charles Mingus and Oscar Pettiford built directly on what he had shown, and every bassist since has inherited some part of it.

lafaro.blurb: The bass as a second melodic voice.
lafaro.bio: Scott LaFaro, born in 1936, was an American bassist whose few years of recorded work changed the instrument permanently. In the Bill Evans Trio he set aside the walking bass line for a countermelodic conversation with the piano, so that the three instruments moved as equals rather than as soloist and support. The 1961 Village Vanguard sessions caught it at its peak, in 'Gloria's Step', a luminous 'My Foolish Heart' and his own composition 'Jade Visions', recorded shortly before his death at twenty-five. He had also recorded with Ornette Coleman, whose freedom suited him as readily as Evans's introspection, and he stood alongside Charlie Haden as one of two bassists remaking the role at the same moment. Eddie Gómez carried the approach onward. LaFaro is still ranked among the most influential bassists jazz has produced.

chambers.blurb: The bass on Kind of Blue.
chambers.bio: Paul Chambers, born in 1935, was an American bassist and the anchor of Miles Davis's first great quintet from 1955 to 1963, and thereafter of pianist Wynton Kelly's group. His sound is among the most familiar in all of jazz: the walking line under 'So What', on 1959's Kind of Blue, is his, unhurried and absolutely certain. Alongside Red Garland and Philly Joe Jones he formed a rhythm section that defined the hard bop era, and he recorded with John Coltrane, Art Pepper and almost everyone else of consequence, more than a hundred albums as a sideman and about a dozen of his own, among them 1956's Whims of Chambers and Bass on Top, whose 1957 'Yesterdays' shows the bowed solo playing he was famous for. Ron Carter took up what he built. He died in 1969.

raybrown.blurb: The most swinging bass in jazz.
raybrown.bio: Ray Brown, born in 1926, was an American bassist whose time feel, huge and buoyant and impossible to rush, became the measure other players held themselves against. He came up in Dizzy Gillespie's bebop bands and was a founding member of the group that grew into the Modern Jazz Quartet, but his longest association was with Oscar Peterson, whose trio he powered for years: 1963's Night Train is the definitive document, from the title track through 'Things Ain't What They Used to Be' to his own composition 'Soular'. He worked extensively with Ella Fitzgerald as well, and later took on roles as bandleader and record producer. Christian McBride and Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen are among the bassists carrying his sound forward. He died in 2002, having swung as hard at the end as at the beginning.

pettiford.blurb: Bebop bassist who gave the cello a voice.
pettiford.bio: Oscar Pettiford, born in 1922, was one of the first bassists to carry the double bass into bebop, and he did the same for the cello, an instrument few jazz players had taken seriously as a solo voice. He worked alongside Dizzy Gillespie as the new music was taking shape and recorded with Thelonious Monk, bringing a big, singing tone and a composer's ear to the rhythm section. His own writing gave the repertoire durable pieces: 'Tricrotism' from 1955, the much-covered 'Bohemia After Dark' from the same year, and 'Blues in the Closet' from 1956. He belongs to the bass lineage that runs through Jimmy Blanton, and stood as a peer to Charles Mingus and Vivian Garry. Pettiford died in 1960, at only thirty-eight, having already reshaped what a bassist could be.

garrison.blurb: The bass anchor of Coltrane's classic quartet.
garrison.bio: Jimmy Garrison, born in 1934, was the bassist who held the ground beneath one of the most searching groups in jazz. From 1961 he sat in John Coltrane's quartet alongside McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones, a rhythm section that could move from hymn-like calm to open turbulence without ever losing its centre. His deep, resonant tone and long pedal figures gave the band a floor solid enough to improvise over freely. His playing opens A Love Supreme on 'Acknowledgement' in 1965, and it shapes 'Crescent' from 1964 and the 1961 reading of 'My Favorite Things'. He also recorded with Ornette Coleman as the new music widened. Garrison stayed with Coltrane until 1967, the whole span of that quartet's work, and died in 1976, his sound still audible in every bassist who plays for the band rather than for himself.

peterson.blurb: Canadian virtuoso, the king of swinging piano.
peterson.bio: Oscar Peterson, born in Canada in 1925, was a pianist of overwhelming technique and unfailing swing. Art Tatum was his model, and on that inheritance he built a style of dazzling runs, blues feeling and rhythmic drive that made his trios among the most admired in jazz. With Ray Brown he formed one of the great bass-and-piano partnerships, and later trios paired him with the guitarist Joe Pass and the bassist Niels-Henning Orsted Pedersen. He accompanied Ella Fitzgerald with the same generosity he brought to his own dates. Over a career of more than sixty years he released upwards of two hundred recordings and won eight Grammy Awards, and Duke Ellington called him the Maharaja of the keyboard. His 1962 album Night Train gave him 'Hymn to Freedom', 'C Jam Blues' and the title track, and remains the record most listeners meet him through.

jamal.blurb: Master of space; Miles Davis took notes.
jamal.bio: Ahmad Jamal, born in 1930, was a pianist who made silence part of the music. For six decades he led small groups with a clarity of design that set him apart from the busier keyboards of his era, using space, dynamics and vamps as compositional tools rather than as decoration. Miles Davis studied that approach closely and carried it into his own quintets, one of the clearest lines of influence in modern jazz. Jamal in turn drew on Art Tatum, and worked in the same orbit as his fellow pianist Erroll Garner. His 1958 Pershing date produced 'Poinciana', 'But Not for Me' and 'Music, Music, Music', and became one of the best-loved trio records ever made. Named an NEA Jazz Master and given a Lifetime Achievement Grammy, Jamal remained a working bandleader and educator until his death in 2023.

hines.bio: Earl Hines, born in 1903 and known as Fatha, was one of the small number of pianists who genuinely changed how the instrument is played in jazz. Where his contemporaries kept a steady stride, Hines drove single-note right-hand lines that cut through a band like a horn, freeing the piano from its purely accompanying role. His 1928 duet with Louis Armstrong on 'Weather Bird' is one of the most celebrated exchanges in the music, and his own 'Rosetta' from 1933 became a standard, with 'Piano Man' following in 1939. As a bandleader he gave early berths to Charlie Parker, Billy Eckstine and Sarah Vaughan, making his orchestra one of the crucibles of bebop. A peer of Fats Waller and Art Tatum, Hines kept working until his death in 1983, his influence audible in nearly every pianist who followed.

waller.blurb: Stride piano's greatest showman and songwriter.
waller.bio: Thomas Wright Waller, born in 1904 and known to everyone as Fats, was a pianist, organist, singer and songwriter whose innovations in the stride style spread through a whole generation of players. He was a huge popular success in the jazz age and the swing era, touring Europe as well as America and turning every session into a piece of theatre with his sly asides and comic timing. Beneath the humour lay a formidable technique and a gift for melody that produced 'Ain't Misbehavin'' in 1929 and 'Honeysuckle Rose' in 1934, both later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, along with the roaring 'The Joint Is Jumpin'' of 1938. Art Tatum and Count Basie both took from him, and the pianist Jason Moran has kept his music alive for new audiences. Waller died in 1943, aged thirty-nine.

teddywilson.blurb: The definitive swing pianist, elegant and precise.
teddywilson.bio: Teddy Wilson, born in 1912, played with a poise that critics have called the definitive swing piano style: gentle, elegant and quietly virtuosic. He learned from Earl Hines and Art Tatum and turned their example into something cooler and more linear. The sessions he led for Billie Holiday in the middle thirties are among the finest small-group records of the era, among them 'What a Little Moonlight Can Do' from 1935, the same year as his trio readings of 'Body and Soul' and 'Sweet Lorraine'. Joining Benny Goodman alongside Lionel Hampton, he became one of the first Black musicians to appear prominently on stage with white players, a quietly historic breach of the colour line. He led his own groups and sessions from the late twenties into the eighties and taught for much of his life. Wilson died in 1986.

andrewhill.blurb: Angular, questing composer-pianist of the avant-garde.
andrewhill.bio: Andrew Hill was an American pianist and composer whose music sits at the far edge of what hard bop could hold. Thelonious Monk was the touchstone, but Hill took Monk's angular logic somewhere stranger, writing pieces whose forms shift under the soloist and whose harmony refuses to settle. His run of mid-sixties recordings is among the boldest of that decade: 'Black Fire' in 1963, then 'Refuge' and 'New Monastery' from the 1964 album Point of Departure, made with Eric Dolphy and the drummer Tony Williams. He also worked with the vibraphonist Bobby Hutcherson, whose shimmering sound suited his floating harmonies. In later years he taught, and his mentorship of the pianist Jason Moran carried his thinking into a new generation. Hill died in 2007, long since recognised as one of the music's true originals.

barron.bio: Kenny Barron, born in 1943, has shaped mainstream jazz piano more than almost anyone else to emerge in the wake of bebop, a musician whose touch, harmonic depth and unhurried swing have made him welcome on hundreds of records as both leader and sideman. He came up in Dizzy Gillespie's band, absorbing the bebop language at its source, and Bud Powell remains audible in the way he shapes a line. His long partnership with the saxophonist Stan Getz produced the duet 'Sunshower' in 1991, from the People Time sessions, and the same year gave his original 'Calypso'. Earlier still, 'Voyage' from 1979 became a piece other musicians play, one of the most durable compositions by any pianist of his generation. A dedicated teacher as well as a performer, Barron has passed the tradition on to generations of younger players.

hodges.blurb: Ellington's alto voice, the sweetest sound in jazz.
hodges.bio: Johnny Hodges, born in 1906, played alto saxophone with a tone so luscious and a sense of phrasing so unhurried that Duke Ellington wrote for him the way a composer writes for a singer. He led the Ellington saxophone section for many years, and his solos give the orchestra much of its warmth: 'Jeep's Blues' from 1938, the ravishing 'Passion Flower' of 1941 and 'Things Ain't What They Used to Be' from 1942. He was heard early on soprano saxophone too, but put the instrument down after 1940 and refused ever to take it up again. Alongside Benny Carter, with whom he also collaborated, he is regarded as one of the two definitive alto voices of the big band era. A young John Coltrane worked under him and learned from that sound, carrying the lesson into a very different music.

webster.blurb: Breathy tenor romantic of the Ellington band.
webster.bio: Ben Webster, born in 1909, was the tenor saxophonist who gave Duke Ellington's orchestra its great romantic voice, a player of two temperaments: fierce and rhythmically hard-driving on the fast numbers, and on ballads so breathy that the air around the note became part of the sound. 'Cotton Tail' from 1940 shows the first, 'Chelsea Bridge' from 1941 the second, and his 1957 'Danny Boy', from Soulville, the sound at its most tender. He came out of the same tenor lineage as Coleman Hawkins, with whom he later recorded, and his approach to a ballad left its mark on Stan Getz. He also made records with Billie Holiday and with his Ellington colleague Johnny Hodges. Webster performed on both sides of the Atlantic across a long career and died in 1973.

joehen.blurb: Tenor saxophonist of endless harmonic invention.
joehen.bio: Joe Henderson, born in 1937, was a tenor saxophonist whose sound could turn from smoky and oblique to fiercely urgent inside a single chorus, and whose harmonic imagination made him one of the most sought-after players of his generation. Over more than forty years he recorded for Blue Note, Milestone, Contemporary and Verve, first as a young firebrand and later as an elder statesman. His 1963 album Page One, made with the trumpeter Kenny Dorham, carried Dorham's 'Blue Bossa' and his own 'Recorda Me', two tunes that entered the repertoire for good. He recorded with Lee Morgan and Freddie Hubbard, took much from Sonny Rollins, and later worked with the pianist Renee Rosnes. His 1992 Billy Strayhorn project brought a late flowering, including 'Lush Life'. Henderson died in 2001.

mclean.blurb: Alto saxophonist with a cry all his own.
mclean.bio: Jackie McLean, born in 1931, played alto saxophone with a piercing, slightly sharp cry that no one else has matched, a sound that carried Charlie Parker's language into rougher and more searching territory. He worked with Charles Mingus and had a formative relationship with the drummer Art Blakey before leading his own dates, among them 'Appointment in Ghana' from the 1960 album Jackie's Bag and the 1961 title track 'Bluesnik'. With 'Let Freedom Ring' in 1962 he turned deliberately toward the freer music then emerging, one of the few hard bop players to make that leap convincingly. He was a composer and bandleader as well as a soloist, and a dedicated educator whose teaching mattered to him as much as his records. The DownBeat Hall of Fame took him in during the same year he died, and McLean remains one of the music's most personal voices.

lovano.blurb: Restless multi-instrumentalist of contemporary tenor saxophone.
lovano.bio: Joe Lovano, born in 1952, is a tenor saxophonist of restless curiosity, equally at home on alto clarinet, flute and drums, and one of the defining voices in contemporary post-bop. He was for many years a member of the drummer Paul Motian's trio alongside the guitarist Bill Frisell, a group whose spare, floating music showed how far a standard could be stretched. John Coltrane is the presence behind his big, grainy tone, though Lovano's phrasing is looser and more conversational. His own records include 'Body and Soul' from 1991 and 'Fort Worth' from 1992, both from From the Soul, and the title track of 'I'm All for You' in 2004. He has won a Grammy and placed repeatedly in the Down Beat polls, and he records and performs with his wife, the singer Judi Silvano.

eldridge.blurb: Little Jazz, the bridge from swing to bebop.
eldridge.bio: Roy Eldridge, born in 1911 and nicknamed Little Jazz, was the trumpeter who carried the instrument out of Louis Armstrong's shadow and pointed it toward bebop. His solos were faster, more harmonically adventurous and more highly strung than anything the swing era had heard, using tritone substitutions and daredevil upper-register runs that made Dizzy Gillespie a devoted student. The 1936 'After You've Gone' is a famous display of that fire. With Gene Krupa's orchestra he cut 'Let Me Off Uptown' and 'Rockin' Chair' in 1941, the first a jubilant exchange with the singer Anita O'Day, the second a ballad that shows how lyrical he could be. He recorded with Coleman Hawkins and remained a fiercely competitive presence on the bandstand for decades. Eldridge died in 1989, one of the most influential musicians of his era.

navarro.bio: Fats Navarro, born in Key West, Florida, in 1923, brought a burnished, almost classical evenness of tone to bebop trumpet, playing lines of great complexity as though they cost him nothing. He toured with big bands before making his name in New York, where a run of studio sessions with Tadd Dameron, Bud Powell and Kenny Clarke produced some of the defining records of the new music, among them 'The Squirrel' and 'Our Delight' in 1947 and 'The Chase' the following year. He also worked alongside Dizzy Gillespie. Tuberculosis cut him down at twenty-six, in 1950, but the sound survived him: Clifford Brown built directly on it, and Miles Davis and Lee Morgan carried traces of it through the decades that followed.

chet.blurb: The Prince of Cool, trumpet and voice.
chet.bio: Chet Baker, born in 1929, played trumpet with a soft, middle-register lyricism that made him the emblem of cool jazz, and sang in a fragile, almost unadorned voice that used the same phrasing as his horn. He came to prominence in Gerry Mulligan's pianoless quartet, where the absence of a chording instrument left his melodic line exposed and he proved more than equal to it. Miles Davis was his model, and the two are often heard as branches of the same restrained approach to the trumpet; he also recorded with Stan Getz. 'My Funny Valentine', which he recorded in 1954, became his signature for the rest of his life, and 'But Not for Me' from the same year and 'Let's Get Lost' from 1955 belong to that same golden run. Baker died in 1988.

bookerlittle.bio: Booker Little, born in 1938, was a trumpeter and composer of startling maturity, a player who had absorbed Clifford Brown's warmth and command by his early twenties and was already moving past it into a harmony of his own devising, full of deliberate dissonance and unusual intervals. He worked with the drummer Max Roach, played alongside John Coltrane, and formed a remarkable front line with the multi-instrumentalist Eric Dolphy, the two of them pushing each other toward the edge of the music. Sonny Rollins was another model. 'We Speak' from 1960, and 'Strength and Sanity' and 'Man of Words' from the 1961 album Out Front, show a composer as much as a soloist. He died in 1961, aged twenty-three, leaving a body of work whose promise still startles.

woodyshaw.blurb: Trumpet innovator who rewired modern harmony.
woodyshaw.bio: Woody Shaw, born in 1944, is widely counted among the most important trumpeters of the twentieth century, a virtuoso who rebuilt the harmonic and technical language of the instrument around wide intervals and shapes few players had attempted. He recorded with Eric Dolphy while still very young, took much from Freddie Hubbard, and passed through Art Blakey's orbit, the traditional finishing school for a hard bop trumpeter. As a leader he wrote music of real substance: 'The Moontrane' and 'Sweet Love of Mine' in 1974, then 'Rosewood' in 1977. He was a mentor, an educator and an outspoken advocate for jazz as well as a player and composer. Shaw died in 1989, his innovations by then absorbed into the vocabulary of nearly every trumpeter who came after him.

dorham.blurb: The most underrated trumpeter in jazz.
dorham.bio: Kenny Dorham, born in 1924, was a trumpeter, composer and occasional singer whose warm, slightly veiled tone and unfailing melodic sense made him a favourite of musicians long before critics caught up. He played in Charlie Parker's group, worked with Art Blakey, and later shared a band with the saxophonist Joe Henderson, whose 1963 album Page One introduced Dorham's 'Blue Bossa', a tune now played by more or less everyone. His own 'Una Mas' arrived the same year, and 'Lotus Blossom' in 1955. Despite the admiration of his peers he never received the public recognition many of his contemporaries enjoyed; the writer Gary Giddins observed that his name had become virtually a synonym for underrated. Dorham died in 1972, and the reappraisal of his work has continued ever since.

jimhall.blurb: Guitar's great listener and quiet architect.
jimhall.bio: Jim Hall, born in 1930, was a guitarist, composer and arranger who treated the instrument as a listening device as much as a solo voice, favouring space, soft attack and lines that answer whatever the other players have just said. He worked in Sonny Rollins's group and with the alto saxophonist Paul Desmond, and his 1962 duets with Bill Evans on Undercurrent, including a headlong 'My Funny Valentine', remain a model of two musicians thinking together. From the 1975 album Concierto came 'I Hear a Rhapsody' and 'Romain'. Almost every thoughtful guitarist since has come through him: Pat Metheny and Bill Frisell both name him, and he shared a close musical kinship with Emily Remler. Hall kept playing and writing until his death in 2013, admired above all by other guitarists.

joepass.blurb: Solo guitar virtuoso, a one-man orchestra.
joepass.bio: Joe Pass, born in 1929, was the guitarist who proved the instrument could carry a whole performance alone. Playing bass line, chords and melody at once, with a bebop player's command of harmony, he made unaccompanied jazz guitar a serious form rather than a party trick. His 1973 album Virtuoso is the demonstration piece, with headlong readings of 'Cherokee', 'Night and Day' and 'How High the Moon' that guitarists have been studying ever since. He was also an ideal accompanist: he recorded with Ella Fitzgerald, worked in Oscar Peterson's group, and made records with Duke Ellington. Among his contemporaries only Wes Montgomery stood at the same height, and the two represent the twin poles of modern jazz guitar. Pass died in 1994, still regarded as one of the century's most complete guitarists.

grantgreen.blurb: Single-note bluesman of the jazz guitar.
grantgreen.bio: Grant Green, born in 1935, played jazz guitar with a directness nobody else quite managed: long single-note lines, no chords to hide behind, phrased with the cadence of a blues singer and swung hard. He was at his best in organ groups, recording with Jimmy Smith and Larry Young in the smoky, gospel-inflected setting that suited his attack, and 'Grant's First Stand' from 1961 announced him fully formed. The 1963 'Idle Moments' is his masterpiece, a slow, hypnotic performance that stretches far past the usual length and never loses its spell. By 1970 he had moved toward funk, and 'Ain't It Funky Now' from that year shows how far he was willing to follow a groove. A contemporary of Wes Montgomery and George Benson, Green died in 1979.

burrell.blurb: Blues-drenched elegance on the jazz guitar.
burrell.bio: Kenny Burrell, born in 1931, is a guitarist, singer and composer whose playing joins the elegance of Charlie Christian, Oscar Moore and Django Reinhardt to the grit of blues players like T-Bone Walker and Muddy Waters. He has recorded for most of the important jazz labels: Blue Note, Verve, Prestige, CTI, Muse and Concord among them. The albums he made with the organist Jimmy Smith were especially fruitful, including the 1965 set Organ Grinder Swing, which reached the Billboard Top Twenty. He also made a fine record with John Coltrane, and stands alongside Wes Montgomery among the guitarists who defined the era. 'Midnight Blue' from 1963 is the album most listeners know him by, its title track joined by the slow-burning 'Chitlins con Carne' and 'Soul Lament'. He has long taught at university level.

haynes.blurb: Snap Crackle, eight decades behind the drums.
haynes.bio: Roy Haynes, born in 1925, drummed for more than eight decades and was nicknamed Snap Crackle in the fifties for the crisp, conversational snare sound that no one has successfully copied. Few drummers in jazz appear on more records, and his career touches nearly all of it: swing, bebop with Charlie Parker, sessions with Thelonious Monk and John Coltrane, the freer playing of the sixties, and later fusion with Chick Corea. Rather than simply keeping time he broke the beat into fragments and scattered it across the kit, an approach that helped free jazz drumming from plain timekeeping. His 1962 album Out of the Afternoon, made with Roland Kirk, gave him 'Snap Crackle' and 'Moon Ray'. A pioneer of the instrument, Haynes kept playing into old age and died in 2024.

phillyjoe.blurb: The drummer who drove Miles Davis's first quintet.
phillyjoe.bio: Philly Joe Jones, born in 1923, was the drummer whose crackling snare and impeccable time powered Miles Davis's first great quintet, where he and the bassist Paul Chambers formed a rhythm team that other groups measured themselves against. He had a rare gift for adjusting his playing to whatever a band or a soloist needed, which is why he appears on so many essential records of the period; 'Billy Boy' from the 1958 Davis album Milestones is a small masterpiece of light, swinging interplay. That same year brought his own 'Blues for Dracula', its title track a comic spoken routine that shows the showman in him, with 'Two Bass Hit' alongside it. A peer of Art Blakey and an heir to the bebop drummers, he kept working until his death in 1985.

dejohnette.blurb: Fluid, orchestral drummer of the modern era.
dejohnette.bio: Jack DeJohnette, born in 1942, was a drummer of extraordinary fluidity, a trained pianist who heard the kit as a melodic instrument and coloured a band rather than merely propelling it. He played with Miles Davis as the music turned toward fusion, spent decades in Keith Jarrett's trio, worked with Dave Holland, and appeared on records with Charles Lloyd, Bill Evans, Alice Coltrane, Sonny Rollins, Herbie Hancock and Pat Metheny, among many others. As a leader he made more than thirty-five albums, including 'Silver Hollow' from 1978 and, from his group Special Edition, 'One for Eric' and 'Zoot Suite' in 1980. He won two Grammy Awards and entered the Modern Drummer Hall of Fame in 2007. Alongside his contemporary Billy Cobham, he shaped what jazz drumming could mean after the sixties.

jojones.blurb: The drummer who lightened the swing beat.
jojones.bio: Papa Jo Jones, born in 1911, anchored the Count Basie Orchestra's rhythm section from 1934 to 1948 and changed how jazz drummers keep time. By shifting the pulse from the bass drum to the hi-hat he made the beat lighter and more elastic, and the famous Basie swing, the sound of a band floating rather than marching, follows from that decision. The 1936 Jones-Smith Inc. session with Basie, which produced 'Shoe Shine Boy', catches him early and already fully formed. His own 1955 date The Jo Jones Special gave the drum features 'Caravan' and 'Old Man River'. Max Roach and Kenny Clarke both built on his innovations, carrying the pulse onto the ride cymbal and into bebop. He was called Papa Jo to distinguish him from the younger Philly Joe Jones, and he died in 1985.

krupa.blurb: The drummer who made drumming a star turn.
krupa.bio: Gene Krupa, born in 1909, was the drummer who turned his instrument into a solo voice and, in the process, into a source of stardom. His extended tom-tom feature on Benny Goodman's 1937 recording of 'Sing, Sing, Sing (With a Swing)' lifted the drummer out of the back line for good and became one of the defining performances of the swing era. Leading his own orchestra from the late thirties, he cut 'Drummin' Man' in 1939 and 'Drum Boogie' in 1941, the latter sung by Irene Daye, and he later hired Anita O'Day, whose brash phrasing suited the band perfectly. Chick Webb was his great contemporary, and he and Buddy Rich shared stages in duels that are part of drumming folklore. Krupa died in 1973, among the most influential drummers in popular music.

hutcherson.blurb: Vibraphonist who took the instrument avant-garde.
hutcherson.bio: Bobby Hutcherson, born in 1941, was the vibraphonist who carried his instrument out of the swing era and into the music's most adventurous corners. Milt Jackson gave him his starting point, but Hutcherson developed a shimmering, harmonically open style, on marimba as well as vibraphone, that made him the ideal partner for the new writing of the sixties. He recorded with Eric Dolphy and with the pianist Andrew Hill, whose shifting forms his sound seemed made for. As a leader he wrote 'Little B's Poem', from the 1965 album Components, whose title track is also his, and 'Maiden Voyage' followed in 1966 on Happenings. His influence runs through the vibraphonists who came after him, among them Steve Nelson, Joe Locke and Stefon Harris. Hutcherson died in 2016.

burton.blurb: Four-mallet vibraphone innovator and duet pioneer.
burton.bio: Gary Burton, born in 1943, is an American vibraphonist, composer and educator whose four-mallet approach turned the instrument into something close to a piano. Where earlier players, Milt Jackson among them, worked with two mallets, Burton spread four across the bars and drew out full harmony, a sound so widely imitated that it became the standard. He came up in the band of Stan Getz before leading his own groups and helping open the door to jazz fusion. His long partnership with Chick Corea made the duet a serious jazz format: their 1972 album Crystal Silence, with its title track alongside 'Senor Mouse' and 'Falling Grace', remains the benchmark. Burton also mentored the young Pat Metheny and spent three decades teaching at Berklee, shaping generations of players. He is one of jazz education's most consequential figures.

jjjohnson.blurb: Bebop's trombone pioneer and gifted composer.
jjjohnson.bio: J.J. Johnson, born James Louis Johnson in 1924 and sometimes billed as Jay Jay, was the trombonist who proved his instrument could keep pace with bebop. Where the horn had been a swing-band voice, he played it with the speed and precision of a saxophone, recording alongside Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and Miles Davis at the music's most demanding tempos. He was also a formidable composer and arranger: the ballad 'Lament', first cut in 1954 with the Jay and Kai group, became a standard, 'Wee Dot' from 1949 shows the bop writer at work, and 'Blue Trombone' from 1957 the quartet leader. His writing reached into hard bop, third stream and eventually film scoring. He belongs to a trombone line that runs through Jack Teagarden, Melba Liston, Curtis Fuller and Frank Rosolino. Johnson died in 2001.

brubeck.blurb: Cool jazz pianist who reshaped rhythm.
brubeck.bio: Dave Brubeck, born in 1920, was an American pianist and composer whose quartet made unusual time signatures sound like popular music. Often named as a leading voice of cool and West Coast jazz, he built his sound from odd meters, contrasting rhythms layered against one another, and a willingness to set classical form, jazz and blues in the same frame. The 1959 album Time Out gave him two enduring pieces: 'Blue Rondo a la Turk', his own, and 'Take Five', written by his bandmate Paul Desmond, which became the group's signature. 'Unsquare Dance', from 1961's Time Further Out, carried the rhythmic experiment further. He also collaborated with Gerry Mulligan, and his third stream leanings drew jazz toward the concert hall. A composer as much as a pianist, Brubeck remained a public face of the music until his death in 2012.

garner.bio: Erroll Garner, born in 1921, was an American jazz pianist and composer celebrated for his buoyant swing and his way with a ballad. He came up in the long shadow of Art Tatum and stood alongside Ahmad Jamal as a pianist who could hold an audience by touch and timing rather than sheer velocity. His 1954 ballad 'Misty' became a jazz standard and later lent its title to a 1971 motion picture. The 1955 concert issued as Concert by the Sea caught him at full stretch, with 'I'll Remember April' and 'Where or When' showing the swing and lyricism that made his playing recognisable within a few bars. He also appeared as an actor. Garner died in 1977, leaving a body of work that still sounds like the sheer pleasure of playing.

hankjones.blurb: Bebop's most elegant and dependable pianist.
