hankjones.bio: Hank Jones, born Henry Jones Jr. in 1918, was an American pianist, bandleader, arranger and composer whose playing drew words like eloquent and impeccable from critics and musicians alike. Schooled by the example of Art Tatum, he became one of bebop's most refined and dependable accompanists, recording with Charlie Parker and with Ella Fitzgerald, settings where taste and touch mattered far more than display. His own dates show the same qualities: the ballad 'We'll Be Together Again' from 1955, and a 1977 reading of Toots Thielemans's 'Bluesette' with The Trio. Honours arrived steadily in his later decades, among them an NEA Jazz Masters award in 1989, ASCAP's Jazz Living Legend award in 2003, the National Medal of Arts in 2008 and an honorary doctorate from the University of Hartford in 2009. He worked almost to the end, dying in 2010.

flanagan.bio: Tommy Flanagan, born in Detroit in 1930, was an American pianist and composer who grew up on the example of Art Tatum, Nat King Cole and Teddy Wilson before bebop and Bud Powell redirected him. Months after his 1956 move to New York he was recording with Miles Davis and appearing on Sonny Rollins's album Saxophone Colossus, and he was the pianist on John Coltrane's Giant Steps. His own 1957 debut as a leader, Overseas, holds the originals 'Eclypso' and 'Verdandi' alongside Charlie Parker's 'Relaxin' at Camarillo'. From 1962 he served three years as Ella Fitzgerald's full-time accompanist, returning in 1968 as her pianist and musical director for a further decade. That work made him the model of the sympathetic accompanist, while his own trios revealed a leader of quiet refinement. Flanagan died in 2001.

garland.blurb: Block-chord pianist in Miles Davis's band.
garland.bio: Red Garland, born William McKinley Garland Jr. in 1923, was an American pianist whose light, swinging touch and glittering block chords became one of the defining sounds of 1950s modern jazz. His years in Miles Davis's group, alongside Paul Chambers and John Coltrane, placed him on some of the most admired records of the decade and helped make the block chord style, a right hand moving in locked parallel harmony, standard equipment for the pianists who followed. As a leader he was just as persuasive: the 1957 trio showcase 'Billy Boy', a swinging 'C-Jam Blues' from Groovy, and 'But Not for Me', where the chords fall like soft rain. Few pianists have ever made swing sound so unforced or so welcoming. Garland died in 1984.

wkelly.bio: Wynton Kelly, born in 1931, was an American pianist and composer whose lively, blues-soaked playing made him one of the most sought-after accompanists in jazz. He was working professionally at twelve and played on a number one rhythm and blues hit at sixteen, making his own leader debut three years after that while building a reputation behind Dinah Washington and in Dizzy Gillespie's band. Two years in the army interrupted the rise, after which he worked with Cannonball Adderley, John Coltrane, Hank Mobley, Sonny Rollins, Betty Carter, Billie Holiday and Abbey Lincoln. With Miles Davis he played 'Freddie Freeloader' on Kind of Blue and recorded 'On Green Dolphin Street'; his own 'Kelly Blue', from 1959, is the signature. Together with Paul Chambers he formed a rhythm section that went on to back Wes Montgomery. Kelly died in 1971.

tristano.blurb: Cerebral pianist and legendary improvisation teacher.
tristano.bio: Lennie Tristano, born in 1919, was an American pianist, composer, arranger and, above all, a teacher of jazz improvisation whose influence travelled through his students rather than the charts. He worked in the orbit of Charlie Parker and stood as a peer to Bud Powell, yet pursued a cooler, more linear music of his own: long winding melodic lines laid over an even pulse, heard early on 'Tautology' from 1949. His 1955 'Line Up' was a landmark of overdubbed piano, a method almost unheard of in jazz at the time, while 'Requiem', from the same year, is his elegy for Parker. As a teacher he shaped Lee Konitz and a whole school of players who prized invention over showmanship. Tristano died in 1978, more revered by musicians than by the listening public.

gonzalo.blurb: Cuban pianist bridging Havana and modern jazz.
gonzalo.bio: Gonzalo Rubalcaba, born in Cuba in 1963, is a pianist and composer who carries the rhythmic inheritance of Havana into modern jazz. His technique is formidable, but the quality musicians most often remark on is control: a player able to fill every space who repeatedly chooses to leave them open. Chick Corea's harmonic reach is audible in his writing, and he stands beside Chucho Valdés among the great Cuban pianists of the era. 'Circuito', from 1991's The Blessing, catches him already fully formed, and a 1992 'Autumn Leaves' on the album Images shows how completely he could remake a standard. His long partnership with Charlie Haden produced its finest moment in 'Besame Mucho', from the 2001 album Nocturne, where restraint and Latin American song meet. He remains among the most admired pianists in jazz.

desmond.blurb: Cool alto voice who wrote 'Take Five'.
desmond.bio: Paul Desmond, born in 1924, was an American alto saxophonist and composer and one of the purest voices in cool jazz. As the melodic centre of the Dave Brubeck Quartet he made the ideal counterweight to the pianist's heavier attack, floating long, unhurried lines through the group's rhythmic puzzles on 'Blue Rondo a la Turk' and elsewhere. He also wrote the quartet's biggest hit, the 1959 'Take Five', which went on to become the best-selling jazz song ever recorded, and revisited the idea under his own name with 'Take Ten' in 1963. Away from Brubeck he found an ideal partner in Jim Hall, whose warmth suited a saxophonist who valued understatement above all. He stands with Lee Konitz among the alto players who chose lyricism over fire. Desmond died in 1977.

konitz.blurb: Alto saxophonist who sidestepped Charlie Parker.
konitz.bio: Lee Konitz, born in 1927, was an American alto saxophonist and composer who found a way past Charlie Parker without ever ignoring him. Studying with Lennie Tristano gave him a cooler, more linear conception, all long melodic lines and restless invention, and his 1949 'Subconscious-Lee' became the signature statement of that school. He played in Stan Kenton's orchestra and in bands led by Miles Davis, then spent the following decades turning standards inside out, as on 'Lover Man' from 1955 and the 1961 album Motion, where 'All the Things You Are' is dismantled and rebuilt in real time. Lester Young and Parker are the poles his sound is measured against, and Paul Desmond his closest peer in tone. Konitz went on improvising almost to the last, dying in 2020.

stitt.blurb: Relentless bop saxophonist on alto and tenor.
stitt.bio: Sonny Stitt, born in 1924, was an American saxophonist of the bebop and hard bop idiom and one of the most heavily documented players of his era, with more than a hundred albums to his name. Early on he was dismissed by some as a Charlie Parker imitator, a charge he answered by moving to tenor and building a warm, driving voice unmistakably his own, occasionally taking up baritone as well. The critic Dan Morgenstern nicknamed him the Lone Wolf for his habit of touring relentlessly without settling into any fixed band. Even so, the encounters count: 'Blues Up and Down' with Gene Ammons in 1950, dates with Dizzy Gillespie and Bud Powell, and the celebrated 1957 saxophone duel with Sonny Rollins, 'The Eternal Triangle', from Sonny Side Up. His 1962 'Stardust' shows the ballad player. Stitt died in 1982.

pepper.blurb: West Coast alto of raw emotional force.
pepper.bio: Art Pepper, born in 1925, was an American alto saxophonist who also played tenor, clarinet and bass clarinet, and the most emotionally exposed player West Coast jazz produced. He first came to notice in Stan Kenton's big band and absorbed Charlie Parker without surrendering his own singing tone. The 1957 session Meets the Rhythm Section, which placed him alongside Paul Chambers, produced 'You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To' and remains the classic meeting of West Coast lyricism and East Coast drive. His career moved through several distinct phases, each return bringing a changed style: 'Patricia', from 1977's Living Legend, and the 1979 recording of his own 'Straight Life' belong to a late period of unguarded intensity. The critic Scott Yanow judged that by his death in 1982 he had become the world's greatest altoist.

mobley.blurb: Hard bop's middleweight champion of the tenor.
mobley.bio: Hank Mobley, born in 1930, was an American tenor saxophonist and composer whom Leonard Feather christened the middleweight champion of the tenor saxophone, meaning a tone neither as aggressive as John Coltrane's nor as mellow as Lester Young's. His playing was laid-back, subtle and melodic, qualities that cost him attention in an era drawn to extremes; the critic Stacia Proefrock ranked him among the bop era's most underrated musicians. He learned the trade under Art Blakey, worked alongside Horace Silver, and later took the tenor chair in Miles Davis's group. His masterpiece is the 1960 album Soul Station, whose title track and 'Dig Dis' are his own compositions, with 'This I Dig of You' completing a record that has grown steadily in reputation ever since.

kirk.blurb: Multi-instrumentalist who played several horns at once.
kirk.bio: Rahsaan Roland Kirk, born in 1936, was an American multi-instrumentalist who played tenor saxophone and flute alongside a whole armoury of other horns, frequently several at once. He spent his early career billed simply as Roland Kirk. In lesser hands that would have been a novelty; in his it was harmony, a one-man horn section. His shows joined virtuoso improvisation to comic banter and political speech, and their sheer vitality is what everyone who saw him remembers. He worked in Charles Mingus's band and stood alongside Eric Dolphy and John Coltrane among the players stretching what a wind instrument could do. 'Rip, Rig and Panic' from 1965 and 'Volunteered Slavery' from 1969 catch his range, while the 1973 'Bright Moments' is the live signature, the sound of a musician insisting that jazz should be joy. Kirk died in 1977.

branford.blurb: Saxophonist moving freely between jazz and classical.
branford.bio: Branford Marsalis, born in 1960, is an American saxophonist, composer and bandleader, best known for the quartet that carries his name. Taught first by his father Ellis and then schooled in the hardest classroom of all, Art Blakey's band, he took Wayne Shorter's example on tenor and soprano and built from it a voice of his own. He has played and recorded with his brothers Wynton, Delfeayo and Jason, and moves with unusual freedom between worlds: soloist with classical ensembles, leader of the group Buckshot LeFonque, and from 1992 to 1995 the head of The Tonight Show Band. 'The Wrath of God', from 1986's Royal Garden Blues, shows the young player; the 1990 theme to Spike Lee's Mo' Better Blues reached a far wider audience; and 2004's 'Eternal' stands as his ballad statement.

clarkterry.blurb: Trumpeter, flugelhorn pioneer and beloved teacher.
clarkterry.bio: Clark Terry, born in 1920, was an American trumpeter, composer and educator who bridged swing and bebop and made the flugelhorn a jazz instrument in its own right. He held chairs in both of the great orchestras, Count Basie's and Duke Ellington's, and his 1957 recording of 'Take the A Train' belongs to that world. His tone was bright and chuckling, recognisable within two bars, and he was a natural comedian: 'Mumbles', from 1964, turns half-swallowed scat singing into a hit, while 'Misty' from the same year shows the ballad player behind the jokes. Terry's deepest legacy may be as a teacher. He mentored the young Miles Davis and later Quincy Jones, and spent decades encouraging students, making him one of the warmest and most generous figures in jazz education.

cootie.bio: Cootie Williams, born Charles Melvin Williams in 1911, was an American trumpeter whose growling, vocalised plunger work became one of the signature colours of the Duke Ellington orchestra. He built from Louis Armstrong's example a voice so distinctive that Ellington wrote pieces around it: 'Echoes of Harlem' in 1936 spotlights the plunger, and the 1940 'Concerto for Cootie' is an entire feature composed for him, later fitted with a lyric to become the 1943 hit 'Do Nothin' Till You Hear from Me'. He also played with Benny Goodman and led bands of his own, moving easily into jump blues and rhythm and blues as the music around him changed. Few sidemen have been so completely identified with a sound: to describe the Ellington brass is often to describe Cootie Williams. He died in 1985.

byrd.blurb: Hard bop trumpeter who crossed into funk.
byrd.bio: Donald Byrd, born Donaldson Toussaint L'Ouverture Byrd II in 1932, was an American trumpeter, composer, vocalist and educator, and one of the very few hard bop players to move into funk and soul without ceasing to be a jazz musician. He learned the trade in Art Blakey's band and alongside Horace Silver, and his 1963 'Cristo Redentor' is a gospel-tinged ballad of extraordinary calm. A decade later 'Black Byrd' made him a genre-crossing success, and 1975's 'Places and Spaces', a Mizell-produced landmark, sealed the sound: bright, danceable jazz-funk that reached far beyond the jazz audience. As a bandleader he was also a talent-spotter, giving the young Herbie Hancock early work, and he spent much of his life teaching. Byrd died in 2013.

blanchard.blurb: New Orleans trumpeter and film composer.
blanchard.bio: Terence Blanchard, born in 1962, is an American trumpeter and composer whose work runs from the jazz quintet to the opera house. Taught by Ellis Marsalis and then seasoned in Art Blakey's band, he emerged alongside Wynton Marsalis and Roy Hargrove among the trumpeters who renewed the jazz mainstream. He has since written more than eighty film and television scores, many of them for Spike Lee, and earned Academy Award nominations for his music for BlacKkKlansman in 2018 and Da 5 Bloods in 2020, as well as composing two operas and teaching at university level. His deepest personal statement is the 2007 album A Tale of God's Will, a requiem for Hurricane Katrina, where 'Funeral Dirge', 'Levees' and 'Wandering Wonder' turn a city's drowning into music of grief and endurance.

teagarden.bio: Jack Teagarden, born Weldon Leo Teagarden in 1905, was an American trombonist and singer who made his instrument sound unhurried. He drew a warm, blues-inflected line out of a horn most bands used for effects, and his singing had the same easy quality: 'Stars Fell on Alabama', from 1934, is the definitive feature for both. He led bands of his own, worked as a sideman in Paul Whiteman's orchestra and recorded with Benny Goodman, but the partnership that defined his later years was with Louis Armstrong, whose All-Stars he joined from 1946 to 1951. Their 1947 readings of 'Basin Street Blues' and 'St. James Infirmary' are among the great duets in jazz, two voices that seem to be talking. The trombone line runs on from him toward J.J. Johnson and modern jazz. Teagarden died in 1964.

cfuller.blurb: Warm hard bop trombone, a Jazz Messenger.
cfuller.bio: Curtis Fuller, born Curtis DuBois Fuller in 1932, was an American trombonist whose full, singing tone made him the trombone of choice on several of hard bop's finest records. He took J.J. Johnson's bebop vocabulary and gave it more warmth and less hurry. In 1957 he joined John Coltrane's sextet for Blue Train, the third horn whose weight gives that record much of its depth, and the following year he was with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers for the Moanin' date. As a leader his 1959 album Blues-ette produced 'Five Spot After Dark', a minor-key theme that became his calling card and one of the most recognisable tunes of the era. Blakey's band gave him a long musical home, and he remained an active player for decades after hard bop's heyday. Fuller died in 2021.

benson.blurb: Virtuoso guitarist who became a pop star.
benson.bio: George Benson, born in 1943, is an American guitarist and singer who turned a jazz career into pop stardom without ever losing the chops. He began working professionally at nineteen, recording with Jimmy Smith and taking Wes Montgomery as his starting point, and he stands alongside Grant Green and, later, Emily Remler in the jazz guitar tradition. In 1976 the album Breezin' broke him wide open: its title track and 'This Masquerade', which won the Grammy for Record of the Year, carried him to an audience far beyond jazz. 'Give Me the Night', produced by Quincy Jones in 1980, made him a fixture on the radio. He has also recorded with Earl Klugh. Few musicians have carried so much technique so lightly, and fewer still have been able to sing as well as they play.

scofield.blurb: Funk-leaning guitarist with an unmistakable tone.
scofield.bio: John Scofield, born in 1951, is an American guitarist and composer whose music folds jazz, fusion, funk, blues, soul and rock into something instantly identifiable: a slurred, vocal tone and a rhythmic sense that leans hard on the backbeat. He came to wide notice in Miles Davis's band, an apprenticeship that pushed him toward groove without blunting his harmonic edge. Since then he has been one of jazz guitar's great collaborators, co-leading the 1994 album I Can See Your House from Here with Pat Metheny and working repeatedly with Bill Frisell. His 1998 record with Medeski Martin and Wood, A Go Go, found a new audience entirely; the title track and the greasy 'Chank' are the sound of a jazz guitarist completely at home inside a groove band.

talfarlow.bio: Tal Farlow, born Talmage Holt Farlow in 1921, was an American guitarist known for a speed and reach that earned him the nickname Octopus, after the way his large, quick hands covered the fretboard. He took Charlie Christian's single-note conception and pushed it to bebop tempos: his 1956 'Cherokee' is the standing demonstration, long, clean, headlong lines played without apparent effort. He could also slow down, as 'Autumn in New York' from 1955 shows, and swing hard, as on 'Stompin' at the Savoy' from the album The Swinging Guitar of Tal Farlow. He stands with Wes Montgomery among the guitarists who shaped the instrument's post-war voice. Farlow died in 1998, a player always better known to guitarists than to the wider public.

stanclarke.blurb: Fusion bassist who made bass a lead voice.
stanclarke.bio: Stanley Clarke, born in 1951, is an American bassist, composer and film scorer who took the bass out of the background and set it at the front of the stage. As a founding member of Return to Forever, alongside Chick Corea and Al Di Meola, he helped invent jazz fusion, and he became the first bassist from that world to headline his own tours, sell out halls internationally and earn gold records. 'Lopsy Lu', from his 1974 debut, showed what a solo bass could carry; 'School Days' in 1976 became his anthem, a piece bass players have worked at ever since, with 'Silly Putty' from the same album showing the funk side. He stands beside Jaco Pastorius as a defining electric bass voice of the era, and his influence runs straight through to Christian McBride.

nhop.blurb: Danish bass virtuoso of astonishing technique.
nhop.bio: Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen, known to musicians simply as NHØP, was a Danish double bassist, born in 1946, and one of the most technically astonishing players the instrument has produced. Building on Ray Brown's example, he combined a huge, singing tone with a speed and accuracy that let him play melodic lines most bassists would attempt only on another instrument. His long partnership with Oscar Peterson, a pianist who demanded everything from a rhythm section, made his name internationally, and he also recorded with Dexter Gordon. As a leader he made the album Jaywalkin' in 1975 and recorded his best-known original, 'My Little Anna', the following year. He composed and taught at university level as well as playing, and by his death in 2005 he had become the model for European jazz bass.

egomez.blurb: Bill Evans's bassist for eleven years.
egomez.bio: Eddie Gómez, born Edgar Gómez in 1944, is a Puerto Rican double bassist whose name is inseparable from the Bill Evans Trio, where he held the bass chair from 1966 to 1977. He inherited the role Scott LaFaro had invented, in which the bass converses with the piano rather than merely keeping time, and extended it with a singing, high-register sound and a soloist's confidence. The 1968 readings of 'Nardis' and 'Waltz for Debby' show that interplay at its most searching, three musicians finishing one another's phrases. Eleven years is a long time in any working trio, and the partnership gave Evans's later music much of its restless energy. Gómez has since worked widely across jazz and Brazilian popular music, but that decade with Evans remains the heart of his story.

rich.blurb: Explosive drummer and driving big-band leader.
rich.bio: Buddy Rich, born Bernard Rich in 1917, was an American drummer, bandleader, songwriter and conductor widely held to be among the most influential drummers who ever lived. His technique was close to freakish, a blur of speed, control and stamina applied to swing with unrelenting force. He came up through Tommy Dorsey's band, worked alongside his fellow drummer Gene Krupa, and was in demand for sessions and recording dates with Count Basie and Charlie Parker. From the mid-1960s he led a big band of extraordinary discipline, and its showpieces are his monuments: the 1966 West Side Story Medley, a tour de force of dynamics and gear changes, 'Love for Sale' from the album Swingin' New Big Band, and the extended 'Channel One Suite' from 1968. Rich died in 1987.

higgins.blurb: The drummer who swung free jazz.
higgins.bio: Billy Higgins, born in 1936, was an American drummer whose light, buoyant swing made him one of the most recorded percussionists in jazz. He sat at the centre of the music's biggest upheaval, joining Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry and Charlie Haden in the quartet that cut 'Lonely Woman' in 1959 and announced free jazz to the world. Yet he was never only an avant-gardist: the freedom of that band sat comfortably beside the hard bop groove he brought to Lee Morgan's 'The Sidewinder' in 1964 and to Kenny Dorham's 'Una Mas' the year before. That rare double citizenship, at ease in the most open playing and the deepest bop, made him the drummer everybody wanted. He worked steadily until his death in 2001, remembered as much for his beaming presence on the bandstand as for the lift of his cymbal beat.

cobb.blurb: The drummer at the heart of Kind of Blue.
cobb.bio: Jimmy Cobb, born in 1929, was the American drummer whose brushes and cymbals carry one of the most famous records jazz ever made. As a member of the first great Miles Davis sextet he played on 'So What', 'All Blues' and 'Freddie Freeloader' in 1959, holding the pulse of Kind of Blue so lightly that the music seems to float rather than swing. Alongside him in that band stood John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley, and Cobb's unfussy, deeply musical time gave both of them room to think. That single session kept his name in circulation for the rest of his life, and he was named an NEA Jazz Master in 2009. He kept playing and recording until his death in 2020, a drummer prized for taste rather than display.

motian.blurb: Freed the drums from keeping time.
motian.bio: Paul Motian, born in 1931 to an Armenian-American family, was a drummer and composer who quietly rewrote what a jazz drummer was for. In Bill Evans's trio he abandoned strict timekeeping for colour and conversation, shading 'Blue in Green' in 1960 and the Village Vanguard 'Waltz for Debby' in 1961 into something closer to chamber music. He went on to work with Keith Jarrett before building the group that defined his later life, the long-running trio with guitarist Bill Frisell and saxophonist Joe Lovano, whose 1985 album 'It Should've Happened a Long Time Ago' remains its calling card. As a composer he wrote spare, haunting melodies his bandmates could pull in any direction. Motian played on until his death in 2011, and generations of drummers who think in texture rather than tempo trace the idea back to him.

hartman.blurb: The baritone who sang with Coltrane.
hartman.bio: Johnny Hartman, born in 1923, was an American singer whose warm baritone made him the definitive interpreter of the jazz ballad. He served his apprenticeship in the big bands of Earl Hines and Dizzy Gillespie and in the company of pianist Erroll Garner, but his name rests above all on one 1963 meeting: the album made with John Coltrane, where 'Lush Life', 'My One and Only Love' and 'They Say It's Wonderful' were sung with an unhurried tenderness the saxophonist answered rather than merely accompanied. It was a landmark for both men and has never lost its glow. Hartman took Duke Ellington's sense of elegance as a model and never chased fashion, working as a ballad specialist through decades when the style was out of favour. He died in 1983, his reputation growing steadily ever since.

porter.blurb: Soul-warmed baritone who widened jazz's audience.
porter.bio: Gregory Porter, born in 1971, is an American singer and songwriter whose deep, soul-warmed baritone carried vocal jazz back towards the pop mainstream. His 2010 debut Water set out the range early with the slow-burning '1960 What?', the work of a jazz singer with the reach of a preacher and the instincts of a storyteller. The 2013 album Liquid Spirit made him a star: the handclapping title track and the bruised 'Hey Laura' won him the Grammy for Best Jazz Vocal Album in 2014, and Take Me to the Alley won it again in 2017. He learned from Nat King Cole and Joe Williams, singers who let warmth and diction do the heavy work, and he has acted on the stage as well. Few contemporary jazz voices reach so far beyond the jazz audience.

samara.bio: Samara Joy, born in 1999, is an American singer who made an old vocabulary sound startlingly new. Her self-titled debut arrived in 2021 and was enough for JazzTimes to name her Best New Artist; the follow-up, Linger Awhile, topped the Billboard jazz albums chart in 2022 on the strength of the aching 'Guess Who I Saw Today', the buoyant 'Can't Get Out of This Mood' and its title track. She sings with the plush low register and harmonic daring of Sarah Vaughan and the rhythmic poise of Ella Fitzgerald, the two singers she most openly claims as models. Six Grammy Awards have followed, among them Best New Artist in 2023, a rare crossover for a straight-ahead jazz vocalist. With Cécile McLorin Salvant she leads a generation proving the standards still have plenty left to say.

chucho.blurb: Founder of Irakere, giant of Cuban piano.
chucho.bio: Chucho Valdés, born in Cuba in 1941, is a pianist, composer, bandleader and arranger whose career now spans more than fifty years. He had been in the Orquesta Cubana de Música Moderna from its first days; in 1973 he founded Irakere and turned it into the loudest and most inventive Latin jazz band of its era, welding Afro-Cuban percussion to the harmony he had absorbed from Dizzy Gillespie's bebop. 'Bacalao con Pan' in 1974 caught the group at full tilt, and his own composition 'Mambo Influenciado', recorded with the band in 1979, became a standard of the repertoire. Beside him in Irakere stood the saxophonist Paquito D'Rivera, and his example runs through younger Cuban pianists such as Gonzalo Rubalcaba. Classically schooled and thunderous at the keyboard, Valdés remains the towering figure of Cuban jazz piano and a teacher to those who followed.

paquito.blurb: Cuban reed virtuoso bridging bebop and Havana.
paquito.bio: Paquito D'Rivera, born in Cuba in 1948, is an alto saxophonist, clarinettist and composer who carried Cuban virtuosity into American jazz. He came up in Irakere alongside the pianist Chucho Valdés, then settled in the United States and launched his own career with the 1981 debut Paquito Blowin', whose reading of 'On Green Dolphin Street' announced a bebop player with a Cuban heartbeat. Charlie Parker gave him his phrasing; Dizzy Gillespie, whose bands he later joined, gave him licence to fuse that phrasing with Afro-Caribbean rhythm. He moves as easily into classical repertoire on clarinet as into a Latin jazz burn-up, and his silvery tone is recognisable within a bar. As bandleader, composer and advocate he has spent four decades insisting that Cuban music and jazz were never two separate things.

shirleyscott.blurb: The Queen of the Hammond organ.
shirleyscott.bio: Shirley Scott, born in 1934, was an American organist known as the Queen of the Organ, and few players ever made the Hammond speak with such economy. Her 1958 debut Great Scott! set the template: a headlong 'Cherokee' that showed she had bebop lines at her fingertips, and a hushed 'Goodbye' that showed she could hold a ballad with nothing but drawbars and space. Her playing braided three traditions at once, the harmonic bite of bebop, the plain-spoken feeling of the blues and the rolling cadences of the church, and it swung without ever needing to shout. She worked in the same era as Jimmy Smith and Larry Young, the other architects of jazz organ, and stands with them as an equal rather than a follower. Scott played and recorded until her death in 2002.

emily.blurb: Straight-ahead guitar brilliance, gone too soon.
emily.bio: Emily Remler, born in 1957, was an American guitarist, bandleader and composer whose career ran barely a dozen years and still left a deep mark. Her 1981 debut Firefly announced a player of unusual maturity: Wes Montgomery's 'Movin' Along' taken with the octaves and warm thumb tone of her great model, a Horace Silver line delivered with hard bop snap, and Ellington's 'In a Sentimental Mood' handled with the patience she had learned from Jim Hall. She played the straight-ahead tradition at a time when fusion dominated the guitar, and swung hard enough to stand comfortably alongside George Benson. As a bandleader she chose her own repertoire and led from the front, one of very few women at the centre of the jazz guitar world. Her death in 1990, in her early thirties, cut short one of the instrument's most promising voices.

rosnes.blurb: Post-bop pianist trusted by the masters.
rosnes.bio: Renee Rosnes, born in Canada in 1962, is a pianist, composer and arranger who built her name as the sidewoman every major leader wanted, then established herself as a leader in turn. She worked in the bands of the saxophonists Joe Henderson and Wayne Shorter, an education in accompanying players who leave nothing predictable, and her touch, at once crisp and lyrical, owes much to Kenny Barron, whose 'Malaga Moon' she recorded in 1990. That same year the title track of For the Moment showed her own writing: harmonically rich, unhurried, built for improvisers rather than for display. She has since become a fixture of the post-bop mainstream, a peer of the bassist Christian McBride, and a bandleader whose groups are prized by the musicians inside them. Rosnes remains one of the most complete musicians in modern jazz piano.

nubya.blurb: Tenor voice of new British jazz.
nubya.bio: Nubya Garcia, born in 1991, is a British saxophonist, composer and bandleader, and one of the defining voices of the current British jazz scene. Her tenor tone is broad and unhurried, shaped by John Coltrane's example yet never merely imitative, and her writing treats jazz as porous rather than sealed off from the music around it. The 2020 album Source made the case in full: a title track built on a long, patient groove, the springing 'Pace' that introduced it, and 'The Message Continues', which unfolds with the slow burn of spiritual jazz. She belongs to a generation, with Shabaka Hutchings and Kamasi Washington among them, that has drawn young audiences back to improvised music by refusing to wall it off from club culture. Her rise has been steady and entirely on her own terms.

shabaka.blurb: Sons of Kemet leader, jazz as ritual.
shabaka.bio: Shabaka Hutchings, born in 1984, is a British saxophonist, composer and bandleader who spent a decade making jazz feel urgent again. He led Sons of Kemet, whose relentless drive and defiance turned the 2018 album Your Queen Is a Reptile into a carnival with teeth: 'My Queen Is Ada Eastman' opened it and 'My Queen Is Harriet Tubman' became its rallying cry, the record naming queens of its own in place of the crown. On 'Black' in 2021, with the poet Joshua Idehen, the band grew starker still. He also fronted Shabaka and the Ancestors and played as King Shabaka in The Comet Is Coming, and he has worked with the Sun Ra Arkestra, Mulatu Astatke and Andre 3000. Pharoah Sanders and Sun Ra pointed the way: jazz as ritual and possibility rather than repertoire.

ellis.blurb: The patriarch who taught a generation.
ellis.bio: Ellis Marsalis, born in 1934, was an American pianist and educator whose influence on modern jazz is measured less in records than in students. Active from the late 1940s, he played a lyrical, harmonically alert piano heard on albums such as 1985's Syndrome and the 1998 trio record Twelve's It, but he was known first of all as a teacher. Out of his classrooms came Terence Blanchard and his own four musician sons, Wynton, Branford, Delfeayo and Jason, whose rise in the 1980s made their father the patriarch of America's best-known jazz family. He taught the fundamentals without dogma, insisting that discipline was what made freedom possible, and he kept teaching at a point when his reputation could have taken him anywhere. Ellis Marsalis died in 2020, having shaped two generations of musicians from the piano bench.

cobham.blurb: Fusion's thunder, the drummer behind Spectrum.
cobham.bio: Billy Cobham, born in Panama in 1944, is a drummer and composer who gave jazz fusion both its power and its precision. He came to notice with Miles Davis around the turn of the 1970s, then joined the guitarist John McLaughlin in the Mahavishnu Orchestra, where his enormous kit and split-second control made odd metres land with the force of rock and roll. His 1973 album Spectrum is the fusion drummer's calling card: 'Quadrant 4' opens at a sprint, 'Red Baron' rides a slow funk backbeat, and 'Stratus' has been sampled so often, by Massive Attack among others, that its groove has outlived its genre. Thunderous and unusually musical with dynamics, he stands with Jack DeJohnette among the drummers who redrew the instrument's limits. Cobham has led bands and taught ever since, still the reference point for jazz played through amplifiers.

airto.blurb: Brazilian percussion that reshaped jazz fusion.
airto.bio: Airto Moreira, born in Brazil in 1941, is a percussionist, drummer and composer who changed the sound of jazz by bringing a whole cabinet of Brazilian instruments into it. He came to notice with the ensemble Quarteto Novo, later crossed to the United States and became the percussion voice of the fusion era, recording with Miles Davis and playing in Weather Report, Return to Forever and Santana. Under his own name the 1972 CTI album Free carried 'Return to Forever' and 'Flora's Song', the latter for the singer Flora Purim, his wife and lifelong collaborator, while 'Tombo in 7/4' from 1973 became one of the most sampled grooves in his catalogue. In his hands, hand percussion stopped being decoration and became a lead voice. Airto remains the model for percussionists who colour the music rather than merely keep time.

eckstine.bio: Billy Eckstine, born in 1914, was an American singer and bandleader with a bass-baritone so rich it was often called operatic. He sang with Earl Hines before forming his own orchestra in the 1940s, and that band became an incubator for bebop: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and the young Sarah Vaughan all passed through its ranks. As a solo star he sold romantic ballads to a mass audience, with 'Everything I Have Is Yours' in 1947, the 1948 hit 'I Apologize', later given a Grammy Hall of Fame award, and 'Caravan' in 1949. His suave, full-throated phrasing shaped a whole line of singers, Johnny Hartman and Joe Williams among them. A Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award came in 2019, long after his death in 1993 and long overdue.

glennmiller.blurb: One of swing's most popular bands.
glennmiller.bio: Glenn Miller, born in 1904, was an American trombonist, arranger and bandleader whose orchestra was among the most successful of the entire big band era. His signature was a sound rather than a soloist: a smooth, instantly recognisable ensemble blend, heard at its most seductive on 'Moonlight Serenade' in 1939, which became his theme. That same year 'In the Mood' turned swing into a national craze, and 'Chattanooga Choo Choo' followed in 1941. Where Benny Goodman and Tommy Dorsey built bands around their soloists, Miller built his on arrangement and polish. In wartime he set the civilian band aside for the US Army Air Forces, where he served as an officer. He died in 1944, at the height of his fame, and his sound has never left circulation.

dorsey.bio: Tommy Dorsey, born in 1905, was an American trombonist and bandleader, the Sentimental Gentleman of Swing, a nickname earned by the smooth, seemingly endless tone he drew from the horn. He played alongside his older brother Jimmy until the two split in the mid-1930s, then led one of America's most successful bands from the end of the 1930s into the 1950s. 'I'm Getting Sentimental Over You' became his theme in 1935, 'Marie' with the vocalist Jack Leonard was a hit in 1937, and 'Boogie Woogie' followed in 1938. His orchestra was a proving ground as much as a hit machine: Buddy Rich drove it from the drums and Frank Sinatra sang out front on 'This Love of Mine'. Among swing bandleaders only Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller rivalled him. Dorsey died in 1956.

eartha.blurb: The purring stylist behind Santa Baby.
eartha.bio: Eartha Kitt, born in 1927, was an American singer, actress and songwriter whose voice was unmistakable within a syllable: a purring, rolled-consonant drawl that could be playful and dangerous at the same moment. Nineteen fifty-three was her year, giving the world 'C'est Si Bon', the sly 'I Want to Be Evil' and 'Santa Baby', a Christmas novelty she turned into a small masterpiece of comic seduction that has never left the season. She worked as an actress and dancer as much as a singer, and carried the same theatrical precision into everything she did. Where peers such as Sarah Vaughan and Dinah Washington built their reputations on sheer vocal power, Kitt built hers on character, timing and nerve. She kept performing for more than half a century, and died in 2008.

dimeola.blurb: Fusion guitar speed with flamenco fire.
dimeola.bio: Al Di Meola, born in 1954, is an American guitarist who arrived fully formed, landing in Chick Corea's Return to Forever in 1974 and playing beside the bassist Stanley Clarke in fusion's most virtuosic band. From 1976 he ran a solo career of his own, opening with Land of the Midnight Sun and its headlong 'Egyptian Danza', then reaching a high-water mark on 1977's Elegant Gypsy, where 'Race with Devil on Spanish Highway' displayed the speed everybody talked about and 'Mediterranean Sundance', a duet with the flamenco master Paco de Lucia, displayed the musicianship they sometimes missed. That partnership widened into the acoustic trio with John McLaughlin captured on Friday Night in San Francisco. Latin and Mediterranean forms have shaped his writing ever since, through the World Sinfonia records. Few guitarists combine that much technique with that much appetite for other traditions.

klugh.blurb: Acoustic fingerstyle warmth in modern jazz.
klugh.bio: Earl Klugh, born in 1953, is an American guitarist and composer who built a career on the instrument most jazz players had set aside: the unamplified acoustic guitar, played fingerstyle. His self-titled 1976 debut opened with 'Angelina', a melody so lyrical it needed no solo to justify it, and the same year 'Living Inside Your Love' and 'Captain Caribe' set the pattern for everything that came after, warm, songful, rhythmically light and entirely unhurried. Wes Montgomery gave him his sense of melody, and George Benson, with whom he later recorded, gave him a model for reaching listeners well beyond the jazz audience. Critics filed him under crossover and smooth jazz; other players noticed the touch, which is immaculate. A Grammy Award and thirteen nominations followed. Klugh made the acoustic guitar a lead voice on his own quiet terms.

liebman.blurb: Soprano saxophone searcher and dedicated teacher.
liebman.bio: Dave Liebman, born in 1946, is an American saxophonist, flautist, composer and educator, and one of the leading soprano voices to emerge in the wake of John Coltrane. He learned on the bandstand in demanding company, playing with the drummer Elvin Jones, then joining Miles Davis in his electric years and turning up on On The Corner. Under his own name he made a run of records for ECM that revealed a searching, texture-minded bandleader: 'Pablo's Story' from 1974's Lookout Farm and 'Goli Dance' from Drum Ode the following year. He has since played on more than five hundred recordings, around two hundred of them as leader or co-leader. The NEA made him a Jazz Master in 2011. He set up the International Association of Schools of Jazz, and teaching has been as central to his life as playing.

tomscott.blurb: The studio saxophone of Los Angeles.
tomscott.bio: Tom Scott, born in 1948, is an American saxophonist, arranger and composer who spent his career where jazz meets the working music of Los Angeles. He led the jazz-funk group L.A. Express, whose 1974 album Tom Cat and its live favourite 'Sneakin' in the Back' became a sample source for later generations of producers, and he played in the Blues Brothers. Screen work took up much of his energy: 'Gotcha', his 1977 theme for Starsky and Hutch, put his horn into millions of living rooms every week. Alongside David Sanborn and Michael Brecker he defined the sound of the studio saxophone in that era, a tone bright enough to cut through a pop mix but rooted in real jazz phrasing. Few players have made so much music that listeners know without knowing whose it is.

sanborn.blurb: The crying alto tone everyone copied.
sanborn.bio: David Sanborn, born in 1945, was an American alto saxophonist whose crying, vocal tone became one of the most imitated sounds in popular music. He took up the horn at eleven and spent the 1970s as a first-call session player, appearing on records by Stevie Wonder, Aretha Franklin, James Brown and the Rolling Stones, and recording with the arranger Gil Evans. His own career began with Taking Off in 1975 and grew to more than twenty albums, among them 1980's Hideaway and the 1986 single 'Chicago Song', his most recognisable. Charlie Parker was the starting point, but Sanborn bent bebop phrasing towards rhythm and blues until the result belonged to nobody else, and six Grammy Awards followed. With Tom Scott he made the saxophone a lead pop instrument again. He died in 2024, his sound still everywhere.

evanparker.blurb: Solo saxophone as continuous, breathing invention.
evanparker.bio: Evan Parker, born in 1944, is a British saxophonist who took free improvisation further into the instrument itself than almost anyone. Starting from the example of late Coltrane, he built a solo soprano language out of unbroken breath and layered overtones, producing continuous streams of sound that seem to come from more than one player at once. 'Aerobatics 1' from the 1976 record Saxophone Solos and 'Monoceros 1', cut direct to disc in 1978, remain the clearest statements of that method. With the guitarist Derek Bailey he was central to the British free improvisation scene and the independent labels that carried it, and he has worked across Europe with players including Peter Brötzmann. Parker treats improvisation as a discipline rather than a gesture, spontaneous but rigorously worked, and his solo records are now standard listening.

bailey.blurb: Guitar remade as pure free improvisation.
bailey.bio: Derek Bailey, born in 1930, was an English guitarist and the defining figure of free improvisation. He set aside the conventional vocabulary of jazz guitar entirely, working instead with atonality, noise and whatever unlikely sounds the instrument could be persuaded to make, so that a Bailey solo sounds less like playing than like thinking aloud. 'Where Is the Police?' and 'Christiani Eddy', both from the 1971 Solo Guitar Vol. 1, laid out the approach in full. He built his own institutions to house the music, releasing much of it on his Incus label and working inside collectives such as Company and the Spontaneous Music Ensemble, and he improvised with everyone from Evan Parker to John Zorn. His influence reached far beyond the free scene, Bill Frisell being among the guitarists who absorbed it. Bailey played on his own uncompromising terms until his death in 2005.

brotzmann.blurb: European free jazz at maximum intensity.
brotzmann.bio: Peter Brötzmann, born in 1941, was a German saxophonist and clarinettist who gave European free jazz its ferocity. His 1968 octet recording Machine Gun is the landmark: a wall of overblown horns taken at a volume and density nobody had risked before, with 'Responsible', dedicated to Jan van de Ven, alongside it on the record. Albert Ayler showed him that raw sound could carry feeling, and like Archie Shepp in America he pushed the music towards protest as much as art. He released more than fifty albums as a leader and improvised with Derek Bailey, Evan Parker, Anthony Braxton, Cecil Taylor and, later, musicians from noise and rock such as Keiji Haino. His tone was enormous, unmistakable and never merely loud. Brötzmann worked at that intensity until shortly before his death in 2023.

viviangarry.blurb: Bebop bassist who led her own quintet.
viviangarry.bio: Vivian Garry, born in 1920, was an American bassist and bandleader at a time when both roles were all but closed to women. She led her own quintet and trio through the bebop years, working from the bass chair rather than out front, which made her one of the very few women of the era shaping a band's rhythm section from the inside. In 1946 her quintet cut sides for RCA Victor, among them the standard 'Body and Soul' and a title that made the point with a wink, 'A Woman's Place Is in the Groove'. She worked in the same scene as the pianist and arranger Mary Lou Williams and the bassist Oscar Pettiford, and those recordings survive as evidence of a career jazz history has been slow to account for. Garry died in 2008.

nancywilson.blurb: The song stylist with the honeyed voice.
nancywilson.bio: Nancy Wilson, born in 1937, was an American singer active from the mid-1950s until she stepped away in the early 2010s, and her work took in jazz, blues, rhythm and blues, pop and soul. She rejected all those labels for one of her own, song stylist, a phrase that captures how she worked, shaping a lyric like an actress rather than showing off her range. Her 1960 reading of 'Guess Who I Saw Today' became definitive, her 1962 collaboration with Cannonball Adderley produced 'Save Your Love for Me', and '(You Don't Know) How Glad I Am' in 1964 gave her the biggest hit of her life. More than seventy albums and three Grammy Awards came of it. Her name belongs with those of Dinah Washington and Carmen McRae among singers who made phrasing the whole point. Wilson died in 2018.

nomalice.blurb: Clipse co-founder who found faith and returned.
nomalice.bio: No Malice, born Gene Elliott Thornton Jr. in 1972, is an American MC out of Virginia Beach, Virginia, and one half of the duo Clipse alongside his younger brother Pusha T. Rapping as Malice he built a reputation for cold, meticulous storytelling, heard at its sharpest on 'Nightmares' from the 2006 album 'Hell Hath No Fury'. A change of faith then reshaped the work, and he re-emerged under the name No Malice with the 2013 solo debut 'Hear Ye Him', with 'Let the Dead Bury the Dead' arriving in 2017. The turn cost him none of his precision; it simply pointed it somewhere new. In 2025 the brothers reunited as Clipse, with 'Chains & Whips' featuring Kendrick Lamar. His career traces one of hip hop's most unusual arcs, from street reportage to conscience without ever loosening the craft.

blu.blurb: Los Angeles MC behind Below the Heavens.
blu.bio: Blu, born Johnson Barnes III in 1983, is a Los Angeles rapper who produces as well as raps. He introduced himself in 2007 as one half of Blu & Exile, whose debut 'Below the Heavens' arrived that July and became a touchstone for a generation of underground listeners: warm, dusty soul loops beneath writing that was searching and unguarded. 'Dancing in the Rain', 'So(ul) Amazin' (Steel Blazin')' and 'The Narrow Path' all come from that record. He is the leading figure in the California collective Dirty Science and has built an unusually prolific catalogue of collaborative albums with producers including Mainframe, Ta'Raach, Bombay, Damu the Fudgemunk, Madlib, Nottz and Union Analogtronics. The influence of J Dilla and Madlib runs through both his rapping and his own beats, and few of his peers have released as much, as restlessly.

kota.blurb: Independent Brooklyn rapper of warm, self-produced records.
kota.bio: Kota the Friend, born Avery Marcel Joshua Jones in 1992, is an American rapper, singer and producer raised in Brooklyn, New York. He took the name from the Disney film Brother Bear, understanding it as a Native American word for friend, and the warmth in it suits the music: unhurried, largely self-produced records about family, city life and staying level. 'Colorado', released in 2018, was the song that carried him beyond New York, and 'Alkaline' followed in 2019 on the album FOTO. He has stayed independent, handling much of the production himself and keeping his catalogue in his own hands. The rhythmic ease of Joey Bada$$ and the soft, off-kilter drum feel J Dilla left behind both shape his sound, and he has become one of the more quietly durable voices in contemporary Brooklyn hip hop.

feloni.blurb: Detroit MC, first out lesbian rap album.
feloni.bio: Feloni, born Trish Best, is an American rapper from Detroit, Michigan. She arrived with the single 'Brand New' in 2005 and followed it in 2007 with 'A Woman's Revenge', the first album by an out lesbian rapper, a record that made her sexuality part of the work rather than a footnote to it at a moment when hip hop offered almost no room for that. Her coming out was later featured on the LOGO documentary series Coming Out Stories, carried by MTV, which took her story far outside Detroit rap circles. She built a career without major-label backing and without softening what she said. Feloni matters to this map less for chart position than for the door she pushed open, and for the queer rappers who have come through it since.

koolherc.blurb: The Bronx DJ who invented the breakbeat.
koolherc.bio: DJ Kool Herc, born Clive Campbell in 1955, is a Jamaican-American DJ widely called the father of hip hop. At a Bronx party in 1973 he did something simple and consequential: he isolated the instrumental stretch of a hard funk record, the break, and used two copies of the same disc to hold it open, cutting from one break to the next so the dancers never had to stop. That technique, breakbeat DJing, is the foundation the whole music sits on. His shouted encouragements to the floor, extended by his partner Coke La Rock, pointed straight toward rapping. Alongside Afrika Bambaataa, Grandmaster Flash, Pete DJ Jones, DJ Hollywood and Busy Bee Starski he built the Bronx DJ scene, and b-boys such as Crazy Legs grew up inside the space his breaks created. Almost everything downstream begins there.

cokelarock.blurb: Often called the first MC in hip hop.
cokelarock.bio: Coke La Rock, born in 1955, is an American MC out of New York City, often credited as the first MC in hip hop. He was the voice at DJ Kool Herc's earliest Bronx parties in 1973, working the microphone over Herc's extended breaks with shout-outs, catchphrases and rhythmic asides addressed straight to the people on the floor. None of it was conceived as a record; it was crowd control and showmanship, and it became the template for rapping. Because those parties were never pressed to vinyl, his contribution survives mostly in the memory of the people who were there and in the practice everyone who followed inherited. Amsterdam's High Times Counterculture Hall of Fame took him in during 2010, a rare piece of formal recognition. He remains the quiet answer to the question of who spoke first.

afrikabambaataa.blurb: Electro pioneer who took hip hop electronic.
afrikabambaataa.bio: Afrika Bambaataa, born Lance Taylor in 1957, was an American DJ, record producer and rapper, and one of the originators of breakbeat DJing. Where his peers DJ Kool Herc and Grandmaster Flash worked funk breaks for the dancers, Bambaataa pushed the music toward the machines, and the records he cut in the early 1980s with the Soulsonic Force redrew the map: 'Planet Rock' in 1982, then 'Looking for the Perfect Beat' and 'Renegades of Funk' in 1983. Drum machines and synthesizers laid over Bronx party rhythm, they defined electro and carried hip hop into electronic dance music. He ran with Fab 5 Freddy and with Kool DJ Red Alert, and his influence is plain in Mantronix and the Jungle Brothers. He died in 2026, leaving one of the widest-reaching legacies the music has.

grandmasterflash.bio: Grandmaster Flash, born Joseph Robert Saddler in 1958, is a Barbadian-American DJ who turned the turntable into an instrument. His Quick Mix Theory used duplicate copies of a record to extend a drum break precisely and on cue, giving b-boys a bed to dance on and MCs a seamless one to rhyme over; cutting and scratching came out of it, and he invented the slipmat that makes it possible. 'The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel' in 1981 put live turntable technique on record for the first time. With the Furious Five, the group he founded, he made 'The Message' in 1982, and 'White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)' followed in 1983 billed to Grandmaster and Melle Mel. His lineage runs from Pete DJ Jones through Grand Wizzard Theodore to DJ Jazzy Jeff and every turntablist since.

grandwizzardtheodore.blurb: The Bronx DJ who invented scratching.
grandwizzardtheodore.bio: Grand Wizzard Theodore, born Theodore Livingston in 1963, is an American DJ widely credited with inventing the scratch. As a teenager in the Bronx, moving in the orbit of Grandmaster Flash, he found that dragging a record back and forth beneath the needle produced a sound of its own rather than a mistake, and he built a vocabulary out of it. He is known too for mastering the needle drop, landing the stylus exactly on the start of a break without cueing, and for a handful of other techniques he either invented or perfected. His playing reached a wide audience through the 1983 film Wild Style, where 'Subway Theme' and 'Military Cut - Scratch Mix', the latter with Kevie Kev Rockwell, sit on the soundtrack. Every turntablist since has been working in the language he opened up.

mellemel.bio: Melle Mel, born Melvin Glover in 1961, is an American rapper, the lead voice and chief songwriter of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five. He is the reason 'The Message' exists as it does: released in 1982, it took rap off the party floor and pointed it at the conditions outside the door, and his delivery, weighty and deliberate, gave those words the authority they needed. 'White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)' followed in 1983, billed to Grandmaster and Melle Mel, and 'Beat Street Breakdown' came in 1984 from the film Beat Street. He came up beside his crewmate Cowboy, and the technical command of his writing fed directly into Rakim and the more intricate rapping of the decade that followed. He remains the first great writer this music produced.

furiousfive.blurb: The crew that made rap tell the truth.
furiousfive.bio: The Furious Five, an American crew out of the South Bronx, formed in 1978 and ran until 1988, and they turned party rapping into something closer to reportage. Working with Grandmaster Flash, the line-up gathered Melle Mel, Kidd Creole, Keef Cowboy, Scorpio and Rahiem, five MCs trading and stacking lines over his turntable work. Early singles Superrappin' in 1979 for Enjoy Records and 'Freedom' in 1980, their first for Sylvia Robinson at Sugar Hill, showed how much a group could do with routines and vocal interplay. Then came 'The Message' in 1982, still the record most often named when people ask when rap began telling the truth about where it came from. Their rivalry with the Cold Crush Brothers sharpened both crews. Nearly every group format in hip hop descends from theirs.

keithcowboy.blurb: Furious Five MC who named hip-hop.
keithcowboy.bio: Cowboy, born Robert Keith Wiggins in 1960, was an American MC, one of the five voices Grandmaster Flash gathered around him in the Furious Five, and the man most often credited with inventing the term hip-hop itself: a scrap of chanted nonsense that ended up naming an entire culture. On stage he was the crowd's man, the hype man in the original sense, the one whose job was to lift a room and then keep it lifted, and much of what a live rap show still does was worked out by him. He appears on Superrappin' in 1979, 'Freedom' in 1980 and 'The Message' in 1982, trading lines alongside his crewmate Melle Mel, and he ran as a peer of Lovebug Starski. He died in 1989, with the music he had named still young.

sugarhillgang.blurb: Rapper's Delight took rap to the world.
sugarhillgang.bio: The Sugarhill Gang, an old-school American trio, came together in Englewood, New Jersey, in 1979 and were launched by Sylvia Robinson through her Sugar Hill Records. 'Rapper's Delight', cut that same year, put rap on the radio for good: it was the first rap single to reach the US Top 40, peaking at number 36 in January 1980. It also stayed their only American hit, though Europe kept taking them in until the middle of the 1980s. '8th Wonder' followed in 1980 and 'Apache' in 1981, built on the same loose, conversational trading of verses. The trio reformed in 1994 and were still touring the world in 2016, decades after the fact. Labelmates and peers of the Sequence, they are the group that proved a rap record could sell.

sylviarobinson.blurb: Sugar Hill founder who put rap on record.
sylviarobinson.bio: Sylvia Robinson, born in 1936, was an American singer, songwriter, producer and label executive, the businesswoman who first put rap on record. She had two careers before that: half of Mickey and Sylvia, whose 'Love Is Strange' arrived in 1956, and a solo artist with 'Pillow Talk' in 1973, a hit that helped fund what came next. As founder and chief executive of Sugar Hill Records she assembled and released the Sugarhill Gang, then produced the Furious Five, the Sequence and Funky 4 + 1. Her instinct that party rapping could be sold as a single changed the economics of the entire music, and her willingness to release women MCs shaped who got heard in the first place. She died in 2011, the most consequential executive of hip hop's first decade.

grandmastercaz.blurb: Cold Crush writer of Rapper's Delight, uncredited.
grandmastercaz.bio: Grandmaster Caz, born Curtis Brown in 1959 and also known as Casanova Fly, is an American MC, DJ and songwriter, and one of the finest writers of the Bronx park-jam era. He joined the Cold Crush Brothers in 1979 and stayed into the mid-1980s, in a crew celebrated for elaborate group routines. He is also hip hop's most famous uncredited author: much of Big Bank Hank's verse on the Sugarhill Gang's 'Rapper's Delight' in 1979 came out of his rhyme book, and he received neither royalties nor a credit for the record that took rap worldwide. His own singles arrived later on Tuff City, among them 'Yvette' in 1985 and 'Get Down Grandmaster' in 1987. His standing among his peers has never depended on chart returns.

coldcrush.blurb: Bronx crew of legendary live routines.
coldcrush.bio: The Cold Crush Brothers, an American crew, came together in the Bronx in 1978 and are among the most admired live crews of hip hop's formative years. Built around the writing of Grandmaster Caz, they were known for tightly drilled group routines and a stage presence that made a park jam feel like a proper show. Their rivalry with the Furious Five is the era's defining crew battle, fought in halls and on cassettes that circulated hand to hand long before either group had much on vinyl, and it is a large part of why both are remembered. Records came late and sparingly: 'Punk Rock Rap' in 1983, an early collision of rap and rock, and 'Fresh, Wild, Fly and Bold' in 1984, the single they are best remembered for. Their reputation rests on performance rather than pressings.

djhollywood.blurb: Club DJ credited among the first rappers.
djhollywood.bio: DJ Hollywood, born in 1954, is an American DJ and MC credited as one of the first people ever to rap. His reputation was made live, in clubs and large rooms rather than on record, talking in rhythm over the discs he played with a polish and crowd-handling ease that owed as much to the disco tradition as to the block party. Where DJ Kool Herc's parties gave the music its breaks, Hollywood supplied much of its microphone style: the call and response, the rhymed introductions, the running commentary that turns a DJ set into a performance. He and his peer Lovebug Starski were the great live MCs of the late 1970s, and Hollywood is named among the possible originators of rapping as a form. 'Shock, Shock the House' in 1980 stands as his signature recording.

lovebugstarski.blurb: Disco Fever DJ who may have named hip-hop.
lovebugstarski.bio: Lovebug Starski, born Kevin Smith in 1960, was an American DJ, MC and record producer who came up with the music itself. He started as a record boy in 1971, just as hip hop was surfacing in the Bronx, and by 1978 was the DJ at Disco Fever, the club that did more than any other to carry the sound from the parks into nightlife. Two men have a claim on coining the phrase hip-hop and he is one of them, by his own account improvising the syllables back and forth with Keef Cowboy of the Furious Five at a send-off for a friend about to join the army. As a recording artist he made 'Positive Life' with the Harlem World Crew in 1981, 'You've Gotta Believe' in 1983 and 'Amityville (House on the Hill)' in 1986. He died in 2018.

sharock.blurb: The first woman to rap, Mother of the Mic.
sharock.bio: Sha-Rock, born Sharon Green in 1962, is an American MC generally recognised as the first woman to rap, and known within hip hop as the Mother of the Mic. Born in Wilmington, North Carolina and raised in the South Bronx, she grew up inside the culture as it was forming and joined Funky 4 + 1 as the plus one, the crew's only woman and its most distinctive voice. With them she made 'Rappin and Rocking the House' in 1979 and 'That's the Joint' in 1980, and appeared on national television at a moment when scarcely any rapper had. Her phrasing, confident and unhurried and never asking permission, fed directly into Roxanne Shante and MC Lyte, and into DMC of Run-DMC. Every woman with a microphone in this music stands somewhere behind her.

funky4.blurb: First crew with a woman MC.
funky4.bio: Funky 4 + 1 were an American crew out of the Bronx, formed in 1979 around K.K. Rockwell, Keith Caesar, Rahiem and Sha-Rock, with Jazzy Jeff, DJ Breakout, Guy Williams, Keith Keith, The Voice of K.K. and Rodney Cee passing through the line-up. The plus one was Sha-Rock, and they were the first crew to carry a woman MC. They collected a remarkable run of firsts besides: the first hip-hop group to sign a record deal, the first to sell their records commercially, and the first to appear live on national television. Sylvia Robinson produced them, and 'Rappin and Rocking the House' arrived in 1979, followed by 'That's the Joint' in 1980, a sprawling, joyful record that still shows how a five-voice routine was supposed to sound. Two members later worked on as the duo Double Trouble.

kurtisblow.blurb: First rapper signed to a major label.
kurtisblow.bio: Kurtis Blow, born Kurtis Walker in 1959, is an American MC, songwriter and producer, and the first rapper to be commercially successful on his own terms. He was the first MC signed to a major label, and 'The Breaks', from his 1980 debut album, became the first rap single certified gold, proof to a sceptical industry that this was a business rather than a novelty. Christmas Rappin' had come the year before, and 'Basketball' in 1984 gave him another standard. Across his career he released seventeen albums and worked as a producer, opening doors for younger artists; Run-DMC in particular came up in his slipstream. A peer of Grandmaster Flash and Whodini, he is now an ordained minister and leads the Hip Hop Alliance, still arguing for the people who make this music.

spooniegee.blurb: Smooth 1970s MC who foreshadowed gangsta rap.
spooniegee.bio: Spoonie Gee, born Gabriel Jackson in 1963, is an American MC and one of very few rappers with records out in the 1970s. Spoonin' Rap, released in 1979, is his signature: a long, easy, first-person tale delivered in a smooth conversational drawl, and the street themes in it, told without moralising, ran ahead of what would later be called gangsta rap by the better part of a decade. 'Love Rap' followed in 1980, a record he shared with the Treacherous Three, the crew he worked alongside through those years. 'The Godfather' came in 1987, a nickname the scene had already given him. He is among those credited with coining the term hip hop. For a rapper with a small discography, his fingerprints on the music's voice and subject matter run unusually deep.

treacherousthree.blurb: The crew that made rapping fast and technical.
treacherousthree.bio: The Treacherous Three were an American hip-hop group formed in 1978, made up of Kool Moe Dee, L.A. Sunshine, Special K and Spoonie Gee with DJ Easy Lee, and joined at times by DJ Dano B, DJ Reggie Reg and DJ Crazy Eddie. They reached vinyl in 1980 with 'The New Rap Language', tucked onto the B-side of Spoonie Gee's 'Love Rap', and quickly became the crew that pushed rapping toward speed and complexity: interlocking verses, rapid-fire delivery and a technical bar other MCs then had to meet. 'Feel the Heartbeat' in 1981 is their best-known record and reached a wide audience through the film Style Wars. 'Yes We Can-Can' followed in 1982. Kool Moe Dee's solo run began here, and the group's appetite for difficulty shaped rapping for a decade.

koolmoedee.blurb: Battle-hardened MC of How Ya Like Me Now.
koolmoedee.bio: Kool Moe Dee, born Mohandas Dewese in 1962, is an American rapper, songwriter and actor who came up in the Treacherous Three and then made himself one of the defining solo MCs of the late 1980s. He is remembered first for technique: fast, clipped and precise, hardened in a celebrated rivalry with Busy Bee Starski that helped set the standard for how MCs test one another. 'Go See the Doctor' in 1986 was a hit built on nerve, 'How Ya Like Me Now' in 1987 gave his platinum album its title and its swagger, and 'Wild Wild West' in 1988 became his biggest chart record. He is considered one of the forerunners of hip hop's new jack swing sound, and his long public feud with LL Cool J was the era's great rap rivalry. Seven albums, the last in 1994.

busybee.blurb: Old-school party MC and battle legend.
busybee.bio: Busy Bee Starski, born David James Parker in 1962, is an American old-school MC and one of the great crowd-movers of the early New York party scene. He appeared on that scene in 1977 and worked with much of the founding generation, among them Melle Mel, Disco King Mario, Afrika Bambaataa and Kool DJ AJ. His gift was the room rather than the record: call and response, catchphrases, a party audible in the voice, the sort of MCing DJ Kool Herc's dances had called into being. That approach was put to the test in his famous rivalry with Kool Moe Dee, a clash that changed what a rap battle was expected to sound like and is still argued over. On vinyl he made 'Making Cash Money' for Sugar Hill in 1981 and 'Suicide' in 1987.

thesequence.blurb: First women to score a rap hit.
thesequence.bio: The Sequence were an American hip-hop trio formed in Columbia, South Carolina, in 1979, made up of Angie B., Blondy and Cheryl the Pearl. Signed and produced by Sylvia Robinson for Sugar Hill Records, they cut 'Funk You Up' that same year: no women had landed a rap hit before them, and few singles of any kind in this young music sold as well. Their 1980 debut album, Sugar Hill Presents The Sequence, was the first time an all-female act put hip hop on vinyl. 'Funky Sound (Tear the Roof Off)' followed in 1981 and 'I Don't Need Your Love (Part One)' in 1982. Labelmates and peers of the Sugarhill Gang, they came from outside New York entirely, and they proved from the very beginning that this was never going to be only a men's form.

fab5freddy.blurb: Bridge between graffiti, rap and the art world.
fab5freddy.bio: Fab 5 Freddy, born Fred Brathwaite in 1959, is an American visual artist, filmmaker and broadcaster, and one of the true architects of hip hop as a culture rather than only a music. He emerged from the late 1970s New York graffiti scene and became the bridge between the uptown rap world and the downtown No Wave art crowd, moving freely between two rooms that barely acknowledged each other; the street art movement as now understood was built partly by him. Blondie name-checked him on 'Rapture' in 1981, which put him in front of the pop audience. As a recording artist he made 'Change the Beat' in 1982, its female version credited to Beside and a French counterpart titled 'Une Sale Histoire', among the most sampled records ever cut. He was the first host of Yo! MTV Raps, and published a memoir in 2026.

crazylegs.blurb: Rock Steady b-boy who took breaking global.
crazylegs.bio: Crazy Legs, born Richard Colon in 1966, is an American b-boy and president of the Rock Steady Crew, the dancer who did most to carry breaking beyond the Bronx. He was at the centre of the earliest stories about hip hop dancing to appear in the mainstream press, and in 1983 he took the form to London and Paris, turning a local street dance into something with an audience across Europe. That same year he appeared in Wild Style, the film that showed the whole culture, dancing included, to people who had only read about it. The dance itself grew out of the extended breaks DJ Kool Herc played for exactly this purpose, and Crazy Legs came up alongside Fab 5 Freddy. He now teaches dance, stages theatre work, keeps up community programmes, and still leads Rock Steady.

djredalert.blurb: New York radio DJ and hip hop tastemaker.
djredalert.bio: Kool DJ Red Alert, born Frederick Crute in 1956, is an Antiguan-American disc jockey and one of the acknowledged founding fathers of hip hop culture. His authority came from radio: the show he built in New York on WRKS 98.7 Kiss FM made him one of the voices that decided what the city heard, at a point when a record's life depended on a DJ deciding it was worth playing. He ran in Afrika Bambaataa's circle, and his mixes carried the Bronx sound to listeners who would never make it to a park jam. He recorded 'We Can Do This' in 1989. Decades on he is still on air, broadcasting six evenings a week on WBLS 107.5 FM, which makes him one of the longest-serving voices the culture has produced.

mantronix.blurb: Electro-funk duo who mechanised the beat.
mantronix.bio: Mantronix were an American hip-hop and electro-funk group formed in New York City in 1984 by the producer and DJ Kurtis Mantronik and the rapper MC Tee. Mantronik's productions were startlingly clean and mechanical for their moment, all snapping drum machines, elastic synthetic bass and hard edits, and they pushed old-school hip hop into direct conversation with electronic and club music. 'Needle to the Groove' and 'Bassline' both come from the 1985 debut The Album, first of the five they released. Line-ups and styles shifted repeatedly across a seven-year run that ended in 1991, moving toward house and dance-pop; 'Got to Have Your Love', featuring Wondress, became their signature hit in 1990. They took Afrika Bambaataa's electro further into the machine age, and the way producers still build a hip hop track owes them a great deal.

whodini.blurb: Brooklyn trio who made rap sing.
whodini.bio: Whodini came together in Brooklyn in 1982: Jalil Hutchins wrote and sang lead, John Fletcher, who performed as Ecstasy, took the second voice, and Drew Carter, better known as Grandmaster Dee, handled the turntables. They arrived in hip hop's foundation era, when the music was moving from park jams and cassettes onto records that could travel. Their run of 1984 sides put melody and songcraft at the centre of rap: 'Freaks Come Out at Night' remains their signature, and 'Five Minutes of Funk' and 'Friends' gave the group hooks a listener could carry home. Working alongside peers such as Kurtis Blow, Whodini helped show that a rap record could be shaped like a pop record without losing its street footing. Their sound stayed warm, danceable and unmistakably New York, and it still marks them as one of the era's most quietly influential groups.

petedjjones.blurb: Mobile DJ who taught the founders.
petedjjones.bio: Pete DJ Jones, who died in 2022, was an American DJ of hip hop's foundation era, known for the mobile sets he ran through the 1970s. A peer of DJ Kool Herc on New York's early circuit, he was an influence on Grandmaster Flash, carrying sound-system craft into the music's first generation.

rundmc.blurb: The Queens trio who took rap mainstream.
rundmc.bio: Run-DMC formed in Hollis, Queens, in 1983 around Joseph Simmons, Darryl McDaniels and Jason Mizell, the DJ known as Jam Master Jay. Managed and guided by Russell Simmons and produced by Rick Rubin, they stripped rap back to hard drums, guitar and two voices trading lines, and in doing so pioneered new-school hip hop and helped usher in the golden age. Their debut single 'It's Like That' arrived in 1983; 'Walk This Way', the 1986 collision with Aerosmith, carried rap onto rock radio and into living rooms that had never heard it, while 'It's Tricky' the same year showed how much fun the formula could be. They were among the first to make the MC and DJ partnership a public act rather than a backroom one. Peers of the Beastie Boys, Public Enemy, Heavy D and DJ Jazzy Jeff, they connect directly back to Kurtis Blow.

jammasterjay.bio: Jason Mizell, born in 1965 and known everywhere as Jam Master Jay, was the DJ of Run-DMC and one of the musicians who made the turntable a lead instrument rather than a support act. As Run-DMC became one of the biggest groups of the 1980s and pushed hip hop into the mainstream, Jay's cuts were its spine. 'Peter Piper' from 1986 is the landmark showcase of his hands, and the group thought enough of him to name a 1984 track 'Jam Master Jay' in his honour. He also worked as a producer, and as a mentor he gave an early platform to the young 50 Cent. He stood among peers like DJ Jazzy Jeff who were turning DJing into a headline craft. Mizell died in 2002; seven years later, in 2009, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted him with Run-DMC.

llcoolj.bio: James Todd Smith, born in 1968 and known as LL Cool J, is one of the first rappers to turn crossover success into a career rather than a moment. Signed as a teenager, he was guided by Russell Simmons and produced by Rick Rubin, whose stripped-down drums suited a voice built for boasting. 'Rock the Bells' in 1985 announced a teenager with more force than anyone his age had shown; 'I Need Love' two years later proved rap could carry a ballad without embarrassment; and 'Mama Said Knock You Out' in 1990 answered everyone who had written him off. His long-running rivalry with Kool Moe Dee sharpened both men and gave the golden age one of its defining battles. Alongside acts like Run-DMC he made the new school commercially undeniable, and he has since built a parallel life as an actor and producer.

beastieboys.blurb: Punks who became restless hip-hop innovators.
beastieboys.bio: The Beastie Boys formed in New York City in 1981, a group that began in hardcore punk and ended up remaking hip hop: Adam Horovitz (Ad-Rock), Adam Yauch (MCA) and Michael Diamond (Mike D). Guided by Russell Simmons and produced by Rick Rubin, they broke through in 1986 with the bratty rap-rock of '(You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!)' and 'No Sleep Till Brooklyn', records that shared the guitar-and-drums logic their peers Run-DMC were pushing. But the joke act refused to stay one. By 1994 they were playing their own instruments and cutting 'Sabotage', a snarl of fuzz bass and shouted vocals that belonged as much to punk as to rap. Restless, funny and endlessly curious, they spent three decades widening what a hip-hop group was allowed to be.

rickrubin.blurb: The producer who built Def Jam.
rickrubin.bio: Rick Rubin, born in 1963, is an American record producer whose ear shaped the sound of hip hop's golden age and a great deal of what followed. With Russell Simmons he co-founded Def Jam Recordings, and the label's first release, T La Rock's 'It's Yours' in 1984, already carried his signature: enormous drums, almost nothing else, and total confidence in the voice on top. He produced LL Cool J, the Beastie Boys and Public Enemy, and in 1986 he produced Run-DMC's 'Walk This Way', the record that carried rap onto rock radio. That same year the Beastie Boys' '(You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!)' proved the formula could sell to anyone. He later founded American Recordings and served as co-president of Columbia Records, working across rock, metal and country with the same instinct for stripping a song to its bones.

russellsimmons.blurb: The mogul who made rap an industry.
russellsimmons.bio: Russell Simmons, born in 1957, is the entrepreneur and record executive who turned hip hop from a scene into an industry. He managed Run-DMC through their 1983 debut single 'It's Like That' and co-founded Def Jam Recordings with Rick Rubin, serving as executive on early releases including T La Rock's 'It's Yours' in 1984. The artists who came up under his guidance, among them Run-DMC, LL Cool J and the Beastie Boys, became the commercial spine of the golden age, and his instinct was to sell rap as itself rather than dress it up for other audiences. Beyond music he built the clothing lines Phat Farm, Argyleculture and Tantris, produced television, and wrote books on health, lifestyle and entrepreneurship. More than any single record, his legacy is the business architecture that let hip hop scale.

rakim.blurb: The MC who rewrote rap's rhythm.
rakim.bio: William Michael Griffin Jr., born in 1968 and known as Rakim, changed how rappers use rhythm. As one half of Eric B. & Rakim, he made 'Paid in Full' in 1987 the calling card of a new kind of MC: calm, unhurried, laying multisyllabic rhymes across the beat instead of riding on top of it. 'I Ain't No Joke' from the same year and 'Microphone Fiend' from 1988's Follow the Leader show a writer thinking in internal rhyme and shifting cadence while everyone else was still counting bars.
