He took cues from Melle Mel, traded verses with Kool G Rap, and stood alongside peers such as EPMD and the Ultramagnetic MCs. His influence on Nas, and through Nas on almost everyone after, is one of the clearest lines in the music. Solo albums followed across the decades, but the golden-age work remains the standard.

ericb.blurb: The DJ half of a perfect duo.
ericb.bio: Louis Eric Barrier, born in 1963 and known as Eric B., is a New York DJ and producer who formed one half of hip hop's most admired duo. He put Eric B. & Rakim together in 1986, taking on both the production and the DJing, building the tracks that Rakim's voice would make legendary. Their debut single 'Eric B. Is President', released that year, set the template: hard, spare, and built on soul records dug up and turned into rhythm. 'I Know You Got Soul' and 'Paid in Full' followed in 1987, the latter an album MTV would name the greatest in hip hop in 2006. In 2011 the pair earned a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame nomination. His work is a lesson in restraint: leave room, let the MC breathe, and let the break do the talking.

bigdaddykane.bio: Antonio Hardy, born in 1968 and known as Big Daddy Kane, started out in 1986 among the ranks of the Juice Crew and quickly became one of the most admired technicians in rap. Working with producer Marley Marl, he made speed sound effortless, switching from double-time flurries to a slow, seductive drawl without breaking stride. His 1988 single Ain't No Half-Steppin' is the performance most often cited, later ranked 25th by Rolling Stone among the fifty greatest hip-hop songs of all time. 'Set It Off' from the same year showed his hunger, and 'Smooth Operator' in 1989 showed the ladies-man persona that made him a star as much as a rapper. Kane brought showmanship, sharp suits and dance routines to a music still working out how to hold a stage, and a generation of MCs learned wordcraft from him.

koolgrap.blurb: Multisyllabic rhyme and mafioso street storytelling.
koolgrap.bio: Nathaniel Wilson, born in 1968 and known as Kool G Rap, is among the most influential MCs the music has produced. He surfaced in the mid-1980s, half of the duo Kool G Rap & DJ Polo and one of the Juice Crew, working with producer Marley Marl. With DJ Polo he made 'Road to the Riches' in 1989, 'Men at Work' the same year and 'Streets of New York' in 1990, records that built the vocabulary of mafioso rap and hardcore street storytelling. His multisyllabic rhyme schemes, dense and stacked, gave later writers a technical model to chase. He traded verses with Rakim, later worked with Jedi Mind Tricks, and his fingerprints are all over Nas. Long revered by rappers more than by radio, he remains a writers' writer, the MC other MCs quote when they want to settle an argument.

marleymarl.blurb: Queensbridge producer behind the Juice Crew.
marleymarl.bio: Marlon Williams, born in 1962 and known as Marley Marl, is the producer and DJ who gave the golden age much of its sound. He grew up in the Queensbridge houses in Queens and worked his way up through local talent shows as rap was finding its feet. Around him formed the Juice Crew, the collective he founded, and through it he produced Big Daddy Kane, Kool G Rap, Roxanne Shanté and MC Shan. 'The Bridge', his 1986 track with MC Shan, put Queensbridge on the map and set off one of rap's great rivalries; 'Eric B. Is President' came the same year; and in 1988 he gathered his crew for 'The Symphony', still the model for how a posse cut should be built. His drums and chopped soul made sampling a craft rather than a shortcut.

juicecrew.blurb: Queensbridge collective at the golden age's centre.
juicecrew.bio: The Juice Crew was a hip-hop collective drawn largely from Queensbridge, New York, and it stood at the centre of the golden age. Built around producer Marley Marl and radio DJ Mr. Magic, and housed by the Cold Chillin' label, it gathered a startling roster: Big Daddy Kane, Kool G Rap, MC Shan, Roxanne Shanté, Biz Markie, Masta Ace, Tragedy and Craig G. The crew specialised in answer records and thrived on argument, trading shots with Kool DJ Red Alert, a rival on the radio, and with the South Bronx's Boogie Down Productions in the rivalry that began with MC Shan's 'The Bridge' in 1986. In 1988 they turned that competitive energy inward on 'The Symphony', a posse cut in which each MC tries to outdo the last, and which remains the format's high-water mark.

mcshan.blurb: The voice at the Bridge Wars' centre.
mcshan.bio: Shawn Moltke, born in 1965 and known as MC Shan, is a rapper from the Queensbridge houses in Queens, New York. He started out in the early 1980s and found his moment in 1986 with 'The Bridge', produced by his Juice Crew colleague Marley Marl, a record that claimed Queensbridge as hip hop's home ground and reached the R&B and hip hop chart. KRS-One heard it as a challenge, and the exchange that followed became the Bridge Wars, the most quoted rivalry of the era. Shan answered with 'Kill That Noise' in 1987, the same year as 'Down by Law', the title track of his best-known album. He has also worked as a singer, songwriter and producer. Whatever the scoreboard on the feud, his early records fixed Queensbridge in hip hop's geography for good.

roxanneshante.bio: Lolita Shanté Gooden, born in 1969 and known as Roxanne Shanté, was still a teenager when she made herself one of rap's first great characters. In 1984 she recorded 'Roxanne's Revenge', an answer record cut with Marley Marl that set off the Roxanne Wars, a chain of responses that turned a local argument into a national event and proved a woman could hold the floor in a music dominated by men. She became part of the Juice Crew, following the trail Sha-Rock had opened and running alongside peers such as Salt-N-Pepa. 'Have a Nice Day' in 1987 and 'Go On Girl' in 1992 kept her sharp tongue in circulation. Her life was dramatised in the 2017 film Roxanne Roxanne, a reminder of how young she was and how much she changed.

bizmarkie.blurb: The Clown Prince of hip hop.
bizmarkie.bio: Marcel Hall, born in 1964 and known as Biz Markie, was the rapper, singer, beatboxer, DJ and producer who gave hip hop's golden age its sense of humour. A member of the Juice Crew, he built a persona out of warmth and self-deprecation and earned the nickname the Clown Prince of Hip-Hop. His 1986 record 'Make the Music with Your Mouth, Biz' showcased the beatboxing that first made his name, and 'Vapors' in 1988 told the story of friends who doubted him and then came around. Then came 'Just a Friend' in 1989, a song built on a gloriously off-key sung chorus that turned him into a household presence and has outlived almost everything around it. Biz died in 2021, remembered as a rapper who never needed to sound tough to be loved.

slickrick.bio: Ricky Walters, born in 1965 and known as Slick Rick, is a British-American rapper and producer based in New York, and hip hop's most quoted storyteller. He rose to prominence in the mid-1980s with Doug E. Fresh & the Get Fresh Crew, and the pair's 'La Di Da Di' in 1985, Rick's voice alone over Doug's beatbox, became an early classic and one of the most sampled recordings in music. His narrative gift peaked with 'Children's Story' in 1988, a bedtime tale that turns into a chase and a warning, told in character voices with perfect timing. 'Hey Young World' the following year showed the tenderness under the swagger. An English accent and a gift for character made him unmistakable, but it is the writing, patient and funny and cinematic, that later generations kept borrowing.

dougefresh.bio: Douglas Davis, born in Barbados in 1966 and known as Doug E. Fresh, is an American rapper, producer and beatboxer, and the pioneer of beatboxing in the United States. Billed as the Human Beat Box, he could reproduce drum machines and studio effects with nothing but a microphone and the working parts of his own mouth and throat, a party trick he turned into an instrument. With the Get Fresh Crew he cut 'The Show' in 1985, and its B-side 'La Di Da Di', where his beatbox carries Slick Rick alone for the length of a record, became one of hip hop's most borrowed pieces of music. 'Keep Risin' to the Top' followed in 1988. A performer first, he built a reputation on stagecraft and on the sheer improbability of the sounds he made, and every beatboxer since has worked in the space he opened.

krsone.bio: Lawrence Parker, born in 1965 and known as KRS-One or the Teacha, is a rapper from the Bronx. In the mid-1980s he formed Boogie Down Productions with DJ Scott La Rock, and their debut Criminal Minded announced a writer who argued as naturally as he rhymed. His answer to MC Shan's 'The Bridge', first 'South Bronx' in 1986 and then 'The Bridge Is Over' the following year, remains the sharpest volley in hip hop's most famous feud. La Rock was shot and killed soon after, and KRS-One carried the group on almost single-handedly, starting the Stop the Violence Movement in his friend's memory. 'My Philosophy' set out his thinking; from 1993 he recorded under his own name, and 'Sound of da Police' from that year became his best-known solo record. Politically restless and a longtime vegan activist, he has influenced generations of rappers.

bdp.blurb: Bronx group that fought the Bridge Wars.
bdp.bio: Boogie Down Productions formed in the Bronx in 1986, taking its name from a nickname for the South Bronx, and brought together KRS-One, D-Nice and DJ Scott La Rock. The group was built for argument. 'South Bronx', released that year, staked the Bronx's claim as hip hop's birthplace against all comers, and 'The Bridge Is Over' pressed the point in 1987 with a taunting delivery that gave no quarter. Their early records matched hard, funny street writing to La Rock's spare production. Then, on 27 August 1987, Scott La Rock was murdered, and BDP continued effectively as a vehicle for KRS-One alone. 'My Philosophy' in 1988 marked the turn towards teaching and politics that would define the rest of his work. Few groups have done more with so short a first act.

scottlarock.blurb: BDP's founding DJ, lost too early.
scottlarock.bio: Scott Sterling, born in 1962 and known as DJ Scott La Rock, was a hip-hop DJ and producer from the Bronx and a founding member of Boogie Down Productions. He worked as a social worker as well as a musician, a detail that says something about the world the early Bronx scene came out of. As DJ and producer he shaped BDP's first records: 'South Bronx' in 1986, the opening shot in the Bridge Wars, and in 1987 'The Bridge Is Over' and '9mm Goes Bang', which set the group's spare, menacing sound. He was murdered in 1987, still in his mid-twenties and only months after those records. KRS-One, his partner in the group, carried the work forward in his name. What survives is a producer's instinct for leaving space, and a body of work almost everyone agrees was only a beginning.

publicenemy.bio: Public Enemy formed in Roosevelt, New York, in 1985 around Chuck D and Flavor Flav, and turned hip hop into a vehicle for argument about American racism and the American media. Behind them the Bomb Squad built a dense, sirens-and-noise production style unlike anything else on record, with Rick Rubin among the producers who backed them. 'Bring the Noise' arrived in 1987, and the following year 'Don't Believe the Hype' anchored It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back, which became the first rap album ever to win the Village Voice critics' poll. 'Fight the Power', written for Do the Right Thing in 1989, became the era's anthem. Fear of a Black Planet and Apocalypse 91 followed, and the group has kept recording for decades since. Peers of Run-DMC, they made political rap loud enough that later artists such as Immortal Technique had somewhere to stand.

chuckd.blurb: The booming voice of political rap.
chuckd.bio: Carlton Ridenhour, born in 1960 and known as Chuck D, leads and fronts Public Enemy, the group he started with Flavor Flav in 1985. His voice is the group's foundation: a deep, declamatory boom that sounds less like a rapper than a man addressing a crowd, and it made political rap sound authoritative rather than pleading. 'Rebel Without a Pause' in 1987 introduced that voice against a shrieking loop; 'Bring the Noise' the same year made an argument out of volume itself; and in 1989 'Fight the Power' gave a generation its slogan. He has also worked as a radio personality and a writer, joined the rock supergroup Prophets of Rage, and released solo albums, most notably 'Autobiography of Mistachuck' in 1996. Few rappers have taken the responsibility of the microphone as seriously.

flavorflav.bio: William Drayton Jr., born in 1959 and known as Flavor Flav, is the founding member who, alongside Chuck D, made Public Enemy work. He invented the modern hype man as a role rather than an accessory: the clock round his neck, the interruptions, the comic energy that cut through Chuck D's gravity and kept the group human. He could carry a record on his own, and did. '911 Is a Joke' in 1990 turned a complaint about ambulance response times into one of the group's most pointed songs, while 'Cold Lampin' with Flavor' in 1988 was pure surreal play, and he is there on the 1989 anthem 'Fight the Power' too. Public Enemy has earned six Grammy nominations, and Flav himself now sits in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Beneath the clowning is a musician with sharp timing.

bombsquad.blurb: The production team behind Public Enemy's noise.
bombsquad.bio: The Bomb Squad is the American production team that gave Public Enemy its sound, and with it changed what a hip-hop record could be made of. Formed in 1986, the collective layered samples until the tracks became something closer to collage than to beat-making: sirens, squalls of noise, fragments of horn and funk stacked so densely that no single element could be picked out. 'Bring the Noise' in 1987 was a statement of method as much as a song. In 1989 they produced 'Fight the Power', the group's defining anthem, and 'Welcome to the Terrordome', perhaps the most claustrophobic record of the era. They also worked with Ice Cube, carrying the approach west. Few production teams have had so identifiable a signature, and none made noise itself sound so purposeful.

icet.blurb: West Coast pioneer of gangsta rap.
icet.bio: Tracy Marrow, born in 1958 and known as Ice-T, is a rapper and actor who moved between hip hop and heavy metal without apology. He spent the 1980s coming up underground, and the 1986 single 6 in the Mornin' laid down a template for gangsta rap: plain, unhurried reporting from the street with no moral attached. He took his cue from Schoolly D's records. Signed to Sire in 1987, he released Rhyme Pays and founded his own Rhyme $yndicate label; 'Power' in 1988 became his only platinum album, and 'O.G. Original Gangster' in 1991 gave him a title track and a nickname. The 1988 song 'Colors', written for the film, took his voice to a wider audience. A peer of N.W.A and a collaborator with 2 Live Crew and Too $hort, he spent the era arguing for rap's right to describe what it saw.

schoollyd.bio: Jesse Bonds Weaver Jr., born in 1962 and known as Schoolly D, is a rapper from Philadelphia and one of the quiet pivots in hip hop's history. In 1985, while most rap records were still about the party, he cut 'P.S.K. What Does It Mean?', a slow, echoing, deadpan account of street life that is widely treated as the first gangsta rap single. 'Gucci Time' came the same year and 'Saturday Night' in 1986, both carrying the same cavernous drums and unhurried delivery. Where his New York contemporaries competed on technique, Schoolly D competed on atmosphere, letting silence and reverb do half the work. Ice-T has pointed to those records as a direct influence, and the whole West Coast turn towards street narrative runs back through them to Philadelphia.

nwa.blurb: The Compton group that changed rap.
nwa.bio: N.W.A formed in Compton, California, in 1986, founded by Eazy-E and built around Ice Cube's writing and Dr. Dre's production. They are among the earliest and most significant acts in gangsta rap, and among the most influential in hip hop full stop. Their 1988 title track 'Straight Outta Compton' introduced each member in turn over a beat with no ornament and no apology, and 'F--- tha Police' from the same album made the group a national argument, condemned by authorities and adopted by everyone who felt policed. 'Express Yourself' in 1989 showed the other side: funk, humour and a producer already thinking about the sound that would define the next decade. Peers of Ice-T on the West Coast, they gave the Geto Boys and countless others licence to report from their own cities.

eazye.bio: Eric Wright, born in 1964 and known as Eazy-E, was the rapper and entrepreneur who founded N.W.A and the label that carried it, Ruthless Records. Often called the Godfather of Gangsta Rap, he propelled West Coast rap out of the clubs and into the national conversation, and his high, nasal, unmistakable voice cut through everything around it. 'Boyz-n-the-Hood' in 1987 was his signature solo single: a cold, funny, matter-of-fact street story delivered as though nothing in it were remarkable. 'We Want Eazy' and the title track 'Eazy-Duz-It' followed in 1988 from his debut album, playing the persona for all it was worth. He worked closely with Dr. Dre, and as a label boss he had a genuine ear, signing and mentoring Bone Thugs-N-Harmony. Eazy-E died in 1995, having done as much as anyone to make the West Coast the centre of rap.

icecube.blurb: West Coast rap's fiercest political voice.
icecube.bio: Ice Cube, born O'Shea Jackson in 1969, is an American rapper, songwriter, actor and film producer who helped write the vocabulary of West Coast hip hop. As a member of N.W.A, his work on the 1989 album Straight Outta Compton pushed gangsta rap into the mainstream. Striking out alone, he cut his solo debut with The Bomb Squad, whose dense, siren-heavy production frames the title track 'AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted' (1990). 'Death Certificate' followed in 1991, alongside the scalding N.W.A diss 'No Vaseline', and 'The Predator' arrived in 1992 carrying his most beloved song, 'It Was a Good Day'. He mentored Yo-Yo, opening a lane for women in West Coast rap, and later built a second career in film. N.W.A took their place in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2016, Cube among the inductees.

2livecrew.blurb: Miami bass pioneers who tested free speech.
2livecrew.bio: 2 Live Crew are an American hip hop group formed in Miami in 1984, originally built around DJ Mr. Mixx, Fresh Kid Ice and Amazing Vee. The best-known line-up came later, with Brother Marquis added and Luther Campbell taking Amazing Vee's place while also managing and promoting the group. Their sound married booming, fast Miami bass with raunchy, comic party rhymes, and the 1986 debut 'The 2 Live Crew Is What We Are' laid out the formula. 'Me So Horny' (1989) turned them into a national phenomenon, and the explicit content that made them popular also made them a target: 'Banned in the U.S.A.' (1990) answered the censorship fight head on. Collaborators with Ice-T, they are pioneers of Miami bass and foundational figures in the rise of Southern hip hop.

epmd.blurb: Long Island duo of laid-back funk rap.
epmd.bio: EPMD are an American hip hop duo from Brentwood on Long Island, formed in 1987 by the emcees Erick Sermon and Parrish Smith. The name is an initialism for Erick and Parrish Making Dollars, trimmed from a longer version partly because Eric Wright of N.W.A was already using Eazy-E. Their debut single 'It's My Thing' (1987) announced a style with no wasted motion: heavy funk breaks, a rolling low end and two unhurried, conversational voices trading verses. 'Strictly Business' (1988) turned that formula into a landmark album, with its title track and the endlessly quoted 'You Gots to Chill' becoming touchstones of the golden age. Peers of Rakim in the East Coast vanguard, they made cool understatement a virtue and have kept the partnership running for close to four decades.

saltnpepa.blurb: Hip hop's first female superstar group.
saltnpepa.bio: Salt-N-Pepa came together in New York City in 1985, an American hip hop group of Salt, Pepa and DJ Spinderella. Their debut 'Hot, Cool & Vicious' (1986) sold more than a million copies in the United States, making them the first female rap act to be certified gold and then platinum. 'Push It', released in 1987 as the B-side to 'Tramp', climbed into the top twenty of the Billboard Hot 100 and became the record that carried rap onto pop radio and dancefloors alike. They kept frankness and fun in balance across 'Let's Talk About Sex' (1991) and 'Shoop' (1993). Peers of Roxanne Shante and collaborators with MC Lyte, they made room for the women who followed, Da Brat among them, and remain the template for the female rap group.

mclyte.blurb: Pioneer who made solo female rap possible.
mclyte.bio: MC Lyte, born Lana Michele Moorer in 1970, is an American rapper, songwriter, actress and businesswoman, and one of the founding figures of female rap. In 1988 she became the first woman to release a full solo rap album with the acclaimed 'Lyte as a Rock', which carried 'Paper Thin' and the battle record '10% Dis'. Her voice is low, dry and unhurried, and her authority comes from phrasing rather than volume, as 'Cha Cha Cha' (1989) demonstrates from end to end. 'Ruffneck' (1993) became the first gold-certified single by a solo female rapper. She followed a path opened by Sha-Rock and worked alongside Salt-N-Pepa and Yo-Yo, later building a long second life as an actress and television announcer. Her run set the standard for every solo woman in hip hop who came after.

queenlatifah.blurb: Regal MC who became a cultural institution.
queenlatifah.bio: Queen Latifah, born Dana Elaine Owens in 1970, is an American rapper, singer and actress whose bearing gave hip hop a new kind of authority. Her debut single 'Wrath of My Madness' (1988) arrived with her poise already fully formed, and 'Ladies First' (1989), cut with Monie Love, remains one of rap's great statements of solidarity. Running with the Jungle Brothers and De La Soul in the same crew, she made Afrocentric warmth and wit central to the golden age. 'U.N.I.T.Y.' (1993), a flat refusal of disrespect towards women, won her a Grammy. She has since collected an Emmy, a Golden Globe and an Academy Award nomination, in 2006 became the first rapper given a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2026.

delasoul.blurb: Playful Long Island pioneers of alternative hip hop.
delasoul.bio: De La Soul are an American hip hop group formed in Amityville on Long Island in 1988 by Posdnuos, Trugoy the Dove and Maseo, who met in high school. A demo of their song 'Plug Tunin' caught the ear of the producer Prince Paul, and the records that followed rewired what rap could sound like: eclectic, oddly sourced samples, private jokes and language, and a colourful, deliberately unmacho sensibility. 'Me Myself and I' (1989) became their signature single almost against their will, while 'The Magic Number' showed the sweetness underneath. Core members of the Native Tongues circle with the Jungle Brothers, A Tribe Called Quest and Queen Latifah, they gathered the whole family on the posse cut 'Buddy' (1989). Following the lead of Stetsasonic, they helped make jazz rap and alternative hip hop a lasting tradition.

atcq.bio: A Tribe Called Quest came together in Queens, New York City, in 1985, an American hip hop group built around Q-Tip as lead rapper and chief producer, with Phife Dawg on the mic, Ali Shaheed Muhammad co-producing and DJing, and Jarobi White also rapping. Co-founders of the Native Tongues collective in 1988, they ran with De La Soul and the Jungle Brothers and turned round bass, warm loops and easy conversational rhyming into a whole school of music. 'Can I Kick It?' (1990) made the approach irresistible, the posse cut 'Scenario' (1992) with Leaders of the New School gave the era one of its wildest moments, and 'Award Tour' (1993) is the group at cruising altitude. Later work with J Dilla deepened the sound further. Critics have placed them ever since among the greatest acts the music has produced.

qtip.blurb: The Abstract, rapper and jazz-rap architect.
qtip.bio: Q-Tip, born Kamaal Ibn John Fareed in 1970, is an American rapper, singer and record producer, nicknamed the Abstract and central to A Tribe Called Quest as both lead voice and main producer. His jazz-rooted production, built from warm bass and unhurried loops, led a jazz-based revolution in nineties rap, and his writing pairs everyday observation with a philosophical, introspective streak. Stepping out under his own name, he scored with 'Vivrant Thing' (1999) and 'Breathe and Stop' (2000), then returned with the reflective 'Gettin' Up' (2008). A frequent collaborator with Busta Rhymes, he has shaped records far beyond his own catalogue, and Billboard has ranked him among the greatest producers the music has known. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the group in 2024.

junglebrothers.blurb: Hip-house innovators at the Native Tongues root.
junglebrothers.bio: Jungle Brothers are an American hip hop group formed in 1987 around Michael Small and Nathaniel Hall. Fostered by the radio kingmaker Kool DJ Red Alert, they fused jazz, hip hop and house music and were the first rap group to make a record with a house producer. Their debut album 'Straight Out the Jungle' (1988) set out an Afrocentric, open-hearted alternative to the harder styles around them, and the hip-house club hit 'I'll House You' was folded into pressings later that year. 'What U Waitin 4?' (1989) kept the party running. Their success drew in De La Soul and A Tribe Called Quest and grew into the Native Tongues collective, with Queen Latifah and Monie Love among the family. Working in the wake of Afrika Bambaataa, they turned Afrocentric hip hop into a movement.

stetsasonic.blurb: The original hip hop live band.
stetsasonic.bio: Stetsasonic are an American hip hop group formed in Brooklyn in 1981, and among the very first rap acts to work with a full band and live instrumentation on record. Beat-boxing, sampling technology and a working rhythm section sat side by side in their music, which drew in rhythm and blues, jazz, dancehall reggae and rock. 'Float On' (1986) showed how naturally they could bend a soul record to their own ends, while 'Talkin' All That Jazz' (1988), their signature single, answered critics of sampling with a defence that has long outlived the argument. 'Sally' (1988) carried the same live swing. They are counted among the pioneers of jazz rap, they shaped De La Soul directly, and the path they opened for hip hop bands runs forward to the Roots.

ultramagnetic.blurb: Bronx eccentrics who rewrote rap's rhyme science.
ultramagnetic.bio: Ultramagnetic MCs are an American hip hop group from the Bronx, founded by Kool Keith with Ced Gee, TR Love and Moe Love. Their music runs on unorthodox sampling, polysyllabic rhyme schemes and lyrical imagery so strange it still sounds like it arrived from somewhere else. 'Ego Trippin' (1986) rearranged what a rap verse could do with syllables, and the album 'Critical Beatdown' (1988), with its title track, remains a high-water mark for producers as much as for rappers. 'Poppa Large' (1992) proved the group had lost none of its bite. The line-up widened over the years, taking in the hype man Big D and, unofficially, Tim Dog, while a young Rahzel worked as a roadie early on. Peers of Rakim in the era's technical arms race, they remain a rapper's group above all.

tooshort.blurb: West Coast pioneer with unhurried blunt swagger.
tooshort.bio: Too $hort, born Todd Anthony Shaw in 1966, is an American rapper, producer and music executive, and one of the first West Coast artists to win national recognition in the late 1980s. His subject matter is famously blunt, running from pimping and promiscuity to drug culture and plain street survival, delivered in a slow, conversational drawl over spare, heavy funk. 'Life Is...Too Short' (1988) established the persona, 'The Ghetto' (1990) revealed the social eye underneath it, and 'Blow the Whistle' (2006) proved decades later that he could still build a national hit out of almost nothing. A collaborator with Ice-T and with E-40, he is one of very few artists to have worked with both 2Pac and the Notorious B.I.G. at the height of their careers. Few rap careers have run so long on so consistent a formula.

getoboys.blurb: Houston hardcore group who rapped paranoia.
getoboys.bio: The Geto Boys were an American hip hop group formed in Houston in 1986, best known for the 1990s line-up of Bushwick Bill, Willie D and Scarface. Working in the wake of N.W.A, they pushed hardcore rap somewhere new by turning it inward. 'Mind Playing Tricks on Me' (1991) is a study in paranoia, guilt and insomnia rather than bravado, and it reached number twenty-three on the Billboard Hot 100 without softening a line. 'Damn It Feels Good to Be a Gangsta' (1992) supplied the swagger, but the group's real subject was always the cost of the life it described. Scarface emerged from the ranks as one of the most respected writers in the music. The group remained active until the death of Bushwick Bill in 2019, and their shadow lies across Southern rap, Three 6 Mafia included.

heavyd.blurb: Rap's smoothest bridge to rhythm and blues.
heavyd.bio: Heavy D, born Dwight Arrington Myers in 1967, was a Jamaican-American rapper, record producer and actor who led Heavy D & the Boyz with the dancers and hype men G-Whiz and Trouble T. Roy and the DJ and producer Eddie F. Light on his feet and generous in tone, he made rap that welcomed singers and dancers in, and the group held a sizeable American audience through most of the 1990s. Their five albums drew production from Teddy Riley, Marley Marl, DJ Premier and his cousin Pete Rock alongside Eddie F. 'We Got Our Own Thang' (1989) and the Aaron Hall collaboration 'Now That We Found Love' (1991) fused hip hop with new jack swing and a reggae lilt, and 'Nuttin' but Love' followed in 1994. A peer of Run-DMC, he discovered Soul for Real and Monifah before his death in 2011.

drdre.blurb: The producer who built West Coast hip hop.
drdre.bio: Dr. Dre, born Andre Romell Young in 1965, is an American record producer, rapper and executive, and the most consequential architect of West Coast hip hop. He began with the World Class Wreckin' Cru in 1984 and in 1987 formed N.W.A with Eazy-E, Ice Cube and Arabian Prince, whose 'Straight Outta Compton' (1989) made gangsta rap a national force. In the early 1990s he crafted G-funk, a slow, synthesiser-heavy sound heard at its purest on 'Nuthin' but a G Thang' (1992) and 'Let Me Ride'. Co-founder of Death Row Records and later of Aftermath Entertainment and Beats Electronics, he mentored Snoop Dogg, produced 2Pac, worked with Nate Dogg, and signed and guided Eminem, 50 Cent, The Game and Kendrick Lamar. 'Still D.R.E.' (1999) announced a second act that has never really ended.

snoopdogg.blurb: The coolest drawl in West Coast rap.
snoopdogg.bio: Snoop Dogg, born Calvin Cordozar Broadus Jr. in 1971, is an American rapper, singer, songwriter and producer, and a defining figure of West Coast hip hop. Discovered and mentored by Dr. Dre, he arrived on Death Row Records with a drawled, unhurried delivery and a melodic sense that made G-funk feel effortless. 'Who Am I (What's My Name)?' (1993) introduced him, and 'Gin and Juice' (1994), from his debut album 'Doggystyle', became the era's most quoted party record. He ran with Nate Dogg, collaborated with 2Pac, and kept extending his reach, hitting a second commercial peak with the Pharrell collaboration 'Drop It Like It's Hot' (2004). His lyrics have never stopped circling social realities, drug use and gun violence among them, and his ease has carried him from gangsta rap into reggae and general fame.

deathrow.blurb: The label that ruled nineties gangsta rap.
deathrow.bio: Death Row Records is an American record label founded in 1991 by Dr. Dre and Suge Knight with The D.O.C. and Dick Griffey, and for a few years the most powerful name in hip hop. Its releases carried G-funk out of Los Angeles and around the world: Dr. Dre's 'Nuthin' but a G Thang' (1992) was the flagship, Snoop Dogg arrived with 'Who Am I (What's My Name)?' (1993), and the signing of 2Pac brought 'California Love' (1995), cut with Dre. At its peak the label was taking in more than a hundred million dollars a year. Its rivalry with Bad Boy Records defined the mid-nineties and turned commercial competition into something far darker. Suge Knight ran it as chief executive, and the roster assembled in those few years still defines the era.

sugeknight.blurb: Executive behind Death Row's rise and fall.
sugeknight.bio: Suge Knight, born Marion Hugh Knight Jr. in 1965, is an American music executive and record producer, co-founder and former chief executive of Death Row Records. A former American football player, he moved into the record business and became the central commercial figure behind gangsta rap's rise through the 1990s. Two early releases carried the label: 'The Chronic', which Dr. Dre delivered in 1992, and 'Doggystyle', which Snoop Dogg followed with in 1993. Around them sat hits like 'Nuthin' but a G Thang' (1992) and 'California Love' (1995). Knight ran the operation by force of personality, and his combative style gave the era its worst tensions as surely as its biggest hits. He is now serving a twenty-eight-year prison sentence for a fatal hit-and-run in 2015.

tupac.blurb: The defining voice of nineties rap.
tupac.bio: 2Pac, the American MC who lived from 1971 to 1996, remains the defining voice of nineties rap. Signed to Death Row and produced by Dr. Dre, he cut 'California Love' and 'Dear Mama' in 1995 and Hit 'Em Up in 1996. His rivalry with the Notorious B.I.G. shaped the era; his influence runs through Kendrick Lamar and Polo G.

natedogg.blurb: The singer who made rap hooks soar.
natedogg.bio: Nate Dogg, born Nathaniel Dwayne Hale in 1969, was an American singer, rapper and songwriter whose smooth, slightly weathered baritone became the sound of the hook in West Coast rap. Between the early 1990s and the late 2000s he sang guest choruses on a remarkable run of records, earning the honorific King of Hooks. He ran with Snoop Dogg, singing on 'Ain't No Fun (If the Homies Can't Have None)' (1993), and reached his widest audience alongside Warren G on 'Regulate' (1994), a record built entirely around the pull of his voice. He returned for the hook on Dr. Dre's 'The Next Episode' (1999). Neither quite a singer's singer nor a rapper, he invented a role that hip hop has relied on ever since. He died in 2011.

notoriousbig.blurb: Brooklyn storyteller with the smoothest flow.
notoriousbig.bio: The Notorious B.I.G., born Christopher George Latore Wallace in 1972, was an American rapper also known as Biggie Smalls, and is widely counted among the greatest ever to hold a microphone. His delivery was laid-back and conversational, an easy cadence that made the grim content of his lyrics land all the harder. Signed to Bad Boy Records and produced by Sean Combs, he told semi-autobiographical stories of hardship and criminality shot through with celebration: 'Juicy' (1994) is a rags-to-riches parable, 'Big Poppa' (1994) is pure charm and 'Hypnotize' (1997) his final flourish. DJ Premier also produced for him, he collaborated with Jay-Z and he mentored Lil' Kim. His rivalry with 2Pac hardened into the defining conflict of nineties rap, and both men were killed at the height of their powers, Wallace in 1997.

puffdaddy.blurb: The producer who made rap a pop empire.
puffdaddy.bio: Sean Combs, born in 1969 and known professionally as Diddy, is an American record producer, executive and rapper who founded Bad Boy Records and turned nineties hip hop into a pop-scale business. His ear was for stars: he is credited with finding and developing Mary J. Blige, Usher and the Notorious B.I.G. among others, and his production style, built on big, unmistakable samples of familiar hits, put rap at the centre of radio. In 1997 he was inescapable, with 'Can't Nobody Hold Me Down' featuring Mase, 'Mo Money Mo Problems' alongside Biggie and Mase, and the elegy 'I'll Be Missing You' with Faith Evans and 112. He also produced for Lil' Kim. A peer of later moguls such as Rick Ross, he made the rap executive a public figure in his own right.

badboy.blurb: The label that made rap sound like pop.
badboy.bio: Bad Boy Records is an American record label founded in 1993 by Sean Combs, and the house that defined the shiny, sample-driven sound of mid-nineties hip hop. Its first signee, Craig Mack, broke through with 'Flava In Ya Ear' in 1994, and the label quickly assembled a roster of the Notorious B.I.G., Faith Evans and Mase, plus 112, Total, the Lox, Carl Thomas and Shyne. 'Juicy' (1994) was its flagship record, and 1997 belonged to it entirely, from 'Mo Money Mo Problems' to the label all-star elegy 'I'll Be Missing You'. That year Bad Boy was valued at around a hundred million dollars. Its rivalry with Death Row Records shaped and scarred the era. In the 2000s it signed French Montana, Machine Gun Kelly, Janelle Monae and Cassie Ventura.

lilkim.blurb: The rapper who rewrote female rap's rules.
lilkim.bio: Lil' Kim, born Kimberly Denise Jones in 1974, is an American rapper, singer, songwriter and model who changed what a woman was allowed to say on a rap record. Mentored by the Notorious B.I.G., she emerged with a hard, sexually charged style delivered with total command, and 'No Time' (1996), featuring Puff Daddy, and 'Crush on You' (1997) with Lil' Cease established her as a star in her own right rather than a protegee. Sean Combs produced much of that early work. In 2001 she topped the charts as part of the all-star 'Lady Marmalade'. Her rivalry with Foxy Brown and her later friction with Nicki Minaj played out in public, but the influence is not in dispute: she is the second best-selling female rapper of all time and a fashion figure whose risks became the norm.

jayz.blurb: MC turned mogul, hip hop's greatest hustler.
jayz.bio: Jay-Z, born Shawn Corey Carter in 1969, is an American rapper, record executive and businessman, and in 2023 Billboard and Vibe named him the greatest rapper of all time. His writing is dense with double entendre, wordplay and braggadocio, all built on a rags-to-riches narrative he has never stopped refining, from 'Can't Knock the Hustle' (1996) with Mary J. Blige through the crossover 'Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)' (1998) to the defiant '99 Problems' (2004). He collaborated with the Notorious B.I.G., Foxy Brown and Timbaland, worked closely with Kanye West and Just Blaze, and traded rap's most famous exchange of blows with Nas. He has signed and mentored a further generation, Rapsody and J. Cole among them. Forbes calls him the wealthiest music artist in history, worth an estimated 2.8 billion dollars.

nas.blurb: Street poet of the boom bap era.
nas.bio: Nas, born Nasir bin Olu Dara Jones in 1973, is an American rapper, producer and entrepreneur, and one of the finest writers hip hop has produced. The son of the jazz musician Olu Dara, he began in 1989 as Nasty Nas, cut demos under the wing of Large Professor and announced himself with a guest verse on Main Source's 'Live at the Barbeque' in 1991. His own records turned street reportage into something close to poetry: 'N.Y. State of Mind' and 'The World Is Yours', both from 1994, and 'If I Ruled the World (Imagine That)' (1996) with Lauryn Hill. He worked repeatedly with DJ Premier, and with Mobb Deep and Common. Following Kool G Rap's lead, he shaped J. Cole and Joey Bada$$ in turn, and his rivalry with Jay-Z remains rap's most storied battle.

mobbdeep.blurb: Queens duo of hip hop's darkest realism.
mobbdeep.bio: Mobb Deep were an American hip hop duo from Queens, New York, made up of the rappers, writers and producers Prodigy and Havoc. Their sound is cold and claustrophobic, built from sparse minor-key loops and hard drums, and their subject is survival with the glamour stripped out. 'Shook Ones, Pt. II' and 'Survival of the Fittest', both from 1995, gave East Coast hardcore rap its definitive texture and anchored 'The Infamous', the album that made their name. 'Hell on Earth' (1996) and 'Murda Muzik' (1999) followed, the latter carrying 'Quiet Storm'. They sold more than three million records and count among the most influential acts in East Coast hip hop. Nas collaborated with them, and 2Pac took aim at them in the era's crossfire. Little in hardcore rap since has matched the pressure of that sound.

prodigy.blurb: Half of Mobb Deep, hardcore rap's bleak poet.
prodigy.bio: Prodigy, born Albert Johnson in 1974, was an American rapper and record producer, best known as one half of Mobb Deep alongside Havoc. His writing was plain, cold and unnervingly specific, and his voice carried a flat menace that made ordinary lines land like threats. 'Shook Ones, Part II' (1995) is the record most often cited as the purest example of it, with 'Survival of the Fittest' from the same year close behind. Across his career he released eight albums with Mobb Deep, six solo studio albums and a posthumous record, and the solo single 'Keep It Thoro' (2000) showed how well that mode suited him. He worked regularly with the producer The Alchemist. He died in 2017, leaving a body of work that remains a touchstone for hardcore East Coast rap.

bigl.blurb: Harlem's sharpest punchline rapper, lost too early.
bigl.bio: Big L, born Lamont Coleman in 1974, was an American rapper and record producer who emerged from Harlem in 1992 and built a reputation among underground listeners on the strength of his freestyling. His gift was the punchline, delivered fast and deadpan, and 'Ebonics' (1998), a whole record devoted to decoding street slang, shows the wit and control behind it. Signed to Columbia Records, he released his debut album 'Lifestylez ov da Poor & Dangerous' in 1995, and its single 'Put It On' and the posse cut 'Da Graveyard', which featured a young Jay-Z, remain fixtures of the era. He worked with DJ Premier and with Big Pun. He was shot and killed in a drive-by in Harlem in 1999, leaving one of hip hop's great unfinished careers.

bigpun.blurb: Bronx virtuoso of breath and internal rhyme.
bigpun.bio: Big Pun, born Christopher Rios in 1971, was a Bronx MC whose dexterity and sheer breath control made him one of the most technically gifted rappers of the boom bap era. He came up in the borough's underground before fellow Bronx rapper Fat Joe discovered and mentored him, bringing him in alongside Cuban Link and Triple Seis and putting him on record in 1995. His own singles followed: 'I'm Not a Player' in 1997 and the reworked 'Still Not a Player' with Joe in 1998, a crossover hit that carried dense internal rhyme onto pop radio. A Latin hip hop pioneer within East Coast rap, he collaborated with Big L and stood beside his crew mates Fat Joe and Remy Ma. He died in 2000, the year 'It's So Hard' with Donell Jones appeared.

fatjoe.blurb: New York MC who built Terror Squad.
fatjoe.bio: Fat Joe, born Joseph Cartagena in 1970, is a New York MC and label executive whose career has run from the underground to the pop charts. He started out in 1991 with the Diggin' in the Crates crew and went solo with his debut album 'Represent' in 1993. In the late nineties he formed Terror Squad as both a group and a label, signing New York talent: Big Pun, Remy Ma, Cuban Link and Triple Seis, and giving early homes to the then unknown producers DJ Khaled and Cool and Dre. Discovering and mentoring Big Pun remains his most consequential act of talent-spotting. As a hitmaker he scored with 'What's Luv?' featuring Ashanti in 2002, the Terror Squad anthem 'Lean Back' in 2004, and 'All the Way Up' with Remy Ma in 2016.

dmx.blurb: Growling, raw-nerved voice of Ruff Ryders.
dmx.bio: DMX, born Earl Simmons in 1970, was an American rapper and actor whose bark, growl and confessional intensity made him one of the defining voices of the late nineties. Signed to Ruff Ryders and working closely with the label's producer Swizz Beatz, he broke through with 'Ruff Ryders' Anthem' in 1998 and dominated radio a year later with 'Party Up (Up in Here)'. His music swung between hardcore aggression, horrorcore imagery and unguarded songs about trauma and childhood abuse, often ending in spoken prayer. That range earned four Grammy nominations along with American Music and Billboard Music Awards, and made him a magnetic screen presence as well. 'X Gon' Give It to Ya' arrived in 2003 and became his most widely recognised anthem. He died in 2021, remembered as one of hip hop's most emotionally exposed performers.

ruffryders.blurb: Yonkers label and crew behind DMX.
ruffryders.bio: Founded in 1988 by the siblings Joaquin, Darrin and Chivon Dean, Ruff Ryders Entertainment is a hip hop label and management outfit based in Yonkers, New York. Operating as a Universal subsidiary distributed by Interscope, with Def Jam handling the DMX albums, it became one of the definitive engines of late nineties New York rap. Its flagship artist was DMX, whose 'Ruff Ryders' Anthem' in 1998 served as the label's calling card, and the roster grew to include Eve, The Lox, Drag-On and MC Jin, with in-house beats from Swizz Beatz, the Deans' nephew, and Dame Grease. The name also described a loose collective of those signees, who came together on posse cuts such as 'Ryde or Die' and 'Down Bottom' with Drag-On and Juvenile in 1999. Powerhouse Studios remains its home base.

thelox.blurb: Yonkers trio of hard, unhurried lyricists.
thelox.bio: The Lox formed in Yonkers, New York, in 1994, a trio of Sheek Louch, Styles P and Jadakiss. Two years on they signed to Puff Daddy's Bad Boy Records and arrived as street-hardened foils to that label's glossier instincts, first on the 1997 tribute 'We'll Always Love Big Poppa' and then on their debut album, whose title track 'Money, Power & Respect' brought in DMX and Lil' Kim in 1998. They soon moved to Ruff Ryders, a change of home that suited their grittier register and produced tracks such as 'Wild Out' in 2000. Three distinct voices, never blurred: Jadakiss with his rasp and punchlines, Styles P with his coiled menace, Sheek Louch with his bluntness. They remain among New York rap's most respected working units, still recording together decades on.

jadakiss.blurb: Raspy Lox lyricist with punchline precision.
jadakiss.bio: Jadakiss, born Jason Phillips in 1975, is an East Coast MC prized for his raspy delivery, sly punchlines and unhurried authority over a beat. He began recording in the early nineties and in 1994 formed the trio the Lox with Styles P and Sheek Louch, who signed to Puff Daddy's Bad Boy Records and released 'Money, Power & Respect' in 1998 before moving to Ruff Ryders for their second album in 2000. Both records reached the top five of the Billboard 200. Solo, he cut 'Knock Yourself Out' and 'We Gonna Make It' with Styles P in 2001, then found a far wider audience with 'Why' featuring Anthony Hamilton in 2004, a song that turned his questioning cadence into social commentary. Later Lox albums arrived through Jay-Z's Roc Nation, and he has collaborated often with Fabolous.

eve.blurb: Ruff Ryders first lady turned pop crossover.
eve.bio: Eve, born Eve Jihan Cooper in 1978, is an American rapper, singer and actress who became the first lady of Ruff Ryders. Her 1999 debut, 'Let There Be Eve', topped the Billboard 200 and was certified double platinum, spinning off 'Gotta Man' among its singles and establishing a voice that was tough, playful and unmistakably her own inside a famously hard-edged crew. That same year she guested on the Roots' 'You Got Me' and Missy Elliott's 'Hot Boyz', both top forty hits, marking her as a rapper equally at home among soul and rhythm and blues singers. In 2001 she crossed over fully with 'Let Me Blow Ya Mind' alongside Gwen Stefani and 'Who's That Girl?'. Television acting followed, but that run of records remains a template for women in mainstream hip hop.

wutang.blurb: Staten Island collective that remade East Coast rap.
wutang.bio: Wu-Tang Clan formed in Staten Island in 1992 and rebuilt East Coast hip hop almost single-handedly. The core members were RZA, GZA, Method Man, Raekwon, Ghostface Killah, Inspectah Deck, U-God, Masta Killa and Ol' Dirty Bastard, who died in 2004, with the close affiliate Cappadonna later made official. RZA produced, giving the group its grimy, off-kilter sound of dusty soul loops, kung fu dialogue and sparse drums. 'Protect Ya Neck' announced them in 1992 as an unruly relay of voices, and 'C.R.E.A.M.' in 1993 became their enduring statement, cold and clear-eyed about money and survival; 'Triumph' in 1997 showed that crowded microphone at full stretch. Their structure proved as influential as their sound, a collective built to launch solo careers, and their shadow falls on groups from Jedi Mind Tricks onward.

rza.blurb: Wu-Tang architect of dusty soul-sample beats.
rza.bio: RZA, born Robert Diggs in 1969, is the producer, rapper and de facto leader of Wu-Tang Clan, and one of the most influential beatmakers hip hop has produced. His signature was scarcity: soul samples chopped raw, drums left sparse and unpolished, snatches of kung fu dialogue used like scene-setting, an aesthetic that made 'C.R.E.A.M.' in 1993 and 'Triumph' in 1997 sound like nothing else on the radio. He produced most of the group's albums and shaped the solo records of GZA, Raekwon, Ghostface Killah, Method Man and Ol' Dirty Bastard, effectively designing a whole school of East Coast rap. Under the alias Bobby Digital he stepped forward himself, on tracks such as 'Tragedy' in 1998. The Source, Vibe and NME have all placed him among the greatest producers of any genre, and he composes and directs films too.

gza.blurb: The Genius, Wu-Tang's coolest, sharpest pen.
gza.bio: GZA, born Gary Grice in 1966, is a founding member of Wu-Tang Clan and its spiritual head, the oldest of the group and the first to land a record deal. His pen is the coolest in the crew, favouring dense, chess-like construction and quiet menace over volume, which is how he came to be known simply as the Genius. His second album, 'Liquid Swords', released in 1995 and produced by RZA, is often named among the finest solo records to come out of the Clan: the title track, 'Cold World' and '4th Chamber' set his measured delivery against RZA's bleakest, most cinematic beats. He has appeared across his fellow members' solo projects throughout, and his precision remains the standard by which lyrically minded rappers who followed the Wu measure themselves.

methodman.bio: Method Man, born Clifford Smith in 1971, is the Wu-Tang member who broke out first and broke out biggest, a rapper with a gravel-and-honey voice and a natural performer's charisma. His 1994 solo debut 'Tical' reached number four on the Billboard 200 and gave him 'Bring the Pain' and the title character track 'Method Man', two of the murkiest and most quotable singles of the era, built on RZA's production. The following year his duet with Mary J. Blige, 'I'll Be There for You / You're All I Need to Get By', reached the top five of the Hot 100 and won the Grammy for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group. He is also half of the long-running duo Method Man and Redman, a producer, and a busy screen actor who later starred opposite Blige again.

odb.blurb: Wu-Tang's wild, half-sung force of nature.
odb.bio: Ol' Dirty Bastard, born Russell Jones in 1968, was a founding member of Wu-Tang Clan and the most unpredictable voice in a group full of them. His style was half rapped and half sung, profane and free-associative, closer to a blues shouter or a street preacher than to anything else in nineties rap. His 1995 solo debut 'Return to the 36 Chambers: The Dirty Version' gave him 'Shimmy Shimmy Ya' and 'Brooklyn Zoo', the first loose and giddy, the second a snarling one-take assault, both set on RZA's productions. In 1999 he had his widest crossover moment with 'Got Your Money' featuring Kelis. He died in 2004, and the Clan never replaced him, because the role he played in it was one that nobody else could have occupied.

raekwon.bio: Raekwon, born Corey Woods in 1970, is a founding member of Wu-Tang Clan and the group's great cinematic storyteller, a rapper who builds scenes out of brand names, coded slang and hard detail. After the Clan's 1993 breakthrough he released 'Only Built 4 Cuban Linx' in 1995, produced by RZA and shadowed throughout by his closest collaborator Ghostface Killah; critics routinely count it among the greatest hip hop albums ever made and a staple of the decade. 'Incarcerated Scarfaces' and 'Criminology' show the record at its most tense, while 'Ice Cream', with Ghostface and Method Man, shows its lighter side. His partnership with Ghostface, two voices seeming to finish each other's thoughts, is one of the most productive in rap. He has kept working steadily in the decades since.

ghostface.blurb: Vivid, emotional storyteller from the Wu.
ghostface.bio: Ghostface Killah, born Dennis Coles in 1970, is the most emotionally direct member of Wu-Tang Clan, a rapper whose verses run on colour, panic, tenderness and vivid non-sequitur. He took his name from a character in The Mystery of Chess Boxing, a kung fu film released in 1979, and after the Clan's breakthrough he launched his solo career in 1996 with the well-received 'Ironman' and its aching family portrait 'All That I Got Is You' featuring Mary J. Blige. 'Supreme Clientele' in 2000 is his high-water mark, with 'Cherchez LaGhost' and 'Apollo Kids' featuring his constant foil Raekwon, and 'Fishscale' in 2006 drew equally strong notices. RZA produced much of his best work, and he founded his own label, Starks Enterprises. Few rappers have written so consistently well for so long.

outkast.blurb: Atlanta duo who reinvented Southern rap.
outkast.bio: OutKast, the American duo of Big Boi and André 3000, came together in Atlanta in 1992 and did more than any other act to prove the South had something entirely its own to say. Working closely with the production team Organized Noize and alongside their Atlanta peers Goodie Mob, they turned intricate lyricism, memorable melody, positive themes and an appetite for funk, psychedelia, jazz and techno into a run of records that were both critically adored and commercially enormous. 'Rosa Parks' in 1998 brought harmonica and handclaps to a rap single; 'B.O.B.' in 2000 pushed hip hop to breakneck tempo; 'Ms. Jackson' the same year turned an apology into a worldwide hit. They collaborated with UGK, and their influence runs straight through Killer Mike and Future.

andre3000.blurb: Restless OutKast innovator who sang his raps.
andre3000.bio: André 3000, born André Benjamin in 1975, is one half of OutKast, the duo he formed in Atlanta with Big Boi in 1992, and one of the most restless figures in hip hop. Born and raised in the city, he was an early adopter of rap-singing, blurring the line between verse and melody long before that became the mainstream default, and few rappers are held in higher regard. His writing turned inward and eccentric as the duo grew, and in 2003 it produced 'Hey Ya!', an irresistible and faintly desolate pop song that became inescapable, along with 'Roses' and 'Prototype' from the same period. He has since favoured guest verses and instrumental work over albums. In 2025 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with OutKast.

bigboi.bio: Big Boi, born Antwan Patton in 1975, was born in Savannah and raised in Atlanta, where he formed OutKast with André 3000 in 1992. He is the duo's rhythmic anchor, a rapper of extraordinary agility whose verses ride funk and bounce with a technical control that is easy to miss because he makes it sound so casual. He co-piloted the group through its entire run, taking the lead on 'The Way You Move' with Sleepy Brown in 2003, then stepped out under his own Purple Ribbon banner with 'Kryptonite (I'm on It)' in 2005 before releasing the swaggering 'Shutterbugg' in 2010. He is a record producer in his own right and a patient mentor to the Atlanta artists who followed him, Killer Mike among them. His catalogue rewards close listening.

goodiemob.blurb: Atlanta group of soul-food social commentary.
goodiemob.bio: Goodie Mob are an American hip hop group from Atlanta, made up of CeeLo Green, Khujo, T-Mo and Big Gipp. Formed at the start of the nineties, they were central to the same Atlanta circle as OutKast, sharing both a neighbourhood and the production team Organized Noize, whose warm, live-sounding tracks gave the group its distinctive Southern soul weight. Their 1995 debut paired that sound with plain-spoken commentary on poverty, surveillance and Black Southern life; its title track 'Soul Food' and the paranoid 'Cell Therapy' remain their best known songs. In 1998 they returned the favour to their neighbours on 'Black Ice (Sky High)' with OutKast. These early records are where Atlanta first found its conscience as well as its voice, and where a Southern rap that could carry hard news took shape.

organizednoize.blurb: Atlanta production team behind OutKast's rise.
organizednoize.bio: Organized Noize are an American production team from Atlanta, formed in 1992 and now composed of Ray Murray and Sleepy Brown, having begun as a trio with the Dungeon Family co-founder Rico Wade, who remained central until his death in 2024. They gave the South its own sonic signature: live players, elastic bass and gospel and funk warmth, everything looser and more humid than the sample-chopping that dominated elsewhere. They produced 'Player's Ball' for OutKast in 1993, launching that duo's career, and 'Cell Therapy' for Goodie Mob in 1995, a group they ran with as much as worked for. The same year they crossed fully into pop with 'Waterfalls' for TLC. Their studio became the workshop where an entire Atlanta scene was built, and their fingerprints are on almost everything the city sent out afterwards.

masterp.blurb: No Limit founder who built a Southern empire.
masterp.bio: Master P, born Percy Miller in 1970, is a rapper, actor and entrepreneur who turned a record label into a Southern empire. He founded No Limit Records in 1991 and built it on independence and sheer volume, releasing records at extraordinary speed with instantly recognisable artwork, and he recorded as part of the label's groups TRU and 504 Boyz and under his own name. 'Bout It, Bout It' in 1995 was the early signature, and his 1996 album 'Ice Cream Man' widened his reach before 'Make 'Em Say Uhh!' in 1997 went platinum and became his defining single, followed by 'I Got the Hook Up!' with Sons of Funk in 1998. His rivalry with Cash Money Records, and his crew alongside Mia X, shaped the Southern rap boom of the late nineties.

cashmoney.blurb: New Orleans label behind the Hot Boys.
cashmoney.bio: Founded in 1991 by the brothers Ronald Slim Williams and Bryan Baby Williams, better known as Birdman, Cash Money Records became the engine of the New Orleans rap boom in the late nineties, signing local acts including Juvenile, B.G., Young Turk and Lil Wayne, who together formed the Hot Boys. Juvenile's 'Ha' and 'Back That Azz Up' in 1998 and B.G.'s 'Bling Bling' in 1999 carried the city's slang into the national vocabulary. Becoming an imprint of Universal in March 1998 turned regional dominance into national reach, a relationship that continued through Universal Motown and eventually Republic, and later years brought Drake onto the roster. Its rivalry with Master P set the terms of Southern rap for a decade, and its signings shaped much of what came after.

juvenile.blurb: Bounce-fluent voice of Cash Money's peak.
juvenile.bio: Juvenile, born Terius Gray in 1975, is a Louisiana rapper who translated his city's bounce tradition into national hits. Signed to Birdman's Cash Money Records, he became the label's biggest solo star at its late nineties peak and a member of its flagship group the Hot Boys, running as a crew alongside Lil Wayne. His 1998 album '400 Degreez' produced 'Ha', a hypnotic single built on a rhythmic tic at the end of every line, and 'Back That Azz Up' with Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, a record so durable it has never left a dancefloor since. In 2004 he had another enormous hit with 'Slow Motion' featuring Soulja Slim. His drawl and his sense of pocket made him, for a few years, simply the sound of a city.

birdman.blurb: Cash Money co-founder and public face.
birdman.bio: Birdman, born Bryan Williams in 1969 and also known as Baby, is the public face of Cash Money Records, which he founded in 1991 with his older brother, Ronald Slim Williams. More mogul than MC, he assembled the roster that carried Southern rap into the mainstream, signing Juvenile, with whom he also ran as a crew mate, and mentoring a young Lil Wayne into the label's defining star. He rapped too, forming the duo Big Tymers with the producer Mannie Fresh, whose '#1 Stunna' in 2000, featuring Lil Wayne and Juvenile, and 'Still Fly' in 2002 made luxury and excess into comedy. His self-titled solo debut arrived in 2002 through a joint venture with Republic, and 'Pop Bottles' with Lil Wayne followed in 2007. Few executives have been so visible on their own records.

ugk.blurb: Port Arthur duo, Southern rap royalty.
ugk.bio: UGK came together in Port Arthur, Texas, in 1987, an American hip hop duo made up of Chad Butler, known as Pimp C, and Mitchell Queen, who left to pursue football and was replaced by Bernard Freeman, known as Bun B. Together they made country rap tunes: slow, blues-soaked, organ-heavy tracks that let Pimp C's drawling melodies play against Bun B's dense, authoritative verses. 'Pocket Full of Stones' in 1992 and 'One Day' in 1996 built them a fiercely loyal Southern following long before the wider industry paid attention. Vindication came with 'Int'l Players Anthem (I Choose You)' in 2007, a collaboration with OutKast that became their signature record. They also worked with Scarface, and their influence carries down to later Southern acts including Suicideboys.

pimpc.blurb: UGK's drawling singer, rapper and producer.
pimpc.bio: Pimp C, born Chad Butler in 1973, was a rapper, singer and record producer, one half of UGK with Bun B, and the sound of Southern rap's soulful side. He produced much of the duo's music himself, building slow, organ-heavy tracks out of Southern soul and blues, then singing over them in a drawl that could turn from comic to menacing within a line. 'Pocket Full of Stones' in 1992 showed the formula early, and 'Int'l Players Anthem (I Choose You)' with OutKast in 2007 gave the duo their crowning moment, released the year he died. His solo single 'Knockin' Doorz Down', with Lil' Keke and P.O.P., had arrived in 2006. His cadences and his production instincts echo through a generation of Southern rappers, Megan Thee Stallion among them.

bunb.bio: Bun B, born Bernard Freeman in 1973, is one half of UGK, the duo he formed with Pimp C in 1987. He is the group's anchoring voice, a rapper of unhurried authority whose verses are packed tight with rhyme yet delivered as though he has all the time in the world, and he became an elder statesman of Southern hip hop almost by default. The duo's guest turn on Jay-Z's 'Big Pimpin' in 1999 took them national, and 'Int'l Players Anthem (I Choose You)' with OutKast in 2007 stands as their signature record. His solo work includes 'Draped Up' in 2005 and five albums in all, among them 'Trill OG' in 2010, which earned the rare five-mic rating from The Source. He is also an entrepreneur, an actor and a producer.

scarface.bio: Scarface, born Brad Jordan in 1970, is a Houston rapper and record producer, raised in the city's South Acres neighbourhood, and the most introspective voice in Southern hip hop. As a member of the Geto Boys he wrote the verses that made 'Mind Playing Tricks on Me' a landmark in 1991, a song about paranoia and dread with no real precedent in rap that changed what the form could carry. His solo work deepened that vein with 'I Seen a Man Die' in 1994, an unflinching account of mortality, and 'On My Block' in 2002, a warmer portrait of the neighbourhood that raised him. He has also collaborated with UGK. The Source has ranked him among the top fifty lyricists of all time, and his fellow rappers tend to rank him higher still.

8ballmjg.blurb: Memphis duo of smooth pimp-talk soul.
8ballmjg.bio: 8Ball & MJG are an American duo out of Orange Mound in Memphis, Tennessee, who met at Ridgeway Middle School in 1984 and have worked together ever since. Their debut, 'Comin' Out Hard', arrived in 1993 and set the template: slow, luxurious tracks, a deep low end, and a smooth conversational trade between 8Ball's heavier voice and MJG's leaner one. 'Space Age Pimpin' and 'Lay It Down', both from 1995, are their best loved songs, unhurried and full of Southern charm, while albums including 'On Top of the World', 'In Our Lifetime' and 'Living Legends' kept them working steadily for two decades. In 2005 they joined Three 6 Mafia on 'Stay Fly', a hit that introduced them to a new generation. They remain foundational to Memphis rap.

three6mafia.blurb: Memphis horrorcore pioneers turned crunk hitmakers.
three6mafia.bio: Three 6 Mafia formed in Memphis in 1991 and turned the darkest corners of Southern rap into an entire aesthetic. They began as a horror-themed underground group working with sinister minor-key loops and chanted hooks, and their 1995 debut 'Mystic Stylez' became a cult record whose influence far outstripped its sales. Releasing through independent labels including their own Hypnotize Minds before moving on to Relativity, Loud and Columbia, they took that sound overground with 'Tear da Club Up '97' in 1997, 'Sippin' on Some Syrup' with UGK and Project Pat in 2000, and the enormous 'Stay Fly' in 2005, which also featured 8Ball & MJG. Gangsta Boo was among the members who gave the group its edge. Their fingerprints are all over what followed: Lil Jon and crunk, Gucci Mane, GloRilla.

bonethugs.blurb: Cleveland harmonizers who pioneered chopper rap.
bonethugs.bio: Bone Thugs-n-Harmony formed in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1991 and consist of Bizzy Bone, Wish Bone, Layzie Bone, Krayzie Bone and Flesh-n-Bone. They arrived sounding like nothing else in rap: five voices harmonising in close formation, rapping at double and triple speed, sliding between sung melody and rapid-fire syllables in a way that helped pioneer both chopper rap and the rap-singing that would later dominate the charts. Mentored by Eazy-E, they broke through in 1994 with 'Thuggish Ruggish Bone', followed by '1st of tha Month' in 1995 and the elegiac 'Tha Crossroads' in 1996, a mourning song that became one of the decade's biggest hits. They also brought Midwestern hip hop into a conversation dominated by the coasts, and have sold more than sixteen million records.

common.blurb: Conscious MC, actor and enduring lyricist.
common.bio: Common, born Lonnie Rashid Lynn in 1972, is an American MC whose conscious, unhurried lyricism has outlasted a long run of passing trends. He signed to the independent Relativity Records at twenty, and the label issued his first three albums, among them 'Resurrection' in 1994, the record that carried 'I Used to Love H.E.R.'. He held an underground following through the late nineties before his work with the Soulquarians collective carried him to a wider audience, with production from J Dilla and Kanye West shaping later singles such as 'The Light' and 'Go!'. He has traded verses with Nas, Mos Def, Talib Kweli and The Roots, and stands as an elder peer to Chance the Rapper and Noname. Acting and activism run alongside the music, bringing him Grammy, Academy, Emmy and Golden Globe recognition.

theroots.blurb: Philadelphia hip hop band playing it live.
theroots.bio: The Roots formed in Philadelphia in 1987, an American hip hop band built by the rapper Black Thought and the drummer Questlove. Where most of their peers built tracks from samples, the group played hip hop live, a working band whose sound drew as freely on soul and rock as on rap. That approach carried 'The Next Movement' and 'You Got Me', the 1999 single featuring Erykah Badu, and then 'The Seed (2.0)' in 2002, which pushed the fusion further towards rock. Common is among the many artists they have backed and recorded with. Since 2009 they have doubled as a television house band, first on Late Night with Jimmy Fallon and from 2014 on The Tonight Show, a nightly role that has made them the most widely seen band in hip hop while their albums stayed restless and searching.

blackthought.blurb: The Roots' lead MC, a rapper's rapper.
blackthought.bio: Black Thought, born Tariq Trotter in 1973, is the lead MC of The Roots, the Philadelphia band he co-founded with the drummer Questlove. His reputation rests on craft: dense multisyllabic rhyme schemes, double entendres stacked several deep, and politically alert writing delivered with a live performer's command of a room. That control is audible from 'Mellow My Man' in 1995 through 'The Next Movement' and 'You Got Me' in 1999, records where a rapping voice had to hold its own against a full band rather than a loop. Widely rated among the most skilled and prolific rappers of his generation, he has nonetheless spent most of his career inside a group rather than out in front of one, and now performs nightly with The Roots as house band of The Tonight Show. Few MCs are as admired by other MCs.

questlove.blurb: Drummer, producer and hip hop's great connector.
questlove.bio: Questlove, born Ahmir Thompson in 1971, is a drummer and record producer, co-founder and joint frontman of The Roots. His playing gave the band its human swing, audible on 'The Next Movement', 'You Got Me' and 'The Seed (2.0)', where the drums breathe rather than repeat. Away from the kit he has been one of the music's great connectors and curators: a DJ, a filmmaker, a music journalist, a broadcaster through the Questlove Supreme podcast, a producer of the 2015 Hamilton cast album, and a co-founder of the Okayplayer and OkayAfrica websites, which gave a generation of alternative rap a home online. He ran with J Dilla, whose feel for imperfect time is close to his own. Since 2016 he has taught at New York University, and he anchors The Roots nightly as house band of The Tonight Show.

laurynhill.blurb: Singer and rapper who changed both at once.
laurynhill.bio: Lauryn Hill, born in 1975, is an American MC and singer who moves between rapping and singing so fluidly that she is credited with founding the modern habit of doing both. She reached the world first as a member of the Fugees, then alone with 'The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill' in 1998, an album that gave her 'Doo Wop (That Thing)', a debut single that entered the charts at number one, alongside 'Ex-Factor' and 'Everything Is Everything'. A defining figure in neo soul, she stood as the only woman on MTV's list of the greatest MCs of all time and on Billboard's ten greatest rappers, and NPR counted her among the fifty great voices. She has recorded with Nas, and her writing runs straight through to Rapsody. Her influence has never depended on the volume of her output.

fugees.blurb: New Jersey trio fusing rap, soul and reggae.
fugees.bio: The Fugees were an American hip hop trio formed in New Jersey in the early nineties by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Pras Michel. Their name, shortened from refugees, nodded to the Haitian heritage of Jean and Michel and to the themes of displacement and resilience running through the songs. In an era dominated by gangsta rap they sounded like an argument for something else: live instrumentation, socially conscious writing, and a sound stitched together from hip hop, R&B, soul and reggae across the African diaspora. In 1996 they made that case commercially, with 'Fu-Gee-La', 'Ready or Not' and a reading of Roberta Flack's 'Killing Me Softly With His Song' that became their signature. The three went on to substantial solo careers, but the trio remains one of the most significant acts alternative hip hop has produced.

wyclef.blurb: Haitian-American producer, guitarist and Fugees architect.
wyclef.bio: Wyclef Jean, born in Haiti in 1969 and raised in the United States, is an MC, producer and guitarist who gave the Fugees much of their musical shape. Within the trio he built alongside Lauryn Hill and Pras he served as lead producer as well as a rapper, and it was his guitar and his ear for Caribbean melody that helped make their 1996 album sound unlike anything else selling in that quantity. He stepped out in 1997 with 'Wyclef Jean Presents The Carnival', a sprawling solo record that produced 'We Trying to Stay Alive' and 'Gone Till November', and followed it with 'The Ecleftic', home to '911' with Mary J. Blige. Across all of it he has worked as a bridge, carrying Haitian music into American pop and never letting the two sit far apart.

gangstarr.blurb: The definitive boom bap duo, MC and DJ.
gangstarr.bio: Gang Starr were an American duo in hip hop, the Boston-based rapper Guru paired with the Houston-born producer DJ Premier. Their division of labour became the template for boom bap: one voice, level and unhurried, riding hard drums and chopped jazz records that Premier cut into hooks in place of sung choruses. 'Mass Appeal', from 1994's 'Hard to Earn', made the formula a hit without softening any of it, and 'Moment of Truth' in 1998 and 'Full Clip' the following year showed how much weight the pairing could carry as the decade turned. East Coast rap in the nineties is difficult to describe without them, and producers are still reaching for the sound Premier built inside this duo. Few partnerships in the music have been so evenly matched or so plainly imitated.

guru.blurb: Monotone Boston MC who married rap to jazz.
guru.bio: Guru, born Keith Elam in Boston in 1961, was an American MC and the voice of Gang Starr, the duo he formed with the producer DJ Premier. His delivery was famously level, a dry unraised monotone that let the words land without theatre, and it gave records like 'DWYCK' in 1992, made with Nice and Smooth, and 'Mass Appeal' in 1994 their unhurried authority. He also carried rap towards jazz more literally than most: the Jazzmatazz series, begun in 1993, put him in the studio with players from the jazz tradition, the trumpeter Donald Byrd among them. A producer and songwriter as well as a rapper, he spent his career arguing that hip hop belonged in the same lineage as the music it sampled. He died in 2010, leaving one of the era's most recognisable voices.

djpremier.blurb: Boom bap's architect, chopping jazz into drums.
djpremier.bio: DJ Premier, born Christopher Martin in 1966, is an American producer and DJ, and the architect of the sound most people mean when they say boom bap. He built it as one half of Gang Starr alongside the rapper Guru, across seven albums, and exported it to almost everyone who mattered in nineties New York: 'N.Y. State of Mind' for Nas on 'Illmatic', 'Ten Crack Commandments' for The Notorious B.I.G., records with Big L, and his own 'Mass Appeal'. The method stayed consistent. Hard, dusty drums, a bassline dug out of an old record, and a chorus scratched together from other rappers' words rather than sung. He has traded ideas with Pete Rock and stands alongside DJ Jazzy Jeff among the turntablist producers of his generation. In 2014 he formed a second duo, PRhyme, and kept working.

peterock.blurb: Soulful producer of warm horns and swinging drums.
peterock.bio: Pete Rock, born Peter Phillips in 1970, is an American producer, DJ and rapper who came up as one half of Pete Rock and C.L. Smooth. Where his peers chased hardness, he chased warmth: looped horns, deep basslines and drums that swung rather than stomped. 'They Reminisce Over You (T.R.O.Y.)' in 1992 is the case in point, a memorial record built on a saxophone figure imitated ever since, and the pair were still at it in 1994 with 'Lots of Lovin'. That same year he gave Nas 'The World Is Yours' on 'Illmatic'. He made his early name as a remixer too, rebuilding other people's singles from the ground up. He is routinely bracketed with DJ Premier, RZA and Q-Tip among the mainstays of nineties East Coast production, and he and Premier have long swapped ideas.

busta.blurb: Explosive MC with the wildest delivery in rap.
busta.bio: Busta Rhymes, born Trevor Smith in 1972, is an American MC whose delivery arrives like weather, a rush of double-time syllables, elastic voices and sudden roars that made him unmistakable on any crowded record. The name came from Chuck D of Public Enemy, borrowed from an American footballer nicknamed Buster Rhymes. His solo run through the second half of the nineties turned that energy into hits: 'Woo Hah!! Got You All in Check' in 1996, 'Put Your Hands Where My Eyes Could See' the following year and 'Gimme Some More' in 1998, each paired with videos as hyperactive as the rapping. He has worked closely with Q-Tip and Missy Elliott, kindred spirits in playing games with rhythm and voice. Twelve Grammy nominations have yet to yield a win, but the lists of the greatest rappers rarely leave him off.

missy.blurb: Futurist MC and producer who rewrote pop rhythm.
missy.bio: Missy Elliott, born Melissa Arnette Elliott in 1971, is an American MC, songwriter and producer who arrived from behind the scenes. She started in the R&B group Sista, part of the Swing Mob collective led by DeVante Swing of Jodeci, and their 1994 album won praise without selling. What followed mattered more. Alongside her Swing Mob cohort Timbaland she wrote and produced for Aaliyah, SWV, 702 and Total, the pair building a rhythmic language of stutters, silences and odd sounds that pop has not stopped borrowing. Her own debut single, 'The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)' in 1997, put that language in her own voice, and 'Get Ur Freak On' and 'Work It' pushed it deeper into the mainstream. She has recorded with Busta Rhymes, Trina and Da Brat, and remains equally decisive as writer, producer and performer.

timbaland.blurb: The producer who taught pop to stutter.
timbaland.bio: Timbaland, born Timothy Mosley in 1972 and raised in Norfolk, Virginia, is an American record producer whose rhythms reorganised popular music around the turn of the century. His signature was a stutter, beats that skipped and hiccupped and left holes where a kick drum was expected, filled instead with clicks, breaths and sounds borrowed from far outside American pop. He built that language with Missy Elliott, his collaborator from the same Virginia circle, on 'The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)' in 1997, refined it for Aaliyah on 'Are You That Somebody?' in 1998, and carried it to Jay-Z with 'Big Pimpin' in 1999. By 2007 critics were tracing most current pop trends back to him. Four Grammy Awards from twenty-two nominations only partly measure how thoroughly other producers absorbed his ideas.

blackstar.blurb: Brooklyn duo who made conscious rap a pleasure.
blackstar.bio: Black Star are a Brooklyn hip hop duo, two American rappers, Mos Def and Talib Kweli, who came together in the late nineties. They took their name from the Black Star Line, the shipping company founded by Marcus Garvey, and the choice announced their intent: rap as a conversation about history, self-regard and the city, delivered with enough wit to keep it clear of the pulpit.
