saweetie.blurb: Bay Area rapper built on hooks.
saweetie.bio: Saweetie, born Diamonte Harper in 1993, is a rapper, actress and model whose career began with a freestyle that outgrew the internet. 'Icy Grl' in 2017 went double platinum and took her to Warner Records, in a joint venture with Artistry Worldwide, the label run by her then-manager Max Gousse. 'My Type' followed in 2019 and 'Tap In' in 2020, both built on the same principle: an unmissable hook, a familiar sample and a cool, unhurried delivery that never oversells. She grew up on the Bay Area tradition and cites E-40 among the figures who shaped her sense of phrasing, and she stands as a peer of Megan Thee Stallion in the wave of women who dominated rap radio at the turn of the decade. Saweetie treats a single as a piece of design.

doechii.blurb: Tampa shapeshifter signed to Top Dawg.
doechii.bio: Doechii, born Jaylah Hickmon in 1998, is a rapper, singer and songwriter whose restless shifts between styles have made her one of the most watched artists of her generation. She broke through virally on TikTok in 2021, and in 2022 she signed with Top Dawg Entertainment and Capitol Records, joining the label that built Kendrick Lamar. 'Persuasive' arrived that year, and 'What It Is (Block Boy)' with Kodak Black followed in 2023, giving her a first Billboard Hot 100 entry and a platinum certification, while she made her acting debut in the film Earth Mama. 'Denial Is a River', from Alligator Bites Never Heal in 2024, showed her writing at its most theatrical and self-aware. She takes clear cues from Nicki Minaj's shape-shifting personae. Doechii can rap, sing and perform a character within a single verse.

stefflondon.bio: Stefflon Don, born Stephanie Allen in 1991, is a British rapper whose writing moves fluidly between hip hop, dancehall, grime and contemporary R&B. She announced herself in 2016 with the mixtape Real Ting and its title track, alongside '16 Shots', a hard, patois-inflected record that made her impossible to place in any single scene. 'Hurtin' Me' with French Montana followed in 2017 and became her signature hit, reaching number seven in the UK singles chart, and a second mixtape, Secure, arrived in 2018. She has collaborated with Nicki Minaj and stands as a peer of Skepta in the London generation that made British rap a genuinely international export. Her strength is versatility used with purpose rather than as a display. Stefflon Don sings, toasts and raps as though the distinctions were never real.

dizzeerascal.blurb: The first UK rapper to travel.
dizzeerascal.bio: Dizzee Rascal, born Dylan Mills in London in 1984, is a rapper and MC widely credited as a pioneer of grime and British hip hop, and as the first UK rapper to achieve international recognition. His debut single 'I Luv U' in 2002 was jagged, claustrophobic and unlike anything in British music, and 'Fix Up, Look Sharp' followed in 2003 with a swagger that reached far beyond the pirate stations. Wiley mentored him in the early Bow scene, and he has since worked with Skepta and stood alongside Kano as a peer of the founding generation. His music has absorbed UK garage, bassline, dubstep and house, culminating in the 2009 number one 'Bonkers' with Armand Van Helden. Dizzee proved a British MC did not have to sound American to be heard anywhere.

wiley.bio: Wiley, born Richard Cowie in Bow, east London, in 1979, is an MC and producer known universally as the Godfather of Grime. From the early 2000s he put out eskibeat instrumentals himself, on white label vinyl, beginning with 'Eskimo', cold, skeletal tracks that gave the emerging genre its rhythmic identity. He led the crew Roll Deep and named the sound itself on 'Wot Do U Call It?' in 2004, then crossed over with 'Wearing My Rolex' in 2008 and reached number one with 'Heatwave' featuring Ms D in 2012. His influence runs through almost everyone who followed: he mentored Dizzee Rascal and Skepta, recorded with Kano and JME, and shaped the writing of Ghetts. Wiley built the scene, walked away from it repeatedly, and kept returning with another beat nobody else had made.

kano.blurb: East London's most literary grime MC.
kano.bio: Kano, born Kane Robinson in East Ham, London, in 1985, is a rapper, songwriter and actor whose command of narrative set him apart from the first wave of grime. 'P's and Q's' in 2005, from his debut Home Sweet Home, remains one of the genre's defining singles, and 'Typical Me' the same year, featuring Ghetto, showed a writer already thinking in scenes rather than bars. He recorded with Wiley and Ghetts and stood alongside Dizzee Rascal as a peer of the founding generation, later reuniting with Wiley and Giggs for '3 Wheel-Ups' in 2016. Made in the Manor, his fifth, reached the 2016 Mercury Prize shortlist and took Best Album at that year's MOBO Awards. He played Sully in Top Boy across its long run. Kano writes about London with a novelist's eye.

giggs.bio: Giggs, born Nathaniel Thompson in Peckham, south London, in 1983, is a rapper whose deep, slow, half-swallowed delivery became the template for UK road rap. 'Talkin da Hardest' in 2007 is his career-defining record, a track so unhurried and so certain of itself that it made speed sound like insecurity. His debut album Walk in da Park arrived in 2008 and Let Em Ave It followed, yielding the 2010 single 'Look What the Cat Dragged In', and 'Lock Doh' with Donae'o came in 2016. He has recorded with Drake, who sought him out, and stands as a peer of Skepta, while his cadence runs directly into Headie One and the drill generation that followed. Giggs never chased the charts or the scene's fashions. He simply changed how British rappers hold a bar.

ghetts.bio: Ghetts, born Justin Clarke-Samuel in 1984, is an English grime MC known for hard-hitting lyrics and rhyme schemes of unusual intricacy. He came up through N.A.S.T.Y. Crew and absorbed the example of Wiley before establishing himself as one of the scene's most respected technicians, touring internationally with Kano and recording with him repeatedly. Rebel with a Cause, his first album, was released independently in March 2014 through Disrupt, and 'Black Rose' followed in 2018 from Ghetto Gospel: The New Testament. In 2021 he released 'Mozambique' with Jaykae and Moonchild Sanelly and 'Skengman' with Stormzy, records that paired his density of writing with real scale. He has also worked with Little Simz. Ghetts is the MC other MCs cite when they want to explain what technical command in grime actually sounds like.

skepta.blurb: Boy Better Know's architect of grime's return.
skepta.bio: Skepta, born Joseph Adenuga in London in 1982 to Nigerian parents, is an MC, producer, DJ and designer who led grime's second life. With his younger brother JME he passed briefly through Roll Deep before the two founded Boy Better Know in 2005, and his clash with Devilman for Lord of the Mics 2 still counts as one of the biggest in the genre's history. Wiley mentored him early; he later recorded with Dizzee Rascal and with Drake, and stands as a peer of Giggs and Stefflon Don. 'That's Not Me' with JME in 2014 stripped the sound back to first principles and triggered a full grime resurgence, followed by 'Shutdown' in 2015 and 'Man' in 2016, both from Konnichiwa. His influence runs straight into AJ Tracey and the generation after.

jme.blurb: Boy Better Know co-founder, independent to the bone.
jme.bio: JME, born Jamie Adenuga in Tottenham, north London, in 1985, is a grime MC, producer and DJ who co-founded Boy Better Know, both crew and label, and has run it as a business ever since, incorporating Boy Better Know Limited in 2008. He came through Meridian Crew and then Roll Deep alongside his older brother Skepta, releasing his debut album Famous? independently and keeping every subsequent release under his own control. 'Serious' in 2010 caught his flat, deadpan wit at full strength; 'Man Don't Care' with Giggs in 2015 became his signature single, and '96 Fuckries', from Integrity that same year, showed how much personality he could wring from restraint. He has recorded with Wiley. JME is the scene's proof that an MC can build an institution without ever signing anything away.

littlesimz.blurb: North London rapper of orchestral ambition.
littlesimz.bio: Little Simz, born Simbiatu Ajikawo in London in 1994, is a rapper and actress whose independence and ambition have made her one of British music's most decorated artists. She released her first three albums herself: A Curious Tale of Trials + Persons in 2015, Stillness in Wonderland in 2016, and Grey Area in 2019, the last shortlisted for the Mercury Prize and named Best Album at the Ivor Novello and NME awards alike. 'Venom' carried that record with cold fury. In 2021 she went further still, opening Sometimes I Might Be Introvert with the orchestral 'Introvert' and following it with 'Woman', featuring Cleo Sol. She has cited Kendrick Lamar's example, collaborated with Ghetts and stands as a peer of Dave. Little Simz writes in long arcs, treating an album as an argument rather than a collection.

ajtracey.blurb: Ladbroke Grove MC bridging grime and garage.
ajtracey.bio: AJ Tracey, born Che Grant in Ladbroke Grove, west London, in 1994, is a rapper and record producer who moves easily between grime, drill and UK garage. He rose to attention in 2016, named by The Guardian among the best new acts to catch at that year's festivals, and the same year he joined Dave for 'Thiago Silva', a raw two-hander that became a generational anthem. 'Ladbroke Grove' in 2019 was the pivot: a garage-driven ode to his own postcode that reached the UK top three and reintroduced the genre to a young audience. 'Butterflies' with Not3s followed in 2021. He came up on Skepta's example and has kept collaborating with Dave. AJ Tracey produces much of his own material, which is why his records sound like one person's taste rather than a committee's.

headieone.blurb: The measured, melodic voice of UK drill.
headieone.bio: Headie One, born Irving Ampofo Adjei in 1994, is a British rapper and singer who became one of the defining voices of UK drill. He broke through with the 2018 mixtape 'The One' and its underground hit 'Know Better', cut with RV, and has since folded trap, UK rap and Afrobeats into a style built on flat, conversational menace rather than volume. '18HUNNA' with Dave carried him further in 2018, 'Both' put him beside Drake in 2019, and 'Ain't It Different' gathered AJ Tracey and Stormzy onto one record in 2020. He belongs to the drill lineage that runs from Giggs through his peer Central Cee and across the Atlantic to Pop Smoke and Fivio Foreign, a strand of British rap whose reach ran well beyond Britain.

kingvon.bio: King Von, born Dayvon Daquan Bennett in 1994, was an American rapper from the South Side of Chicago and one of the most compelling figures in drill. His gift was narrative: 'Crazy Story' in 2018 unfolded as a tightly plotted tale told in plain, unhurried language, and it made him a name well beyond his neighbourhood. He worked closely with fellow Chicago rapper Lil Durk, and built on the drill blueprint that Chief Keef had laid down in the same city a few years earlier. 'How It Go' arrived in 2020 as a single from his album 'Welcome to O'Block', and 'Took Her to the O' became a posthumous hit after his death that year. The storytelling voice he left behind still shapes how drill rappers structure a verse.

fiviforeign.blurb: Brooklyn drill's booming, ad-libbed hometown voice.
fiviforeign.bio: Fivio Foreign, born Maxie Lee Ryles III in 1990, is an American rapper from Brooklyn and one of the central figures of the borough's drill scene. His 2019 single 'Big Drip' broke him nationally, earning platinum certification and a remix with Lil Baby and Quavo, and it led to a deal with Mase's RichFish Records in partnership with Columbia. He came up alongside Pop Smoke in the same Brooklyn scene, and shares a transatlantic kinship with the UK drill rapper Headie One. 'Demons' followed in 2021 with Sosa Geek, later credited with a Drake appearance, and in 2022 'City of Gods' placed him beside Kanye West and Alicia Keys on one of the year's biggest rap records. His barked ad-libs are the sound of Brooklyn drill itself.

d12.blurb: Detroit's six-man horrorcore crew around Eminem.
d12.bio: D12 are an American hip-hop group from Detroit, formed in 1996 and built around a lineup of Eminem, Proof, Bizarre, Denaun Porter, Kuniva and Swifty McVay. Founded by Proof, the group set out as a collective of alter egos, each member rapping under a second name, and their humour ran to the grotesque: horrorcore imagery and comedy delivered over hard Midwest beats. Eminem's rise made them a mainstream proposition, and 'Devil's Night' gave them the 2001 breakout single 'Purple Pills' along with the harder 'Fight Music'. 'D12 World' followed, its 2004 single 'My Band' a self-mocking joke about the group being treated as one star and five sidemen. Proof's death took away the crew's founder and its heart, and D12 stand as one of Detroit rap's defining collectives.

proof.blurb: Detroit's connector: hype man and D12 founder.
proof.bio: Proof, born DeShaun Dupree Holton in 1973, was an American rapper from Detroit and the founder of D12. Before that group he passed through Soul Intent, 5 Elementz, Funky Cowboys, Promatic and Goon Sqwad, a run that made him one of the best-connected figures in the city's rap scene. A childhood friend of Eminem, he was the hype man at his concerts and a peer rather than a follower, the man who put the D12 lineup together and kept its balance. He stepped out under his own name with 'Searching for Jerry Garcia' in 2005, which carried his signature solo track 'Kurt Kobain' along with 'Forgive Me'. He died in 2006. Detroit hip hop still treats him as the connective tissue that held its scene together.

immortaltech.blurb: Uncompromising political rapper of the underground.
immortaltech.bio: Immortal Technique, born Felipe Andres Coronel in 1978, is a Peruvian-American rapper, activist and songwriter whose work sits at the far militant end of underground hip hop. His lyrics take on politics, religion, institutional racism and government conspiracy, delivered with a debater's precision and no interest in radio. 'Dance with the Devil', from 2001's 'Revolutionary Vol. 1', remains his signature song, a brutal cautionary narrative that spread by word of mouth long before streaming. 'Revolutionary Vol. 2' followed in 2003 with 'Point of No Return' and 'Industrial Revolution', and he has collaborated with Mos Def among others. He carries forward the tradition of Public Enemy, treating a record as an argument rather than entertainment, and he built a substantial following while remaining outside the major-label system entirely.

jmt.blurb: Philadelphia's dark, cinematic underground rap duo.
jmt.bio: Jedi Mind Tricks came out of Philadelphia, an underground American rap act begun by two friends from high school: Vinnie Paz on the microphone and Stoupe the Enemy of Mankind behind the boards. Stoupe's beats, built from orchestral and film-score samples, gave Paz's blunt, apocalyptic verses a cinematic weight that set the group apart from its East Coast peers. Rapper Jus Allah joined in 1999 for the second album 'Violent by Design', left soon after, returned in 2006 for 'A History of Violence', then departed again in 2013; Stoupe stepped away in 2011 and came back in 2015. 'Animal Rap' in 2003 brought in the veteran Kool G Rap, 'Scars of the Crucifix' followed on 2004's 'Legacy of Blood', and 'Suicide' appeared on 2006's 'Servants in Heaven, Kings in Hell'. The Wu-Tang Clan's dense, grimy blueprint is audible throughout.

suicideboys.blurb: New Orleans cousins who built punk-rap from SoundCloud.
suicideboys.bio: Suicideboys are an American hip-hop duo out of New Orleans, formed by cousins Scott Arceneaux Jr., who records as Scrim, and Aristos Petrou, who records as Ruby da Cherry. They rose on SoundCloud with abrasive, self-produced beats and unsparing lyrics about substance abuse and despair, and their sound draws directly on the Memphis horror of Three 6 Mafia and the Southern drawl of UGK. 'Kill Yourself (Part III)' in 2014 was an early signature from the long series that gave them their following, and 'Paris' followed in 2016. Rather than sign away control, they run their own label, G*59 Records, and release everything they make through it. That independence, as much as the punk-rap and emo-rap sound itself, made them a template for the SoundCloud generation that came after.

coxsone.blurb: Studio One founder who built Jamaican music.
coxsone.bio: Clement Dodd, known to everyone as Coxsone, was a Jamaican record producer born in 1932 who did more than anyone to shape ska, rocksteady and reggae. Through his Studio One operation he ran what amounted to Jamaica's conservatory: the house band, the audition, the session, the record. He produced the Skatalites, Alton Ellis, the Heptones, Jackie Mittoo, Burning Spear, Bob Andy and Delroy Wilson, and recorded with Leroy Sibbles, whose basslines became the backbone of the catalogue. In 1964 he cut 'Simmer Down' with the young Wailers, their debut and a Jamaican number one. 'I've Got to Go Back Home' with Bob Andy followed in 1966, and 1968's Sound Dimension instrumental 'Full Up' became one of the most versioned riddims ever made. His rivalry with Duke Reid drove the whole island forward. He died in 2004.

dukereid.blurb: Treasure Isle boss who made rocksteady sing.
dukereid.bio: Duke Reid, born Arthur Reid in 1915, was a Jamaican record producer, disc jockey and label owner, and Coxsone Dodd's great rival. A former policeman turned label owner, he ran Treasure Isle and gave rocksteady its plush, unhurried sound, all horns and space where ska had been all speed. He produced Alton Ellis, John Holt, Phyllis Dillon, the Paragons and the saxophonist Tommy McCook. 'Get Ready - Rock Steady' with Ellis in 1966 helped name the era; the Paragons' 'The Tide Is High' in 1967 later became a worldwide number one for Blondie; and the Jamaicans' 'Ba Ba Boom' won the Festival Song contest the same year. His sessions with U-Roy toasting over old rocksteady cuts opened the door to deejay music. He died in 1975.

princebuster.blurb: Ska's swaggering singer, producer and provocateur.
princebuster.bio: Prince Buster, born Cecil Bustamente Campbell in 1938, was a Jamaican singer, songwriter and producer whose 1960s records set the course of the island's popular music. He worked both sides of the glass, writing and singing his own hits while producing others, and his sense of theatre gave ska its swagger. 'Madness' arrived in 1963; 'Al Capone' in 1964 became his best-known single and the direct inspiration for the Specials' 'Gangsters'; and 'Enjoy Yourself' in 1968 turned into a standard. His long feud with Derrick Morgan, fought out in answer records, was the great rivalry of Jamaican vocal music, and he stood alongside Coxsone Dodd and Laurel Aitken as a founding figure. British bands of the next generation drew on his catalogue almost wholesale. He died in 2016.

skatalites.blurb: The house band that invented ska.
skatalites.bio: The Skatalites are a Jamaican ska band, formed in the early 1960s from the finest players in Kingston and effectively the house band of the island's recording boom. Their first run lasted barely two years, but in that time they cut a catalogue that defined the music: 'Man in the Street' in 1964, then 'Guns of Navarone' and 'Phoenix City' in 1965. Trombonist Don Drummond, saxophonists Tommy McCook and Roland Alphonso, and the young keyboard player Jackie Mittoo gave the group a jazz musician's command of harmony over a relentless offbeat. Working for Coxsone Dodd, they backed sessions for Prince Buster and for Bob Marley and the Wailers, whose 'Simmer Down' they played on. The guitarist Ernest Ranglin was a peer from the same scene. The band re-formed in 1983 and has played on ever since.

dondrummond.blurb: Ska's brooding trombone genius and composer.
dondrummond.bio: Don Drummond, born in 1932, was a Jamaican trombonist and composer and one of the founding members of the Skatalites. He wrote a great many of the group's tunes, and his playing gave ska something no one expected of dance music: a dark, meditative, minor-key voice that owed as much to modern jazz as to the offbeat beneath it. 'Man in the Street' in 1964 and 'Confucius' and 'Eastern Standard Time' in 1965 remain the clearest statements of that sensibility, melodies that sound like laments played at a party. His life ended in tragedy. In 1966 he was convicted of the murder of his partner Anita Mahfood, and he died three years later, in 1969. Jamaican music has never produced another composer quite like him.

tommymccook.bio: Tommy McCook, born in 1927, was a Jamaican saxophonist and flautist, trained in jazz and a founding member of the Skatalites. He played on the group's essential sides, among them 'Music Is My Occupation' with Don Drummond in 1964 and 'Guns of Navarone' and 'Confucius' in 1965, bringing a cool, considered tone to music built for the dancehall. When ska gave way to rocksteady he directed the Supersonics for Duke Reid, and shaped the horn arrangements behind that era's great vocal records, including sessions with Phyllis Dillon. Through the 1970s he backed countless recordings for Bunny Lee and played with the Revolutionaries at Channel One Studios, keeping his horn at the centre of reggae as it changed around him. He died in 1998.

rolandalphonso.blurb: The Chief Musician: ska's steady tenor saxophone.
rolandalphonso.bio: Roland Alphonso, born in 1931 to Cuban and Jamaican parentage, played tenor saxophone and helped found the Skatalites. Known as the Chief Musician, he was the group's most dependable soloist, a player whose warm, unhurried lines held the centre while the music raced beneath him. His own composition 'Phoenix City' became one of the band's best-loved instrumentals in 1965, the same year he cut 'El Pussy Cat Ska' and played on 'Guns of Navarone'. Where other soloists in the band brooded, Alphonso swung, and that contrast is much of what makes the Skatalites catalogue endure. He kept working for decades after the band's first breakup, carrying the ska repertoire through the reggae years and into the group's later revival. He died in 1998.

ernestranglin.blurb: The guitarist who shaped the ska chop.
ernestranglin.bio: Ernest Ranglin, born in Jamaica in 1932, is a guitarist and composer whose playing sits underneath a remarkable amount of Jamaican music. Hired as a session guitarist and music director by labels including Studio One and Island, he played on many of the earliest ska recordings and helped create the chopped rhythmic guitar style that gave the form its pulse. His approach is chordal and percussive, blending jazz, mento and rhythm and blues into solos that swing hard without ever crowding a singer. His credits run from the Eric Deans Orchestra and Theophilus Beckford to Prince Buster, the Skatalites, Monty Alexander, Jimmy Cliff and Bob Marley, and he recorded with Millie Small. Surfin', from 1967, remains his signature Studio One instrumental, and 1996's 'Below the Bassline' brought his jazz side to a wider audience.

desmonddekker.bio: Desmond Dekker, born in 1941, was a Jamaican singer and songwriter and a pioneer of ska, rocksteady and reggae. With his backing group the Aces he took Jamaican music abroad ahead of almost anyone: '007 (Shanty Town)' in 1967 gave the rude-boy era its anthem, and 'Israelites' in 1968 became one of the earliest international reggae hits, a song whose clipped, keening vocal made sense to listeners who could not make out half the words. 'It Mek' followed in 1969, and 1970 brought 'You Can Get It If You Really Want'. He came into the business under the wing of Derrick Morgan, who helped him find his first sessions, and he stood alongside Jimmy Cliff as one of the two Jamaican voices British audiences knew first. He died in 2006.

derrickmorgan.blurb: Ska's hit-making rival and generous mentor.
derrickmorgan.bio: Derrick Morgan, born in 1940, is a Jamaican singer who was among the most popular voices of the 1960s and 1970s, at home in rhythm and blues, ska, rocksteady and skinhead reggae. 'Forward March' in 1962 caught the mood of Jamaican independence and became his signature hit; 'Tougher Than Tough', a Beverley's production from 1966, defined the rude-boy record; and 'Moon Hop' in 1969 made him a favourite of Britain's skinhead audience. His running feud with Prince Buster, conducted in answer records, was the great rivalry of the era. He worked with Bob Marley and Jimmy Cliff, mentored the young Desmond Dekker into the business, and much later encouraged Queen Ifrica, making him one of the few figures whose influence stretches across three generations of Jamaican singers.

laurelaitken.bio: Laurel Aitken, born Lorenzo Aitken in Cuba in 1927 and raised in Jamaica, was a singer and one of the true pioneers of ska, widely called the Godfather of the music. He was recording before the form had a name, working the boundary between American rhythm and blues, Jamaican mento and the offbeat shuffle that was about to become something new. 'Boogie in My Bones' in 1959 was a Jamaican number one and the first Jamaican record issued in Britain, a small event with large consequences: it opened the route by which Jamaican music reached the United Kingdom. 'Judgement Day' followed in 1960. A later ska generation would claim him as an ancestor. Alongside his peer Prince Buster, he stands at the very start of the story. He died in 2005.

milliesmall.blurb: The teenager who took ska worldwide.
milliesmall.bio: Millie Small, born in Jamaica in 1947, was a singer who did more in one record than most artists manage in a career. 'My Boy Lollipop', released in 1964 when she was still a teenager, reached number two in both the British and American charts and sold over seven million copies, becoming Island Records' first major hit and setting that label on its way. Overnight she made Jamaican music a pop proposition abroad: no Caribbean performer had reached that far before, and no woman from the region has gone further since. 'Sweet William' followed the same year. She recorded with the guitarist Ernest Ranglin, whose guitar gave the hit its bounce, and she belonged to the same moment as Byron Lee. She died in 2020, her single still the doorway through which millions first heard ska.

byronlee.blurb: Bandleader who took Jamaican music to the stage.
byronlee.bio: Byron Lee, born in Jamaica in 1934, was a bass player, bandleader, producer and entrepreneur, best known for leading Byron Lee and the Dragonaires. His band was the polished, professional face of Jamaican music, the outfit sent abroad to present ska to audiences who had never heard it, and 'Jamaica Ska' in 1964 was exactly that: an invitation set to a beat. 'Sammy Dead' followed in 1965, and 1968's 'Soul Limbo' turned a Booker T. and the M.G.'s instrumental into a Caribbean party record. He was a peer of Millie Small in the years when the island's music first travelled, and as an entrepreneur he built the recording and touring infrastructure that later generations relied upon. He died in 2008, having spent five decades keeping Jamaican dance music in front of the world.

jimmycliff.blurb: The Harder They Come: reggae's global ambassador.
jimmycliff.bio: Jimmy Cliff was a Jamaican singer, songwriter and producer who moved between ska, rocksteady, reggae and soul, and did as much as anyone to carry the music to the wider world. 'Many Rivers to Cross' in 1969 and 'You Can Get It If You Really Want' in 1970 showed a gospel-deep voice that could carry a hymn or a hustle, and in 1972 the film 'The Harder They Come' and its title song made him the face of Jamaican music internationally, the record that sent a generation of listeners looking for more. He was a peer of Desmond Dekker, Toots Hibbert and Bob Marley, a whole front rank arriving at once. Nominated seven times for a Grammy and twice a winner, he was among the very few musicians honoured with Jamaica's Order of Merit.

tootshibbert.blurb: The voice that named reggae itself.
tootshibbert.bio: Toots Hibbert, born in 1942, was a Jamaican singer and songwriter and the lead voice of Toots and the Maytals, a performer whose great roaring instrument owed as much to American gospel and soul as to anything in Kingston. 'Do the Reggay', which he cut in 1968, is generally taken as the moment the genre got its name, and the same year '54-46 That's My Number' turned a prison sentence into one of the most quoted basslines in Jamaican music. 'Pressure Drop' followed in 1969 and became the song by which the rest of the world knew him, and 'Funky Kingston' in 1973 made the soul connection explicit. A peer of Jimmy Cliff and Bob Marley, he performed for six decades and won a Grammy for the album 'True Love' in 2005. He died in 2020.

altonellis.bio: Alton Ellis, born in 1938, was a Jamaican singer and songwriter and the man most responsible for the slowing of ska into rocksteady, a shift that gave Jamaican music its romantic voice. 'Rock Steady' in 1966 helped name the era and 'Cry Tough' arrived the same year, while 'I'm Still in Love with You' in 1967 carried a riddim later reused for 'Uptown Top Ranking' and countless other records. He was that rare artist who worked for both of the great rivals, cutting sides for Coxsone Dodd and then for Duke Reid. He stood among peers including Ken Boothe, Hopeton Lewis and Slim Smith, and mentored the young Delroy Wilson. Known as the Godfather of Rocksteady, he took his place in the International Reggae and World Music Awards Hall of Fame in 2006. He died in 2008.

kenboothe.bio: Ken Boothe, born in 1948, is a Jamaican vocalist known for a distinctive vibrato and a timbre that carries real ache, and he built an international reputation on a run of records that reached reggae audiences and mainstream listeners alike. 'Freedom Street' in 1970 set social conscience to a soul melody, and in 1974 he had two of his best-known sides, 'Crying Over You' and 'Everything I Own', the latter reaching number one in Britain and making him one of the few Jamaican singers of his generation to top that chart. A peer of Alton Ellis from the rocksteady years, he shares with him the ability to sing a love song as though something serious depends on it. His voice remains one of the most immediately recognisable in Jamaican music.

johnholt.blurb: Rocksteady's romantic voice, from Paragons to solo star.
johnholt.bio: John Holt, born in 1947, made his name as a Jamaican reggae singer with the vocal group the Paragons before building a long career of his own. Recording for the producer Duke Reid, he brought a light, unforced tenor to the group's harmonies, a voice with no strain in it at all, and it became one of the defining sounds of rocksteady. 'Ali Baba' followed in 1969 and 'Stick by Me' in 1972, from a long association with the producer Bunny Lee. His biggest solo hit came in 1974 with a reading of 'Help Me Make It Through the Night', part of a lush, string-laden approach that took Jamaican singing into the British pop mainstream. He died in 2014, leaving a songbook that later artists have never stopped versioning.

theparagons.blurb: The rocksteady group behind The Tide Is High.
theparagons.bio: The Paragons sang rocksteady and ska harmony in Kingston through the 1960s, and few groups of that decade blended better. They recorded for Duke Reid, whose spacious, horn-led arrangements suited their smooth, close-voiced sound perfectly. 'On the Beach' and 'Wear You to the Ball' both arrived in 1967 and remain rocksteady staples, versioned repeatedly by later singers and deejays. Their best-known song, 'The Tide Is High', came from the pen of their own John Holt and was cut the same year; it would go on to become a worldwide hit for others and one of the most widely known melodies to come out of Jamaica. Holt went on to a major solo career, but the group's records stand as a high point of the rocksteady era.

heptones.blurb: Studio One's great three-part harmony trio.
heptones.bio: The Heptones are a Jamaican vocal trio whose strongest years ran through the 1960s and into the early 1970s, and whose three-part harmony helped carry the island's music out of ska, through rocksteady and into reggae. With Leroy Sibbles in the lineup, they stood as contemporaries and equals of the Wailers and the Maytals. They recorded for Coxsone Dodd at Studio One, where 'Fattie Fattie' in 1966 became their first single for the label and a scandalous local hit. 'Book of Rules' in 1973 showed the group at its most reflective, a piece of sung philosophy that has outlived its era, and 'Party Time' followed in 1977 under the hand of Lee Perry. Few groups sit so squarely at the centre of the Jamaican songbook.

leroysibbles.blurb: The Heptones' lead voice and bass player.
leroysibbles.bio: Leroy Sibbles, born in 1949, is a Jamaican singer, bass player and producer who occupies two important places in reggae at once. As lead voice of the Heptones through the 1960s and 1970s he sang some of the most enduring harmony records made in Kingston, and at Studio One he recorded with Coxsone Dodd, laying down basslines that were versioned again and again for decades afterwards. A great deal of the foundation catalogue rests on parts he played. Under his own name he cut 'Express Yourself' for Studio One in 1971 and 'Garden of Life' in 1979, his best-known solo single. Singer and session musician in equal measure, he is one of the figures whose work shaped the sound of Jamaican music from inside the studio as well as in front of the microphone.

delroywilson.blurb: Jamaica's first child star, then rocksteady mainstay.
delroywilson.bio: Delroy Wilson, born in 1948, was a Jamaican singer of ska, rocksteady and reggae, often regarded as the island's first child star: he was cutting records for Coxsone Dodd at Studio One while still a teenager, and 'I'm Still Waiting' in 1965 already showed a voice of unusual poise. Alton Ellis, who mentored him, was a guiding presence through those early studio years. 'Dancing Mood' in 1966 became an early rocksteady smash and remains one of the era's essential records, all easy swing and lightness of touch. In 1971 'Better Must Come' gave Jamaica something rarer still, a hopeful song taken up as a PNP campaign anthem. He died in 1995. His youngest son, Karl Wilson, records as Konan in the British duo Krept and Konan.

phyllisdillon.blurb: The pure soprano of Treasure Isle rocksteady.
phyllisdillon.bio: Phyllis Dillon, born in Jamaica in 1944, was the reigning female voice of rocksteady, a clear and unhurried soprano that could turn a love song into something close to a hymn. She recorded through the late 1960s and early 1970s for Duke Reid at his Treasure Isle label, whose lush rhythms defined the era, and her sessions were carried by Tommy McCook and the house players who gave those records their glide. 'Perfidia' in 1967 remade a bolero standard as Jamaican pop; 'Don't Stay Away', from the same year, and 'One Life to Live' in 1969 confirmed her as Reid's most reliable star. She sang with restraint rather than force, which is why the records still sound modern rather than merely old. Dillon died in 2004, her Treasure Isle sides long since accepted as standards.

hoptonlewis.blurb: The singer who slowed ska into rocksteady.
hoptonlewis.bio: Hopeton Lewis, born in Jamaica in 1947, was a singer, arranger and later radio presenter whose 1966 hit 'Take It Easy' is widely counted as the record that opened the rocksteady era. The story is in the title: the ska beat dropped its gallop, the tempo eased, and a singer suddenly had room to phrase. 'Sounds and Pressure', from the same year, pushed the new feel further, and 'Grooving Out on Life' in 1971 showed how comfortably his warm, conversational delivery sat on top of it. He worked in parallel with Alton Ellis, the other great voice of that changeover, and between them they set a template that reggae singers would inherit. Lewis kept performing and broadcasting for decades, and died in 2014, remembered as one of rocksteady's founding voices.

bobandy.bio: Bob Andy, born Keith Anderson in Jamaica in 1944, was a vocalist and, above all, a songwriter, widely regarded as the most influential writer reggae produced. He came up at Clement 'Coxsone' Dodd's Studio One, where 'I've Got to Go Back Home' in 1966 became both his breakthrough and his signature: a song about leaving that Jamaica took as its own. 'Too Experienced', in 1967, entered the rocksteady canon and has been covered ever since by singers who often had no idea who wrote it. His partnership with Marcia Griffiths gave him his widest audience, their 1970 reading of 'Young, Gifted and Black' reaching number five in Britain. Andy wrote with unusual interiority, plain language carrying real weight, and his songs passed into the repertoire of generations. He died in 2020.

marciagriffiths.blurb: The Queen of Reggae, still recording.
marciagriffiths.bio: Marcia Griffiths, born in Jamaica in 1949, has been called the Queen of Reggae, and few careers justify a title so thoroughly. She broke through at Studio One with 'Feel Like Jumping' in 1968, then formed one of reggae's great duos with Bob Andy, their 1970 version of 'Young, Gifted and Black' reaching number five in Britain. She also sang alongside Rita Marley and Judy Mowatt in the harmony trio behind Bob Marley, a role that put her voice on some of the most widely heard records ever made in Jamaica. Then came 'Electric Boogie' in 1982, the song that gave the Electric Slide line dance its music and outsold every other single by a woman in reggae. Griffiths is still recording, a living link between Studio One and everything that followed.

slimsmith.blurb: The most aching voice of rocksteady.
slimsmith.bio: Slim Smith, born in Jamaica in 1948, sang rocksteady with a catch in his voice that nobody else quite matched; one standard history of the music calls him simply the greatest vocalist the era produced. He sang beside Jimmy Riley as a bandmate and recorded under Winston Riley's production, but his best-known sides came from Studio One in 1967, where 'Never Let Go' and its double-sider 'Rougher Yet' arrived together and 'The New Boss' followed. His singing carried a gospel intensity into secular songs of longing and pride, and it shaped how the young Jamaican tenor was expected to sound for a decade afterwards. He worked at the same moment as Alton Ellis, at the height of the form. Smith died in 1973, still in his twenties, leaving a small catalogue later singers kept returning to.

kingtubby.bio: King Tubby, born Osbourne Ruddock in Jamaica in 1941, was an electronics and sound engineer who turned the mixing desk into an instrument and, in doing so, brought dub into being. Working from his own small studio, he stripped the vocals away from finished rhythms, drenched what remained in reverb and delay, and let bass and drum carry everything, a method that reordered how records could be made anywhere. He mixed for Bunny 'Striker' Lee, cut sides with Johnny Clarke, Linval Thompson and Mikey Dread, and traded ideas with Lee 'Scratch' Perry. 'King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown', made with Augustus Pablo in 1976, remains dub's defining album; 'Dub You Can Feel' in 1975 shows the method in full flow. He trained Scientist and King Jammy, and shaped later artists from Alborosie to Fat Freddy's Drop. Tubby died in 1989.

leeperry.blurb: The Black Ark alchemist of Jamaican production.
leeperry.bio: Lee 'Scratch' Perry, born in Jamaica in 1936, was a producer, singer and songwriter whose studio functioned less as a workplace than as a laboratory. At his Black Ark he layered, echoed and half-buried sounds until reggae records took on a murky, three-dimensional depth nobody had heard before, and in doing so he became, with King Tubby, a founder of dub. He produced Bob Marley in the formative years, cut 'Police and Thieves' with Junior Murvin in 1976, made 'War Ina Babylon' with Max Romeo the same year and 'Curly Locks' with Junior Byles in 1974, and led his own house band, The Upsetters. He worked with The Congos, with Sly and Robbie, with Dillinger, and later with Mad Professor. Perry stayed strange and prolific until his death in 2021, an acknowledged ancestor of remix culture everywhere.

bunnylee.blurb: Prolific producer at the heart of dub.
bunnylee.bio: Bunny 'Striker' Lee, 1941 to 2020, was among Jamaica's most prolific producers and a constant presence through the dub years. He cut Delroy Wilson's 'Better Must Come' in 1971 and Johnny Clarke's 'None Shall Escape the Judgement' in 1974 and 'Move Out of Babylon' in 1975, also producing John Holt and Cornell Campbell. His rhythms were King Tubby's raw material.

niney.blurb: Producer of roots reggae's fiercest anthems.
niney.bio: Niney the Observer, born in Jamaica in 1944, is a producer of the roots era. His own 'Blood and Fire' in 1970 became an anthem of the new militancy, and his long work with Dennis Brown gave reggae 'Money in My Pocket' in 1972 and 'Westbound Train' in 1973, the records that turned a young singer into a star.

joegibbs.blurb: The producer who made roots reggae pop.
joegibbs.bio: Joe Gibbs, who lived from 1942 to 2008, was one of the defining Jamaican producers of the 1970s, a hit-maker with an ear for the exact moment a rhythm turns catchy. Working closely with the engineer Errol Thompson, he assembled a run of records that carried roots reggae out of Jamaica and into the British charts. He produced Culture's 'Two Sevens Clash' in 1977, the apocalyptic warning that became the defining roots album of its year, and in the same year cut Althea and Donna's 'Uptown Top Ranking', a teenage deejay record that crossed over completely. His long association with Dennis Brown produced the 1979 re-cut of 'Money in My Pocket', the version that made Brown a star in Britain. Gibbs proved that roots seriousness and pop instinct could share a single record.

augustuspablo.blurb: The melodica voice of dub's meditative side.
augustuspablo.bio: Augustus Pablo, born Horace Swaby in Jamaica in 1953, took a schoolroom instrument, the melodica, and made it the loneliest and most recognisable sound in reggae. The brooding minor-key mood of his playing gave dub a meditative streak that ran against the music's dancehall energy. 'Java' in 1972 announced it as an instrumental hit, and 'East of the River Nile' in 1977 extended it into a full album statement. His collaboration with King Tubby produced 'King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown' in 1976, generally held to be the greatest dub album ever made, Pablo's melodica floating over Tubby's mixes like weather. He was a composer and producer as well as a player, working most notably with the singer Jacob Miller. Pablo died in 1999, and nobody has convincingly claimed his instrument since.

scientist.blurb: King Tubby's protege, dub's second generation.
scientist.bio: Scientist, born Hopeton Overton Brown in Jamaica in 1960, learned dub at King Tubby's mixing desk and then carried it into the 1980s with a sharper, cleaner sound of his own. As Tubby's protege he came up among the engineers who had built the vocabulary in the 1970s, and he treated the desk with the same freedom, dropping instruments in and out and letting echo do the arranging. 'Taxi to Baltimore Dub' and 'Drum Song Dub', both from Scientific Dub in 1981, show the method at its most economical: a rhythm reduced to bass, drum and space. Much of his strongest work was cut over rhythms by the Roots Radics, the band that defined the decade's heavier, slower feel. For a great many listeners outside Jamaica, his mixes were the first dub they ever heard.

kingjammy.blurb: The producer who made reggae go digital.
kingjammy.bio: King Jammy, born Lloyd James in Jamaica in 1947, began as a dub mixer at King Tubby's studio, where he earned a reputation for mixes of unusual clarity, and ended up redirecting the music entirely. Recording as Prince Jammy he cut 'Ism Skism' with Wayne Smith in 1982 and produced Half Pint's 'One in a Million' in 1984, but it was 'Under Me Sleng Teng' in 1985, again with Wayne Smith, that broke the ground: a stark, wholly electronic rhythm that made the session band optional and set off the digital dancehall era. He produced Nitty Gritty, Cocoa Tea, Admiral Bailey, Pinchers and Little John through the boom that followed, kept pace with peers like Steely and Clevie, and trained Bobby Digital. Few single records have redirected a genre so completely.

slyrobbie.blurb: Reggae's greatest rhythm section and production duo.
slyrobbie.bio: Sly and Robbie were the drummer Sly Dunbar and the bassist Robbie Shakespeare, two Jamaican players who had each built a reputation alone before pairing up around the middle of the 1970s, and who between them turned up on hundreds of records. As a unit they were unmistakable: a drum sound that kept shifting with the times and a bass that never hurried. They played behind Peter Tosh, The Mighty Diamonds, Gregory Isaacs, Barrington Levy, Half Pint and Michael Rose, produced Black Uhuru, and worked with Lee 'Scratch' Perry and Gussie Clarke. They also made hits in their own right, including 'Boops (Here to Go)' in 1987, which reached number twelve in Britain, and their production of Chaka Demus and Pliers' 'Murder She Wrote' in 1992 became one of dancehall's most enduring records. No pairing shaped more of reggae's sound.

familyman.blurb: The bass that anchored Bob Marley's Wailers.
familyman.bio: Aston 'Family Man' Barrett, born in Jamaica in 1946, was the bassist and bandleader of Bob Marley and the Wailers, and one of the quietly decisive figures in reggae. He did more than hold the bottom end: he co-produced the albums and took charge of the arrangements, deciding how each song would be built around Marley's voice. With the drummer Carlton Barrett he formed a rhythm section first heard with The Upsetters and then at the centre of everything the Wailers recorded, from 'Stir It Up' on Catch a Fire in 1973 through 'Jamming' on Exodus in 1977 to 'Could You Be Loved' on Uprising in 1980. His lines are melodies in their own right, patient and unmistakable. He later recorded with Alpha Blondy, and kept the Wailers band going until his death in 2024.

carltonbarrett.blurb: The drummer behind reggae's one drop.
carltonbarrett.bio: Carlton Barrett, born in Jamaica in 1950, was the drummer of Bob Marley and the Wailers, and the man who carried the one drop into common use, the rhythm that hands the weight to the third beat and leaves the first one open. His playing was more intricate than that description suggests: broken triplets flicked across the hi-hat in tight syncopation, and startling introductions that other drummers learned by heart. He worked in permanent partnership with the bassist Aston 'Family Man' Barrett, the two of them forming the engine of the band. 'Get Up, Stand Up' on Burnin' in 1973, the title track of Exodus in 1977 and 'One Drop' on Survival in 1979 all show what he could do inside a groove that never seems to hurry. His life ended in 1987.

jackiemittoo.blurb: Studio One's musical director and organ master.
jackiemittoo.bio: Jackie Mittoo, born Donat Roy Mittoo in Jamaica in 1948, was a keyboardist, songwriter and musical director whose fingerprints are on more Jamaican records than almost anyone's. He played in the Skatalites during the ska years and then became musical director at Clement 'Coxsone' Dodd's Studio One, where he arranged sessions, wrote rhythms and cut a steady stream of organ instrumentals under his own name. 'Drum Song' in 1967 became his most-sampled composition, a rhythm later generations built on again and again; 'Darker Shade of Black' from the same year and 'Hot Milk' in 1968 show the same taste for a simple hooking figure played with total authority. He later settled in Canada and kept recording. Mittoo died in 1990, having supplied the raw material for decades of reggae and dancehall.

bobmarley.blurb: The voice that carried reggae to the world.
bobmarley.bio: Bob Marley, born in Jamaica in 1945, is the figure through whom most of the world met reggae. He began in the harmony group the Wailers with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer, recorded a formative run of sides under Lee 'Scratch' Perry, and built his mature band on Aston 'Family Man' Barrett's bass and Carlton Barrett's drums, with Marcia Griffiths among his harmony singers. His songs joined a plain, indelible melodic gift to Rastafarian spirituality and outspoken politics, and he used the platform to argue for democratic reform and pan-Africanism. 'No Woman, No Cry' in 1974, 'One Love / People Get Ready' on Exodus in 1977 and 'Redemption Song' on Uprising in 1980 have long since passed out of one genre and into common property. He stood among peers like Toots Hibbert, Jimmy Cliff and Dennis Brown, and died in 1981, by then a figure the whole world recognised.

petertosh.blurb: The Wailers' militant, uncompromising second voice.
petertosh.bio: Peter Tosh, born in Jamaica in 1944, was a core member of the Wailers from 1963 until 1976, alongside Bob Marley and Bunny Wailer, and then a solo artist who made confrontation his subject. Where the group's records balanced anger with sweetness, Tosh sharpened them. He co-wrote 'Get Up, Stand Up' with Marley in 1973, and his solo titles read as manifestos: 'Legalize It' in 1976 arguing openly for cannabis, 'Equal Rights' in 1977 demanding justice rather than calm. He was a guitarist as well as a singer, and he recorded with the rhythm section of Sly and Robbie, whose weight suited his blunt delivery. A committed promoter of Rastafari, he refused to soften his politics for an international audience. Tosh was murdered during a home invasion in 1987, and remains an influence on later singers such as Lucky Dube.

bunnywailer.blurb: The Wailers' third voice, roots to the core.
bunnywailer.bio: Bunny Wailer, born Neville O'Riley Livingston in Jamaica in 1947, was a singer, songwriter and percussionist, and an original member of the Wailers with Bob Marley and Peter Tosh. When the trio came apart he went his own way, and his 1976 solo debut Blackheart Man showed what he valued: patient, hymn-like songs steeped in Rastafarian devotion, carried by one of reggae's most distinctive voices, high and slightly withdrawn. The title track, 'Dream Land' and 'Rastaman' all come from that record, and none of them concedes anything to an international rock audience. He won three Grammy Awards in the decades that followed and was regarded as a standard-bearer for the music, the keeper of what the Wailers had originally meant. He died in 2021, an original Wailer to the end.

burningspear.blurb: Roots reggae's deepest historian and chanter.
burningspear.bio: Burning Spear, born Winston Rodney in Jamaica in 1945, has spent half a century turning Jamaican history into song. He first recorded for Clement 'Coxsone' Dodd, but it was the Marcus Garvey album of 1975 that fixed his identity: the title track set Garvey's teachings to a slow, hypnotic rhythm, and 'Slavery Days', from the same record, made remembrance itself the subject. His voice is closer to chant than to croon, circling a phrase until it becomes an incantation, and the horns and hand drums around it give the records a ceremonial weight. 'Social Living' in 1978 carried the same seriousness into a leaner sound. A Rastafarian and one of the longest-standing roots artists of the 1970s generation, he remains a direct influence on younger singers such as Chronixx.

dennisbrown.bio: Dennis Brown, born in Jamaica in 1957, started recording at eleven and never really stopped, leaving more than seventy-five albums behind him. Bob Marley called him his favourite singer and gave him the name that stuck, the Crown Prince of Reggae. The voice was smooth, warm and unforced, equally at home in lovers rock and in roots. He cut the original 'Money in My Pocket' for Niney the Observer in 1972 and recorded it again years later for Joe Gibbs, who produced much of his best-known work; 'Wolf and Leopards' in 1977 and 'Here I Come' in 1978 caught him at his peak. He also recorded for Clement 'Coxsone' Dodd, worked with the saxophonist Dean Fraser and the engineer Errol Thompson, and sang with Gregory Isaacs. He died in 1999, having shaped nearly every reggae singer who followed, Buju Banton among them.

uroy.blurb: The originator of the deejay art.
uroy.bio: U-Roy, born Ewart Beckford in Jamaica in 1942, is the man who made talking over a record into an art form. Working with Duke Reid, he took the producer's rocksteady rhythms, already several years old, and rode them with a melodic, perfectly timed stream of exhortation and comment, turning old hits into new ones. In 1970 'Wake the Town', 'Rule the Nation' and 'Wear You to the Ball' arrived in quick succession and rewrote what a Jamaican single could be. What he invented, the deejay style, ran straight through Jamaican music into dancehall and beyond. He mentored Big Youth, worked alongside his peer I-Roy, and stayed a presence on sound systems and stages for another fifty years. U-Roy died in 2021, his sense of timing never bettered.

iroy.blurb: The wittiest deejay of the roots era.
iroy.bio: I-Roy, born Roy Samuel Reid in Jamaica in 1944, was among the most prolific deejays of the 1970s, and among the most articulate. Where others chanted, he talked, in a dry, well-spoken voice that made room for jokes, boasts and social observation, and he could fill a rhythm without ever crowding the music underneath. 'Sidewalk Killer' in 1972 rode Tommy McCook's 'Sidewalk Doctor', and 'Black Man Time', from his 1973 album Presenting I Roy, showed how much substance the style could carry. 'Welding', cut at Channel One in 1975, caught him on the harder rhythms of the mid-decade. He worked alongside his peer U-Roy at the height of the form and collaborated with Dillinger. His run through the decade helped make the deejay a headline artist rather than an accompaniment.

bigyouth.blurb: The chanting deejay who preached Rastafari.
bigyouth.bio: Big Youth, born Manley Augustus Buchanan in Jamaica in 1949, was the deejay who took the style U-Roy invented and filled it with Rastafarian conviction. His voice was rougher and more urgent than his mentor's, and where the first generation had mostly celebrated, he testified. 'S.90 Skank' in 1972, produced by Keith Hudson, was the breakthrough, and the following year 'Screaming Target' gave its title to a debut album that stands among the essential deejay records; 'Hit the Road Jack' came from the same period. He worked amid a generation of peers including Prince Far I and Tapper Zukie, all of them pushing the deejay from entertainer towards preacher, and his best work still sounds like a man thinking aloud over a rhythm. Big Youth remains one of the definitive voices of the roots era.

dillinger.blurb: Second-wave deejay with an unlikely signature hit.
dillinger.bio: Dillinger, born Lester Bullock in Jamaica in 1953, arrived with the deejays of the mid-1970s, a second generation who inherited a style already established and pushed it somewhere stranger. He had a light, insinuating delivery and an ear for the absurd hook. 'Cokane in My Brain', from the 1976 album CB 200, became the record most people know him by, a nonsense-verse chant riding a rock-solid rhythm; 'Crank Face' came from the same album, and 'Marijuana in My Brain' followed in 1977 with a knowing sequel's logic. He recorded with Lee 'Scratch' Perry and collaborated with I-Roy, two very different senior figures, and moved easily between the roots studios of the era. Dillinger showed how far the deejay style could travel once it left the dancehall behind.

princefari.blurb: The voice of thunder in roots reggae.
princefari.bio: Prince Far I, born in Jamaica in 1944, was a deejay and producer with a voice like gravel and a preacher's cadence, so distinctive that his records seem to shake as they play. He used it to indict the Jamaican government: 'Under Heavy Manners' in 1976 took its title from the measures announced against violent crime and turned the phrase back on the authorities. 'Black Man Land', from the same year, is cut from the same cloth, and 'Deck of Cards' in 1977 shows his gift for recitation, holding an audience with nothing but rhythm and speech. A Rastafarian who chanted rather than sang, he stood beside peers such as Big Youth and Mutabaruka, and his collaboration with the producer Adrian Sherwood carried the roots chant to new listeners. He died in 1983.

tappazukie.blurb: Deejay and producer of the militant era.
tappazukie.bio: Tapper Zukie, born in Jamaica in 1955, is a deejay and producer who arrived at the moment when the Jamaican deejay was at his most militant. 'MPLA', released in 1976, is his signature: a chant of solidarity named after the Angolan liberation movement, riding a rhythm stripped back to its bones, and it made his name well beyond the dancehall. 'Oh Lord' and 'Pick Up the Rockers', both from the same year, show the same combination of spare delivery and heavy backing. He belonged to the generation of Big Youth and the roots chanters, and like several of them he moved behind the mixing desk as well, producing other artists rather than only voicing rhythms of his own. That double role has kept him working across the decades since.

culture.blurb: The roots group behind Two Sevens Clash.
culture.bio: Culture were a roots reggae group out of Jamaica, formed in 1976 and known at first as the African Disciples, built around the voice of Joseph Hill, the single fixed point in the line-up until he died in 2006. Their subject was prophecy. 'Two Sevens Clash', produced by Joe Gibbs and released in 1977, took a Rastafarian reading of the calendar and turned it into a warning, and it became one of the defining albums of the roots era. 'See Them a Come' and 'I'm Not Ashamed', from the same year, share its mixture of harmony singing and unblinking judgement. Hill sang with a rasping urgency that the harmony voices behind him smoothed out, a contrast that gave the group its character. Culture kept the roots message intact long after fashion had moved on, and carried it to audiences worldwide.

abyssinians.blurb: Close-harmony architects of the Rastafari anthem.
abyssinians.bio: The Abyssinians formed in Jamaica in 1968 and are remembered for two things: close harmony singing of exceptional beauty, and lyrics that placed the Rastafari movement at the centre of reggae. 'Satta Massagana', cut in 1969 for Clement 'Coxsone' Dodd, is the group's monument, a slow minor-key hymn that became an anthem of the faith and a rhythm later singers returned to again and again. 'Declaration of Rights' followed in 1971 with the same grave, patient delivery, and 'Y Mas Gan' in 1976 kept the devotional thread going. Their sound is unhurried and almost churchlike, voices moving together rather than one leading and the rest supporting, and it gave roots reggae much of its spiritual vocabulary. Few groups with so small a catalogue have left so deep a mark.

mightydiamonds.blurb: Jamaican harmony trio of the roots era.
mightydiamonds.bio: The Mighty Diamonds came together in Jamaica in 1969 and became one of the most graceful vocal groups of the roots reggae era. Their close three-part singing carried a strong Rastafarian message, and their 1976 debut 'Right Time', produced by Joseph Hoo Kim, stands among the defining albums of the period. The title song, along with 'Have Mercy' and 'I Need a Roof', matched sweet lovers-style harmony with hard words about poverty, judgement and survival in Kingston. 'Deeper Roots' followed in 1979. Across a long career the Diamonds worked with the rhythm section of Sly and Robbie, whose drum and bass shaped much of the reggae that came after them. They proved that three voices in close harmony could carry the full weight of roots consciousness, and generations of Jamaican vocal groups took the lesson.

blackuhuru.blurb: Militant roots group powered by Sly and Robbie.
blackuhuru.bio: Black Uhuru formed in Jamaica in 1972, at first simply as Uhuru, and became the hardest and most militant of the great roots vocal groups. Line-ups changed often around the mainstay Derrick Duckie Simpson, with Michael Rose supplying the keening lead voice of the classic years. Their records were driven by the rhythm section of Sly and Robbie, whose stark, mechanised drum and bass gave 'Guess Who's Coming to Dinner' and 'Shine Eye Gal' in 1979, and 'Sponji Reggae' in 1981, a weight no other group of the time could match. That partnership carried them onto international stages alongside peers such as Grace Jones, and in 1985 their album 'Anthem' won the first Grammy Award ever given for Best Reggae Album. Black Uhuru remain the sound of roots reggae turning modern.

israelvibration.blurb: Kingston harmony trio of unshakable roots devotion.
israelvibration.bio: Israel Vibration are a roots reggae harmony group from Kingston, formed in 1976 by Cecil Skelly Spence, Lascelle Wiss Bulgin and Albert Apple Gabriel Craig. Each of the three had contracted polio as a child, and they first met at a rehabilitation centre, and that shared history gives their singing an extraordinary steadiness: three plain, unpolished voices leaning into one another rather than reaching for showmanship. 'The Same Song' and 'Crisis', both from 1978, established them as one of the most devout groups of the roots era, while 'Ball of Fire' in 1980 confirmed the sound. They sang Rastafari faith as lived experience rather than doctrine, a quality that placed them close to peers such as Horace Andy. Israel Vibration have remained working singers for decades, and their harmonies are among the most instantly recognisable in Jamaican music.

wailingsouls.blurb: Studio One harmony group of remarkable durability.
wailingsouls.bio: The Wailing Souls trace their origins to Jamaica in the 1960s, and across many changes of line-up the voices of Lloyd Bread McDonald and Winston Pipe Matthews have remained constant. They came up through Studio One under Clement Coxsone Dodd, learning the discipline of harmony singing in the same rooms that trained most of the island's great groups, and they carried it forward into the roots years and beyond. 'War' and 'Bredda Gravalicious', both from 1979, and 'Things and Time' from 1981 show the group at full strength, tough, unhurried and beautifully blended. Their durability is remarkable: across a career spanning decades they have picked up three Grammy nominations. Few Jamaican groups have held a sound so consistent for so long without ever settling into nostalgia.

congos.blurb: Falsetto harmony reborn in Lee Perry's Black Ark.
congos.bio: The Congos formed in Jamaica in the mid-1970s as a duo, the tenor of Ashanti Roy Johnson set against the high falsetto of Cedric Myton, later becoming a trio with the baritone of Watty Burnett. That unusual spread of voices found its perfect setting with the producer Lee Scratch Perry, who recorded their album 'Heart of the Congos'. 'Fisherman', 'Congoman' and 'Row Fisherman Row', all from 1977, are the heart of it, songs built on biblical imagery and Rastafarian devotion, sunk in echo and layered until the voices seem to come from inside the rhythm rather than above it. Widely regarded as one of the greatest reggae albums ever made, it changed how producers think about space and texture. The Congos have worked on and off from that moment to the present day.

maxromeo.blurb: Protest singer behind Chase the Devil.
maxromeo.bio: Max Romeo, born in Jamaica in 1944, was one of reggae's great topical singers, a songwriter who moved from bawdy early hits to some of the fiercest protest music the island produced. He first found success with the vocal group the Emotions, then scored a notorious solo hit with 'Wet Dream' in 1968, whose frank lyrics opened a whole new lane in Jamaican pop. His lasting work came with Lee Scratch Perry, whose productions gave the 1976 album 'War Ina Babylon' its swampy, hallucinatory depth. 'Chase the Devil' from those sessions, with its image of the sinner sent flying out into space, became one of the most borrowed records in all of reggae, while 'One Step Forward' and the title track carried plain political anger. Romeo kept working until his death in 2025.

horaceandy.blurb: Trembling tenor of Skylarking and beyond.
horaceandy.bio: Horace Andy, born in Jamaica in 1951, has one of the most distinctive voices in reggae, a light, trembling tenor that sounds fragile and utterly certain at the same time. He made his name at Studio One under Clement Coxsone Dodd, where 'Skylarking' in 1972 became a defining Jamaican record, followed by 'Government Land' the same year and 'Money Money' in 1973. Where peers such as Israel Vibration sang in close harmony, Andy has always been a solo voice, floating above the rhythm. His songs 'Angel' and 'Spying Glass' and his reading of 'Ain't No Sunshine' show the same quality, and his long association with the English trip hop group Massive Attack, including 'Five Man Army', carried that voice far outside reggae. He has also worked with the dub engineer Mad Professor.

gregoryisaacs.blurb: The cool, wounded voice of Night Nurse.
gregoryisaacs.bio: Gregory Isaacs, born in Jamaica in 1951, was reggae's supreme romantic singer, a performer whose cool, wounded delivery made even the hardest rhythms sound like late-night confidences. The New York Times judged him the most exquisite vocalist the music had produced, and 'Night Nurse' in 1982 remains his signature, a song so smooth that its ache is easy to miss. 'Soon Forward' in 1979 and 'Front Door' in 1981 show the same balance of sweetness and menace. He recorded across the eras with the rhythm section of Sly and Robbie and with the Roots Radics, the band that defined early dancehall, and he shared both stages and songs with Dennis Brown and with his peer Sugar Minott. Isaacs died in 2010, having set the template for nearly every reggae love song that followed.

johnnyclarke.blurb: Flying cymbals hitmaker for Bunny Lee.
johnnyclarke.bio: Johnny Clarke, born in Jamaica in 1955, was the defining voice of the mid-1970s Bunny Striker Lee production line, the singer who carried the flying cymbals sound to the top of the Jamaican charts. 'None Shall Escape the Judgement' in 1974 is the record that made him, its hissing hi-hat pattern and stern Rastafarian warning becoming the template for a whole run of hits. 'Move Out of Babylon' followed in 1975, backed by Lee's studio band the Aggrovators, along with his own cut of the Abyssinians song 'Declaration of Rights'. Because Lee sent his rhythms straight on to King Tubby, Clarke's voice also sits at the centre of the early dub explosion, on countless versions mixed at Tubby's board. He later recorded for the singer and producer Linval Thompson.

juniormurvin.blurb: High voice behind Police and Thieves.
juniormurvin.bio: Junior Murvin, born in Jamaica in 1946, was a singer and guitarist whose high, keening voice made him one of the most recognisable vocalists of the roots era. His name rests above all on 'Police and Thieves', recorded in 1976 with Lee Scratch Perry, a song about street violence and state violence that became an anthem in Jamaica and far beyond it. 'Roots Train' followed from the same album in 1977, and 'Cool Out Son' arrived in 1979 from the Joe Gibbs camp. Perry's production is inseparable from the effect: the voice floats high and clear while the rhythm underneath stays soft, murky and endlessly detailed. Murvin also worked in soul and later as a film producer, but he is remembered for one of the most enduring songs reggae ever produced. He died in 2013.

ijahmanlevi.blurb: Devotional roots chanter of Haile I Hymn.
ijahmanlevi.bio: Ijahman Levi, born in Jamaica in 1946 and long resident in Britain, is a conscious roots chanter whose music sits closer to devotional song than to the dance. He was tutored in his early years by Joe Higgs, the vocal teacher who trained much of the first generation of Jamaican singers, and he took the name Ijahman Levi after converting to Rastafari while in prison between 1972 and 1974. His first album, 'Haile I Hymn', appeared on Island Records in 1978 and carried the long, hymnlike 'Jah Heavy Load' along with a reworking of 'I'm a Levi'. 'Are We a Warrior' followed as the title track of his second album in 1979. His records preach Rastafari and Twelve Tribes of Israel doctrine, and place him among peers such as Bob Marley.

judymowatt.blurb: I Threes singer who made Black Woman.
judymowatt.bio: Judy Mowatt, born in Jamaica in 1952, is a singer and songwriter who did more than almost anyone to give women a voice in roots reggae. From 1974 she sang in the I Threes, the trio that backed Bob Marley and the Wailers alongside Rita Marley and Marcia Griffiths, and that platform carried her around the world. Her own album 'Black Woman' in 1979 is the record that matters most, a work of quiet authority whose title track became her signature and whose self-penned 'Slave Queen' set the condition of Jamaican women inside a Rastafarian frame. 'Sisters Chant', from the same album, has the same devotional cast. Written and sung from a woman's point of view at a moment when that was rare, 'Black Woman' remains one of the great roots albums.

ritamarley.blurb: I Threes singer and keeper of a legacy.
ritamarley.bio: Rita Marley, born in Cuba in 1946 and raised in Jamaica, is a singer whose life sits at the centre of reggae's best-known story and whose own music deserves a hearing on its own terms. With Marcia Griffiths and Judy Mowatt she formed the I Threes, the vocal trio that backed Bob Marley and the Wailers through the years of their greatest fame, her voice one of the three answering his on record after record. She was Marley's wife and later his widow, and she has gone on recording and working with the next generation, including Ziggy Marley. Her 1981 album 'Who Feels It Knows It' produced 'One Draw', a best-selling reggae single, alongside the title song and 'Many Are Called'. She remains a formidable figure in Jamaican music.

freddiemcgregor.blurb: Studio One prodigy turned enduring reggae statesman.
freddiemcgregor.bio: Freddie McGregor, born in Jamaica in 1956, is a singer, musician and record producer who has worked in reggae for almost his entire life, having started out at the age of seven. Growing up under Clement Coxsone Dodd at Studio One gave him a grounding in harmony and discipline that later carried him through roots, lovers rock and dancehall without ever sounding out of place. 'Bobby Bobylon' in 1980, the title track of his Studio One album, is his roots statement, while 'Big Ship' in 1982 became the hit that defined him, a buoyant song still played wherever reggae is played. 'Push Comes to Shove' followed in 1984. He has recorded often with the saxophonist Dean Fraser and mentored younger singers, notably Luciano, extending the Studio One tradition of teaching into the modern era.

sugarminott.blurb: Roots singer who opened the door to dancehall.
sugarminott.bio: Sugar Minott, born in Jamaica in 1956, was a singer, a record producer and a sound-system man who stood exactly at the hinge between roots reggae and dancehall. He learned his craft at Studio One under Clement Coxsone Dodd, where he took to singing fresh lyrics over the label's older rhythms, a habit that became standard method for the dancehall generation. As a producer and sound-system man he gave many young Kingston singers their start, mentoring Barrington Levy among others. His own records ranged from the sweet, soul-inflected 'Good Thing Going', which reached number four in Britain in 1981, to 'Vanity' in 1983 and the Sly and Robbie production 'Herbman Hustling' in 1984. A peer of Gregory Isaacs, Minott died in 2010, as influential a talent-spotter as he was a singer.

ericdonaldson.blurb: Festival Song champion behind Cherry Oh Baby.
ericdonaldson.bio: Eric Donaldson, born in Jamaica in 1947, is a singer-songwriter from Saint Catherine whose name is inseparable from the island's annual Festival Song competition. 'Cherry Oh Baby' won that contest in 1971 and became his signature, a light, high-voiced song whose loping rhythm has been covered and versioned far outside reggae. 'Love of the Common People', cut for Dynamic Sounds the same year, showed his gift for turning a simple melody into something that sounds as though it had always existed, and 'Land of My Birth' in 1978 spoke plainly of home. Donaldson's music sits a little apart from the militant roots current running through the work of peers such as Bob Marley, closer to country soul and to Jamaican popular song. That warmth is exactly why the records have lasted.

cornellcampbell.blurb: Falsetto master known as the Gorgon.
cornellcampbell.bio: Cornell Campbell, born in Jamaica in 1945, is a singer known throughout reggae for his trademark falsetto, a light, boyish sound he has kept remarkably intact across six decades. He recorded at Studio One for Clement Coxsone Dodd in the late 1960s before finding his defining partnership in the 1970s with the producer Bunny Striker Lee. From that work came 'The Gorgon' in 1976, a swaggering piece of Kingston mythmaking that gave him both his biggest hit and the nickname Don Gorgon, and it was followed by 'Boxing Around' for Joe Gibbs in 1981. Campbell's voice cuts through the heavy rhythms of the period without ever forcing, which is why singers as different as roots chanters and lovers-rock crooners have looked to him. He remains one of reggae's great survivors.

johnnyosbourne.blurb: Roots singer who crossed into digital dancehall.
johnnyosbourne.bio: Johnny Osbourne, born in Jamaica in 1948, is a singer whose career bridges the roots era and the dancehall boom that followed. His 1980 album 'Truths and Rights', made at Studio One for Clement Coxsone Dodd, is the roots landmark, its title track a plain call for justice that has been versioned endlessly since. From there he moved with the music: 'Water Pumping' in 1983 caught the harder, faster sound of the new decade, and in 1985 'Buddy Bye' rode the Sleng Teng rhythm for King Jammy, the digital track that changed Jamaican music overnight. Much of that later work was cut with the Roots Radics, the band that supplied the era with its rhythms. Osbourne's warm, elastic voice made him one of the few singers equally at home in both worlds.

linvalthompson.blurb: Roots singer turned prolific dancehall-era producer.
linvalthompson.bio: Linval Thompson, born in Jamaica in 1954, is a conscious roots vocalist who became one of the most productive producers of the late 1970s and early 1980s. His own records came first: 'Don't Cut Off Your Dreadlocks' and 'Jah Jah Is the Conqueror', both cut in 1976 with Bunny Striker Lee, staked out a devout Rastafarian position, and 'I Love Marijuana' in 1978 became his best-known track. He worked closely with King Tubby, whose mixes turned those rhythms into dub, and he moved steadily behind the desk himself, producing sessions for singers including Johnny Clarke. That double life as vocalist and producer is typical of Jamaican music, where the distance between the microphone and the mixing board has always been short. His productions helped carry roots reggae into the dancehall era.

thirdworld.blurb: Jamaica's polished crossover band of the seventies.
thirdworld.bio: Third World formed in Jamaica in 1973 and became the island's most polished crossover band, playing reggae shot through with soul, funk and disco. Where the roots groups of the period stripped the music down, Third World added keyboards, horn arrangements and a smooth vocal front, and the strategy worked: 'Now That We Found Love', from the album 'Journey to Addis', became a transatlantic hit in 1978, and 'Cool Meditation' followed in 1979. In 1982 they recorded 'Try Jah Love', written for them by Stevie Wonder, which showed how far outside reggae their audience now reached. Through many changes of line-up, Richard Daley has stayed with the band from its inception. Peers of Bob Marley and of Inner Circle, they proved that a Jamaican band could tour the world without leaving the music behind.

steelpulse.blurb: Birmingham's great British roots reggae band.
steelpulse.bio: Steel Pulse formed in 1975 in the Handsworth district of Birmingham, coming together at Handsworth Wood Boys School around David Hinds, Basil Gabbidon and the bassist Ronald McQueen, with Mykaell Riley also in the early line-up. They were the great British roots band, singing about racism and inner-city life in England with a directness Jamaican groups rarely attempted. 'Ku Klux Klan', their Island debut single in 1978, named white supremacist terror outright, and 'Prediction', also from 1978, taken from the album 'Handsworth Revolution', showed how sophisticated their arrangements had become. 'Your House' followed in 1979 on 'Tribute to the Martyrs'. No act from outside Jamaica had ever taken the Grammy for Best Reggae Album until they did, and eight more nominations followed; they stood alongside peers such as Aswad and Misty in Roots.

aswad.blurb: British reggae band with soul in its bones.
aswad.bio: Aswad formed in Britain in 1975 and became, with Steel Pulse, one of the two great British reggae bands, though their route was a different one. Where their peers sharpened the roots edge, Aswad folded in strong currents of soul and rhythm and blues, and the mixture eventually carried them into the pop charts. Their name is the Arabic word for black. 'Warrior Charge' in 1980 is the roots instrumental that made their reputation in the dances, while 'Don't Turn Around' reached number one in Britain in 1988 and 'Shine' returned them to the top five in 1994. Across more than twenty albums and three Grammy nominations they worked within the same British scene as Dennis Bovell, Maxi Priest and UB40, and shared stages with Jamaican singers such as Dennis Brown.

innercircle.blurb: Kingston band with two very different lives.
innercircle.bio: Inner Circle formed in Kingston in 1968 and have had two distinct lives. The first came in the 1970s, when the band backed The Chosen Few and then joined forces with the singer Jacob Miller, whose huge voice fronted a run of records including 'Tenement Yard' in 1976, one of the sharpest songs ever written about crowded Kingston living. That era ended abruptly in 1980, when Miller was killed in a car crash. The band regrouped and found an unlikely second act as international hitmakers, with 'Bad Boys' in 1987 becoming known worldwide as the theme to the television series COPS, and 'Sweat (A La La La La Long)' turning into a global hit in 1992. Peers of Third World, they carried Jamaican music to about the widest audience it has ever reached.

theupsetters.blurb: Lee Perry's house band at dub's origin.
theupsetters.bio: The Upsetters played house band to the Jamaican producer Lee Scratch Perry, taking their name from his own nickname, which came in turn from his song 'I Am the Upsetter', a record that dismissed his former boss Clement Coxsone Dodd. Assembled in 1968, the band gave Perry the raw material for everything that followed: 'Return of Django' in 1969 was an instrumental hit in Britain, 'Live Injection' from the same year is an early piece of proto-dub, and 'Clint Eastwood' in 1970 catches the spaghetti-western swagger the group loved. Their ranks passed through many of Jamaica's best players, among them the bassist Aston Family Man Barrett.
