Because Perry recorded them constantly and then took the results apart at the mixing desk, the Upsetters sit at the very origin of dub.

madprofessor.blurb: British dub engineer who kept the tradition alive.
madprofessor.bio: Mad Professor, born Neil Fraser in 1955, is a British-Guyanese dub engineer, producer and remixer who kept the form alive long after its Jamaican founders had moved on. Working from his own studio, he built a style that treats the mixing desk as an instrument, dropping parts in and out and drenching whatever remains in echo and reverb. He has recorded with reggae figures including Lee Scratch Perry and the singer Horace Andy, and with many artists from outside the music. His best-known work is the 1995 album that dubbed Massive Attack's 'Protection' from the ground up, yielding 'Radiation Ruling the Nation', 'Eternal Feedback' and 'Bumper Ball Dub', a version of 'Karmacoma'. Alongside his peer Adrian Sherwood, he made dub a living British art rather than a historical style.

adriansherwood.blurb: Dub producer who founded On-U Sound.
adriansherwood.bio: Adrian Sherwood, born in England in 1958, is a record producer who took the techniques of Jamaican dub and applied them to almost everything else. In 1979 he founded On-U Sound, the label that became home to his own extended family of musicians, among them Skip McDonald, Doug Wimbish and Keith LeBlanc, the players at the centre of Tackhead, a band he joined himself. He produced 'Mind At The End Of The Tether' for them in 1985, 'Off the Beaten Track' for African Head Charge in 1986 and, that same year, 'Hey Luciani' for The Fall. He has remixed work by Depeche Mode, Primal Scream, Coldcut and Sinead O'Connor among many others. A collaborator of Prince Far I and a peer of Mad Professor, he calls himself tone deaf and works purely by sound.

mikeydread.blurb: Broadcaster, singer and producer of roots radio.
mikeydread.bio: Mikey Dread, born Michael Campbell in Jamaica in 1954, was a singer, record producer and radio broadcaster, a rare combination that let him champion reggae from both sides of the microphone. His own records carried the same mission as his broadcasting: 'Roots and Culture' and 'Barber Saloon', both from 1979, the latter reaching number one on the reggae chart, followed by the roots single 'Break Down the Walls' in 1980. He worked with King Tubby, whose mixing board gave those tracks their depth, and produced widely himself, treating the studio as a place to build atmosphere rather than simply capture a song. Dread died in 2008, remembered as one of the figures who carried dub out of the mixing room and into everyday Jamaican listening.

rootsradics.blurb: The rhythm section that built early dancehall.
rootsradics.bio: The Roots Radics were formed in 1978 by the bassist Errol Flabba Holt, the guitarist Eric Bingy Bunny Lamont and the drummer Lincoln Style Scott, and they went on to dominate Jamaican music through the first half of the 1980s. Holt and Lamont had worked together before in the Morwells and in the Arabs, the band behind Prince Far I. What the Radics brought was a slower, heavier, sparser rhythm than the roots bands before them, and that sound became the foundation of early dancehall. They backed Gregory Isaacs, Johnny Osbourne, Barrington Levy, Bunny Wailer, Eek-A-Mouse, Half Pint and Israel Vibration, and their rhythms were raw material for the engineer Scientist, whose 1982 album gave them 'Dangerous Match One'. Almost every dancehall record of the era rests on their playing.

deanfraser.bio: Dean Fraser, born in Jamaica in 1957, is the saxophonist whose horn runs through an extraordinary share of the island's recorded music, having played on thousands of sessions since the mid-1970s. His debut 'Black Horn Man', produced by Joe Gibbs in 1978, announced a player with a big, singing tone who could carry a melody as convincingly as any vocalist. Since then he has been the first call for horn work across every era of reggae, recording with Dennis Brown and Freddie McGregor among countless others. In later years he has taken on the role of producer and mentor, guiding the career of the singer Tarrus Riley and playing on his records. The Jamaican government gave him the Musgrave Medal in 1993, honouring his long service to the music.

barringtonlevy.blurb: Soaring teenage voice of early dancehall.
barringtonlevy.bio: Barrington Levy, born in Jamaica in 1964, is a singer from Clarendon who arrived as a teenager and became one of the founding voices of dancehall. Sugar Minott took him under his wing early on, and the Roots Radics supplied the sparse, weighty rhythms his voice needed, a startling instrument full of swoops and wordless cries that could turn a plain line into a hook. 'Under Mi Sensi' and 'Murderer', both from 1984, are dancehall classics, the first of them cut with Jah Screw, and 'Here I Come' in 1985 carried him well beyond Jamaica on the strength of that soaring delivery. He has also recorded with the rhythm section of Sly and Robbie. Levy's phrasing shaped a generation of singers and deejays, and his hooks have been borrowed steadily ever since.

yellowman.bio: Yellowman, born Winston Foster in Jamaica in 1956, is the deejay who carried dancehall out of the Kingston sound systems and into the wider world. He became the island's most in-demand toaster in the early 1980s with a rush of singles including 'Mad Over Me' and the swaggering title cut of 1982's 'Mister Yellowman'. A year later 'Zungguzungguguzungguzeng' gave him an anthem whose singsong melody has been sampled, versioned and quoted across dancehall and hip hop ever since. Working the same dances as Eek-A-Mouse and Josey Wales, he perfected the deejay art of riding a riddim with wit, boast and comic timing, answering the crowd line by line. His style reached across the water to British deejays such as Smiley Culture. Crowned King Yellowman, he remains reggae's most imitated microphone voice.

eekamouse.blurb: Eccentric singjay who scatted over the riddim.
eekamouse.bio: Eek-A-Mouse, born Ripton Joseph Hylton in Jamaica in 1957, is one of the first artists ever described as a singjay, a performer who neither quite sings nor quite toasts but slides between the two. His trademark is a wordless scat of swooping nonsense syllables, a sound that set him apart from the straight-talking deejays around him in the early 1980s. 'Wa-Do-Dem' made his name in 1981, and the next year brought both the Junjo Lawes hit 'Ganja Smuggling' and 'Wild Like a Tiger'. He has always been as much a showman as a singer, given to flamboyant stage costume and dancing, on the principle that an audience comes to see something and not only to hear it. Alongside peers Yellowman and Josey Wales, he made the dancehall a stage for characters.

joseywales.bio: Josey Wales, born in Jamaica in 1959, is a dancehall deejay who took both his name and his nickname, The Outlaw, from the Clint Eastwood western of 1976. He came up through the sound systems with Charlie Chaplin as his partner on the microphone, the pair trading turns over the same riddims, and he is remembered alongside Chaplin, Brigadier Jerry and Yellowman as one of the finest Jamaican deejays of the 1980s. Junjo Lawes produced his breakthrough 'Leggo Mi Hand' in 1983, and the same year brought 'It Pays to Pray', a reminder that his toasting could turn from street talk to sermon within a bar. 'It's Raining' followed in 1984. His delivery is unhurried and conversational, the sound of a man who learned his craft in front of a live dance.

charliechaplin.blurb: Cultural deejay of the sound-system era.
charliechaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin, born in Jamaica in 1959, is a dancehall deejay from the golden age of the Jamaican sound systems. He cut 'Diet Rock' for producer George Phang in 1984 and 'Them Nuh Like We' the year after. He worked closely with Josey Wales and shared the cultural deejay ground of his peer Brigadier Jerry.

brigadierjerry.blurb: Cultural deejay who preached on the microphone.
brigadierjerry.bio: Brigadier Jerry, born Robert Russell in Jamaica in 1957, is a deejay known for cultural lyrics rather than slackness. Where much of the dancehall around him traded in boast and bawdry, his toasting carried Rastafari teaching and social comment, delivered in a steady, sermonising cadence built for the sound systems. Among his records are 'Pain', voiced on the Never Let Go riddim, together with 'Three Blind Mice' and 'Jah Jah Move', all from 1985. His peer Charlie Chaplin worked the same conscious ground, and the two are named together whenever the cultural deejays of the era are counted. In a decade remembered for its wildest entertainers, Brigadier Jerry made the case that a deejay could hold a crowd by preaching, and he remains a touchstone for artists who took dancehall seriously.

frankiepaul.bio: Frankie Paul, born Paul Blake in Jamaica in 1965, was one of the defining voices of 1980s dancehall, a singer of enormous range and easy emotional directness. Blind from birth, he was dubbed the Jamaican Stevie Wonder, a comparison that spoke to his phrasing and his ear as much as to his circumstances. 'Worries in the Dance' announced him in 1983, and 'Pass the Tu-Sheng-Peng' made him a star the following year, a record that still sums up the sound of the dance in that period. 'Sara' followed in 1987. Those records belong to the moment when a singer's job was to carry a warm melody over a rhythm built for the floor, and few did it more naturally. His peer Cocoa Tea shared the same era and the same gift. He died in 2017.

halfpint.blurb: Sweet-voiced dancehall singer covered by the Stones.
halfpint.bio: Half Pint, born Lindon Andrew Roberts in Jamaica in 1961, is a dancehall, ragga and reggae singer with a light, keening voice that cuts through the heaviest rhythm. He worked with the two great backing units of the era, the Roots Radics and the drum-and-bass partnership of Sly and Robbie, whose playing gave his records their spring. 'Winsome' arrived in 1983 and travelled further than most Jamaican singles of its moment: the Rolling Stones cut their own version of it as 'Too Rude'. 'Greetings' and 'Mr. Landlord' followed in 1985, the first a standing invitation to the dance, the second a complaint every tenant understood. His songs work as singalongs without losing their edge, which is why they have kept their place in sound-system sets ever since.

tenorsaw.blurb: Digital-era singjay behind Ring the Alarm.
tenorsaw.bio: Tenor Saw, born Clive Bright in Jamaica in 1966, was a singjay whose short career left one of the deepest marks on Jamaican music. His voice had a keening, hymn-like ache to it, and he used it to ride the new digital rhythms as though they were church organ. 'Ring the Alarm', cut for Winston Riley on the Stalag riddim in 1985, became the anthem of the moment and has been versioned ever since; the same year brought 'Pumpkin Belly', voiced on the Sleng Teng riddim, and 'Lots of Sign'. He belonged to a small group of singers, among them Nitty Gritty and Wayne Smith, who worked out what the digital era would sound like almost as it was being invented. He died in 1988, aged twenty-two, leaving records that have never left circulation.

nittygritty.blurb: Unmistakable voice of the first digital riddims.
nittygritty.bio: Nitty Gritty, born Glen Augustus Holness in the August Town district of Kingston in 1957, was a singer with one of the most distinctive deliveries of the early digital era, a voice no listener confuses with another. The second of eleven children in a religious household, he came through to record for King Jammy at the moment Jammy's studio was remaking Jamaican music from the rhythm up. 'Hog inna Minty', voiced on the Sleng Teng riddim in 1985, was his breakthrough, and 'Run Down the World' followed the same year, with 'Sweet Reggae Music' in 1986. He and his peer Tenor Saw were the two voices most closely identified with that first wave of computerised riddims, singers who could make a stiff electronic rhythm feel human. He died in 1991.

coccotea.blurb: Smooth tenor from dancehall to conscious reggae.
coccotea.bio: Cocoa Tea, born Colvin George Scott in Jamaica in 1959, was a reggae singer and songwriter whose smooth, unhurried tenor carried him from the dancehall boom through the digital era and well beyond it. 'Rocking Dolly' broke him in 1984 on Volcano, and 'Weh Dem a Go Do' followed in 1985 as the computerised riddims took hold. He voiced records for King Jammy, the producer setting the pace for the whole island, and shared the decade with his peer Frankie Paul. In 1991 'Rikers Island' showed the other side of him, a singer willing to turn a sweet melody towards hard subject matter. That balance of ease and comment ran through everything he did and made him a favourite of singers and sound systems alike. He died in 2025.

admiralbailey.blurb: Booming deejay of King Jammy's late eighties.
admiralbailey.bio: Admiral Bailey, born in Jamaica in 1963, is a deejay who was rated the hottest attraction dancehall had in the late 1980s. His records for King Jammy came in a rush in 1987, among them 'Punanny', 'Big Belly Man' and 'Healthy Body', riding the producer's computerised riddims with a booming, good-humoured delivery that could fill a dance without ever sounding strained. He worked the slack and the comic sides of the music with equal appetite, and his greatest success ran from the mid-1980s into the early 1990s, the years when Jammy's studio was turning out hit after hit and the deejay, not the singer, was the star attraction. He still lives in Jamaica, his best-known records still working every time a selector reaches for them.

waynesmith.blurb: Sang the record that digitised reggae.
waynesmith.bio: Wayne Smith, born in Jamaica in 1965, was the singer on the record that changed Jamaican music. 'Under Mi Sleng Teng', voiced for King Jammy in 1985, was built on a preset electronic rhythm rather than a live band, and it is regarded as the track that opened the digital era of reggae. Within months the island's studios had followed, and the Sleng Teng riddim itself was versioned endlessly. Smith followed it with 'Ain't No Meaning' the same year and 'Come Along' in 1986, singing plainly and insistently over rhythms nobody had heard before. He shared that new territory with peers such as Tenor Saw. He died in 2014, remembered for a single record whose consequences reached into every corner of reggae and dancehall that came after it.

shabbaranks.blurb: The deejay who took dancehall global.
shabbaranks.bio: Shabba Ranks, born Rexton Rawlston Fernando Gordon in Jamaica in 1966, is the deejay who took dancehall global. A rough, barking delivery and an unhurried sense of timing made him the most popular Jamaican musician in the world at the turn of the 1990s. 'Wicked inna Bed' established him at home in 1989, the album 'Just Reality' carried him into North America in 1990, and 'As Raw as Ever' and 'X-tra Naked' won Best Reggae Album Grammys in 1992 and 1993. 'Mr. Loverman', cut with Chevelle Franklyn, and 'Ting-A-Ling' became his signature songs. He recorded for Bobby Digital and Gussie Clarke, sparred with peers Super Cat and Cutty Ranks, crossed over alongside Maxi Priest, and left a template that Shaggy and Sean Paul would later carry to the pop charts.

supercat.blurb: Wild Apache, the don dada of deejays.
supercat.bio: Super Cat, born William Anthony Maragh in Jamaica in 1963, is a deejay widely counted among the greatest the dancehall has produced. His nickname, Wild Apache, came from his mentor Early B, and it suited a delivery that was fast, sharp-edged and full of menace held in reserve. 'Boops' made him a star in 1985, a sugar-daddy anthem that everyone in the dance could recite. He carried that authority into the 1990s and into the American market, where 'Ghetto Red Hot' and 'Don Dada' arrived in 1992 as dancehall was being absorbed into hip hop and rhythm and blues. Working the same circuit as peers Shabba Ranks and Ninjaman, he had the rare gift of sounding entirely unbothered by competition. His phrasing remains among the most copied in Jamaican music.

ninjaman.blurb: Theatrical gun-talk deejay and clash legend.
ninjaman.bio: Ninjaman, born Desmond John Ballentine in Jamaica in 1966, is a deejay whose stuttering, melodramatic delivery made him one of the most theatrical performers dancehall has known. Styling himself Don Gorgon, he built his reputation on gun talk and on clashes, above all his long rivalry with Bounty Killer, contests staged before crowds who came as much for the sparring as for the songs. 'Murder Dem' in 1989 became his signature, and 'Permit to Bury' and 'My Weapon' followed in 1990, records whose pro-gun lyrics drew controversy then and since. His peer Super Cat worked the same era at the same pitch. In 2017 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, an ending that has shadowed the reputation of one of the era's most formidable microphone talents.

cuttyranks.blurb: Dry-voiced ragga deejay behind The Stopper.
cuttyranks.bio: Cutty Ranks, born Philip Thomas in Jamaica in 1965, is a dancehall deejay of the ragga years, when the computerised riddims ran hot and fast and a deejay needed the breath control to keep up with them. 'The Stopper' gave him his breakthrough in 1991 and remains his signature tune, a record built on a threat delivered with complete calm. 'A Who Seh Me Dun' followed in 1992 and 'Limb by Limb' in 1993, the latter versioned and rebuilt far beyond Jamaica, its clipped, percussive vocal turning up wherever producers wanted a voice with an edge on it. He came up alongside Shabba Ranks in a period when the deejays were the biggest stars on the island. His delivery, dry and cutting, is one of the most recognisable of the era.

beenieman.blurb: Dancehall's long-reigning king of the microphone.
beenieman.bio: Beenie Man, born Moses Anthony Davis in Jamaica in 1973, is a dancehall deejay who has held the top of the music longer than almost anyone, collecting eight consecutive DJ of the Year awards. 'Slam' established him in 1995, and 'Who Am I', known to everyone as Sim Simma, took him worldwide in 1997 on the Playground riddim. 'Girls Dem Sugar', cut with Mya in 2000, pushed further into American pop, and his album 'Art and Life' won a Grammy in 2001. His long rivalry with Bounty Killer defined a decade of clash culture, while he collaborated freely with Buju Banton, Spragga Benz, Sean Paul and Vybz Kartel, and recorded with Steely and Clevie and with Spice. Few deejays have stayed so consistently central for so long.

bountykiller.blurb: The Warlord of nineties dancehall lyricism.
bountykiller.bio: Bounty Killer, born Rodney Basil Price in Jamaica in 1972, is the deejay they call the Warlord, one of the most aggressive stars of 1990s dancehall and, by wide agreement, among its greatest and most influential lyricists. 'Cellular Phone' announced him in 1994, and 'Look Into My Eyes' in 1997 showed the other side of his writing, gun talk giving way to a plea on behalf of the poor. 'Fed Up' turned that anger into a ghetto anthem in 2002. His clashes with Ninjaman and his long rivalry with Beenie Man set the terms of dancehall competition for a generation. He also built the next one, mentoring Vybz Kartel and Mavado and recording with Spragga Benz, while Busy Signal is among the deejays who came up in his shadow.

capleton.bio: Capleton, born Clifton George Bailey III in Jamaica in 1967, is a deejay whose Rastafari conviction runs through everything he records. Known variously as King Shango, King David, The Prophet and, most enduringly, The Fireman, he turned the imagery of purifying fire into an entire persona, and founded the David House Productions label to house it. 'Tour' broke him in 1995 and 'Wings of the Morning' followed the same year, records that caught him at the hinge between dancehall bravado and something more devotional. By 'Jah Jah City' in 2000 the change was complete, the fireman preaching over hard modern riddims. He has worked repeatedly with Sizzla and Anthony B, the two deejays closest to him in outlook and intensity, and together they carried conscious lyrics back into the dance.

sizzla.bio: Sizzla, born Miguel Orlando Collins in Jamaica in 1976 and known also as Sizzla Kalonji, is one of the reggae artists of his generation with the widest commercial and critical success, and certainly the most prolific: by 2018 he had released fifty-six solo albums. He sings and deejays in the same breath, moving from a rough chant to a high, keening melody without seeming to change gear. 'Black Woman & Child' and 'Praise Ye Jah', both from 1997, are his defining statements, Rastafari devotion set to hard, spacious rhythms built with producer Bobby Digital; 'Thank U Mamma' followed in 2002. He has recorded with Capleton, Anthony B and Jah Cure, and stands with peers Richie Spice and Glen Washington in the conscious wave that reshaped Jamaican music in the late 1990s.

anthonyb.blurb: Fiery conscious deejay of the Rastafari revival.
anthonyb.bio: Anthony B, born Keith Anthony Blair in Jamaica in 1976, is a deejay and a member of the Rastafari movement whose records put the two things together without compromise. He arrived fully formed in 1996: 'Fire Pon Rome' was the anti-establishment broadside that broke him, 'Raid the Barn' matched conscious lyrics to a hard dancehall rhythm, and 'Cold Feet', from the album 'So Many Things', showed he could hold a tune as securely as a position. He belongs to the same late-1990s wave as Capleton and Sizzla, both frequent collaborators, deejays who took the fire-and-brimstone register of Rastafari preaching into a music that had spent much of the previous decade on slackness and guns. His delivery is urgent, high and impossible to mistake for anyone else.

ladysaw.bio: Lady Saw, born Marion Marie Hall in Jamaica in 1972, was known as the Queen of Dancehall, and she took the title by beating the men at their own game. Her early records made slackness a woman's weapon: 'If Him Lef' in 1994, then 'No Long Talking' in 1996 and 'Sycamore Tree' in 1997, the last of them her signature. She recorded with Steely and Clevie, the production team that ran the digital era, and crossed into American pop as a guest voice, appearing on Vitamin C's 'Smile' in 1999 and on No Doubt's 'Underneath It All' in 2002, a triple-platinum single that won No Doubt a Grammy. Across a career spanning more than two decades she cleared the ground that Spice and the women after her still work.

garnettsilk.blurb: Golden voice of the roots revival.
garnettsilk.bio: Garnett Silk, born in Jamaica in 1966, was the singer who brought roots reggae back to the centre of Jamaican music in the early 1990s, and he did it with a voice of unusual warmth and power, smooth and emotive at once. 1992 was his year: 'Hello Mama Africa' gave him his first international hit, 'It's Growing' became a roots-revival classic, and 'Zion in a Vision' set his Rastafari faith to melody. Much of that work was made with producer Bobby Digital. He shared the moment with his peer Luciano and collaborated with the deejay Tony Rebel, the three of them proof that conscious singing could compete with the hardest dancehall. He died in 1994, still being hailed as a rising talent, while trying to rescue his mother from a house fire.

tonyrebel.blurb: Cultural deejay who chose Rastafari over slackness.
tonyrebel.bio: Tony Rebel, born Patrick George Anthony Barrett in Jamaica in 1962, is a deejay who chose culture over slackness at a moment when the dancehall was running hard the other way. 'Fresh Vegetable' broke him in 1990, and 1992 brought both 'Sweet Jamaica', an affectionate anthem for the dance, and 'Nazarite Vow', which set out his Rastafari commitments plainly. He worked closely with the singer Garnett Silk, the two of them leading voices of the conscious revival that ran through Jamaican music in those years, and he later mentored Queen Ifrica, passing the same principles on to a younger artist. His toasting is measured and clear, built for listeners rather than for clashes, and it helped make room for the roots reggae that followed him.

bujubanton.bio: Buju Banton, born Mark Anthony Myrie in Jamaica in 1973, ranks among the most significant and best regarded artists Jamaica has produced, a deejay whose voice deepened into a growl and whose subject matter turned, in mid-career, from the dancehall towards Rastafari. 'Murderer' in 1993 was the turning point, a condemnation of gun violence from an artist who had traded in bravado; by 1995 he had made 'Til Shiloh', which gave him 'Champion' and the acoustic 'Untold Stories', the record most listeners name first. He recorded for producers Donovan Germain and Gussie Clarke, collaborated with Beenie Man, and carried forward the singing tradition of Dennis Brown. He has since worked with hip-hop, Latin and punk artists as well as with the sons of Bob Marley.

luciano.blurb: Second-generation roots singer of the nineties.
luciano.bio: Luciano, born Jepther McClymont in Jamaica in 1964, is a second-generation roots reggae singer and poet, and one of the central figures of the conscious revival of the 1990s. He has been closely linked with Freddie McGregor, and 1995 brought the run of records that made his name: 'It's Me Again Jah', still his signature anthem, along with 'Lord Give Me Strength' and 'Who Could It Be' from the album 'Where There Is Life'. His singing is plain and devotional, closer to a hymn than to a hit, and it offered listeners an alternative to the gun talk then dominating the dancehall. He shared that ground with his peer Garnett Silk and later collaborated with Gentleman. He holds the Order of Distinction for his service to Jamaican music.

chakademus.blurb: Duo who carried dancehall to number one.
chakademus.bio: Chaka Demus and Pliers are a Jamaican duo formed in the early 1990s, pairing a deejay with a singer: Chaka Demus toasts, Pliers carries the melody, and the contrast between them is the whole trick. Both had solo careers before the partnership, but together they reached a mainstream pop audience neither had found alone. Sly and Robbie produced 'Murder She Wrote' in 1992, still the record their name is attached to and one of the defining dancehall singles of the decade. 'Tease Me' reached the UK Top 5 in 1993, and their cover of 'Twist and Shout' went to number one there the same year. The duo showed how much room there was between the dance and the pop chart, and how easily a good riddim could travel.

dawnpenn.blurb: Rocksteady singer with one immortal song.
dawnpenn.bio: Dawn Penn, born in Jamaica in 1952, is a singer with one of the strangest career shapes in reggae. She cut 'You Don't Love Me' at Studio One in 1967, a rocksteady lament sung with cool, wounded detachment, then stepped away from music at the end of the decade after a career of barely three years. Nearly thirty years later she returned to the same song with the production team Steely and Clevie, who rebuilt it for the dancehall era, and the 1994 version became a worldwide hit, known far beyond Jamaica and still instantly recognisable from its opening line. Her voice had barely changed in the interval: the same flat, unhurried delivery that made the original haunting is what made the remake irresistible.

michaelrose.blurb: Waterhouse wail that voiced Black Uhuru.
michaelrose.bio: Michael Rose, born in Jamaica in 1957, is a singer from the Waterhouse district of Kingston and the man who gave Black Uhuru their voice, fronting the group from 1977 to 1984, its most celebrated period. He sang over the drum-and-bass foundation of Sly and Robbie, with whom he continued to record afterwards. His delivery, a keening cry that bends notes into wails, founded a whole school of singing that started in his home neighbourhood and spread across the island, and critics have ranked him among Jamaica's most distinguished vocalists. Solo, he issued 'Bogus Badge' on his own Grammy Rose label in 1985, and a decade later cut 'Short Temper' for an album produced by Niney. His later work has kept that roots tradition in circulation.

spraggabenz.blurb: Rasping deejay who bridged dancehall rivalries.
spraggabenz.bio: Spragga Benz, born Carlton Errington Grant in Jamaica in 1969, is a dancehall deejay with a rasping, conversational delivery that sits somewhere between a taunt and a shrug. 'Could a Deal', produced by Winston Riley in 1994, was his breakout and remains the record his name is attached to. He worked easily across the divides of the era, collaborating with both Bounty Killer and Beenie Man at a time when those two were locked in the most famous rivalry in the music. In 2000 he cut 'Backshot' with Lady Saw for Fully Loaded, and the following year 'Oh Yeah' with the rapper Foxy Brown, part of the traffic between dancehall and hip hop that ran in both directions through those years. His timing is his signature.

pinchers.blurb: Dancehall singer of Agony and Bandelero.
pinchers.bio: Pinchers, born Delroy Thompson in Jamaica in 1965, is one of the sweetest voices of the dancehall era, a singer whose pleading delivery gave the digital rhythms of the late 1980s a romantic centre. He came to prominence recording for King Jammy, whose studio was then the engine room of Jamaican music, and his 1987 sides 'Agony' and 'Mass Out' remain the records that define him: lovers-rock feeling carried over hard, spare dancehall backing. In 1991 he returned with 'Bandelero', the title track of the album of the same name, a swaggering outlaw tune that broadened his reach beyond the yard. Across that run he showed how the singer, and not only the deejay, could thrive in the dancehall, and later vocalists working romantic themes over dancehall rhythms follow the path he cut.

littlejohn.bio: Little John, born John McMorris in Jamaica in 1970, was one of the defining voices of 1980s dancehall, and one of the youngest, cutting hit records while still a teenager. His 1984 sides 'True Confession', made for George Phang at Channel One, and 'Fade Away' caught the moment when the deejay style was loosening into something more melodic, half chatted and half sung. He also recorded for King Jammy, whose studio was reshaping the sound of Jamaican music at exactly that time, and the pairing placed him at the centre of the dancehall's most productive years. His high, agile delivery and prolific run of singles made him a fixture on sound systems across the island, and the sung-deejay approach he helped popularise became one of dancehall's standard voices for the generation that followed.

steelyclevie.blurb: Dancehall production duo who digitised the riddim.
steelyclevie.bio: Steely and Clevie were the Jamaican production duo of Wycliffe Johnson and Cleveland Browne, formed in 1982 and among the most influential rhythm teams of the digital dancehall era. Working as a keyboard and drums partnership, they built riddims that were spare, springy and instantly recognisable, and their 1990 'Poco Man Jam', voiced by Gregory Peck, became a signature rhythm that a whole run of records was cut over. They produced 'Sorry' in 1989 with Foxy Brown and, in 1994, 'You Don't Love Me (No, No, No)' with Dawn Penn, a record that carried Jamaican music around the world. They also worked with Beenie Man and Lady Saw, and stood as peers to King Jammy in the studio rivalry that drove the era forward. Their rhythms remain foundational to how dancehall is built.

gussieclarke.blurb: Producer who gave dancehall a polished sheen.
gussieclarke.bio: Gussie Clarke, born Augustus Clarke in Jamaica in 1953, is a producer who made his name in the roots and dub years of the 1970s and then, from his own Music Works studio, gave Jamaican music one of its most influential modern sounds. Where much of the dancehall of the late 1980s was raw, his productions were rich and immaculately finished, and the run of records he cut in 1988 and 1989 proves it: 'Rumours' with Gregory Isaacs, 'Telephone Love' with J.C. Lodge, and the combination anthem 'Pirate's Anthem' with Home T, Cocoa Tea and Shabba Ranks. He produced Shabba Ranks and Buju Banton, collaborated with the rhythm section Sly and Robbie, and worked alongside Donovan Germain as one of the two producers who set the era's standard for studio craft.

bobbydigital.blurb: Digital B producer behind Shabba and Sizzla.
bobbydigital.bio: Bobby Digital, born Bobby Grantley Dixon in Jamaica in 1961, was one of the great producers of the digital era, and he took his nickname from the moment itself: he was working alongside King Jammy in the mid-1980s just as Jammy began experimenting with computerised rhythms. Mentored in that studio, he set up his own Digital B label and made it a home for the biggest voices of the day. He produced 'Wicked Inna Bed' with Shabba Ranks in 1989, a record that helped push the deejay towards international fame, and in 1992 cut 'It's Growing' with Garnett Silk, whose singing signalled the conscious turn dancehall was about to take. He went on to produce Sizzla and influenced artists including Admiral Tibet. He died in 2020, leaving a catalogue central to modern reggae.

shaggy.blurb: Deejay who took dancehall to global number one.
shaggy.bio: Shaggy, born Orville Richard Burrell in Jamaica in 1968, is the deejay who carried the dancehall voice furthest into the pop mainstream. His gruff, unmistakable chat, learned from the Jamaican deejay tradition and from Shabba Ranks in particular, made 'Boombastic' a hit in 1995 and won him a Grammy for the album of the same name. In 2000 he did it again on a far larger scale with 'It Wasn't Me', a duet with Rikrok that went to number one around the world, and 'Angel' with Rayvon. A second Grammy followed for the album he made with Sting, along with a Brit Award. A collaborator with Sean Paul, he opened a door that a generation of Jamaican crossover artists walked through, proving a deejay could top charts without leaving the dancehall behind.

seanpaul.blurb: Dancehall deejay who topped the American charts.
seanpaul.bio: Sean Paul, born Sean Paul Ryan Francis Henriques in Jamaica in 1973, is the deejay who made dancehall a fixture of global pop radio in the 2000s. After a first album, 'Stage One', in 2000, he broke through with 'Dutty Rock' in 2002 and its singles 'Gimme the Light' and 'Get Busy', the latter topping the American chart in 2003. He repeated the feat with 'Temperature', from 'The Trinity', in 2005. His appeal lay in the rhythm of his delivery, a rapid, melodic patois chat that sat as easily on a pop production as on a Jamaican riddim. Influenced by Shabba Ranks and a collaborator with Shaggy and Beenie Man, he belongs to the lineage of deejays who exported the dancehall, and he remains among the most widely heard voices Jamaica has produced.

jacobmiller.blurb: Inner Circle voice behind Tenement Yard.
jacobmiller.bio: Jacob Miller, born in Jamaica in 1952, was one of the most charismatic singers of the roots reggae years, a big, playful voice with a real ache underneath it. His first session, as a teenager in the late 1960s, was for Clement Dodd; he then cut a run of sides for Augustus Pablo in the mid-1970s. 'Baby I Love You So', from 1975, is one of them, and its b-side dub, 'King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown', is among the most celebrated records ever made in Jamaica. As lead singer of Inner Circle he had a hit with 'Tenement Yard' in 1976, and the same year 'All Night Till Daylight' finished runner-up in the Festival Song contest. He toured and recorded with the band until his death in a car crash in 1980, aged twenty-seven.

winstonriley.blurb: Producer of Double Barrel and the Stalag riddim.
winstonriley.bio: Winston Riley, born in Jamaica in 1943, was a singer turned producer whose work runs through several decades of Jamaican music. He began as a founding member of the vocal group the Techniques, whose 1967 'You Don't Care' is a rocksteady classic, and he also produced the singer Slim Smith. Moving behind the desk, he wrote and produced 'Double Barrel' for Dave and Ansell Collins in 1970, a record that reached far beyond Jamaica. His deepest legacy may be the Stalag rhythm, one of the most reused backing tracks in the music: Tenor Saw, whom he likewise produced, voiced 'Ring the Alarm' over it in 1985, and producers have been rebuilding it ever since. Riley died in 2012, but few producers have left a rhythm so thoroughly woven into reggae and dancehall.

errolthompson.blurb: Engineer who helped invent dub at the desk.
errolthompson.bio: Errol Thompson, born in Jamaica in 1948 and known throughout the industry as ET, was among the earliest engineers to take dub seriously as studio work, and so one of the men who made the mixing desk an instrument in its own right. At Randy's Studio 17 he engineered Big Youth's 'Screaming Target' in 1973, a landmark of the deejay style. His most celebrated partnership was with the producer Joe Gibbs, and together they engineered and produced Culture's 'Two Sevens Clash' in 1977, one of the defining apocalyptic roots albums. He also recorded with Dennis Brown. Thompson's touch was for space and drama, dropping instruments out and letting echo do the work, and the way he shaped a mix became standard practice for the engineers who came after him. He died in 2004.

donovangermain.blurb: Penthouse producer who shaped conscious dancehall.
donovangermain.bio: Donovan Germain, born in Jamaica in 1953, is the producer behind Penthouse Records, the Kingston studio that gave dancehall much of its conscience in the early 1990s. His most important relationship was with Buju Banton, whom he guided from raw deejay to one of reggae's great voices: 'Murderer', from 1993, and 'Untold Stories', from 1995, were both made at Penthouse, and both became standards. Germain's records are marked by clean, musical production and by a willingness to let an artist grow rather than chase the rhythm of the week. Alongside Gussie Clarke he was one of the two producers who set the standard for studio craft in the era, and Penthouse remains among the most respected names in Jamaican music. His work is a reminder that a producer can shape a career, not just a record.

lintonkwesi.blurb: Dub poet of Black Britain's resistance.
lintonkwesi.bio: Linton Kwesi Johnson, born in Jamaica in 1952 and based in Britain, is the dub poet who put the voice of Black Britain on record. Speaking his verse in patois across dub rhythms built with Dennis Bovell, he made poetry that worked as music and music that worked as testimony. 'Sonny's Lettah', subtitled an anti-sus poem and aimed at the police stop-and-search powers of the day, appeared on 'Forces of Victory' in 1979; 'Inglan Is a Bitch' followed on 'Bass Culture' in 1980, and 'Di Great Insohreckshan' on 'Making History' in 1984. An activist as much as an artist, in 2002 the Penguin Modern Classics series took him on, making him only its second living poet and its only Black one. With Mutabaruka he stands as one of the twin figures of dub poetry.

mutabaruka.blurb: Rastafari dub poet with a broadcaster's reach.
mutabaruka.bio: Mutabaruka, born Allan Hope in Jamaica in 1952, is a Rastafari dub poet whose adopted name, drawn from a Rwandan word, declares him forever victorious. His verse is delivered over reggae rhythms and aimed squarely at power: Black liberation, racism, poverty and religion are his standing subjects, argued rather than merely sung. 'Everytime A Ear De Soun' was his breakthrough single in 1981, and 'Dis Poem', from 'The Mystery Unfolds' in 1986, is the piece he is most often quoted for. An actor, educator and broadcaster as well as a musician, he built two of the island's most listened-to radio shows, Steppin' Razor and The Cutting Edge. With Linton Kwesi Johnson and Prince Far I as peers, he made the spoken word a serious force in reggae.

dennisbovell.blurb: Architect of British reggae and lovers rock.
dennisbovell.bio: Dennis Bovell, born in Barbados in 1953 and based in Britain, is the producer, guitarist and bass player who did more than almost anyone to give British reggae its own accent. He began in a progressive rock group that turned into Matumbi, a British reggae band whose 1976 'After Tonight' is a landmark of lovers rock, and he issued dub sides under his own name and under the alias Blackbeard. In 1979 he co-wrote and produced 'Silly Games' for Janet Kay, the record that carried lovers rock into the pop charts, and in the same year produced and arranged 'Sonny's Lettah' for Linton Kwesi Johnson, beginning a collaboration that has run for decades. A peer of Aswad in the London scene, Bovell built the sound that British reggae singers and poets alike have worked inside ever since.

janetkay.blurb: The voice of lovers rock's biggest hit.
janetkay.bio: Janet Kay, born Janet Kay Bogle in Britain in 1958, is the singer whose light, soaring soprano became the defining sound of lovers rock, the gentle and romantic strain of British reggae. Her debut single in 1977 was a version of Minnie Riperton's 'Loving You', but it was 'Silly Games', produced by Dennis Bovell in 1979, that made her famous: it reached number two in the British charts and remains the genre's best-known record, its high, delicate vocal line still a test for any singer who takes it on. An actress as well as a vocalist, she has kept performing across the decades since. Alongside Maxi Priest she stands as one of the artists who proved British reggae could produce pop hits entirely on its own terms, without waiting for approval from Kingston.

maxipriest.blurb: Reggae fusion's first international crossover star.
maxipriest.bio: Maxi Priest, born Max Alfred Elliott in Britain in 1961 to a Jamaican family, is the vocalist who fused reggae with rhythm and blues and made it work on a global scale. Where earlier British reggae singers had been heard mainly at home, his smooth, soulful delivery crossed over: 'Some Guys Have All the Luck' reached number twelve in Britain in 1987, his reggae reading of Cat Stevens' 'Wild World' went to number five in 1988, and 'Close to You' topped the American chart in 1990. That run made him one of the first artists to take reggae fusion into the mainstream, and among the most successful the style has produced. He recorded with Shabba Ranks, and stood alongside Janet Kay and Aswad in the British reggae generation that set its own terms.

ub40.blurb: Birmingham band who made reggae British pop.
ub40.bio: UB40 formed in Birmingham in December 1978, an English reggae band whose original line-up was strikingly mixed, with Jamaican, Yemeni, Irish, Scottish, Welsh and English parentage among its members at a time when British pop rarely looked like that. Their early work carried a political edge, among it 'One in Ten' from the 1981 album 'Present Arms'. Then came 'Labour of Love', a set of reggae covers whose 1983 reading of 'Red Red Wine' went to number one in Britain, a feat repeated in 1993 with '(I Can't Help) Falling in Love with You'. More than fifty British chart singles followed, along with over a hundred million records sold worldwide, four Grammy nominations for Best Reggae Album and a Brit nomination in 1984. Peers of Aswad and of Katchafire, they carried reggae into British homes on an unmatched scale.

mistyinroots.blurb: Southall collective who brought roots reggae home.
mistyinroots.bio: Misty in Roots took shape in Southall, in London, during the mid-1970s, and were among the most important of the British roots reggae bands. They began as a loose collective, five lead singers deep, with a shifting cast of musicians behind them, before slimming down to a core of three. Their first album, 'Live at the Counter Eurovision' in 1979, was recorded at an event staged in Brussels as a political alternative to the Eurovision Song Contest, and its songs are steeped in Rastafari; 'Mankind' comes from it, and the twelve-inch 'Wandering Wanderer' followed the same year. 'Own Them Control Them', from the 1983 album 'Earth', is the other song they are known by. Championed by the BBC Radio 1 disc jockey John Peel, they took roots reggae to white audiences that had not sought it out and, with Steel Pulse, defined the late 1970s British scene.

smileyculture.blurb: Fast-chat deejay who translated cockney into patois.
smileyculture.bio: Smiley Culture, born David Victor Emmanuel in Britain in 1963, was a deejay whose fast-chat style and comic timing produced two of the most admired reggae singles Britain made in the 1980s. 'Cockney Translation', his debut for Fashion Records in 1984, set London slang beside Jamaican patois line by line, a joke that was also a serious statement about who belonged where. 'Police Officer' followed the same year and reached number twelve in the British charts. Influenced by the Jamaican deejay Yellowman, he built something distinctly British on that model, though his run of fame was a short and bright one. In 2011, aged forty-eight, he died as police raided his home; the inquest recorded suicide, a verdict his family and campaigners have long disputed.

damianmarley.blurb: Jamrock deejay, Bob Marley's youngest son.
damianmarley.bio: Damian Marley, born in Jamaica in 1978, is Bob Marley's youngest son and the one who took the family name deepest into the deejay tradition. He chats as much as he sings, and his voice carries the hard edge of dancehall over roots foundations. In 2005 he found his signature in 'Welcome to Jamrock', a Grammy-winning single that made his reputation and set the reality of Kingston against the island's postcard image; the same record produced 'Road to Zion' with Nas and 'Beautiful' with Bobby Brown. He has won four Grammy Awards. A bandmate of his brothers Stephen and Ziggy, a peer of Morgan Heritage and a collaborator with Kabaka Pyramid, he sits at the junction where reggae, dancehall and hip hop meet, and he made that crossing sound entirely natural.

stephenmarley.blurb: Marley singer and eight-time Grammy-winning producer.
stephenmarley.bio: Stephen Marley, born in 1972 and holding both Jamaican and American nationality, is a singer and producer, and among the most decorated members of his family: he has won eight Grammy Awards, three as a solo artist, two as producer of his younger half-brother Damian's albums 'Halfway Tree' and 'Welcome to Jamrock', and three more inside his elder brother Ziggy's group, the Melody Makers. That spread tells the story, since he is as significant behind the desk as in front of the microphone, and the sound of the modern Marley records is largely his doing. His own debut, 'Mind Control', appeared in 2007 and produced 'The Traffic Jam' with Damian; 'Made in Africa', featuring Wale, followed in 2011. Rooted in his father's music but restless with it, he keeps the tradition moving rather than preserved.

ziggymarley.blurb: Melody Makers leader, Bob Marley's eldest son.
ziggymarley.bio: Ziggy Marley, born David Nesta Marley in Jamaica in 1968, is the eldest son of Bob and Rita Marley and the first of the family to carry the music forward. He led Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers, the family band, until 2002, by then with eight studio albums behind it; 'Tomorrow People' and 'Tumblin' Down', both from 1988 and the album 'Conscious Party', are the songs that made the group's name. Since then he has recorded for his own label, Tuff Gong Worldwide, winning a Grammy for the 2006 single 'Love Is My Religion'. He has won eight Grammys along with a Daytime Emmy, and works as an author and philanthropist as well as a musician. Alongside his brothers Stephen and Damian, and with his mother Rita, he has kept the Marley tradition a living concern rather than a memorial.

protoje.blurb: Reggae Revival leader with a crossover ear.
protoje.bio: Protoje, born Oje Ken Ollivierre in Jamaica in 1981, is one of the central figures of the movement that returned roots reggae to young Jamaican audiences. He first drew notice with a mixtape in 2005 and released his debut album, 'The Seven Year Itch', in 2011, following it with a steady run of records through the 2010s and into the 2020s. 'Kingston Be Wise' arrived in 2012, and 'Who Knows', a 2014 duet with Chronixx, became the crossover hit of the revival, a slow, hypnotic record that travelled well beyond reggae audiences; 'Blood Money' followed on 'A Matter of Time' in 2018. As much a connector as a soloist, he has recorded with Chronixx, Lila Ike, Jesse Royal, Jah9 and Kabaka Pyramid, and the scene around him is as much his achievement as any single album.

chronixx.blurb: Roots revival voice of a new generation.
chronixx.bio: Chronixx, born Jamar Rolando McNaughton in Jamaica in 1992, is the singer most identified with the Reggae Revival, the return to roots themes and live-feeling rhythms that reshaped Jamaican music in the 2010s. The son of the singer Chronicle, he was first known as Little Chronicle before taking a name of his own. 'Here Comes Trouble' in 2013 was the breakout, followed by 'Smile Jamaica' in 2014 and, from the album 'Chronology', 'Skankin' Sweet' in 2017. His writing moves between anti-war argument, romantic declaration and messages of resilience, delivered in a light, unforced tenor that owes much to Burning Spear and the roots singers before him. He has recorded with Protoje, mentored the young deejay Koffee, and belongs to the British collective Sault. Few artists have done more to make roots reggae feel current again.

koffee.blurb: Grammy-winning deejay who broke through with Toast.
koffee.bio: Koffee, born Mikayla Victoria Simpson in Spanish Town, Jamaica, in 2000, arrived as a teenager with a voice and a confidence that seemed to skip several stages. She released her debut single in 2017 and had signed to Columbia Records within a year. 'Toast', from 2018, was the breakout, a bright and grateful record that became one of the biggest reggae songs of its moment, and the EP it appeared on, 'Rapture', took the Best Reggae Album Grammy, its title track carrying the same buoyancy. 'Lockdown' followed in 2020, and the album 'Gifted' in 2022. Mentored by Chronixx, and now performing as Original Koffee, she came out of the Reggae Revival but writes with an ear tuned to hip hop and pop as much as to roots.

tarrusriley.blurb: Roots-soul singer behind the anthem She's Royal.
tarrusriley.bio: Tarrus Riley, born Omar Riley in 1979 and holding both American and Jamaican nationality, is a singer whose warm, unhurried delivery bridges roots reggae and soul. He was mentored by the singer Jimmy Riley, and his career has been shaped just as much by the musician and producer Dean Fraser, who has both produced his records and worked alongside him in the studio. 'She's Royal', from 2007, became a modern reggae anthem and remains the song he is asked for everywhere; 'Contagious' and 'Just the Way You Are' followed in 2009. A member of the Rastafari movement, he writes with a directness that has kept him on Jamaican radio for two decades while never drifting far from the music's roots. Alongside Romain Virgo he leads the island's contemporary singing tradition.

romainvirgo.blurb: Lovers rock singer from a talent contest.
romainvirgo.bio: Romain Virgo, born in Jamaica in 1990, is a singer who works chiefly in lovers rock, the romantic strain of reggae, and who came to notice through the Jamaican music competition Rising Stars. His self-titled debut album arrived in 2010 and gave him 'Can't Sleep' and 'Who Feels It Knows It', records that showed a young voice with unusual control and none of the strain talent-show singers often carry. In 2014 he turned Sam Smith's 'Stay With Me' into a reggae ballad, the kind of reading that has long been part of the Jamaican tradition and that widened his audience beyond the island. A peer of Tarrus Riley, he belongs to the generation keeping the singer, rather than the deejay, at the centre of contemporary reggae.

jahcure.blurb: Ballad singer with a soaring, pained tenor.
jahcure.bio: Jah Cure, born in 1978 and raised in Kingston, is a Jamaican reggae singer known for a high, keening tenor that suits the ballad above all else. He was given his name by the singer Capleton. 'Longing For', from 2004, is the record that established him, a song of yearning that became a standard of modern reggae, and he built on it with 'Call On Me', from 'The Universal Cure' in 2009, and 'Unconditional Love', from 'World Cry' in 2012. He has recorded with Sizzla. His strength is emotional directness: where much of contemporary Jamaican music is built on rhythm and chat, he works in melody and open sentiment, and that has made him one of the most widely heard reggae voices of the 2000s across the Caribbean and its diaspora.

alborosie.blurb: Italian who became a Kingston reggae fixture.
alborosie.bio: Alborosie, born Alberto D'Ascola in Italy in 1977, is the singer and producer who moved to Jamaica and earned a place inside the music rather than beside it. Known to some as Italy's reggae ambassador, he produces his own records and works in the analogue tradition of the dub engineers; King Tubby is the acknowledged influence, and it shows in the depth and echo of his mixes. His 2008 album 'Soul Pirate' carried 'Kingston Town' and 'Police', and 'Herbalist' came the same year; together they made his name in Europe and Jamaica alike. A collaborator with the singer Gentleman, he is the clearest evidence that reggae long ago stopped being only a Jamaican music, while insisting that the way to play it properly is still to go and learn it at the source.

gentleman.blurb: German singer who made roots reggae abroad.
gentleman.bio: Gentleman is the German vocalist who took up roots reggae far from the island that made it and sang it convincingly enough to be taken seriously inside the music. The breakthrough was 'Dem Gone', from the 2002 album 'Journey to Jah', a record built on the steady, unhurried roots feeling that has stayed at the centre of the work rather than the harder dancehall styles running alongside it. 'Superior' followed in 2004 and 'Intoxication' in 2007, by which point this was among the best-known reggae acts working outside Jamaica. There have been recordings with Alborosie and with Luciano, collaborations that say something about how the reggae world came to regard the name: not as a visitor to the tradition, but as part of the working life of it.

vybzkartel.blurb: Dancehall's most provocative and prolific voice.
vybzkartel.bio: Vybz Kartel, born Adidja Palmer in Jamaica in 1976, is a dancehall deejay whose provocative writing and restless work rate made him the most argued-about voice of his era. Mentored early by Bounty Killer, he built a catalogue that runs from the raw 'Romping Shop' with Spice in 2009 to the sly consumer anthem 'Clarks' in 2010 and the breezy 'Summer Time' in 2011. He collaborated with Beenie Man and conducted a long, bitter rivalry with Mavado that split the island into camps. Nicknamed Worl Boss and Teacha, he became a folk hero at home and, in equal measure, a scandal to those who deplore the music. Singer, producer, songwriter and entrepreneur, he shaped the generation behind him, mentoring Popcaan and seeding the dancehall inflections heard in Western pop; Drake has named him among his biggest inspirations.

popcaan.bio: Popcaan, born Andrae Sutherland in Jamaica in 1988, is a dancehall singer and deejay whose light, keening melodies gave the music one of its most recognisable modern voices. He came up under Vybz Kartel, whose mentorship put him in front of dancehall audiences early and marked his phrasing for good. 'Only Man She Want' broke him in 2011, the single that turned a protege into a headliner. 'Everything Nice' followed in 2014, and by 'Family' in 2018 he was writing with a warmth and reflectiveness that reached well beyond the dancehall floor. Where his mentor pushed provocation, Popcaan leaned into melody and mood, and that sweetness became one of the defining textures of contemporary Jamaican dancehall, a sound that carried well beyond the island.

spice.bio: Spice, born Grace Hamilton in Jamaica in 1982, is a dancehall deejay and singer widely hailed as the Queen of Dancehall. Her name first travelled after a Sting festival appearance in 2000, and in 2003 Dave Kelly's Madhouse Records issued her debut single, 'Complain'. Through the decade that followed she built a reputation on an aggressive flow, outspoken lyrics and real musical range. Her 2009 duet with Vybz Kartel, 'Romping Shop', made her a household name well beyond Jamaica; 'So Mi Like It' in 2014 established her as a signature solo act, and 'Needle Eye' followed in 2015. She has recorded alongside Beenie Man and Jimmy Cliff, and takes her lineage from Lady Saw, who cleared the ground for outspoken women in the dancehall. Spice remains among the most influential Jamaican artists of her generation.

mavado.blurb: Melodic dancehall singer, Kartel's great rival.
mavado.bio: Mavado, born David Brooks in Jamaica in 1981, is a dancehall singer whose keening, gospel-tinged delivery gave the music one of its most emotive modern voices. Taken under Bounty Killer's wing as a young artist, he broke through in 2007 with the crossover hit 'So Special' and with 'Dying', a duet featuring Serani, then consolidated in 2009 with 'On the Rock'. His long rivalry with Vybz Kartel became the defining feud of Jamaican dancehall, dividing audiences and dominating the island's airwaves for years. In 2011 he signed to We the Best Music Group, DJ Khaled's label, at that point housed under Cash Money and Republic Records, and guested on every Khaled album until the pair separated before 2021's Khaled Khaled. 'Give It All to Me', released in 2013, trailed a major-label debut that has still never appeared.

jesseroyal.blurb: Conscious roots voice of the revival.
jesseroyal.bio: Jesse Royal, born in Jamaica in 1989, is a reggae singer and songwriter who emerged as one of the most forceful voices of the island's contemporary roots resurgence. 'Modern Day Judas' announced him in 2012, a breakthrough single whose title told you plainly where its writer stood, and he followed it with 'Generation' in 2014 and 'Finally' in 2017. His writing keeps the roots tradition's habit of moral argument while sitting easily alongside the sounds his own generation grew up with. He has worked closely with Protoje, a collaboration that places him inside the loose circle of young Jamaican artists who turned back towards conscious reggae through the 2010s. Royal holds the line between righteous commentary and pure melodic pleasure, and that balance is what has carried his songs beyond Jamaica.

morganheritage.blurb: Family band at roots reggae's heart.
morganheritage.bio: Morgan Heritage is a reggae band that five of the reggae artist Denroy Morgan's children, Peetah, Una, Gramps, Lukes and Mr Mojo, formed in 1994, turning one musical household into one of the music's most durable groups. Rooted in Jamaica and raised in the United States, they built their reputation on tight family harmony, live-band muscle and songs that argue for Rastafari without preaching. 'Don't Haffi Dread' in 1999 became their signature anthem, insisting that faith is measured by conduct rather than by hairstyle, and 'Down by the River' in 2001 gave them one of the warmest singles of the era. Grammy-winning and almost permanently on tour, they have carried Jamaican roots music to audiences on every continent, working the same contemporary roots ground as their peer Damian Marley.

richiespice.bio: Richie Spice, born Richell Bonner in Jamaica in 1971, is a reggae singer and guitarist whose smooth, conversational delivery carried some of the sharpest social writing of the 2000s roots revival. A Rastafarian, he made his name with 'Earth a Run Red' in 2004, a plain-spoken reckoning with violence at home that became his signature, and with 'Marijuana' the same year. 'Brown Skin' in 2007 showed his other side, tender where the protest songs were unflinching. He comes from a deep musical family: his brothers Pliers, Spanner Banner and Snatcha Lion are all reggae artists in their own right. Ranged alongside peers such as Sizzla and Etana, Richie Spice helped re-establish conscious roots singing at a moment when dancehall dominated Jamaican radio, and his catalogue remains a benchmark for the style.

queenifrica.blurb: Conscious singer who names what others avoid.
queenifrica.bio: Queen Ifrica, born Ventrice Morgan in 1975 and raised in the hill country above Montego Bay, is a Jamaican singer and disc jockey whose work sits at the conscious end of contemporary reggae. Her father is the ska musician Derrick Morgan, though a mother and stepfather brought her up, and she came up under the mentorship of the singer Tony Rebel. Her signature song, 'Daddy' in 2007, confronted the sexual abuse of children in language so direct that it divided Jamaican radio and made her a national voice on the subject. 'Below the Waist' arrived the same year, and 'Lioness on the Rise' in 2009 gave her an anthem of self-possession. Ifrica sings with a preacher's certainty and a folk singer's plainness, and her willingness to name what others leave unsaid defines her place in the music.

etana.blurb: Strong, dignified voice of modern roots.
etana.bio: Etana, born Shauna McKenzie in Jamaica in 1983, is a reggae singer whose full, unhurried voice made her one of the strongest roots vocalists of her generation. She broke through in 2006 with 'Wrong Address', a song about the doors that close on people from the wrong part of town, and consolidated in 2008 with 'Roots' and 'I Am Not Afraid'. Her debut album, The Strong One, arrived in June 2008 and set the template for a career built on dignity rather than provocation. She has since been nominated for Best Reggae Album at the Grammys, at both the 61st and the 64th ceremonies. Working in the same conscious current as her peer Richie Spice, Etana writes about self-worth, womanhood and Jamaican life with a directness that has made her a fixture on reggae stages worldwide.

busysignal.bio: Busy Signal, born Reanno Gordon in Jamaica in 1979, is a dancehall reggae artist with one of the most elastic deliveries in the music, able to switch from rapid-fire patois to smooth singing inside a single bar. 'Night Shift' broke him in 2005 with a gruff, hungry style that owed much to Bounty Killer, whose growl and phrasing shaped a whole generation of Jamaican deejays. He widened his range with 'Come Over (Missing You)' in 2009, a tender crossover that travelled far beyond the dancehall, and returned with 'Watch Out fi Dis (Baddest)' in 2017. That versatility, hardcore on one record and melodic on the next, kept him current across two decades of shifting dancehall fashion and made him one of the most in-demand voices for producers at home and abroad.

lilaike.blurb: Soulful new voice of Jamaican reggae.
lilaike.bio: Lila Iké, born in Jamaica in 1993, is a reggae singer and songwriter whose warm, unhurried voice sits at the centre of the island's contemporary revival. She emerged through a run of singles: 'Where I'm Coming From' in 2019, her signature statement of origin, then 'Second Chance' the same year and 'I Spy' in 2020, all pairing reggae's rhythmic bedrock with the phrasing of soul and rhythm and blues. Her debut EP, The ExPerience, arrived in May 2020. A close collaborator of Protoje, she belongs to the circle of young Jamaican artists who pulled the music back towards songwriting and interiority. Her first album, Treasure Self Love, arrived in August 2025 and drew a Grammy nomination in the reggae category, and she took the stage at the 2026 Grammy Awards.

jah9.blurb: Jazz-toned reggae of breath and stillness.
jah9.bio: Jah9, born Janine Cunningham in Jamaica in 1983, is a singer whose low, jazz-inflected phrasing sets her apart from almost everyone else working in contemporary reggae. 'Steamers a Bubble' in 2013 became her most-streamed song and the clearest statement of her method: a slow, meditative delivery laid across deep roots rhythm. 'Avocado' followed in 2016, and 'Note to Self (Okay)', a 2020 collaboration with Chronixx, carried her writing to a wider audience. A yoga teacher as well as a musician, she has built her work around breath, discipline and inner life, and that stillness travels straight into the music. She has recorded with Protoje and belongs to the loose community of Jamaican artists who returned reggae to conscious songwriting in the 2010s, though her voice within it remains entirely her own.

kabakapyramid.blurb: Where hip hop meets roots reggae.
kabakapyramid.bio: Kabaka Pyramid, born Keron Salmon in Kingston in 1985, is a deejay and singer who folds rap technique into roots reggae without losing the weight of either. He grew up on Peter Tosh and on hip hop, citing Raekwon of the Wu-Tang Clan among his influences, and the result is a dense, rapid lyric style delivered over rhythms drawn straight from roots reggae's foundations. 'Well Done' in 2015, produced by Damian Marley, was the record that defined his career and opened a long partnership; 'Kontraband' in 2018 was made with Marley too. 'Can't Breathe' in 2017 showed the protest edge of his writing. A frequent collaborator of Protoje, Kabaka Pyramid is central to the reggae revival, the artist who made the case that rap and roots are the same argument in different accents.

glenwashington.bio: Glen Washington, born Glenroy Washington in Jamaica in 1957, is a reggae singer and songwriter who also drums and produces, and whose career ran on a famously long fuse. He cut his first hit, 'Rockers Not Crackers', for the Joe Gibbs label in 1978, then spent two decades away from the charts before returning with 'Brother to Brother' in 1997 and, a year later, 'Kindness for Weakness', the breakthrough that finally made his name and remains his signature song. His voice is a soul singer's instrument applied to roots reggae, unhurried and burnished, and his drumming background shows in how carefully he sits behind a rhythm. Ranged alongside peers such as Sizzla, he became one of the most dependable voices of the late-1990s roots resurgence, an artist whose patience was rewarded by an audience waiting for exactly that sound.

jimmyriley.bio: Jimmy Riley, born Martin James Norman Riley in Jamaica in 1954, was a singer and record producer whose career touched almost every phase of the island's music. He began in vocal harmony groups, singing with the Sensations and then alongside Slim Smith in the Uniques, before stepping out as a soloist. His finest run came at the start of the 1980s with Sly and Robbie's Taxi productions: 'Love and Devotion' in 1981 crossed over to the UK pop chart, its companion 'My Woman's Love' turned a Curtis Mayfield song into reggae, and 'Tell the Youths the Truth' in 1982 put his roots conscience plainly on record. He produced as well as sang, and he passed the trade directly to his son Tarrus Riley, whom he mentored into one of modern Jamaica's leading voices. Riley died in 2016.

luckydube.bio: Lucky Dube, born in South Africa in 1964, was the continent's best-selling reggae artist and the voice that carried Jamaican roots music into apartheid-era townships. A Rastafarian steeped in Bob Marley and Peter Tosh, he turned their idiom towards the conditions he knew, addressing the issues facing South Africans and Africans generally for a global audience. 'Slave' in 1987 was his international breakthrough and remains his signature song; 'Together as One' followed in 1988 and 'Prisoner' in 1989. He recorded twenty-two albums in twenty-five years, and the 1996 World Music Awards handed him its Best Selling African Musician prize; he stands with peers such as Alpha Blondy and Majek Fashek at the head of African reggae. He was killed in Rosettenville, a suburb of Johannesburg, in October 2007, a loss still felt across the continent's music.

alphablondy.blurb: The voice of West African reggae.
alphablondy.bio: Alpha Blondy, born Seydou Koné in Ivory Coast in 1953, is the artist who proved reggae could be an African language as much as a Jamaican one. Following Bob Marley's example, he sings mainly in his native Dyula alongside French and English, occasionally reaching for Arabic, Hebrew or Jamaican patois, and most of his songs carry a political or social charge. 'Brigadier Sabari', from his 1982 debut album Jah Glory, was the record that made his name; 'Cocody Rock' followed in 1984 and 'Jerusalem' in 1986. He has recorded with Aston Family Man Barrett, a direct line back to the music's source. With peers Lucky Dube and Majek Fashek he built a continental reggae tradition answerable to African politics rather than to Jamaica, and he remains its most quoted voice.

majekfashek.bio: Majek Fashek, born Majekodunmi Fasheke in Nigeria in 1963, was a singer, songwriter and guitarist who gave African reggae one of its most theatrical figures. Nicknamed the Rainmaker, he broke out in 1988 with 'Send Down the Rain', the single from his album Prisoner of Conscience that won six PMAN Music Awards and carried his name far beyond Nigeria. 'Free Africa, Free Mandela', from the 1989 record I and I Experience, aimed his conscience squarely at the continent's politics. He took his cue from Bob Marley and Jimmy Cliff and, like his peers Lucky Dube and Alpha Blondy, proved that reggae's message travelled intact into African hands. Across a long career his collaborators ranged from Tracy Chapman and Jimmy Cliff to Michael Jackson, Snoop Dogg and Beyoncé. He died in 2020.

katchafire.bio: Katchafire formed in Hamilton, New Zealand, in 1997, an all-Māori group playing roots reggae and steeped in Bob Marley from the beginning. Their easy, sunlit sound, all warm harmony, unhurried tempo and a bassline you can lean on, became the template for a whole New Zealand scene. 'Giddy Up' broke them in 2002 as the best-selling New Zealand single of that year, and 'Get Away' and 'Collie Herb Man', both from the 2003 album Revival, consolidated the breakthrough. Alongside peers such as Fat Freddy's Drop and UB40, they are evidence that reggae long ago became a global working language rather than a Jamaican export. Decades on, they remain one of New Zealand's most enduring reggae bands, the group that made roots music a homegrown tradition rather than an import.

fatfreddysdrop.blurb: Wellington dub collective built on stage.
fatfreddysdrop.bio: Formed in Wellington in 1999, Fat Freddy's Drop grew out of a loose jam between seven musicians already busy in other groups, among them The Black Seeds, TrinityRoots and Bongmaster, before the side project gradually became everyone's main concern. Their music refuses a single label: dub and reggae at the foundation, with jazz, soul, techno and rhythm and blues layered over the top. They are above all a live band, and what reaches their albums is material worked and reworked on stage over years, which is why 'Wandering Eye', 'This Room' and 'Cay's Crays', all from the 2005 album Based on a True Story, sound less written than grown. The dub engineering of King Tubby and Lee Scratch Perry runs through everything they do, and with peers such as Katchafire they made New Zealand an unlikely centre of the music.

gracejones.bio: Grace Jones, born in Jamaica in 1948, is a singer, songwriter, model and actress who bent reggae into shapes nobody had tried before. She modelled first, in New York and then Paris, working for Yves Saint Laurent and Kenzo and landing Elle and Vogue Hommes covers; photographed by Helmut Newton and Guy Bourdin, she ranked among the most visible Black models of the 1970s and became a reference point in early arguments about gender expression. Her music carried that same androgynous force into the studio, where Sly and Robbie's production gave her a spare, elastic Jamaican foundation. 'Private Life' in 1980 recast a Pretenders song as dub reggae, 'Pull Up to the Bumper' in 1981 fused reggae and funk into her signature Compass Point hit, and 'Slave to the Rhythm' followed in 1985. Her peers Black Uhuru worked the same rhythms.
